# Chapter III

## The Creation of Wave Mechanics

### Introduction

On 27 January and 23 February 1926, respectively, the *Annalen der Physik* received two papers from Erwin Schrödinger, bearing the titles ‘*Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem*’ (‘Quantization as a Problem of Eigenvalues’) and ‘*Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem (Zweite Mitteilung)*’ (‘Quantization as a Problem of Eigenvalues, Part II’), which were duly published in the issues of 13 March and 6 April 1926 (Schrödinger, 1926c, d). They constituted the first two of a series of six papers by the same author, which Max Born would later admire as being ‘magnificent’ (‘*großartig*,’ Born, 1961a, p. 85), and which signified the birth of a new quantum theory—wave mechanics. Friedrich Hund described in short, in his *Geschichte der Quantentheorie*, what these papers contained with the following words: ‘In January the first paper was finished; it gave the calculation of the energy values of the hydrogen atom and kept the connection with de Broglie’s ideas somewhat concealed. The second paper, in February 1926, carried out de Broglie’s point of view; namely, that the new mechanics was related to classical mechanics just as wave optics was related to geometrical optics; it also contained simple applications’ (Hund, 1967, p. 137).

Behind these rather simplified statements a fairly complex story is hidden. A little of the complexity of the path, leading to the results in Schrödinger’s first two papers on the quantization as a problem of eigenvalues, may be grasped from what Louis de Broglie reported fifty years after the discovery of wave mechanics. He mentioned especially: ‘I was wondering how to clarify and generalize my results [on matter waves] when, early in 1926, I got to know the fine memoirs of Erwin Schrödinger in the *Annalen der Physik*. Schrödinger, inspired by the results in my thesis and the Hamilton–Jacobi theory, wrote in a correct (Newtonian) albeit nonrelativistic form, the wave equation of Wave Mechanics which he designated by the now famous symbol $\Psi$’ (L. de Broglie, 1973, p. 14). While de Broglie rightly pointed to the fact that Schrödinger had given, in his initial memoirs, only the nonrelativistic wave equations, Paul Dirac recalled, in his obituary notice of Schrödinger, that in fact the nonrelativistic treatment presented in the early papers had been preceded by a relativistic wave equation. Dirac explained:

> He [Schrödinger] has told me how he came to make his great discovery. With his work on spectra he was using, of course, Bohr’s orbit theory, but he always felt that the quantum conditions in this theory were unsatisfactory and that atomic spectra should really be determined by some kind of eigenvalue problem. In 1924, de Broglie

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0009 -->

368 Chapter III The Creation of Wave Mechanics

published his work on waves associated with the motion of free particles. This influenced Schrödinger profoundly, and he set to work to try to generalize de Broglie waves to bound particles. He finally obtained a neat solution to the problem, leading to the appearance of energy-levels as eigenvalues of a certain operator. He immediately applied this method to the electron of the hydrogen atom, duly taking into account relativistic mechanics for the motion of the electron—as de Broglie had done. The results were not in agreement with observation ... Schrödinger was very disappointed and concluded that his method was no good and abandoned it. Only after some months did he return to it, and then noticed that if he treated the electron nonrelativistically his method gave results in agreement with observation in nonrelativistic approximation. He wrote up this work and published it in 1926, and in this delayed manner Schrödinger’s wave equation was presented to the world. (Dirac, 1961, p. 356)

The story recalled by Dirac poses a serious problem for the reconstruction of historical events; the problem is not that it claimed a relativistic precursor of Schrödinger’s nonrelativistic wave equation for the hydrogen atom, but has to do with the timetable for the creation of the whole method. First, there is no indication in any of Schrödinger’s published papers, prior to the winter of 1925/1926, hinting at a relativistic treatment of electron waves in atoms. What is more, if one summarizes all the evidence provided for the steps towards wave mechanics in other original sources, such as letters and notebooks, one is forced to conclude that Schrödinger did not enter into any deeper study of de Broglie’s work much before the beginning of November 1925. This left him only about two-and-a-half months until the submission of the first paper on the nonrelativistic hydrogen wave equation. Hence he could not really have put the problem aside *for several months after* the relativistic wave equation had failed to yield agreement with experiment. From the main source of information about the earliest steps, namely a letter to Einstein dated 3 November 1925, we learn that Schrödinger became interested in de Broglie’s theory because it seemed to connect well, as Einstein had claimed in January 1925, with the new quantum theory of ideal gases. In agreement with this primary interest in gas theory, Schrödinger started work on a paper, ‘*Zur Einsteinschen Gastheorie*’ (‘On Einstein’s Gas Theory’), which he submitted to *Physikalische Zeitschrift* on 15 December 1925; it contained an application of an idea, derived from de Broglie’s concept of matter waves, for dealing with the energy states of an ideal gas (Schrödinger, 1926b). The predominant concern with the quantum statistics of the ideal gas is also reflected by the fact that Schrödinger submitted, during the same period, still another paper on that topic—namely the one entitled ‘*Die Energiestufen des idealen einatomigen Gasmodells*’ (‘The Energy States of the Ideal Monatomic Gas Model’)—to the Prussian Academy of Sciences in Berlin, where it was presented by Einstein in the meeting of 7 January 1926 (Schrödinger, 1926a). Such intense and sustained activity on the problems of quantum statistics and ideal gas theory limited the time which Schrödinger was able to devote to the work on the hydrogen equation. On the other hand, it may explain why Schrödinger later recalled—and told Dirac—that he put the problem aside for quite some time: it may well be

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0010 -->

**Introduction**

369

that he arrived at a kind of relativistic hydrogen equation in November 1925, then recognizing its failure abandoned it, and devoted himself exclusively to the two above-mentioned papers on gas theory, and only after their submission in the middle of December 1925 did he return to the hydrogen problem.

In the case of the creation of matrix mechanics, especially the appearance of Werner Heisenberg's pioneering paper of July 1925, we have been fortunate in having a wonderfully rich source of information: the letters which Heisenberg exchanged with Ralph Kronig, Niels Bohr, and especially Wolfgang Pauli, provide an accurate, at times even daily, timetable of the emergence of ideas and the recognition of new, often unexpected connections. Thus the main steps and their sequence could be fully reconstructed after more than fifty years. No such helpful devices exist in the case of wave mechanics, although the preliminary steps leading to its proposal and formulation were at least as involved as those of the Göttingen mechanics. Certainly, Schrödinger also wrote letters during this crucial period, which we may place between July 1925 and February 1926, and some of these letters are still available. But the letters do not go into any detail as to Schrödinger's thoughts; they just permit, mostly through some side remarks, a few glimpses into the workings of his mind. The creator of wave mechanics was a different person from the young, excitable and outgoing Heisenberg; far less talkative than the Göttingen physicist, he often concealed his ideas rather than expose them to daylight. Therefore, the information in the letters, valuable and indispensable as it is, must be carefully examined, together with what is contained in his published work during that period—these being essentially the two papers on gas statistics—and in his unpublished notes. However, two difficulties arise from the latter notes: first, the notes that have been preserved do not give a complete derivation of the later results, but rather a few, scattered glimpses at parts of them; and second, the notes are not dated. Hence one must, in order to arrive at a reliable, detailed story of the birth of wave mechanics, analyze *as a whole all the available documents*—the publications, the unpublished notes and the letters—before one can settle any particular point.¹ In this detective puzzle the later reminiscences of Schrödinger, of his colleagues, and of those who were around in Zurich during the critical period, might also contribute in establishing the historical facts.²

¹ One should take into account and discuss in this context even manuscripts, which Schrödinger wrote at that time on different topics, such as physiology and philosophy. They include six pages of notes on physiology, dated in August 1925, and a philosophical essay which the author published later. We shall come back to these writings at a suitable place.

² The steps towards the foundation of wave mechanics have frequently been treated in the literature on the history of modern physics. There is, of course, the pioneering study of Martin J. Klein in his article on 'Einstein and the Wave-Particle Duality' (M. J. Klein, 1964). A detailed reconstruction of Schrödinger's thoughts in the fall of 1925 has been attempted by Linda Wessels in her Ph.D. thesis: 'Schrödinger's Interpretations of Wave Mechanics' (Wessels, 1975) and in an article, 'Schrödinger's Route to Wave Mechanics' (Wessels, 1979)—which may be complemented by Paul A. Hanle's doctoral dissertation on 'Schrödinger's Statistical Mechanics' (Hanle, 1975) and two subsequent articles (Hanle, 1977a, 1979)—and by Helge Kragh in his article on 'Erwin Schrödinger and the Wave Equation: The Crucial Phase' (Kragh, 1982).
We shall, however, analyse the available material of these accounts independently in the following sections, and occasionally compare our results with those of the previous studies.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0011 -->

370 Chapter III The Creation of Wave Mechanics

One of the major tasks in this chapter, describing the origin of Schrödinger’s wave mechanics, is the following. From Schrödinger’s remarks in his first paper—‘I originally intended to find the new quantum conditions in a more intuitive manner [i.e., showing the connection of the new wave equation to the idea of real vibrations of electrons within the atom]’ (Schrödinger, 1926c, p. 372)—it has often been concluded that ‘the second part of the paper [i.e., the second paper: Schrödinger, 1926d] could have preceded the first part [i.e., Schrödinger, 1926c] from the logical point of view’ (Jammer, 1966, p. 261), and perhaps even did so. This logical possibility has to be examined carefully, if only because it is contradicted by another of Schrödinger’s statements: ‘The results of the later sections [i.e., of the later papers] were largely unknown to the writer of the earlier ones’ (Schrödinger, 1927d, preface). Another main point is just as subtle; namely, how far was Schrödinger’s wave mechanics a logical continuation, or generalization, of de Broglie’s conceptions on matter waves? As de Broglie mentioned in the above-quoted remarks, he himself was concerned with continuing the work of his thesis. In what direction did he [de Broglie] generalize his ideas, and how far did his generalization overlap with that which Schrödinger had created? Fortunately, Louis de Broglie published some papers about it and later reported on his plans at the Solvay Conference in 1927.

We shall base the organization of this chapter on the assumption that the creation of wave mechanics involved three major distinct stages which also exhibit some overlap in time and ideas. The first stage was formed by Schrödinger’s efforts, during the second half of 1925, to arrive at a more consistent quantum statistics of identical particles, one that would yield in a natural way Einstein’s new quantum theory of ideal gases (Section 1). This stage of development brought him into a very lively scientific exchange with two of his most respected colleagues, Max Planck and Albert Einstein. The Berlin physicists became very interested in Schrödinger’s work and, in return, provided him, with essential help in clarifying his ideas and on how to proceed on new paths. One of the crucial hints, which Schrödinger obtained from Einstein, was the reference to Louis de Broglie’s doctoral thesis (L. de Broglie, 1924e, 1925). While carefully studying this work, it occurred to Schrödinger that he might connect de Broglie’s matter waves with some previous ideas of his own on vibrating systems, and thus he indeed established a foundation for Einstein’s new gas theory. Moreover, the same combination of ideas would also work in the case of atomic structure, and allow him to found the rules and results of the previous quantum theory of atomic structure on an entirely new basis. Hence Schrödinger’s fundamental studies of the quantum statistics, especially the theories of Bose, Einstein and Planck, prepared the way towards his discovery of wave mechanics. The steps which he took will be discussed in Section 2.

In Section 3 we shall analyze the content of the first paper, on *Quantization as an Eigenvalue Problem*, which emerged from the second stage. The third stage in the discovery of wave mechanics is represented by the development of the elements of a general undulatory theory of atomic systems, of which the hydrogen wave equation is just a particular example. This generalization required a thorough

look back at the methods, which the Irish astronomer William Rowan Hamilton had devised about a hundred years earlier, for dealing with the problems of ray optics and their extensions since that time (Section 4). Schrödinger had already become well acquainted with Hamilton's results; he had occasionally discussed and even generalized them in unpublished notes in the late 1910s, as we shall also

372              Chapter III   The Creation of Wave Mechanics

‘notable property of quantum orbits’ of October 1922 on a mathematical formalism which Weyl had derived for his unified theory of electricity and magnetism.⁵ Weyl’s written ideas also continued to attract him during the following years. Schrödinger, therefore, not only read through the new editions of *Raum-Zeit-Materie*, but also through Weyl’s scientific and popular papers on the subject.

For example, the *Naturwissenschaften* issue of 14 March 1924 contained an interesting article by Hermann Weyl entitled ‘*Massenträgheit und Kosmos. Ein Dialog*’ (‘Inertia of Mass and Cosmos. A Dialogue,’ Weyl, 1924a). The author formulated his profound ideas and analysis of the problem in the form of a witty dialogue between St. Peter and St. Paul; St. Peter appeared as a staunch defender of Mach’s assumption or principle that the inertia of bodies is caused by the action and cooperation of all masses in the universe, especially the distant ones; St. Paul, on the other hand, attacked the principle, basing his arguments on general relativity theory and its extensions. Weyl’s dialogue illuminated the most elementary and fundamental question to be asked in relativity theory; that is: in how far did the physical situation, described by the theory, really depend on relative motion, as Mach had demanded since 1883, and not on some absolute motion? It was exactly this question which Schrödinger addressed in an article on ‘*Die Erfüllbarkeit der Relativitätsforderung in der klassischen Mechanik*’ (‘The Satisfiability of the Relativity Requirement in Classical Mechanics’), submitted in June 1925 to *Annalen der Physik* (Schrödinger, 1925e). Instead of discussing the problem in the high-brow general relativistic cosmology, as his predecessors had done, he restricted himself to considering the case in classical mechanics, arguing: ‘In view of the present status, however, it may not be useless to ask oneself if one cannot satisfy Mach’s relativity requirement by a simple modification of classical mechanics’ (Schrödinger, 1925e, p. 326).

Since the expression for the potential energy in classical mechanics already fulfilled Mach’s requirement—because the potential between two mass points depended only on their distances and not on their absolute position—Schrödinger was left with the problem of modifying the expression for the kinetic energy. To achieve his goal he proposed to define the kinetic energies differently from the usual procedure of defining them for single mass points, where they depended on the individual velocities of the particles; but rather ‘to interpret it [i.e., the kinetic energy] similarly as an energy of *interaction* of each couple of mass points and have it depend only on the distance and the velocity of change of the distances of two mass points’ (Schrödinger, 1925e, p. 327).⁶ With the help of this *Ansatz*, he calculated the energy of a mass point in the interior of a hollow sphere, whose surface is covered with a uniform mass density, and indeed derived an expression that agreed with the classical expression for kinetic energy; in the case that a small mass (planet) moved in the vicinity of a larger mass (sun), this system

### III.1 Scientific Exchange with Planck and Einstein  
373  

being placed at the centre of the hollow sphere mentioned, he also arrived at the usual motion following from classical mechanics; even the perihelion rotation of general relativity could be obtained with suitable assumptions. Finally, he indicated how relativistic motions of mass points could be treated in his modified mechanics: ‘I consider it to be probable that one may arrive, by pursuing these ideas ultimately after several changes at general relativity theory’ (Schrödinger, 1925e, p. 335).  

Up to then, that is, up to the middle of 1925, no positive sign of a personal scientific exchange between Schrödinger and Weyl can be found from their respective work.⁷ Only several months later, however, in the course of working out a definite mathematical problem in wave mechanics, would Schrödinger draw on the help of Hermann Weyl. By that time he had also become stimulated a little by some scientific exchange with Peter Debye. We shall present the story in detail in the next section.  

#### Growing Reputation and the Solvay Conference of 1924  

In his early Zurich years Schrödinger obviously did not seek the advice of his colleagues at the university or at the E.T.H. on scientific problems. He worked completely by himself on questions of his own choice, and for the necessary ideas of others he checked their published papers. He was not, at least in the new and foreign surroundings, an outgoing person; it took him time to make friends in Switzerland. In addition, he really struggled with the requirements of the university professorship, with both the teaching load and the prescribed topics—as we have seen from his letter to Sommerfeld dated 19 November 1924, quoted in Section II.3. Finally, he suffered from unstable health, especially at the beginning of the Zurich period. ‘He got a bit of a lung trouble, and he was sent to Arosa to make a “Liegekur”, his widow later recalled, adding: ‘He had to lie down for some time’ ( A. Schrödinger, AHQP Interview, 5 April 1963, p. 5). Schrödinger wrote to Pauli on 8 November 1922: ‘I see that you are so kind as to inquire about my state of health: this is excellent at the moment; the four months in Arosa have done me a world of good. In addition, I was, as I have just found out, so [mentally] down that I couldn’t get any reasonable thought. The cause of this was not least the frequent moves, the constant decisions about one’s fate, dealing with ministries, etc., all which I am not really suited for at all. This situation is now hopefully over for a long time.’  

In spite of the stable professional situation in Zurich, Schrödinger quite regularly returned to Arosa for vacations or cures. The Schrödingers loved the resort in the mountains; Erwin liked mountaineering, although he never made

In this basically historical review Weyl covered the attempted solutions from the ancient times of the Greek philosophers to the present.

374 Chapter III The Creation of Wave Mechanics

difficult and strenuous tours. They also spent several months in the summer of 1925 and around Christmas of the same year in Arosa; and it was there that he began to work seriously on the first ideas towards wave mechanics.

Under these partly unfavourable circumstances, Schrödinger's reputation grew rather slowly in Zurich and in the scientific world. Still he was not ignored. He was invited, for example, to attend the fourth Solvay Conference on Physics, which took place from 24 to 29 April 1924 in Brussels. There were perhaps two main reasons for this invitation. First, the topic of the conference, selected by its Scientific Council, was the electrical conductivity of metals and Schrödinger had just recently, in his paper on gas degeneracy and mean free path (Schrödinger, 1924a), made an interesting contribution to that field. Second, and perhaps even more important, the committee availed itself of the opportunity to invite an Austrian physicist from Switzerland. Such a move was necessary because, after World War I, participants from Germany and Austria had been excluded from most international scientific conferences, especially from those occurring in Belgium which had been invaded by German troops in 1914, and which was not prepared in 1924 to lift the ban.

Whatever the real reasons, Schrödinger must certainly have been pleased to have been invited, together with his far more illustrious E.T.H. colleague Peter Debye, as the only participants from Switzerland.$^8$ He carefully studied the reports which had been prepared: Lorentz ('Application of Electron Theory to the Properties of Metals'), Percy W. Bridgman ('Conduction Phenomena in Metals and their Theoretical Explanation'), Owen Willans Richardson ('Yet Another Theory of Metallic Conduction'), W. Rosenhain ('The Internal Structure of Alloys'), W. Broniewski ('Electrical Resistance and the Expansion of Metals'), Abraham Joffé ('The Electrical Conductivity of Crystals'), Kamerlingh Onnes ('New Experiments with Superconductors'), Edwin H. Hall ('Metallic Conduction and Transverse Effects of the Magnetic Field'), and the short report by Joffé, unrelated to the topic of the conference, on an experiment with N. Dobronravoff ('Propagation of Radiation Momentum'), which seemed to favour the light-quantum hypothesis. Schrödinger also actively participated in the discussions of the reports of Bridgman, Richardson, Rosenhain and Joffé.$^9$

The fourth Solvay Conference was not very successful compared to the previous conferences, especially those before World War I. This was due not only to the

III.1 Scientific Exchange with Planck and Einstein 375

absence of participants from Germany—Albert Einstein, though invited, did not attend—but mainly to the selection of the topic for the conference. As the reports presented and the discussion about them clearly showed, the problem of the electrical conductivity of metals was not ripe for a satisfactory solution in 1924; the appropriate methods for a suitable description of the electrical properties of conductors had not yet been developed. Decisive progress would come, however, within a few years: First, Albert Einstein would, in the summer of 1924, develop a systematic quantum theory of the ideal gas, based on Satyendra Nath Bose’s new statistical method and involving the concept of gas degeneracy (Einstein, 1924c); towards the end of the same year Wolfgang Pauli would discover an important property of the electron, the so-called exclusion principle (Pauli, 1925b), and in early 1926 Enrico Fermi would suggest a proper quantum statistical method for the electrons (Fermi, 1926a, b); by the end of 1926 Pauli would apply Fermi’s statistics to the electron gas and compute its diamagnetic properties (Pauli, 1927a); finally Arnold Sommerfeld would solve in principle the problem of the metallic electrical conductivity in 1927, and, in the following years, Neville Francis Mott, Felix Bloch and others would develop a fully systematic quantum mechanical treatment of electron conduction in metals.<sup>10</sup>

**The Innsbruck *Naturforscherversammlung***

The second conference of 1924, in which Schrödinger participated, was the 88th *Versammlung der Gesellschaft Deutscher Naturforscher und Ärzte* (*Naturforscherversammlung*), which took place in Innsbruck from 21 to 27 September. The German Physical Society, being associated with the *Gesellschaft*, also held its annual meeting together with the *Versammlung*: it constituted Section 2 of the meeting, which arranged a session together with Section 3 formed by *Deutsche Gesellschaft für technische Physik* (German Society for Technical Physics).<sup>11</sup> The 88th *Naturforscherversammlung* was the first one after World War I that took place outside Germany—the previous two having been held in Bad Nauheim (September 1920) and in Leipzig (September 1922)—and the Austrians made a big effort to continue the tradition of the brilliant pre-war Vienna meeting of

***

<sup>11</sup>The *Naturforscherversammlung* met only every second year at that time. In the years between any two meetings the German Physical Society held a separate meeting called *Physikertag*, the last one in Bonn from 17 to 22 September 1923. The German Physical Society and the German Society for Technical Physics belonged to the *Naturwissenschaftliche Hauptgruppe* (Main Science Section) of the *Naturforscherversammlung*; other sections included Section 1 (Mathematics and Astronomy), Section 4a (Chemistry), Section 4b (Physical Chemistry), Section 5 (Applied Chemistry), etc. Altogether the Science Section was divided into 15 sections; the other big portion, the *medizinische Hauptgruppe*, embraced 18 sections—from 16: History of Medicine, Section 17: Anatomy, to Section 33: Veterinary Science. (See *Mitteilungen der Gesellschaft Deutscher Naturforscher und Ärzte* **1**, No. 5, May 1924, pp. 18–19, published as an addendum to *Naturwissenschaften*, Volume 12 of 1924.)

The *Gesellschaft* not only invited scientists and physicians from the three German-speaking countries of Austria, Germany and Switzerland, but also, and in particular, members of the German-speaking minorities now living in foreign countries, such as Czechoslovakia, Hungary and Italy.$^{14}$ The *Naturforscherversammlung* tried to re-establish, on a modest scale, the pre-war relationship with scientists of other countries by inviting the Dutch physicist Hendrik Kramers from Copenhagen to present a report on ‘*Die chemischen Eigenschaften der Atome nach der Bohrschen Theorie*’ (‘The Chemical Properties of Atoms According to Bohr’s Theory’) to the joint session of its science sections held on 23 September 1924. Another physicist from Scandinavia, Lars Vegard of Oslo, gave a review of ‘*Das Nordlichtspektrum und die höheren Atmosphärenschichten*’ (‘The Spectrum of the Polar Light and Upper Layers of the Atmosphere’) in one of the special physics sections.$^{15}$

The programme of the meeting, whose main organizer was the former Viennese physicist Egon von Schweidler, included three ‘General Sessions’ (‘*Allgemeine Sitzungen*’) held on the mornings of 22, 23 and 24 September 1924, with special sessions of the Physics Section (i.e., the German Physical Society) arranged on the afternoon of 24 September, and all day on 25 and 26 September 1924.$^{16}$ The joint session of the science sections, referred to above, presented extremely interesting talks for physicists, especially those interested in quantum and atomic theory. $$Z = \sum_{n} P_{n} \exp \left( - \frac{E_{n}}{k T} \right), \tag{1}$$

where $k$ is the Boltzmann constant, $T$ the absolute temperature, and $P_{n}$ the statistical weight of the discrete energy state $E_{n}$, Bohr’s energy values for the hydrogen atom,

$$E_{n} = - \frac{2 \pi^{2} m_{e} e^{4}}{n^{2} h^{2}}, \quad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots \tag{2}$$

(where $m_{e}$ and $e$ denote the mass and charge of the electron, respectively and $h$ denotes Planck’s constant), were substituted, then the sum over the states would obviously diverge. Niels Bohr, who had already noticed this difficulty in 1916, argued that in reality $n$ could not assume very large values, because the volume available in nature to a single hydrogen atom was finite (Bohr, 1921f, p. 150). Richard Becker, on the other hand, had claimed that the sum converged due to a different reason: the statistical weights $P_{n}$ decreased for higher quantum numbers $n$ (Becker, 1923). ‘However, one then arrives at the dubious conclusion that the statistical weights, which should really refer to a particular atomic model, must depend on the specific volume of the gas,’ argued Planck against this solution to the problem (Planck, 1924b, p. 674). He rather proposed to derive the sum of the states of a gas of $N$ hydrogen atoms—consisting of $N$ hydrogen nuclei and $N$ electrons—by referring directly to the following procedure: Essentially, one splits $Z$ into two parts, one referring to the case of ionized hydrogen atoms (free electrons), the other to the case of normal hydrogen atoms (bound electrons). In particular, in a gas consisting of $N$ hydrogen nuclei with $P$ free electrons and $(N - P)$ bound electrons, he then found the results:

$$Z_{\text {free electrons }} = \frac{z_{1}^{P}}{P !}, \tag{3}$$

and

$$Z_{\text {bound electrons }} = \frac{z_{3}^{N-P} N !}{(N-P) ! P !}, \tag{4}$$

where $z_{1}$ and $z_{3}$ are given, respectively, by the equations,

$$z_{1} = \left(2 \pi m_{e} k T\right)^{3 / 2} \frac{V}{h^{3}}, \tag{3a}$$

and

$$z_{3} = \sum_{n=1}^{n^{\prime}} n(n+1) \exp \left(-\frac{E_{n}}{k T}\right). \tag{4a}$$

From Eqs. (3) and (4) Planck finally arrived at an expression for the free energy of the gas, on which he commented as follows:

> If one compares it with the formulae known from general thermodynamics, one sees that the three terms [there was an extra term for the ionized hydrogen nuclei] represent in sequence the free energy of the isolated nuclei (positive ions), the free energy of the free electrons, and the free energy of the non-dissociated atoms. (Planck, 1924b, p. 684)

On the way to obtaining expressions (3) and (4) Planck made use of his usual method of calculating the statistical probability of identical particles, namely, division by the factors $P!$ and $(N - P)!$. ‘It is known to me,’ he added in a footnote, ‘that some distinguished physicists, for example, P. Ehrenfest and V. Trkal [(1921)] and E. Schrödinger [(1924a)] object to this kind of calculation and call the division by $P!$ an *a posteriori* introduction. Still, I can see in the method used as little an inconsistency as in the procedure of calculating the number of permutations of $n$ objects, among which some are of the same kind, where one divides the factorial $n!$ afterwards by the factorial of the number of alike objects’ (Planck, 1924b, p. 681, footnote 1). Schrödinger carefully followed Planck’s reasoning; he would return to the problem of like particles again in the summer of 1925.

A further contribution to the Innsbruck meeting had an even more immediate effect on Schrödinger’s research, namely, Kratzer’s review of molecular properties and band spectra. Schrödinger was especially impressed by the arguments that Kratzer gave in favour of introducing half-integral quantum numbers in the description of the rotational motion of diatomic molecules (Kratzer, 1924, p. 1058). He would make use of the same assumption in his paper on the specific heat of molecular hydrogen, submitted less than two months after the *Naturforscherversammlung* (Schrodinger, 1924f).<sup>23</sup>

The second general session of the Innsbruck meeting on 23 September 1924 dealt with quite different scientific problems. Three lectures were presented there, the first by Karl von Frisch of Breslau on ‘*Sinnesphysiologie und "Sprache" der Bienen*’ (‘Physiology of Senses and “Language” of Bees’), the second by Fritz Knoll of Prague on ‘*Blütenökologie und Sinnesphysiologie der Insekten*’) (‘Ecology of Flowers and Physiology of Senses of Insects’), and the third by Otto Porsch of Vienna on ‘*Die Zukunftsaufgaben der Vogelblumenforschung auf Grund des neuesten Tatbestandes*’ (‘The Future Tasks of Bird Flower Research on the Basis

All three lectures treated aspects of the colour vision of animals: especially, the Viennese Frisch, from 1923 professor of zoology in Breslau, discussed the details of the problem of colour vision in the case of bees (Frisch, 1924), while Knoll studied the same problem in the case of flies and butterflies (Knoll, 1924). Their results interested Erwin Schrödinger, an expert on physiological-optical and human colour vision, and he referred to both lectures in his paper on the origin of the sensitivity curves of the human eye which appeared in the *Naturwissenschaften* issue of 7 November 1924 (Schrödinger, 1924e).²⁴  
Being a lover of the mountains, we may assume that Schrödinger did not miss the third general session ('*Allgemeine Sitzung*'), in which Albrecht Plenck of Berlin, Otto Ampferer of Vienna and R. von Klebelsberg of Innsbruck spoke on the geology and structure of the Alps. He would also have been interested in the lecture on '*Die physikalischen Grundlagen der Sonnen- und Höhenstrahlung und ihre Anwendung auf die Therapie*' ('The Physical Foundations of Solar and High Altitude Radiation and Its Influence on Therapeutics'), which the meteorologist and pioneer in that field, Carl Dorno of Davos, delivered later in the same session.²⁵ Schrödinger, who had suffered—as we have mentioned earlier—for some time from a lung infection and regularly went to Davos for recreation or cure, certainly knew about the work of Dorno; a further reason for attending the lecture was his interest in solar radiation as a fundamental aspect of physiological optics.  
The Innsbruck *Naturforscherversammlung* formed perhaps the most brilliant scientific conference which, so far, had been organized in post-World War Central Europe. The list of speakers included a large number of the most outstanding researchers on quantum and atomic physics, such as Max Born, James Franck, Hendrik Kramers, Max Planck and Arnold Sommerfeld. Among the other participants were Albert Einstein and Alfred Landé. Schrödinger also met quite a few of his friends from Vienna, for example, Wolfgang Pauli and Karl Przibram. Egon von Schweidler, formerly assistant at Franz Exner’s institute and supervisor

Schrödinger thus had the opportunity of re-establishing contacts with his old acquaintances and of bringing his name back into the consciousness of the academic authorities of his native land of Austria. Nearly a year later the Innsbruck visit seemed to have paid off. As he wrote to Sommerfeld: 'I nearly forgot to tell you—if you do not already know about it—that I am expecting to receive a call to Innsbruck. I would like to return home, because the Swiss are far too uncongenial ('*gar zu ungemütlich*'). However, I must remind myself again and again that Innsbruck still appears gilded to me by the memory of last fall' (Schrödinger to Sommerfeld, 21 July 1925).

The 'gilded' reminiscences of Innsbruck also referred to meeting Arnold Sommerfeld again in Innsbruck. Schrödinger had been a guest at the Munich *Kolloquium* back in 1919; he now renewed and deepened his acquaintance and began to enter, soon after the *Naturforscherversammlung*, into a scientific correspondence with his illustrious senior colleague, or 'highly honoured, dear Professor' ('*hoch verehrter, lieber Herr Professor*'), as he would address him. This correspondence resulted, during the following months, in a lively exchange of scientific ideas, which contributed importantly to Schrödinger's work on two papers concerning atomic and molecular constitution (Schrödinger, 1924f, 1925c).²⁶ An even greater gold mine for Schrödinger's future work and career would turn out to be his meeting with the two eminent Berlin physicists, Albert Einstein and Max Planck.

### Einstein, the Nature of Light and Bose Statistics

Although Einstein did not deliver a lecture at the Innsbruck *Naturforscherversammlung*, his presence in the Tyrolean capital constituted, of course, one of the highlights of the meeting. However, unlike the previous *Naturforscherversammlungen* at Bad Nauheim in September 1920 and at Leipzig in September 1922, his theory of relativity no longer stood at the centre of heated debates.²⁷

²⁶ We have discussed this exchange of ideas and the contents of these papers earlier in Chapter II, Section II.4.
²⁷ In Bad Nauheim an entire session had been devoted to relativity theory, with Hermann Weyl, Gustav Mie, Max von Laue, Leonhard Grebe and Hugo Dingler presenting important talks. Weyl had spoken on the unification of gravitation and electricity (Weyl, 1920), von Laue on the optical tests of relativity (Laue, 1920), Grebe from Bonn on the gravitational shift of (solar) Fraunhofer lines (Grebe, 1920), and Dingler from Munich on the foundations of relativity theory (Dingler, 1920). After Grebe's lecture especially an extended debate had followed, when Philipp Lenard had suggested a return to the ether concept and an abandonment of relativity theory. He had quarrelled with Einstein on the right description of electromagnetic and gravitational phenomena—and Max Born and Gustav Mie had added interesting comments. Hugo Dingler, on the other hand, had presented a critical analysis of some concepts used in relativity theory; he had claimed that the experimental proofs, which had so far been cited as supporting relativity, were not proofs in the strict sense but depended on interpretation. Two years later, at the Leipzig meeting, Einstein had been supposed to deliver the main lecture on relativity theory in one of the general sessions; however, he had not arrived at the meeting. (See Einstein to Planck, 6 July 1922; quoted in Seelig, 1954, p. 213.) However, relativity

In September 1924 another of Einstein’s fundamental ideas, his light-quantum hypothesis, aroused notable interest, although less from the general public, but certainly from the smaller, distinguished group of experts on quantum and atomic theory assembled at Innsbruck. To be more specific, what the quantum physicists discussed was not so much the old hypothesis of 1905, but rather the specific radiation theory, which had been recently formulated by Niels Bohr, Hendrik Kramers and John Slater in Copenhagen, in order to avoid Einstein’s light-quantum concept (Bohr, Kramers and Slater, 1924). Wolfgang Pauli, who had earlier been persuaded to accept the Copenhagen views, reported to Bohr shortly after the Innsbruck meeting:

> As Kramers might have already told you, as a physicist, I am presently completely opposed to this interpretation of the radiation phenomena. I am also supported, very strongly, in this opinion by the fact that many other physicists, perhaps even most of them, reject this view, though partly for different reasons. (Pauli to Bohr, 2 October 1924)

Among the ‘many other’ physicists Pauli included Arnold Sommerfeld, who had been converted to the light-quantum hypothesis in early 1923 after becoming aware of the result of Arthur Compton’s experiment. In his lecture at the Innsbruck meeting he criticized the entire Copenhagen correspondence-approach to the problems of atomic and quantum theory, which seemed to be connected with the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory. But Pauli, in his letter to Bohr, did not put the emphasis on the subtle points that were mainly debated between Sommerfeld and Kramers. He rather reported:

> Among these other physicists, I discussed in the first place this question with Einstein—at last I have finally succeeded in encountering him! You repeatedly told me at Easter [when Pauli was visiting Copenhagen] that you would like to hear Einstein’s arguments. Therefore I will not hesitate any further in writing to you [about them]. In addition, I want to use the occasion freely and let you know, at the end, my arguments too. (Pauli to Bohr, 2 October 1924)

In his letter to Bohr, Pauli then listed four of Einstein’s main (*hauptsächlichste*) arguments: first, Einstein claimed, that any system of atoms and radiation, described by the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory, would exhibit, in the course of time, systematically growing deviations from energy conservation, e.g., the kinetic energy of a cavity having ideally reflecting walls and filled with radiation might increase infinitely as time goes on; second, the available experimental information about elementary processes—such as the electron–atom collisions—always

Einstein had attended the Bonn meeting and especially participated—with Sommerfeld and Cornelius Lanczos—in the debate following the lecture by the astronomer Josef Hopmann of Bonn, who had spoken on ‘*Die Deutung der Ergebnisse der amerikanischen Einsteinepexpedition*’ (‘The Interpretation of the Results of the American Einstein Expedition,’ Hopmann, 1923).

He especially criticized Bohr’s assumption that two physically different types of resonance radiation should exist, one obtained from atoms in the excited state and the other from atoms in the ground state; there was, he thought, no experiment to distinguish between the two types of radiation, hence their difference did not make any sense.³⁰  

Schrödinger had a legitimate interest in these discussions concerning the true nature of light. He had tried experimentally, for example, many years ago, to distinguish between light waves and light-quanta (Schrödinger, 1920a); he had, in 1922 before the discovery of the Compton effect, given an important application of the light-quantum hypothesis in describing the Doppler effect of spectral lines (Schrödinger, 1922a); and he had just recently discussed the radiation theory of Bohr, Kramers and Slater in an extended note in *Naturwissenschaften* (Schrödinger, 1924d). In the latter he expressed sympathy with that theory; and had calculated the energy fluctuation of a (macroscopic) gram-atom of hydrogen on the basis of statistical energy conservation, arriving at the comforting result that only very small relative fluctuations violating energy conservation were obtained in the course of a reasonable finite time interval, which as yet did not contradict observation (Schrödinger, 1924d, p. 723). This conclusion was not at variance with Einstein’s statement (reported by Pauli in his letter to Bohr) as ‘with the help of fluctuation phenomena one could show that, for the statistical independence of the occurrence of elementary processes in spatially distant atoms, a system may exhibit, in the course of time, systematic deviations from the first [heat] theorem’ (Pauli to Bohr, 2 October 1924). Einstein did not give the period of time in which a considerable deviation from energy conservation would

accumulate, but declared, in principle, any deviation to be ‘disgusting’ (‘*dégoutant*’)—as Pauli wrote to Bohr—while Schrödinger, as we have mentioned earlier in Section II.4, rather liked to assume an essentially statistical nature of physical laws.

In the summer of 1924 Einstein had further reason to renew his strong stand in favour of the light-quantum hypothesis. He had just seen Satyendra Nath Bose’s paper providing a derivation of Planck’s radiation law on the basis of a new statistics for light-quanta (Bose, 1924a); it was a derivation which satisfied all of Einstein’s demands with respect to consistency. Einstein was immediately able to generalize Bose’s quantum statistical method in developing a quantum theory of ideal gases, in which some of the difficulties persisting in previous approaches could be removed. In the months following the Innsbruck meeting he continued to work on that theory. ‘The thing with the quantum gas turns out to be very interesting,’ he reported to Paul Ehrenfest by the end of the year. ‘I am increasingly convinced that very much of what is true and deep is lurking behind it. I am happily looking forward to the moment when I can quarrel with you about it’ (Einstein to Ehrenfest, 2 December 1924).

The points of the theory which Einstein especially wished to discuss with his friend in Leyden included three problems. The first was the question of statistical independence in the new gas theory, the second was the occurrence of degeneracy at low temperatures, and the third concerned the existence of a paradox—the so-called Gibbs’ paradox—connected with the mixture of two volumes containing molecules of the same gas. In his second paper on the quantum theory of the ideal gas, communicated to the meeting of 8 January 1925 of the Prussian Academy, Einstein remarked on the first problem: ‘Ehrenfest and other colleagues have criticized Bose’s theory of radiation and my analogous theory of ideal gases with respect to a fact, which we have not specifically mentioned in our papers, namely, that in these theories the [light-] quanta and molecules, respectively, are not treated as being objects statistically independent of each other. This is completely right’ (Einstein, 1925a, p. 5). A complete statistical independence of the objects would result, Einstein continued, in the radiation law of Wilhelm Wien in the case of radiation theory, and in the classical equation of ideal gases in the case of gas theory. While this conclusion contradicted experiment in the first case, it led, in the latter case, ‘either to an offence against Nernst’s theorem or against the demand that the entropy for a given inner state [of a gas] must be proportional to the number of molecules’ (Einstein, 1925a, p. 7).

Einstein by that time had obviously adopted the views of Nernst and Planck insofar as he believed both in the validity of Nernst’s (third) heat theorem—demanding zero entropy for a gas at absolute zero temperature—and in Planck’s concept of the ‘“probability” of a macroscopically defined state’ (‘“*Wahrscheinlichkeit*” eines makroskopisch definierten Zustandes,’ Einstein, 1924c, p. 261), which included the additivity of entropies for two volumes containing the same gas in the same macroscopic state, a point which had been questioned earlier by Ehrenfest.³¹ However, like Ehrenfest, he disagreed with Planck’s method of

deriving the result—and especially with Planck’s division of the probability for a microscopic state by the factorial of the number of identical particles—even claiming that it would result, if properly applied, in a contradiction with Nernst’s heat theorem. Bose’s statistical method, on the other hand, satisfied both the theorem *and* the additivity requirement for the entropies.

Planck also did not remain idle after Innsbruck. After all, he had developed in early 1916 the first quantum theory of ideal gases fulfilling both the requirements of thermodynamics and quantum theory (Planck, 1916b). Six years later he had provided, within the framework of the same theory, an answer to the above-mentioned Gibbs’ paradox by showing how the mixing entropy of two gas volumes approached zero, if the velocity distribution of (chemically) identical molecules in the two volumes differed by less than a quantity determined by the size of the quantum-theoretical phase cells (Planck, 1922b).<sup>32</sup> In the winter of 1924/1925 he treated the quantum theory of ideal gases, especially the definition of its entropy, in a series of lectures given at the University of Munich.<sup>33</sup> In February 1925 he also presented a paper, entitled ‘*Zur Quantelung einatomiger Gase*’ (‘On the Quantization of Monatomic Gases’) to the Prussian Academy (Planck, 1925a).

### First Correspondence with Einstein

From the Innsbruck encounter with Einstein and Planck, Schrödinger might have taken away particular hints for his future work on quantum statistics and gas theory; for example, the impression of Planck’s stubborn insistence on the division of the probability for the state of a gas by the factorial of the number of identical particles, or the possibility of degeneracy occurring in gases at low temperatures in Einstein’s recent gas theory. Although both these points did play an important role later, they would not do so immediately, partly because of Schrödinger’s situation during the following winter semester: he was very much occupied with his teaching duties, which left him little spare time for working on research problems.<sup>34</sup> However, towards the end of the semester he began again to study

<sup>32</sup> The paradox consisted in the observation that in classical theory the mixing of two volumes of different gases, having the same temperature and pressure, was connected with an additional entropy increase, the mixing entropy. In the case of two identical gases, however, no such mixing entropy should exist.

<sup>33</sup> Planck’s lectures at the University of Munich had already been planned in the summer of the year 1923. In a letter to Sommerfeld, dated 8 July 1923, Planck asked for a postponement of those lectures from November 1923, adding: ‘With genuine pleasure I accept your offer to present lectures in the winter semester of 1924–1925; and I would now like to fix a definite month, preferably after Christmas, because I always have more free time then . . . . The general lecture I intend to present in one hour, the lectures on entropy in four hours; this is, altogether five hours, probably on five days.’ Planck would actually present his Munich lectures in December 1924 (see Planck, 1925b, p. 442).

<sup>34</sup> See Schrödinger’s complaint expressed in the letter to Arnold Sommerfeld of 19 November 1924, which we have already referred to in Chapter II, Section II.4.

During the winter semester of 1924–1925 Schrödinger submitted only one paper for publication, that on the specific heat of molecular hydrogen (received on 24 November by *Zeitschrift für Physik*). In this work one may trace a weak reminiscence of Planck’s Innsbruck lecture, namely the use of ‘Planck’s “state sum”’ (‘*Plancksche “Zustandssumme”*’, Schrödinger, 1924f, p. 343) for the rotational degrees of freedom of the hydrogen molecule.

Einstein answered these politely presented objections in a letter, dated 28
February 1925. 'Your reproach is not unjustified, although I have not made a
mistake in my paper,' he stated. 'In the Bose statistics, which I use, the quanta
or molecules are not considered as being *mutually independent* objects' (Einstein
to Schrödinger, 28 February 1925). He then explained, by a simple example, how
the new statistical method differed from the classical Maxwell–Boltzmann statis-
tics of independent molecules; and he informed Schrödinger that he had analyzed
the situation in greater detail 'in a second memoir published since in the *Sitzungs-
berichte* [of the Prussian Academy of Sciences; see Einstein, 1925a]', and that he
had given, finally, 'in a third memoir, which is in print presently, considerations
which are independent of the type of statistics used [see Einstein, 1925b]' and
do confirm his theory of gas degeneracy.

Schrödinger did not acknowledge the receipt of Einstein's letter until much
later. In November 1925, he finally replied by saying:

> Only through your letter [of 28 February] did the uniqueness and originality of
> your statistical method of calculation become clear to me; I had not grasped it
> before at all in spite of the fact that Bose's paper had already come out. It is really
> like this: in Bose's treatment, compared to that of Jeans and Debye, (1) the role of
> energy and aether resonators is exchanged, and (2) the statistics are also turned
> around, hence naturally the same result follows as before. Now at first this did not
> seem particularly interesting to me. Only your theory of gas degeneracy is really
> something fundamentally new, and this I did not grasp at all, at first. Pardon me
> for not having replied to this letter, which has been so valuable to me, before now.
> I heard that you would be in America; hence I postponed my answer and then I
> forgot about it. (Schrödinger to Einstein, 3 November 1925)$^{38}$

On first inspection, it thus appeared to Schrödinger that Bose had merely made
a more-or-less trivial modification of Planck's original procedure—or the Jeans–
Debye formulation of it; that is, he had simply exchanged resonators and energy
packets, and in addition had altered the counting method in such a way that
ultimately the old results (of 1900 or 1910, respectively) followed. Einstein's
theory of gases, however, did involve (in Schrödinger's opinion) a considerable
change, as it provided among other things a new approach to the problem of gas

Einstein explained the implications of his theory in more detail in a second paper on the quantum theory of gases, which he had completed in December 1924 and communicated to the meeting of the Prussian Academy of Sciences on 8 January 1925. The paper was published in issue No. I of the *Sitzungsberichte* and appeared in print during the first half of February 1925 (Einstein, 1925a); thus it was available to Schrödinger at about the time he received the letter from Einstein.

Unlike the case of light-quanta, for which the constant $A$ in Eq. (6a) assumed the value 0, $A$ could take on values between 0 and 1 for the ideal gas. Einstein had actually concluded that, for any given temperature $T$, the atoms of a gas contained in a fixed volume would separate into two parts: 'One part "condensates," the other remains a "saturated ideal gas". ($A = 0, \lambda [= \exp(-A)] = 1$)' (Einstein, 1925a, p. 4). Now the remainder or second part corresponded completely to the situation of the light-quanta (in blackbody radiation); but the first part created a further quantum effect, as it embraced an appreciable portion of the gas at sufficiently low temperatures—thus Einstein had computed that in the case of helium the critical density was only five times smaller than the saturation density at the same temperature, hence in a dense helium gas degeneracy effects should become noticeable. 'There exists a case, in which nature possibly might have realized the situation of a saturated ideal gas; namely, the case of the conduction electrons in the interior of metals,' Einstein had further argued. He found in particular, 'that the saturation concentration of (moving) electrons for usual temperatures is about $5.5 \times 10^{-5}$; hence only a vanishingly small part of the electrons might contribute to the thermal energy' (see Einstein, 1925a, p. 12). These results evidently pleased Schrödinger who had arrived more than a year earlier, although based on quite a different approach to gas degeneracy, at very much the same conclusions (Schrödinger, 1924a).$^{39}$

Another aspect of Einstein's second paper on the quantum theory of the ideal gas also met with Schrödinger's approval. In Section 7 Einstein had made a 'comparison of the gas theory developed with that following from the hypothesis of mutual statistical independence of gas molecules' (Einstein, 1925a, pp. 5–7). The two respective definitions of entropy $S$ for $N$ gas atoms in a volume $V$, according to Bose's statistical method (a), and according to the hypothesis of statistically independent particles (b), yielded the expressions

$$S_a = k \sum_{\nu} \{(n_\nu + z_\nu) \ln(n_\nu + z_\nu) + n_\nu \ln n_\nu - z_\nu \ln z_\nu\}, \quad (7)$$

and

$$S_b = k \{N \ln N + \sum_{\nu} (n_\nu \ln z_\nu - n_\nu \ln n_\nu)\}. \quad (8)$$

$$z_{\nu} = \frac{2 \pi V}{h^{3}} (2m)^{3/2} E^{1/2} \Delta E, \tag{9}$$

$m$ being the mass of the atoms and $h$ Planck's constant. Einstein had then concluded the following from the above entropy expressions: First, Eq. (7), which agreed with

390 Chapter III The Creation of Wave Mechanics

phase space of a physical system is covered everywhere continuously by phase points, and only the density of this space distribution becomes discontinuous in the transition from one phase cell to a neighbouring one' (Planck, 1925a, p. 49). Planck now argued that the outcome of the experiments of Otto Stern and Walther Gerlach three years previously had disproved this quantum condition by showing that atomic systems described very definite orbits in space (Gerlach and Stern, 1922a). In order to take care of that situation, Planck proposed to calculate the free energy $F$ of a gas volume at temperature $T$ containing $N$ identical atoms having no mutual interaction (other than by elastic collisions) by making use of the definition

$$ F = -kT \ln \sum \exp\left(-\frac{U}{kT}\right). \tag{11} $$

He assumed, as seemed obvious, that the total energy $U$ entering the right-hand side of the expression was the sum of the kinetic energies of the individual atoms ($U = u_1 + u_2 + u_3 + \cdots + u_n$).
To determine the energy states of the atoms Planck considered the phase space of the entire gas system, noting: 'To every point in phase space there corresponds a definite state of the gas. However, to each definite state of the gas there does not correspond one definite phase point, but $N!$ different phase points, because for a given state of the gas the numbers of single atoms are not fixed as well; two phase points, which differ only in that two or more different atoms have exchanged their co-ordinates and velocity components, rather denote the same state of the gas' (Planck, 1925a, p. 50). By assigning to each of the $N!$ congruent '*Urzellen*' ('original cells') in phase space, which together represent a single state of the gas, the (phase space) volume $(h^3)^N$, Planck computed the number $z$ of quantum cells for a gas in volume $V$ (whose atoms of mass $m$ have kinetic energy between zero and the value $u$) to be

$$ z = \left(\frac{4\pi e V}{3h^3 N}\right)^N (2mu)^{\frac{3}{2}N}, \tag{12} $$

where $h$ denotes Planck's constant and $e$ is the base of the natural logarithm. This number, however, should be equal to the number of terms in the sum on the right-hand side of Eq. (11). On the other hand, the same sum may also be written as the $N$-fold product of the identical terms $\sum_0^u \exp(-u/kT)$, each of which is associated with a single atom. Hence $z$ could be written as $n^N$, with $n$ denoting the number of quantum states of each atom—not of the free atom but of an atom in volume $V$ filled with gas (i.e., with ($N - 1$) further atoms). By inserting $n^N$ for $z$ in Eq. (12), Planck found the energy of the quantized states of a gas atom as

$$ u_n = \frac{h^2}{2m} \left(\frac{3N}{4\pi e V}\right)^{2/3} \cdot n^{2/3}, \tag{13} $$

with $n = 1, 2, \ldots$. Since the atom did not have to assume exactly the energy states

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0032 -->

III.1 Scientific Exchange with Planck and Einstein 391

$u_n$, but might also take on definite values between $u_{n-1}$ and $u_n$, say $u_{n-\alpha}$ with $\alpha$ lying between 0 and 1, Eq. (13) became generalized to

$$u_n = \frac{h^2}{2m} \left( \frac{3N}{4\pi e V} \right)^{2/3} (n - \alpha)^{2/3}. \tag{14}$$

With the discrete states, Eq. (14), for the single gas atom the free energy $F$ could be calculated. Then the equation of state for the gas assumed, in a reasonable approximation (involving the replacement of the sum by an integral), the form:

$$p = - \frac{\partial F}{\partial V} = \frac{kTN}{V} \left\{ 1 - \frac{(\alpha - \frac{1}{2})h^3 N}{(2\pi m k T)^{3/2} e V} \right\}. \tag{15}$$

For $\alpha = \frac{1}{2}$ the right-hand side passed over into the classical expression for the ideal gas; for any other value of $\alpha$-deviations from the classical case, degeneracy occurred.$^{41}$

Planck commented on his theory by remarking that 'the theory of degeneracy of monatomic gases, recently established by A. Einstein [(1924c)], is fairly related as far as the methods are concerned, although it is basically different both in physical content and results' (Planck, 1925a, p. 56). He noted as the essential difference in Einstein's theory two facts: (i) quantum cells with the lowest occupation numbers (of atoms) occur most frequently; and (ii) the probability of an atom occurring in a given quantum cell also depends on the number of other atoms contained in the cell. In spite of this difference Planck's and Einstein's theory yielded the same equation for the gas in the situation of weak degeneracy—i.e., for not very low temperatures—if one took the special value $\alpha = 0.586$ in Planck's theory.$^{42}$

### **Schrödinger’s Analysis of Entropy Definitions**

In early July 1925, Planck would not have the last word in the discussion of gas theory. The respondent, however, was not Einstein but Schrödinger. Less than half a year after his presentation of the above theory, Planck received a paper from Zurich, entitled 'Bemerkungen zur statistischen Entropiedefinition beim idealen Gas' ('Remarks on the Statistical Definition of Entropy for the Ideal Gas'), which he communicated to the Prussian Academy of Sciences at the meeting of 23 July 1925 (Schrödinger, 1925d).$^{43}$ Unlike Planck, Schrödinger did not develop any

$^{43}$ Schrödinger did not forward the paper to Einstein, as one might have expected from the previous correspondence. So far as he knew Einstein had planned a visit to America at that time. Einstein did indeed go to South America, especially Argentina, in the spring of 1925, but returned to Berlin before 9 July, when he gave a paper on 'Einheitliche Feldtheorie von Gravitation und Elektrizität' ('Unified Field Theory of Gravitation and Electricity') at a meeting of the Prussian Academy of Sciences (Einstein, 1925d).

further quantum theory of ideal gases; he rather referred to the existing ones, concentrating on a single, important aspect of the problem: the proper counting method for identical particles. For that purpose he listed and analyzed what he thought was the possible different ways of defining the entropy of a gas consisting of $N$ atoms.

Altogether he discussed four such definitions, their physical and mathematical foundation and their consequences.$^{44}$ These definitions included the following:

$$S_{\mathrm{I}} = k \ln W_{\max}, \qquad (16)$$

with

$$W = \frac{N!}{N_1! N_2! \dots N_i! \dots}, \qquad (16\mathrm{a})$$

where $N_i$ denotes the occupation number of the $i$th state. Schrödinger claimed that $S_{\mathrm{I}}$ or rather $S_{\mathrm{I}} - k \ln(N!)$ was Planck’s definition, which he criticized as having been evaluated incorrectly, both with respect to the mathematical method and the physical interpretation. While the mathematical defect—i.e., a wrong use of Stirling’s formula in the case of small numbers $N_i$—could be easily corrected, the physical objections remained serious enough. One objection had already been raised earlier by Einstein; he had argued that the expression $S_{\mathrm{I}} - k \ln(N!)$ violated Nernst’s theorem—see (Einstein, 1925a), referred to above—and Schrödinger now repeated this argument.$^{45}$ He also pointed to the consequence of a negative zero-point entropy, stating ‘that the logarithm of a *permutation number* or a sum of such numbers, i.e., in any case that of a natural number, *cannot possibly* assume a negative value in a correct evaluation, whatever assumption one may apply concerning the counting of certain permutations being different or the same’ (Schrödinger, 1925d, p. 438).

In order to avoid such shortcomings Schrödinger proposed the definition

$$S_{\mathrm{IV}} = k \ln(\text{number of all permutations at a given total energy } E), \qquad (17)$$

where each permutation was taken regardless of its permutability property. He showed that $S_{\mathrm{IV}}$ coincided with Planck’s definition, including the subtraction term, $-k \ln(N!)$, for not very low temperatures; however, ‘the quantum phenomena (degeneracy) become already noticeable for the gas at much higher temperatures, that is, in the case when the number of occupied states is no longer very large compared to $N$’ (Schrödinger, 1925d, p. 438). Schrödinger evidently preferred a much larger quantum effect than had been suggested earlier by

III.1 Scientific Exchange with Planck and Einstein                                                                                       393

Planck<sup>46</sup>; such larger effects also followed from Einstein’s new gas theory, the entropy of which coincided with $S_{IV}$, in Schrödinger’s opinion.

Interestingly enough, Schrödinger did not mention in this context Planck’s recent work of February 1925, in which Planck had strongly modified his previous quantum theory of gases, and in which even stronger deviations from the classical gas equation might result than in Einstein’s theory. However, he referred to it later in Section 6 of his paper, where he attempted to use Planck’s idea of quantizing the gas volume $V$, containing $N$ identical atoms at temperature $T$, as a whole. In proceeding along this path he claimed that a further hypothesis had to be called in, stating: ‘One may then rightly assume that each of these *quantized gas states* [of the entire gas system] possesses the “symmetry number” $N!$; and one cannot see any objection against agreeing to count the $N!$ states, emerging from each other simply by all the molecules [atoms] exchanging their roles, as a single state. *We want to stick to this agreement*’ (Schrödinger, 1925d, pp. 438–439). According to Schrödinger, Planck had, in February 1925, introduced this extra ‘agreement,’ thus removing the problems of either violating entropy addition or Nernst’s heat theorem. Even then, however, Planck had not been consistent, because he had ‘yet again not only made the assumption that the total energy of the gas, as in classical gas theory, is composed of adding the kinetic energies of the single molecules, but he also assumed that the quantized states of the [whole] gas are such that in them the single energy of each molecule may adopt only certain discrete values $u^{(1)}, u^{(2)}, u^{(3)}, \dots, u^{(r)}$’ (Schrödinger, 1925d, p. 439). This assumption seemed ‘in no way cogent’ to Schrödinger, who went on to construct an example in which Planck’s treatment led to a contradiction with the above-mentioned ‘agreement.’ He thus concluded: ‘I do not see any *general* reason for demanding ... that for each *individual* distribution of the molecules to the energy values there must correspond exactly *one* quantum state of the gas which is different from all the other states, and is different *regardless* of the individuality of the molecules’ (Schrödinger, 1925d, p. 440).

### Planck’s Last Word

Planck took the opportunity to answer this criticism immediately. At the same meeting of the Prussian Academy of Sciences, to which he communicated Schrödinger’s paper, on 23 July 1925 he spoke ‘*Über die statistische Entropiedefinition*’ (‘On the Statistical Entropy Definition,’ Planck, 1925b). As stated in the introduction, Planck seized the opportunity ‘to report on the result of investigations which have occupied me recently and whose main content I have already developed in my guest lectures delivered in December 1924 at the University of Munich, a little earlier than previously planned ... and to connect with it the discussion of some points touched upon in Schrödinger’s paper’ (Planck, 1925b, p. 442).

394 | Chapter III The Creation of Wave Mechanics
To begin with Planck suggested a new general definition of the entropy, which did not—as he pointed out—agree with any of the four definitions mentioned in Schrödinger’s paper, namely

$$S = k \ln P, \tag{18}$$

where $P$ denoted the number of different stationary states which the system was able to adopt for a given total energy. Planck argued in favour of this definition as follows: ‘Its main advantage consists in that it avoids in principle all probability considerations and the arbitrariness connected with them, by reducing the problem of calculating the entropy to another independent physical problem, namely, the problem of quantizing the processes occurring in the system under consideration. It [the definition] differs from all other previous definitions in that it provides the entropy directly and not through the study of the individual parts (molecules) comprising the system; the latter procedure might easily imply the danger that the interactions of the parts are not properly taken into consideration’ (Planck, 1925b, pp. 442–443).

After demonstrating that the new entropy definition would yield (for systems with very many degrees of freedom) the same free energy as given by the earlier equation (11), Planck turned to particular applications of Eq. (18). For this purpose he distinguished two types of systems according to whether or not a system consisted of a large number of subsystems, which could be completely separated from each other and therefore considered as independent. He claimed: ‘I believe that by neglecting this question quite a number of ambiguities and misunderstandings have resulted,’ and added that: ‘There are indeed a number of theorems, which apply only to the first mentioned special case but have no meaning for the more general [second] case’ (Planck, 1925b, p. 443).

Planck now explored the situation for different cases, treating first a system of $N$ identical harmonic oscillators (frequency $\nu$) of one degree of freedom with total energy $E$. He arrived, by counting the quantized states again, at the well-known expression

$$S = kN \left\{ \left( 1 + \frac{E}{Nh\nu} \right) \ln \left( 1 + \frac{E}{Nh\nu} \right) - \frac{E}{Nh\nu} \ln \left( \frac{E}{Nh\nu} \right) \right\}. \tag{19}$$

He further found that the distribution of oscillators of a given energy $\mathcal{E}_n$ was given by a Boltzmann-like equation, i.e.,

$$N_n = \exp\left( - \frac{\mathcal{E}_n}{kT} \right) / \sum_m \exp\left( - \frac{\mathcal{E}_m}{kT} \right), \tag{20}$$

hence small energies would occur more frequently. This result had to be modified in the case of oscillators possessing several degrees of freedom; there the maximally occupied energy state was above the ground state.$^{47}$

$^{47}$ In the case of oscillators having $f$ degrees of freedom Planck calculated, for the average energy per oscillator $\bar{\mathcal{E}} = fh\nu/[\exp(h\nu/kT) - 1]$, a value slightly higher than the energy of the most frequently occupied state.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0036 -->

III.1 Scientific Exchange with Planck and Einstein 395

In dealing with more general systems Planck first remarked 'that, if one can decompose the system [under investigation] into several, mutually independent partial systems having many degrees of freedom, then the free energy $F$ of the total system is made up additively by the free energies of the partial systems, because each state of a partial system can be combined with each state of another partial system' (Planck, 1925b, pp. 448-449). For a particular example of this case Planck referred to the treatment of the crystal lattice in the theory of Max Born and Theodore von Kármán of 1912 (Born and Kármán, 1912). On the other hand, he noted, 'To the systems, which cannot be considered as being composed of identical, mutually independent elements, there belongs as a typical representative the case of a *gas*. Even if—as we may assume—all $N$ molecules of a gas are identical and unchangeable, they still cannot be considered as being independent of one another, because they exert physical actions on each other, showing up in collisions' (Planck, 1925b, p. 449).

As Planck pointed out, in order to calculate the free energy of the gas one must, for the time being, evaluate the old Eq. (11) for the free energy by determining the number of states of the gas occupying a definite region of the phase space. This evaluation, he further claimed, did not involve any ambiguity or arbitrariness, especially not with respect to the fact that each state of a gas system containing $N$ atoms was represented $N!$ times in the phase space. He continued: 'Therefore I cannot admit that—as Mr. Schrödinger states elsewhere [i.e., in his paper of July 1925 (Schrödinger, 1925d)]—we still need a particular determination or agreement in order to count the $N!$ states of the gas, differing only by molecules exchanging their roles, as a single state, as long as one keeps the point of view of the definition, Eq. (18). This special manner of counting is, in my opinion, necessarily fixed by the fact that the molecules can, in the course of their movement, exchange places, and hence cannot be identified as pairs in two different states of the gas, in contrast to the earlier discussed oscillators at rest, which occupy fixed places and thus remain, whatever their changes, always distinguishable individually' (Planck, 1925b, pp. 449-450).

Planck then went on to calculate the energy states in the following way. For usual densities and temperatures of the gas one could use the phase-cell method and later replace the discrete sum in Eq. (11) by an integral—this procedure yielded, in particular, the entropy constant of Otto Stern and Hugo Tetrode. Planck stated: 'A different and more difficult task must be performed if temperature and volume drop so far that only a limited number of terms in the state sum, Eq. (11), practically contributes to its value (gas degeneracy). In this case it turns out to be necessary, in order to carry out the calculation, to present the actual quantization of the molecular motions—a problem which has been strictly solved so far only in a very few examples, for instance, for a single molecule oscillating between two fixed parallel walls. Already for two molecules difficulties arise, because the individual processes during collision are not known; and these difficulties grow immensely if one takes very many molecules' (Planck, 1925b, p. 450). These difficulties could be approached only by 'a rather plausible, and as

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0037 -->

396 Chapter III The Creation of Wave Mechanics

simple as possible *Ansatz*, say of the kind that had been suggested many years ago by Arnold Sommerfeld (1914b). With respect to his earlier treatment in 1925 Planck accepted Schrödinger’s criticism, ‘that this *Ansatz* is by no means a very satisfactory one and should certainly be replaced once by a better one’—in the better one, perhaps Schrödinger’s idea had to be incorporated that the mean free path of the molecules played an essential role.⁴⁸ Whether such a procedure would finally lead to an empirically substantiated expression for the entropy of a gas had to be left to future investigations. Planck concluded: ‘At any rate I tend to believe that one must try in this direction before one decides to agree with Einstein’s point of view, according to which apart from the interactions between the molecules, stemming from their impenetrability and their mutual attractions—which find their natural place in the theory developed above—there still exists a characteristic dependence of the molecules on each other, which so far can be found only in the analogy to the quanta of radiation’ (Planck, 1925b, pp. 450–451).

In closing his presentation to the Prussian Academy of Sciences, Planck mentioned that he planned to give some details of the points which he had just touched upon in a later publication. The promised paper, entitled ‘*Eine neue statistische Definition der Entropie*’ (‘A New Statistical Definition of the Entropy’) was indeed received on 30 October 1925 by the *Zeitschrift für Physik* and appeared in print before the end of the year (Planck, 1925c). It contained not only extended applications of the entropy definition, Eq. (18), but also revealed a change in Planck’s attitude towards the quantum-theoretical definition of the entropy: while he had formerly considered all his attempts to be ‘a suitable further development of the Boltzmann–Gibbs concepts, caused by the quantum hypothesis,’ he now thought it more appropriate to speak of ‘a new definition’ (Planck, 1925c, p. 155). The main advantage of this new definition was, so Planck claimed, that it embraced both the old Boltzmann statistics and the statistics recently proposed by Einstein. In contrast to his assertion in July 1925 he now said that the definition, Eq. (18), ‘is not restricted to systems having many degrees of freedom, but even provides for those having arbitrarily few degrees of freedom in any case a definite value [of the entropy],’ hence ‘the concept of entropy [defined by Eq. (18)] obtains a significance which reaches even beyond the realm of thermodynamics’ (Planck, 1925c, p. 156).

The examples presented by Planck in his October paper were essentially of the same type as those in the July communication to the Prussian Academy of Sciences, namely, that of systems of harmonic oscillators and of gas atoms in a quasi-classical limit, in which the sum over states could be approximated by an integral. Planck again left out the case of degeneracy, in which one had to deal explicitly with the sum in Eq. (18), and this sum ‘required for its evaluation a particular assumption about the position and shape of the phase cells that cannot
