*collapses like a house of cards*' (Einstein to Millikan, 13 July 1925; reported in Clark, 1972, p. 400; our italics). Although he himself 'did not believe in the accuracy of Miller's results' (Einstein to Millikan, 13 July 1925), Einstein in the summer of 1925 would not play down their principal significance.

The only way to deal with the problem properly and adequately seemed to be to check the results of Miller thoroughly by an additional experiment, possibly at still higher altitudes—because Miller had not observed a definite effect at sea-level.¹²⁹ The theoretician Schrödinger therefore started to get personally involved in such a project. In September 1925 he reported his first steps in that direction; he especially stated: 'The other day I talked to the president of the *Wissenschaftliche Jungfrau-Kommission* (A. de Quervain). We really want to repeat the experiment on the *Jungfraujoch*' (Schrödinger to Wien, 17 September 1925). Apart from Schrödinger, Edgar Meyer—'he actually was the first to discuss it [the repetition of the experiment] seriously'—especially pleaded for the project on the high-altitude laboratory in the Swiss Central Alps.¹³⁰ The practical conditions for the experiment soon seemed to be available, and Schrödinger eagerly reported the following details to Wien:

In the new observatory, whose completion is expected within one to two years, we have been promised a room with a concrete basement, as well as free transportation for observers and instruments with the *Jungfraubahn*. Food there will not be gratis; although provided at a considerably reduced rate, it will constitute an essential part [of the budget]. Of course we need an able optician, if possible one who is also an alpinist and can endure the long stay at an altitude of 3,500 m without damage. (Schrödinger to Wien, 17 September 1925)

Wien reacted very enthusiastically to the news from Zurich. He wrote back: 'The repetition of the experiment in Switzerland should really be undertaken with German and Swiss funds only' (Wien to Schrödinger, 13 October 1925). He emphasized at the same time that he did not see any difficulty in the whole project. He quickly became active in looking for a suitable experimentalist, the 'able optician' demanded by Schrödinger, and was successful after a month. He wrote again: 'As far as the *Jungfrau* project is concerned, I can tell you that Dr. Tomaschek of Heidelberg has agreed to carry out the Michelson experiment. You know that a while ago he did the interference experiment with extraterrestrial light sources. Hence he is well prepared and is an excellent experimentalist. It can hardly be difficult to collect the necessary money. It will be best if you contacted him directly' (Wien to Schrödinger, 16 November 1925).

Rudolf Tomaschek, a student of Philipp Lenard in Heidelberg and then his assistant, was indeed a most suitable candidate, as far as experimental and alpine

skill were concerned.<sup>131</sup> He had performed (two years earlier) the aforementioned interference experiment—a kind of Michelson experiment—with extraterrestrial light sources, which was also scheduled to determine the absolute ether motion (Tomaschek, 1923). He had also just completed another experimental investigation connected with the ether problem, i.e., an experiment on the question as to whether the ether exerted a magnetic influence on a condenser at rest relative to the surface of the earth (Trouton–Noble experiment); and he had ‘carried out the main experiments ..., during the month of October [1925], on the *Jungfraujoch* at an altitude of 3,457 m in a frame constructed of wood, placed at a distance of about 5 m from a rather steeply ascending, 80 m high wall of rock’ (Tomaschek, 1926a, p. 744). In his paper, which was received by the *Annalen der Physik* on 9 November 1925, Tomaschek reported a zero ether effect on the condenser. He further concluded from it: ‘Hence we would also, at high altitudes, expect a negative result of the Michelson interference experiment. In contrast to this there are the positive results of the Michelson interference experiment, obtained by C. D. Miller at an altitude of 1,734 m, which provide a relative velocity [of the ether] of about 30 percent of the earth’s velocity in its orbit. The effect would have been most easily detectable with the present apparatus, since the accuracy of the above experiment of second order [in the velocity of the ether] ... reaches absolutely that of Miller’s apparatus, while the experiment of the first order is even more sensitive by a factor of 100’ (Tomaschek, 1926a, p. 755). He therefore stressed the importance of examining possible sources of error in Miller’s experiments, and of studying the dependence of the results on the place of observation, ‘for which, first of all, it seems to be especially necessary to repeat that experiment at the same place as the present experiment [i.e., Tomaschek’s on *Jungfraujoch*]’ (Tomaschek, 1926a, p. 755).

Clearly, Wien had proposed an excellent candidate, one who was even experienced in carrying out experiments on *Jungfraujoch*, for the project of repeating Miller’s experiments at higher altitudes, and he waited impatiently for the answer from Zurich. Since it did not arrive, he wrote again, a month later, to Schrödinger: ‘You still have not replied to my last letter, in which I suggested Tomaschek for the M[ichelson] and M[iller] experiment. It seems to me to be perfectly in the interest of the experiment to charge him with the task, since he, like hardly any other person, has gathered experience with his experiments on interference from extraterrestrial light sources. In addition, he will perform the experiment in any case, and it would certainly be best, if one concentrates for the moment all resources on one experiment’ (Wien to Schrödinger, 24 December

Lenard in Heidelberg in the early 1920s and his *Habilitation* in 1924 (at the University of Heidelberg). In November 1926 he moved to the *Technische Hochschule* in Munich, and then to the University of Marburg, where he was appointed *Extraordinarius* for experimental physics in late 1927. In 1934 he became full professor at the *Technische Hochschule*, Dresden, and from 1939 to 1945 he occupied the experimental chair at the *Technische Hochschule*, Munich. After the war he worked for several years (1948–1954) in England at the AIOC-Research Centre, Kirklington, near Newark.

### III.3 The Nonrelativistic Hydrogen Equation

1925). Three days later Schrödinger finally replied telling Wien about the reservations against Tomaschek and that the Zurich people had rather selected Georg Joos of Jena for the job. Wien, a little unhappy about the development, wrote back: ‘Of course, I do not have the slightest objection against Joos; but Tomaschek will perform, I believe, the experiment, even if he might not be “acceptable” to E. Meyer.’ And he added: ‘It appears to me really somewhat surprising that Lenard’s political attitude can influence the physical experiments of his pupils. I would regret if this nonsensical antagonism should lead to the result that the experiment (on which now all resources must be concentrated) would finally fail because of it, or at least would suffer from it, insofar as the resources are being split’ (Wien to Schrödinger, 1 January 1926).

Tomaschek’s teacher and professor, Philipp Lenard, director of the *Radiologisches Institut* at the University of Heidelberg, had a reputation as a staunch opponent of relativity theory.¹³² He firmly pleaded for a reinstallation of the ether concept based on pure observation and simple reasoning as opposed to the ‘only mathematical formal treatment of the subject, neglecting physical thinking (relativity “theory”)’ (Lenard, 1923, p. 89). Tomaschek’s investigation on the propagation velocity of light emitted by extraterrestrial sources had been devised as a part of Lenard’s programme (see Tomaschek, 1923, p. 105). His experimental result, however, demonstrating practically zero shift of the interference fringes in a Michelson-type experiment involving light from extraterrestrial sources, could be interpreted as perfectly substantiating relativity theory. Moreover, the young Heidelberg experimentalist was, like his master, skeptical with respect to the positive results of Miller, as we have mentioned above.¹³³ Indeed there existed little evidence for suspecting that Lenard’s prejudice against relativity theory might influence the result of Tomaschek’s repetition of Miller’s experiment on the *Jungfraujoch*.

But the Swiss had decided in favour of Georg Joos, and the latter solved the problem of who should do the experiment in a more elegant manner. ‘Just at this moment Joos writes me that he has agreed with Tomaschek: he will carry out the Michelson experiment, while Tomaschek plans further work on the Trouton–Noble experiment. The interference apparatus will be built by the Zeiß Company,’ Wien reported to Schrödinger on 2 January 1926, adding: ‘Of course, nothing can be held against this agreement; because it is a very great advantage that Joos can construct the apparatus on the spot together with Zeiß. I believe that with this the entire case has been concluded in a favourable manner.’ Schrödinger was relieved, and he expressed to Wien his happiness ‘that the enterprise with the Michelson experiment has now taken a direction, with which you also, *Herr Geheimrat*, agree’ (Schrödinger to Wien, 8 January 1926). 458 Chapter III The Creation of Wave Mechanics

personally had been angry about the procedure of his Zurich colleague, and now commented: ‘This is a really fine and reasonable distribution of work, and the collaboration of the Zeiß Company is invaluable’ (Schrödinger to Wien, 8 January 1926).$^{134}$

As a consequence Rudolf Tomaschek, supported by the *Notgemeinschaft der deutschen Wissenschaft*, continued his Trouton–Noble experiment on the *Jungfraujoch* in April 1926; the previous negative result, i.e., no effect from ether motion, was confirmed. While he would repeat his earlier skeptical attitude towards Miller’s results, the latter reported, in an April meeting of the American Physical Society in Washington, on new experiments carried out in February 1926. He emphasized: ‘There is a periodic displacement of the interference fringes which is clearly systematic and cosmical in character; it is such as would be produced by a relative motion of the earth and the ether of 10 km per second’ (Miller, 1926, p. 812).

In the following months Miller’s experiment was eagerly discussed in America, England and Europe.$^{135}$ In Europe especially, the Swiss physicist Auguste Piccard (1884–1962), together with his collaborator from Brussels, E. Stahel, repeated the Michelson experiment: on a balloon ascent in June 1926 no increase in Miller’s effect was noted up to 2,500 m altitude (Stahel, 1926); later in November they showed that the effect was about a factor ten smaller than that given by the American experimentalist (Piccard and Stahel, 1927). A year later they reported a similar result obtained on the Rigi, Switzerland, at 1,800 m altitude (Piccard and Stahel, 1928). The final death blow to a positive result of the Miller experiment was provided by Georg Joos, who, after four years of preparation and collaboration with the Zeiß Company in Jena, established the necessary apparatus and, in September 1930, arrived at the conclusion:

> The microphotometric evaluation of the pictures made with the apparatus yields the result that a possibly existing effect exerted by the ether wind must be smaller than $10^{-3}$ of the width of the interference fringes, hence the absolute value of the ether wind must be smaller than 1.5 km/sec. (Joos, 1930, p. 407)$^{136}$

Miller [i.e., Miller had claimed that he had also observed the positive effect at low altitudes]; and one may rightly ask whether—in view of this change, and in view of the totally negative result in all the repetitions of the Trouton–Noble effect at higher altitudes, and finally in view of the financial calamity of German science—the expenses for such an expedition could still be justified’ (Joos, 1930, pp. 406–407).

### III.3 The Nonrelativistic Hydrogen Equation
459

Thus the entire enterprise served to strengthen relativity theory beyond further experimental doubt.¹³⁷ Schrödinger’s faith in relativity theory would never be shaken again and, in later years, he would devote a good proportion of his own research to problems of the general theory. For the moment, however, i.e. in the beginning of 1926, his personal involvement in the fundamental experimental problem did terminate, setting all his energies free to attack the problems of atomic theory.

### A Breakthrough During the Christmas Vacation

In spite of serious efforts on both sides the first project proposed by Wien to Schrödinger—the *Handbuch* article on physiological optics—did not materialize, while the second project, initiated by Schrödinger—the repetition of the Michelson–Miller experiment—was soon taken out of their hands. A third enterprise, however, again promoted by Wien, worked much better. Early in their correspondence, back in June 1925, Schrödinger had already ‘taken permission to announce a small paper on the “*Erfüllbarkeit der Relativitätsforderung in der klassischen Mechanik* [On the Realizability of the Relativity Postulate in Classical Mechanics]”, with a request to publish it in the *Annalen*’ (Schrödinger to Wien, 16 June 1925). Wien had promptly accepted, and the paper (also received on 16 June) was published in the August issue of the *Annalen der Physik* (Schrödinger, 1925e). Six months later, on 24 December 1925, Wien closed a letter to Schrödinger by saying: ‘I have not received anything for the *Annalen* from Zurich for a long time. I would very much enjoy obtaining again several Swiss papers soon.’ He repeated this request in the following letter, in which he further encouraged Schrödinger:

> I still want to add that previously the papers published by the Berlin Academy were also very frequently reprinted in the *Annalen*, because they would not get much distribution otherwise. I would like to ask you whether or not you want to submit your papers again to the *Annalen*. With respect to the Vienna Academy the situation is perhaps more difficult, because their proceedings are the general publication journal in Austria. (Wien to Schrödinger, 1 January 1926)

Clearly, Wien referred with that request to recent papers by his Zurich colleague on gas statistics published in the *Sitzungsberichte* of the Prussian Academy of Sciences. Schrödinger soon replied:

> Thank you very much for your kind proposal, which is honourable for me, to accept my last Academy papers for publication in the *Annalen* also. So far *one* has appeared

¹³⁷ Max Born, who had been concerned about Miller’s result in 1922, saw Miller and his apparatus on his visit to the United States in 1926. He later recalled: ‘I . . . went to Pasadena to see a demonstration of the apparatus on top of Mt. Wilson. Miller was a modest little man who very readily allowed me to operate the enormous interferometer. I found it very shaky and unreliable; a tiny movement of one’s hand or a slight cough made the interference fringes so unstable that no readings were possible. From then on I completely lost all faith in Miller’s results. I knew from my visit to Chicago in 1912 that Michelson’s apparatus was very reliable and his measurements accurate’ (Einstein, H. and M. Born, 1971, p. 74).

Another paper on the same subject, he continued, he had sent five weeks earlier
to Einstein, expecting that the latter might add something or agree to submit it
as a joint publication to the Prussian Academy of Sciences. But: ‘Here I still
have to wait to see what has happened.’<sup>138</sup> However, he immediately raised Wien’s
expectation of getting another, completely new paper for the Annalen by
reporting:

Mainly, however, I now want to get on to the vibration theory of the atom at once,
and I hope to be able already very soon to send you a communication on that
problem. (Schrödinger to Wien, 8 January 1926)

Actually, this hint about the ‘vibration theory of the atom’ was not the first
notice which Wien had received concerning Schrödinger’s main recent scientific
research. One and a half weeks earlier Schrödinger had reported:

At the moment I am plagued by a new atomic theory . . . . I believe that I can write
down a vibrating system—constructed in a comparatively natural manner and not
by ad hoc assumptions—which has as its eigenfrequencies the term frequencies of
the hydrogen atom. (Schrödinger to Wien, 27 December 1925)<sup>139</sup>

He then explained in more detail that he actually did not get the spectroscopic
hydrogen terms, -R/n², where R denotes Rydberg’s number and n an integral
number, but rather the term
$$
\frac{m_{\text{e}}c^{2}}{h} - \frac{R}{n^{2}},
$$
(80)
with $m_{\text{e}}$ being the mass of the electron and c and h the velocity of light in vacuo
and Planck’s constant, respectively. Hence, he derived what he called the ‘term
frequencies of the hydrogen atom’ (‘Wasserstofftermfrequenzen’), for the different
integers n and m (with $m_{\text{e}}$ denoting the mass of the electron),
$$
v_{n} = \frac{m_{\text{e}}c^{2}}{h} - \frac{R}{n^{2}},
$$
(80a)
and
$$
v_{m} = \frac{m_{\text{e}}c^{2}}{h} - \frac{R}{m^{2}},
$$
(80b)

neither added his name to the paper as co-author nor included any new material.

III.3 The Nonrelativistic Hydrogen Equation                                                                                                    461

and from those the difference

$$\nu_n - \nu_m = R\left(\frac{1}{m^2} - \frac{1}{n^2}\right), \quad (81)$$

which indeed represented the frequencies of the hydrogen lines. Finally, he had added in the same letter:

> I soon hope to be able to write a bit more in detail and more illuminatingly about this. At the moment I still have to learn the mathematics to handle the vibration problem fully—[it’s] a linear differential equation, similar to Bessel’s, however less known and exhibiting strange boundary conditions; these are connected with it and not imposed from outside. (Schrödinger to Wien, 27 December 1925)

Schrödinger wrote the letter of 27 December to Wien from Arosa, where he spent about two weeks of Christmas vacation.$^{140}$ As usual, he not only tried to recover there from the hardships of semester work, but also tried to find time for new ideas or for making progress in his scientific research problems. Schrödinger distributed his vacation time wisely between recreation and work. As Mrs. Schrödinger recalled: ‘He was a bad sleeper and he was tired [in the morning] because he sometimes worked in the evening and he had to have some recreation in between.’ But also: ‘When he was working on a certain subject, he didn’t do much recreation . . . . He never had a rest in the afternoon; he kept going on. He smoked a lot and that was why we always kept separate rooms, so that I shouldn’t always be surrounded by his smoke’ (AHQP Interview with Mrs. Schrödinger, 5 April 1963). In the Christmas vacation of 1925 Schrödinger indeed had a subject to work on. After completing, in the middle of December, the paper ‘*Zur Einsteinschen Gastheorie*’ (Schrödinger, 1926b), he again threw himself with fresh energy into the approach to atomic structure implying the de Broglie matter waves. ‘In 1925 when he started to work on that, we were in Arosa,’ recalled his widow, emphasizing: ‘I remember that he told me in Arosa about the papers of Einstein and de Broglie’ (A. Schrödinger, AHQP Interview, 5 April 1963).$^{141}$

The content of Schrödinger’s letter to Wien, dated 27 December 1925, thus provides the first documentary evidence of the progress achieved during the Christmas vacation. If compared with the earlier note ‘*H-Atom, Eigenschwingungen*’—which we have analysed in the previous section—several new aspects

---

$^{140}$From this letter and the following one of 8 January 1926 (which was written from Zurich) we know that he arrived in Arosa before 27 December 1925 and left on 8 January 1926.

$^{141}$In the interview with Mrs. Schrödinger the exact date of Schrödinger’s involvement in the atomic problem was discussed. While Mrs. Schrödinger’s recollections pointed to December 1925, her interviewer, Thomas S. Kuhn, also discussed an earlier date. ‘If that much was done to get these ideas [i.e. the relativistic and nonrelativistic wave equation]’, he argued, ‘and then to write several papers in the mind, at least, before the first one was sent in—that must have started before Christmas because the first paper was received by the journal in January’ (AHQP Interview, 5 April 1963). However, the previous vacations of the Schrödingers in Arosa had been in summer 1925, months before Schrödinger received de Broglie’s thesis, which provided the start for his investigations.

462 &emsp; **Chapter III &ensp; The Creation of Wave Mechanics**

appeared here that had not been present in the older treatment. First, Schrödinger explicitly wrote down a formula, Eq. (81), for the frequencies of the hydrogen spectral lines. Second, each hydrogen frequency must be composed as the difference of two ‘term frequencies’. Third, in the result obtained relativistic effects had been neglected—hence Schrödinger attempted at this time a *non-relativistic* theory of the hydrogen atom.

The first aspect mentioned may not seem to imply any real progress beyond the previous note on the relativistic hydrogen equation. Even without explicitly writing down a formula for the hydrogen spectral frequencies, Schrödinger had then obtained a result, from which the corresponding relativistic relation could be immediately derived by copying the procedure in the old Bohr-Sommerfeld quantum theory of atomic structure.$^{142}$ That he had in mind, from the very beginning, Sommerfeld’s procedure is confirmed by a statement which Schrödinger made at the end of January 1926 in a letter to Sommerfeld. He confessed:

> Finally, I still wish to add that the discovery of the whole connection [between the wave equation and the quantization of the hydrogen atom], goes back to your beautiful complex integration method for evaluating the radial quantum integral. It was the characteristic $(-B/\sqrt{A}) + \sqrt{C}$ which suddenly shone out from the exponents $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ like a Holy Grail. (Schrödinger to Sommerfeld, 29 January 1926)

Obviously, the earliest discussion of the relativistic equation had already led to a solution for the hydrogen spectral lines, though it was not an acceptable one.$^{143}$

The second feature emerging from the letter of 27 December 1925, namely the construction of atomic frequencies as differences of term frequencies, did not occur in the note on the hydrogen eigenvibrations either. The earlier investigation had been restricted to dealing with the stationary states of the hydrogen atom, hence only ‘term frequencies’ were involved. The fact that the experimental emission and absorption frequencies could be derived by taking differences of term frequencies still had to be proven within the new theoretical scheme.

The third and very important aspect emerging from Schrödinger’s letter was that he had now left behind him the previous, unsuccessful relativistic approach and was perfectly willing to content himself with a nonrelativistic theory of the hydrogen atom. This meant a decisive spiritual step forward—and to some extent a sacrifice of the intellect (the hydrogen atom had eventually to be treated in a relativistic manner!)—although it could be performed easily on the mathematical

***

$^{142}$ As we have shown in the previous section, Schrödinger obtained from the boundary conditions of the differential equation (see Eqs. (53) and (54)) definite values for the constants $A$, $B$ and $C$. With these values he could calculate the relativistic hydrogen terms, following Sommerfeld’s procedure, in evaluating the relativistic hydrogen atom in 1916 (Sommerfeld, 1916d).

$^{143}$ We disagree therefore strongly with the opinion put forward by Helge Kragh, ‘that Schrödinger did not solve the relativistic eigenvalue equation for hydrogen until after 27 December 1925’ (Kragh, 1982, p. 178). Of course, having in hand the result for the hydrogen frequencies did not yet imply a full wave-mechanical treatment in the sense of Schrödinger’s later published papers, for neither the relativistic case nor the nonrelativistic one.

# III.3 The Nonrelativistic Hydrogen Equation
463

level: Schrödinger just had to drop terms in his previous treatment that were small in the nonrelativistic limit. Then the wave equations (41) and (44) remained essentially unchanged; e.g., the differential equation for the radial function $\psi_r$ still kept the form

$$ \frac{d^2\psi_r}{dr^2} + \frac{2}{r} \frac{d\psi_r}{dr} + \left[ -A + \frac{2B}{r} - \frac{C}{r^2} \right] = 0. \qquad (82) $$

However, for the coefficients $A$, $B$ and $C$, Eqs. (44'a) to (44'c), a nonrelativistic approximation had to be taken, namely,

$$ A = \frac{4\pi^2}{h^2} 2m_{\text{e}}(m_{\text{e}}c^2 - h\nu), \qquad (82\text{a}) $$

$$ B = \frac{4\pi^2}{h^2} m_{\text{e}}e^2, \qquad (82\text{b}) $$

and

$$ C = n_\phi(n_\phi + 1), \qquad (82\text{c}) $$

with $m_{\text{e}}$ and $e$ denoting mass and charge of the electron, $h$ Planck's constant, $\nu$ the matter wave frequency and $n_\phi$ an integer number (the azimuthal quantum number in the old theory).$^{144}$

According to Schrödinger's previous rule—i.e., the one which he had already followed in the relativistic hydrogen case—one of the expressions (54) now had to be an integral number; this was exactly the 'Holy Grail' of which he spoke to Sommerfeld a few weeks later. Let us take, e.g., the condition

$$ \frac{B}{\sqrt{A}} - \sqrt{C + \frac{1}{4}} + \frac{1}{2} = n_r = \text{integer}. \qquad (83) $$

Then by inserting the expressions (82a)–(82c), he obtained the equation

$$ \frac{B}{\sqrt{A}} = \sqrt{\frac{2\pi^2 m_{\text{e}} e^4 / h^2}{m_{\text{e}}c^2 - h\nu}} = (n_r + n_\phi) = n, \qquad (84) $$

or, by taking the square on both sides,

$$ \frac{Rh}{m_{\text{e}}c^2 - h\nu} = n^2, \qquad (85) $$

$^{144}$ The nonrelativistic approximation is obtained in $A$ by replacing the term $(m_{\text{e}}c^2 + h\nu)$ by $2m_{\text{e}}c^2$, in $B$ by replacing the term $h\nu$ by $m_{\text{e}}c^2$, and in $C$ by neglecting the second term as being small compared with the first one.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0105 -->

464 Chapter III The Creation of Wave Mechanics

with $R (=2\pi^2 m_e e^4/h^3)$ denoting Rydberg's constant in spectroscopy. From Eq. (85) there immediately followed Eq. (80a) for the frequency $\nu = \nu_n$ related to the integral number $n$, which Schrödinger wrote in his letter to Wien.
In calculating from Eq. (83) the term frequency, Schrödinger followed exactly the procedure given earlier by Sommerfeld.$^{145}$ The main point, as we wish to emphasize again, is that he performed the transition to the nonrelativistic case, which he considered to be important enough to be treated in some detail, because he began the notebook on 'Eigenwertproblem des Atoms' exactly with a section on 'Ohne Relativistik (erste Näherung)' ('Without Relativity (First Approximation)'). The basic content of this section consists of a derivation of the nonrelativistic hydrogen equation by using the same line of thought as in his previous note on the relativistic hydrogen. That is, Schrödinger started from an equation for the de Broglie phase wave frequency of an electron with velocity $v$ in the electric field of a hydrogen nucleus, i.e.,

$$h\nu = m_e c^2 + \frac{m_e v^2}{2} - \frac{e^2}{r}. \quad (86)$$

From this equation he derived the expression for the (nonrelativistic) momentum $m_e v$ of the electron,

$$m_e v = \sqrt{2m_e \left( h\nu - m_e c^2 + \frac{e^2}{r} \right)}, \quad (87)$$

which he then inserted into the relation for the phase velocity $u$ of the de Broglie wave, i.e.,

$$u = \frac{h\nu}{m_e v} = \frac{h\nu}{\sqrt{2m_e (h\nu - m_e c^2 + e^2/r)}}. \quad (88)$$

The $u$ thus obtained could be used in the wave equation (40), yielding the following differential equation for the nonrelativistic hydrogen atom:

$$\Delta \psi = -\frac{4\pi^2}{h^2} 2m_e \left( h\nu - m_e c^2 + \frac{e^2}{r} \right) \psi. \quad (89)$$

By assuming separability of the wave function $\psi$ in the radial and angular co-ordinates, Schrödinger finally arrived at the differential equation (82) for the radial part $\psi_r$ of the wave function.

$^{145}$ For Sommerfeld's procedure see: *Atombau und Spektrallinien*, fourth edition, Appendix 8 (Sommerfeld, 1924d, p. 806). Sommerfeld not only defined the 'constants' $A, B$ and $C$ in a slightly different manner, he also introduced a different energy term, namely, $W = h\nu - m_e c^2$, instead of Schrödinger's ($h\nu$).

### III.3 The Nonrelativistic Hydrogen Equation &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 465

The coherence of the contents of Section 1 of the new notebook with the results, reported to Wien in the letter of 27 December 1925, leads to the following conclusion: Schrödinger had already begun composing the notebook on ‘*Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. I*’, before he wrote the letter; but he had not gone much beyond the first section of this notebook on that date. That is, he had definitely started to deal with the nonrelativistic hydrogen problem around Christmas 1925, probably the very day he arrived in Arosa for his winter holidays. The next interesting question to be solved is, of course, how far did he proceed before returning to Zurich? An indication of an answer may be taken from the letter which Schrödinger wrote—again to Wien—on 8 January 1926, certainly not long after getting back to Zurich.$^{146}$ There he described the status of his investigations with the following words:

> This is an extremely funny thing. The contrast between light-quanta and wave radiation can be traced even in the atom as: (a) single orbiting electrons; or (b) a standing vibration of the whole atomic region. In the interpretation (a) [we have]: the Hamiltonian partial differential equation; the separation of the variables; and the quantization in the well-known manner. In the interpretation (b) [we have]: the wave equation; the *separation of variables* in the old well-known sense that the unknown function is assumed to be, e.g., the product of a function of [radial co-ordinate] *r*, of a function of [the angle] $\theta$, and a function of [the angle] $\phi$; searching for the “normal vibrations”. The frequencies emitted [by atoms] appear as frequency differences, i.e., as beat frequencies of the normal frequencies. Something must be hidden behind that. I hope to formulate the results soon in an organized way. (Schrödinger to Wien, 8 January 1926)

These remarks, although being very general and vague, reveal the fact that Schrödinger had used his Christmas vacation to probe systematically into what he called ‘interpretation (b).’ This included that he had applied it to several examples of atomic systems—whose solution according to the old Bohr-Sommerfeld theory (called ‘interpretation (a)’ by Schrödinger) was well known. The first half of the notebook on ‘*Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. I*’ dealt with just such applications; hence, it represents exactly the work Schrödinger performed during the Christmas vacation. In the second half, however, Schrödinger introduced new methods, which came closer to the theory which he would report in his first published paper on the eigenvalue problem of the nonrelativistic hydrogen atom.

### **The Notebook on ‘*Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. I*’ (First Part)**

Among the notebooks and memoranda kept in the Schrödinger *Nachlaß* there are three extensive notebooks, which are particularly closely connected with the

---

genesis of wave mechanics. The author gave them the appropriate title of ‘*Eigenwertproblem des Atoms*’ (‘Eigenvalue Problem of the Atom’), and he developed there, more or less systematically, the contents of his three later memoirs on ‘*Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem*’ (Schrödinger, 1926c, d, f) and the paper ‘*Über das Verhältnis der Heisenberg–Born–Jordanschen Quantenmechanik zu der meinen*’ (Schrödinger, 1926e).¹⁴⁷ Especially, the first of these notebooks, No. I, allows a deep insight into the intellectual workshop of creating the wave equation of the hydrogen atom, the first example of the new quantum theory based on matter waves.¹⁴⁸ We shall therefore provide here an analysis and discussion of this most important source of wave mechanics.

Schrödinger did not organize his notes according to an *a priori* logical plan; rather, he wrote down a mixture of sudden inspirations and sketched-out methods of mathematical solution, which he often interrupted at points where he got no further, continuing on a given item at a later time with fresh energy. This method of procedure is already reflected in the titles given by Schrödinger to the sections of his notebook.¹⁴⁹ They are (with the English translation in square brackets):

The individual sections of the notebook had fairly different lengths. One-page notes alternated with detailed evaluation of specific mathematical questions. Schrödinger devoted large portions of the write-up to treating the Zeeman and Stark effects of the hydrogen atom (especially pp. 10–16, pp. 24–26, pp. 38–41, p. 44, pp. 58–72). In other parts he dealt with problems of the spatial oscillation (pp. 47–48), or with the rotational and vibrational modes of molecules (pp. 51–55), or with perturbation theory (pp. 56–57). All these items he would not include in his ‘*Erste Mitteilung*’ on wave mechanics, which exclusively presented the case of the nonrelativistic, free hydrogen atom; nevertheless, the fact that Schrödinger was concerned with these topics at a very early stage, certainly before the completion of the first publication, illuminates well the peculiar progress of his ideas and methods and thus the entire process of creation of wave mechanics. The notes also prove that for that purpose Schrödinger did not place himself in an ivory tower of purely theoretical conceptions—i.e., he did not restrict himself to reflecting deeply on a wave-theoretical reformulation of the atomic problem—but rather used the existing wealth of reliable spectroscopic results and their description within the framework of the old quantum theory of atomic structure, thus testing the new approach piece by piece until he was sure that the reformulation did work in detail. Such a cautious approach, involving a constant comparison between theory and empirical data, was in agreement with Schrödinger’s whole education and scientific temperament. As far as the particular moment of creation of wave mechanics is concerned, it may have played some role in that he was presenting at that time—i.e., in the winter semester of 1925/1926—a lecture course on the theory of spectra, which included the topics of the relativistic hydrogen spectra and the Stark and Zeeman effects in great detail; hence, he had these topics immediately at hand when he attempted the earliest tests of his wave mechanical ideas.²

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0109 -->

468 Chapter III The Creation of Wave Mechanics

In the first section of the notebook Schrödinger treated the nonrelativistic hydrogen problem. He derived there—as we have already reported—the corresponding differential equation for the radial wave function and outlined preliminary steps towards its evaluation. Especially, he obtained the stationary states from a condition which had to be applied in order to arrive at a unique solution of the equation. This mathematical treatment referred heavily to the analogy with Arnold Sommerfeld's evaluation by complex integration of the radial phase integral in the old quantum theory, and did not show any clear hint to the method of eigenfunctions presented later. A first, however modest, step in this direction may be recognized in an incomplete attempt by the author to write down the explicit expression for the radial wave function.<sup>150</sup>

The following three pages of the notebook (pp. 3–5) are interesting for another reason. Here Schrödinger tried, for the first time, to formulate the mathematical problem of deriving the hydrogen equation as a variational problem. He started from the variational problem:

$$
\delta \int \left[ \left( \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial y} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial z} \right)^2 - \frac{1}{c^2} \left( \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial t} \right)^2 \right] \cdot dx\, dy\, dz\, dt = 0 \tag{90}
$$

which leads to the second-order differential equation for the wave function $\phi$, i.e.,

$$
\Delta \phi - \frac{1}{c^2} \ddot{\phi} = 0. \tag{91}
$$

(In Eq. (91), $\Delta$ denotes the Laplacean differential operator, $\partial^2/\partial x^2 + \partial^2/\partial y^2 + \partial^2/\partial z^2$, and the double dots indicate the second time derivative.)<sup>151</sup> He then tried to obtain the variational problem corresponding to the relativistic hydrogen equation,

$$
\Delta \psi + \frac{4 \pi^2 \nu_0^2}{c^2} \left[ \left( \frac{\nu}{\nu_0} + \frac{a}{r} \right)^2 - 1 \right] \psi = 0, \tag{92}
$$

where $\nu_0 = m_e c^2$ and $a = e^2 / m_e c^2$. (See Eq. (41).) He suggested a formulation of the type

$$
\delta \int \left\{ \sqrt{1 - (\text{grad } \psi)^2 + \frac{1}{c^2} \left( \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial t} \right)^2 } \right\} dx\, dy\, dz\, dt = 0, \tag{93}
$$

but did not get anywhere with it.

<sup>150</sup> Schrödinger proposed expanding the solution for $\psi_r$ as a power series in a complex variable; he conjectured that the specific power series obtained might be related to a Legendre polynomial. (See pp. 1-2 of *Notebook I*.)

<sup>151</sup> Schrödinger knew of the relation between the variational problem and the wave equation from his student years. (See the notebook ‘*Physikalisches Seminar*’, filed on AHQP Microfilm No. 39, Section 1, which we have mentioned earlier.)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0110 -->

# III.3 The Nonrelativistic Hydrogen Equation 469

In the next section of his notebook Schrödinger again went back to the second-order differential equation—both the relativistic and the nonrelativistic cases—for the radial wave function. He especially explored the possibility whether the equation could be transformed into a Riccati equation, namely,

$$\frac{dy}{dx} = a_0(x) + a_1(x)y + a_2(x)y^2,$$ (94)

i.e., a differential equation of first order. He soon realized that this did not work out at all.

After a short sketch of the variational formulation of the problem of wave dispersion (p. 9) Schrödinger turned to a new problem, the (relativistic) hydrogen atom in a magnetic field. He observed that the phase velocity in that case had to be represented by a vector **u**,

$$\frac{\mathbf{u}}{u^2} = \frac{1}{h\nu} \left( \frac{m_e\mathbf{v}}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}} + \frac{e}{c}\mathbf{A} \right),$$ (95)

with **A** denoting the electromagnetic vector potential. This observation could be interpreted as the ‘non-reversibility of the “light-path”’ (‘*Nichtumkehrbarkeit des “Lichtweges”*’), as Schrödinger stated in the ‘*Programm*’ (p. 12). Three pages later, in the next section on the Zeeman effect, he wrote down the expression

$$u \approx \pm c[1 \pm s\alpha c],$$ (96)

for the phase velocity, with $\alpha$ denoting the direction cosine (of the angle between the wave propagation and the magnetic field) and $s$ a parameter proportional to the magnetic field strength (p. 15).

In the *Programm* (pp. 12–14), Schrödinger dealt for the first time with the Stark effect.$^{152}$ In this case he had to introduce, like Paul Epstein and Karl Schwarzschild in the old quantum theory, a different set of co-ordinates, the so-called parabolic co-ordinates. He took the following ones,

$$x^2 + y^2 = -(\lambda_1 - e_1)(\lambda_2 - e_1),$$ (97a)

and

$$2z = 2e_1 - \lambda_1 - \lambda_2,$$ (97b)

where $x$, $y$ and $z$ denote the Cartesian co-ordinates (with $z$ being in the direction

H-field. Non-reversibility of the “light path”. Analysis with magnetic rotation. 2. E-field. Parabolic co-ordinates. $\nu$-spectra.’) Only the second item is treated in the following.

III.3  The Nonrelativistic Hydrogen Equation                                                                    471

radial wave function, Eq. (82). For this purpose he transformed the equation by the substitution

$$ \psi_r = r^{\alpha-1/2} U \tag{99} $$

into another second-order differential equation which he called the Laguerre equation—although it is known as Laplace’s differential equation in the literature—namely$^{155}$

$$ \frac{d^2 U}{dr^2} + \frac{2\alpha + 1}{r} \frac{dU}{dr} + \left( A + \frac{2B}{r} \right) U = 0. \tag{100} $$

A solution of Eq. (100) could immediately be given by expanding $U$ in a power series of the variable $r$, i.e.,

$$ U = a_0 + a_1 r + a_2 r^2 + \dots + a_k r^k. \tag{101} $$

Then $U$ satisfied the Laplace equation provided the following relations held between the coefficients:

$$ a_1 = \frac{2B}{\alpha + 1}, \quad a_2 = \frac{Aa_0 + 2Ba_1}{2(\alpha + 2)}, \quad a_3 = \frac{Aa_1 + 2Ba_2}{2(\alpha + 3)}, \dots \tag{102} $$

Schrödinger further observed that the function $\bar{U} = r^{2\alpha} U$ satisfied an equation similar to Eq. (100), or,

$$ \frac{d^2 \bar{U}}{dr^2} + \frac{-2\alpha + 1}{r} \frac{d\bar{U}}{dr} + \left( A + \frac{2B}{r} \right) \bar{U} = 0. \tag{100'} $$

Hence he could restrict himself to take only positive $\alpha$, demanding

$$ \alpha = \sqrt{-C} = n, \tag{103} $$

where $n$ assumed positive integral values with zero excluded.$^{156}$

In the further evaluation of Eq. (100), Schrödinger then referred completely to the method discussed in Ludwig Schlesinger’s textbook on differential equations, the book which he had already consulted earlier for the relativistic hydrogen equation (Schlesinger, 1900).$^{157}$ Schlesinger had written down the

---

$^{156}$ The constant $\bar{C}$ of Eq. (103) is related to the constant $C$ of Eq. (82) by
$$ -C_{103} = C_{82} + \frac{1}{4}. $$
$^{157}$ See our discussion in Section 2. We assume that Schrödinger had Schlesinger’s book (which he also quoted in the first memoir (Schrödinger, 1926c)) in his possession, and that he took it with him when he went to Arosa for the Christmas vacation. It also seems that he continued to consult this book exclusively for most of his preliminary studies on wave mechanics.

general solution as

$$U = \int_L \exp(zr)(z - c_1)^{\alpha_1 - 1}(z - c_2)^{\alpha_2 - 1} dz. \tag{104}$$

The parameters $c_1$ and $c_2$ and the exponents $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ are given by the relations

$$c_1 = +\sqrt{-A}, \quad c_2 = -\sqrt{-A}, \tag{104a}$$

and

$$\alpha_1 = \frac{B}{\sqrt{-A}} + \alpha + \frac{1}{2}, \quad \alpha_2 = -\frac{B}{\sqrt{-A}} + \alpha + \frac{1}{2}. \tag{104b}$$

The path $L$ of the integration on the right-hand side of Eq. (104) is a closed one in the complex $z$-plane$^{158}$; it consists of a double loop around the fixed points $c_1$ and $c_2$. The solution could be expressed as the sum of two terms, i.e.,

$$U = (1 - e^{2\pi i \alpha_2})U_1 - (1 - e^{2\pi i \alpha_1})U_2. \tag{105}$$

$U_1$ and $U_2$ also represented solutions of Eq. (104), however, with closed paths circling only *one* of the two points, $c_1$ and $c_2$, respectively. $U_1$ and $U_2$ possess the following asymptotic expansions for large $r$ (see Schlesinger, 1900, p. 210):

$$\tilde{U}_1 \simeq e^{c_1 r} r^{-\alpha_1} (-1)^{\alpha_1} (e^{2\pi i \alpha_1} - 1) \Gamma(\alpha_1) (c_1 - c_2)^{\alpha_2 - 1}, \tag{106a}$$

and

$$\tilde{U}_2 \simeq e^{c_2 r} r^{-\alpha_2} (-1)^{\alpha_2} (e^{2\pi i \alpha_2} - 1) \Gamma(\alpha_2) (c_2 - c_1)^{\alpha_1 - 1}. \tag{106b}$$

In order to discuss the solution, given by Eqs. (105) and (106), Schrödinger distinguished the two cases

$$A > 0 \tag{107a}$$

and

$$A < 0. \tag{107b}$$

$$\int_L \frac{d}{dz}[\exp(zr)(z - c_1)^{\alpha_1}(z - c_2)^{\alpha_2}] dz = 0.$$

(See Schlesinger, 1900, Eq. (25a) on p. 197.)

III.3 The Nonrelativistic Hydrogen Equation &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; 473

In the first case, i.e., for positive $A$, $c_1$ and $c_2$ both assumed purely imaginary values; hence, the asymptotic expressions $\tilde{U}_1$ and $\tilde{U}_2$ remained finite, and the radial wave function possessed (for large values of $r$) the form

$$\psi_r \simeq \text{const. } r^{\alpha - \alpha_1 - 1/2} \times \text{periodic function} + \text{const.}' r^{\alpha - \alpha_2 - 1/2} \times \text{periodic function}, \tag{108}$$

where the $r$-exponents took the values

$$\alpha - \alpha_1 - \frac{1}{2} = -\frac{B}{\sqrt{-A}} + 1, \tag{108a}$$

and

$$\alpha - \alpha_2 - \frac{1}{2} = \frac{B}{\sqrt{-A}} - 1, \tag{108b}$$

respectively.

The case for negative $A$-values, where $c_1$ and $c_2$ assumed real values, did not prove to be so smooth. Then the $U_1$-part clearly grew indefinitely for large $r$-values, while the $U_2$-part approached zero; and so did $U$, if $\alpha_2$ did not take on negative integral values, or

$$\alpha_2 = -s, \quad \text{with } s = 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots \tag{109}$$

To obtain $U_1$ under the latter condition, Schrödinger had to calculate the residue of the integrand on the right-hand side of Eq. (104), namely

$$U_1 = \text{Res}_{c_2}[\exp(zr)(z - c_1)^{\alpha_1 - 1}(z - c_2)^{\alpha_2 - 1}],$$

that is, he had to calculate the residue of the expression within the square brackets at the point $z = c_2$. After some lengthy evaluations, in which he also used the expression for the exponential function, he arrived at the result

$$U_1 = \exp(-r \cdot \sqrt{-A}) \sum_{k=0}^{s} (-2\sqrt{-A} r)^k \frac{1}{k!} \binom{s + 2\sqrt{-C}}{s - k}. \tag{110}$$

On identifying $U_1$ with $U$, he found for the radial function $\psi_r$ the solution

$$\psi_r = f(r \cdot \sqrt{-A}), \tag{111}$$

with

$$f(r \cdot \sqrt{-A}) = r^{\sqrt{-C}-1/2} \exp(-r \cdot \sqrt{-A}) \cdot \sum_{k=0}^{s} (-2r

Schrödinger concluded with an attempt at a physical interpretation of the result (*Notebook I*, pp. 21–22). He noted that the function \( f(r \cdot \sqrt{-A}) \) exhibited zeros for \( r \) assuming the order of magnitude  

$$
r_i \sim \frac{1}{\sqrt{-A}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(4\pi^2/c^2)(\nu^2 - \nu_0^2)}} \approx \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{2mh(\nu - \nu_0)}}. \tag{112}
$$  

He related this result to the previous observation in the old quantum theory, namely that the perihelion and aphelion distances, \( r_1 \) and \( r_2 \), of the elliptical orbits of the hydrogen atom were determined by the equation  

$$
-\frac{A}{C} = \frac{1}{r_1} \cdot \frac{1}{r_2}, \tag{113}
$$  

with \( C \) a small integral number. Hence he concluded: ‘The radii of the nodal spheres [i.e., the zeros of \( f(r \cdot \sqrt{-A}) \)] therefore have the order of magnitude of the electron orbits [in the Bohr–Sommerfeld quantum theory of atomic structure]’ (*Notebook I*, p. 22). He further registered the following relation between the value for the radial quantum number \( n_r \) (\( = s + \frac{1}{2} \)) and the number of nodes:  

| radical quantum number: | \(\frac{1}{2}\) | \(\frac{3}{2}\) | \(\frac{5}{2}\) |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| number of nodes: | 1 | 2 | 3 |

(114)  

Finally, he stated: ‘The behaviour at \( r = \text{zero} \) depends on the *azimuthal* quantum number’ (*Notebook I*, p. 22).  

Following a short and unsuccessful effort to modify the relativistic hydrogen equation—by inserting a term \( \text{grad}(u/c)^2 \cdot \text{grad} \, \psi \) (see p. 23)—Schrödinger went on with a treatment of the Stark effect.^159 Especially, he tried to evaluate Eqs. (98a) and (98b) in a straightforward manner. He first noticed that both equations could be written in the form  

$$
\psi'' + \frac{1}{x} \psi' + \left( Dx + A + \frac{2B}{x} + \frac{C}{x^2} \right) \psi = 0, \tag{115}
$$  

with  

$$
C < 0, \tag{115a}
$$  

where the variable \( x \) denotes \( \lambda_1 \) or \( \lambda_2 \), and \( \psi' \) and \( \psi'' \), respectively, the first and second derivative with respect to \( x \). Equation (115) now somewhat resembled

**III.3 The Nonrelativistic Hydrogen Equation** 475

the equation for the free hydrogen atom without having exactly the same form; it constituted a linear homogeneous differential equation of second order. Schrödinger again found a full presentation of the mathematical methods of solution in Schlesinger’s book (see especially Schlesinger, 1900, p. 178 ff). As a rule, Eq. (115) exhibited two singular points, namely

$$x = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad x = \infty. \tag{116}$$

In particular, Schrödinger analyzed the situation at infinity by multiplying Eq. (115) by $x^2$. He further got rid of the $C$-term in a way similar to the case of the free hydrogen equation, i.e., by the transformation

$$\psi = x^\alpha u. \tag{117}$$

Thus he arrived at the equation

$$x^2 u'' + x P_1(x) u' + P_2(x) u = 0, \tag{118}$$

with

$$P_1(x) = 2\alpha + 1 \tag{118a}$$

and

$$P_2(x) = D x^3 + A x^2 + 2 B x. \tag{118b}$$

He then applied the transformation

$$y = \frac{1}{x} \frac{d \ln u}{dx}, \tag{119}$$

by which Eq. (118) turned into the first-order differential equation

$$\frac{y'}{x} + y^2 + y \frac{2\alpha + 2}{x^2} + \frac{D}{x} + \frac{A}{x^2} + \frac{2B}{x^3} = 0, \tag{120}$$

that is, a first-order Riccati equation. However, the particular coefficients in Eq. (120) implied a double zero root in the characteristic equation ‘which leads to an unpleasant situation’ (‘was zu *Unannehmlichkeiten führt*,’ p. 26). Schrödinger, therefore, laboured hard to obtain a more suitable Riccati equation by employing alternative transformations to that provided by Eq. (119). But for the moment he did not succeed.

Having gone as far as page 29 of his *Notebook I*, Schrödinger had reached, at least partly, his goal of solving wave equations for the atom. The mathematical

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0117 -->

476 Chapter III The Creation of Wave Mechanics

methods available to him—basically through the information from Schlesinger’s textbook on differential equations—had allowed him to handle successfully the nonrelativistic problem of the free hydrogen atom: there he had found the well-known results, i.e., the continuum solutions for $A > 0$ and the discrete energy states for $A < 0$; he had further explicitly calculated the wave function for the discrete states. On the other hand, in trying to score a similar success with the Stark effect he had been unlucky; and it seemed to him that it was not because of reasons of principle which had caused that failure, but rather his own limited skill in the mathematical methods for solving second-order differential equations. ‘If I only knew more about mathematics!’, he had written to Wilhelm Wien on 27 December 1925. For the moment, the methods derived from Schlesinger’s book did not seem to help Schrödinger in carrying out his arduous programme: the systematic wave equation approach to describe the behaviour of quantized atomic systems.

### Assistance from Colleagues in Zurich

Felix Bloch, then a student at Zurich, recalled that Schrödinger presented, a few weeks after his colloquium on de Broglie’s matter waves, still another colloquium talk in the winter semester of 1925/1926, which he opened with the words: ‘My colleague Debye suggested that one should have a wave equation; well, I have found one’ (Bloch, 1976, p. 24). He meant by this remark the wave equation for the nonrelativistic hydrogen atom. About this second colloquium, Erwin Fues, another Zurich contemporary—at that time assistant to Schrödinger—remembered that it was again Debye who provided the idea of deriving wave mechanical equations from a variational principle; he stated in detail:

> The stimulus occurred in a colloquium discussion, after Schrödinger had presented his nonrelativistic theory. As far as I recall, Debye said—in this sense, not exactly in these words—nothing but that one has succeeded in putting the most important fundamental theories of physics into the form of a variational principle which gives an impressive summary [of the theories]. (Fues, AHQP Interview, 24 July 1963)

These recollections of Schrödinger’s contemporaries in Zurich raise the important question as to what influences helped him in creating wave mechanics. Both Bloch and Fues implied that Schrödinger obtained an essential stimulus at two crucial stages of the development: namely, first, when he passed over from the geometrical approach of matter waves in atoms to the description by a wave equation in November or December 1925; and, second, when he set out in January 1926 to find the systematic and complete solution of the nonrelativistic hydrogen equation.
It is very difficult to trace any of Debye’s influence in Schrödinger’s preliminary notes and the first publication, even apart from the fact that Debye’s name is not mentioned there at all. Debye himself, when later confronted with the story that he might have helped to initiate the idea of the wave equation, replied: ‘No, I

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0118 -->

III.3 The Nonrelativistic Hydrogen Equation
477

don’t remember that. I don’t remember that. I had no influence. Certainly not’ (Debye, AHQP Interview, 5 April 1962). In spite of this rejection, one cannot exclude the possibility that Debye pleaded, in the discussion of Schrödinger’s first Zurich colloquium, for having a wave equation for matter waves, and that his remark played some role in taking the wave equation approach. That is, he either pushed Schrödinger to the idea of developing a wave equation, or he confirmed Schrödinger’s previous thoughts in that direction. With respect to the origin of the idea of using a variational principle as the basis for the wave equations, the available documents tend to answer the question of Debye’s influence rather clearly. Schrödinger had already conceived the possibility of deriving the hydrogen wave equation *before* he presented the second Zurich colloquium—which he did after the Christmas vacation and after 8 January 1926. The proof can immediately be found in the fact that he hinted in the notebook ‘*Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. I*’ early on (i.e., on p. 3) at the formulation of a variational principle for the wave equation, a method which he knew existed from his student days in Vienna.¹⁶⁰ On the other hand, he returned to a variational principle in a latter part of the same notebook, namely on page 32, where he attempted to formulate a new programme allowing him to put his previous results on the hydrogen wave equation into more systematic order. It appears evident that this new programme constituted the first step in the fulfilment of his promise to Wilhelm Wien on 8 January 1926: ‘I soon hope to bring it into some orderly shape.’ As in the earlier situation with the wave equation we cannot, and do not want to, exclude the possibility that Debye’s remark about the usefulness of having a variational principle either paved the way to the new programme or—what is even more plausible—it confirmed Schrödinger’s original ideas formulated soon after returning to Zurich from the Christmas vacation.

Under the title ‘*Programm*’, beginning on page 30 of *Notebook I*, Schrödinger listed two topics, namely: ‘1. Co-motion of the nucleus relativistically. 2. The old Hamiltonian analogy between optics and mechanics.’ As the first item he again treated (on pp. 30–31) the free relativistic hydrogen atom.¹⁶¹ Since the previous evaluations had yielded a wrong result for the fine structure, Schrödinger now hoped for a correction of the result if he considered in addition the motion of the hydrogen nucleus. He therefore planned to find a wave equation for the relativistic two-body system, consisting of a hydrogen nucleus and an electron and having the following properties: (i) The sum of the momenta is constant and may be put equal to zero; (ii) the momenta of the electron and hydrogen nucleus, therefore, can be assumed to have the same magnitude and opposite directions; (iii) the corresponding velocities, *v* and *v'*, have opposite directions, the ratio of

¹⁶⁰ See Schrödinger’s notes entitled ‘*Physikalisches Seminar*,’ filed on AHQP Microfilm No. 39, Section 1. The variational principle, which Schrödinger indicated on p. 3 of his notebook on ‘*Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. I*’, is copied from the early notes.
¹⁶¹ Schrödinger noted explicitly that he did not include in this treatment ‘magnetic forces and [electric] field deformations’ (*Notebook I*, p. 30).

their values is *not* constant but depends on the relative distance $r$ between the electron and the nucleus.

With these assumptions the following equation could be written down for the total energy $W$ of the relativistic hydrogen atom

$$\frac{m_e c^2}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}} + \frac{Mc^2}{\sqrt{1 - v'^2/c^2}} = W + \frac{e^2}{r}, \qquad (121)$$

where the individual contributions from the electron (rest-mass $m_e$) and hydrogen nucleus (mass $M$) were, respectively,

$$\frac{m_e c^2}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}} = \frac{1}{2}\left( W + \frac{e^2}{r} - \frac{M^2 - m_e^2}{W + e^2/r}\right), \qquad (121a)$$

and

$$\frac{M^2 c^2}{\sqrt{1 - v'^2/c^2}} = \frac{1}{2}\left( W + \frac{e^2}{r} + \frac{M^2 - m_e^2}{W + e^2/r}\right). \qquad (121b)$$

From Eq. (121a) Schrödinger derived the following expression for the phase velocity $u$ of the electron,

$$u = \nu c\biggl/\biggl[\frac{1}{4}\left(\nu + \frac{e^2}{hr} - \frac{\nu_0'^2 - \nu_0^2}{\nu + e^2/hr}\right)^2 - \nu_0^2\biggr]^{1/2}, \qquad (122)$$

with

$$\nu = \frac{W}{h}, \qquad (122a)$$

and

$$\nu_0 = \frac{m_e c^2}{h}, \qquad \nu_0' = \frac{Mc^2}{h}. \qquad (122b)$$

He commented on the result as follows: 'This would be quite nice, but now $\nu$ is much damned bigger than before. Obviously, I should not divide the energy of the total system by the momentum of the electron' (*Notebook I*, p. 31). To correct that mistake, he replaced the total energy $W$ by the expression

$$h\nu = W - \frac{Mc^2}{\sqrt{1 - v'^2/c^2}}. \qquad (123)$$

$$S = \int_{(x_0, y_0, z_0)}^{(x_1, y_1, z_1)} \mathcal{T} \, dt = \int_{(x_0, y_0, z_0)}^{(x_1, y_1, z_1)} \sqrt{E - V} \, ds, \qquad \text{[(128)]}$$

Thus far he had only described the procedure of classical dynamics, which had also been used in the old quantum theory.$^{162}$ But now came the crucial point, the connection with the wave equation, which Schrödinger established with the following observation: ‘Instead of $S$ one can introduce [the wave function] $\psi$ into the partial differential equation [(127)] via

$$S = K \cdot \ln \psi, \qquad \text{[(129)]}$$

with $K$ having the dimension of an *action*. [Then one obtains the wave equation]

$$\left( \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial x} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial y} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial z} \right)^2 + \frac{2m}{K^2} (V - E)\psi^2 = 0 \qquad \text{[(130)]}$$

[or the variational principle with $d\tau = dx \, dy \, dz$]

$$\delta \int \left[ \left( \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial x} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial y} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial z} \right)^2 + \frac{2m}{K^2} (V - E)\psi^2 \right] d\tau = 0.’ \qquad \text{[(131)]}$$

He also commented: ‘For the moment we want to express the situation differently. Is the following statement correct? If one demands that the above integral [(131)] should obtain an extremum value by inserting a function $\psi$ which is unique in the whole space, finite and two-fold continuously differentiable, then only an [in-]finite, discrete number of negative $E$-values is possible, but a continuum of positive $E$-values. The negative $E$-values give rise to the Balmer series’ (*Notebook I*, p. 32).

The reference to the mechanical-optical analogy and the use of the transformation (129) undoubtedly constituted a new stage and a major step towards wave mechanics, from the fundamental point of view as much as for practical reasons. Schrödinger now possessed the first elements of a general method by which he was able to derive, from a classical dynamical description of a mechanical system, the corresponding wave equation description. It might appear that only a thorough

162 Karl Schwarzschild especially had introduced the Hamilton–Jacobi theory of periodic systems into Bohr’s quantum theory of atomic structure (Schwarzschild, 1916c). A short summary of the method was presented by Sommerfeld in his book *Atombau und Spektrallinien*. (See Sommerfeld, 1924d, Appendix 7.)

# III.3 The Nonrelativistic Hydrogen Equation

**481**

study of the relations between classical mechanics and wave optics could have provided the above progress; especially, the eiconal concept should have triggered the special transformation (129).¹⁶³ Despite the logical conclusiveness of such an argument the true story did not happen in this way.¹⁶⁴ Schrödinger did not really need any refined eiconal theory when he thought of the old Hamiltonian analogy between optics and mechanics, because he was able to rely for that purpose on his own considerations, written down in Vienna in a notebook entitled 'Tensoranalytische Mechanik. III'.¹⁶⁵ These old results provided especially useful guidance for the ideas which Schrödinger would present in his second publication on wave mechanics (Schrödinger, 1926d). For the moment, i.e., early in January 1926, Schrödinger merely needed the existence of the analogy between the principle of least action in mechanics,

$$
\delta \int (E - V) \, dt = \int \sqrt{(E - V)} \, ds, \tag{132}
$$

and Pierre de Fermat’s variational principle of optics,

$$
\delta \int n \, ds = 0, \tag{133}
$$

establishing the close analogy between the index of refraction, $n$, and the square root of the kinetic energy of a mechanical system, $\sqrt{T}$, which can be expressed as $\sqrt{(E - V)}$ (i.e., the square root of the difference between total energy and potential energy). This analogy provided a direct motivation for the wave equation (130), since in optics a relation

$$
\left( \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial x} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial y} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial z} \right)^2 \quad \text{proportional to } n^2 \tag{134}
$$

482 Chapter III The Creation of Wave Mechanics

was satisfied.$^{166}$ In order to arrive at Eq. (130), he had just to introduce the *Ansatz* (129).$^{167}$
The procedure from the variational principle, Eq. (131), onwards was straightforward. Schrödinger carried it out explicitly in his notebook on *Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. I* (p. 33), finding
$$
2 \int \delta\psi \frac{\partial\psi}{\partial n} df - 2 \int \delta\psi \left[ \Delta\psi + \frac{2m}{K^2}(E - V)\psi \right] d\tau = 0 \tag{135}
$$
with
$$
\Delta\psi = \frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial z^2}. \tag{136}
$$
The first surface term could be neglected, if the gradient of the wave function in the direction normal to the wave front, $\partial\psi/\partial n$, decreased faster than $R^{-2}$ at large distances $R$. Then the wave equation,
$$
\Delta\psi + \frac{2m}{K^2}(E - V)\psi = 0, \tag{137}
$$
was retained, which provided the basic differential equation for nonrelativistic quantum systems having total energy $E$ and potential energy $V$.
In the special example of the nonrelativistic hydrogen atom Eq. (137) assumed the form
$$
\Delta\psi + \frac{2m_e}{K^2} \left( E + \frac{e^2}{r} \right) \psi = 0, \tag{138}
$$
where
$$
K^2 = \frac{h^2}{4\pi^2}, \tag{138a}
$$
and $m_e$ denoted the mass of the electron. With it Schrödinger quickly repeated (*Notebook I*, pp. 33–34) the essential steps of the solution. That is, he wrote $\psi$ as a product of functions in the angular and the radial variables, obtaining for the radial part the second-order differential equation,
$$
\frac{1}{r^2} \frac{d}{dr} \left( r^2 \frac{d\psi_r}{dr} \right) + \left[ \frac{2m_e E}{K^2} + \frac{2m_e e^2}{K^2 r} - \frac{n(n - 1)}{r^2} \right] \psi = 0. \tag{139}
$$

$^{167}$ At a later stage of the development of wave mechanics, Schrödinger would call the transformation described by Eq. (129) ‘not understandable by itself’ (‘*an sich unverständlich*,’ Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 489).

As before, he introduced the function $U$ by the equation

$$\psi_r = r^{\alpha - 1/2} U(r). \qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad (140)$$

The function $U$ now satisfied the equation (see Eq. (100)),

$$\frac{d^2U}{dr^2} + \frac{2\alpha + 1}{r} \frac{dU}{dr} + \left( \frac{2m_e E}{K^2} + \frac{2m_e e^2}{rK^2} \right) U = 0, \qquad\qquad (141)$$

whose solution could be written as (see Eq. (104)),

$$U = \int_L \exp(zr)(z - c_1)^{\alpha_1 - 1}(z - c_2)^{\alpha_2 - 1} dz, \qquad\qquad (142)$$

with the parameters $c_1$, $c_2$, $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ given by

$$c_1 = +\sqrt{-\frac{2m_e E}{K^2}}, \quad c_2 = -\sqrt{-\frac{2m_e E}{K^2}}, \qquad\qquad (142\text{a})$$

and

$$\alpha_1 = \frac{m_e e^2}{K^2 \sqrt{-2m_e E / K^2}} + n + 1, \quad \alpha_2 = -\frac{m_e e^2}{\sqrt{-2m_e E / K^2}} + n + 1, \qquad (142\text{b})$$

and the path of integration $L$ represents a double loop around the points $c_1$ and $c_2$ in the complex $z$-plane, as shown in Figure 1. Schrödinger added the remark: 'In the present case, however, where the *sum* of the exponents assumes an integral value,

$$\alpha_1 - 1 + \alpha_2 - 1 = 2n, \qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad [(143)]$$

In continuing the evaluation of the nonrelativistic hydrogen problem (*Notebook I*, pp. 35-36), Schrödinger considered especially the situation of negative *E*-values. As later in the published paper he separated the cases

$$l > n, \tag{144a}$$

Unlike the published paper, however, he did not go through the calculation in detail, encountering for the moment some mathematical difficulties.$^{168}$ In later pages (i.e., pp. 49-50) of the notebook, he returned to the hydrogen problem in a section on 'Laguerresche Polynome.' He especially noticed then that the radial wave functions, solving Eq. (141) for discrete values of the energy, could be expressed by derivatives of Laguerre polynomials. By the time Schrödinger wrote that section, he had certainly the full solution of the nonrelativistic hydrogen problem in his hands.

III.3  The Nonrelativistic Hydrogen Equation 485  

Schrödinger mentioned explicitly the assistance of another Zurich colleague—that of the mathematician Hermann Weyl.¹⁶⁹ After presenting the equation for the radial wave function of the nonrelativistic hydrogen atom, he stated: ‘For guidance in treating the equation I owe . . . the deepest thanks to Hermann Weyl’ (Schrödinger, 1926c, p. 363, footnote 1).  
    If taken at face value, one might interpret the above statement in the sense that Schrödinger had not progressed much before he obtained Weyl’s assistance. This opinion might even be confirmed by the fact that Schrödinger added, after the acknowledgment, in the same footnote: ‘I refer for statements not proven in the following to L. Schlesinger’s book *Differentialgleichungen* (*Sammlung Schubert*, No. 13, *Göschen*, 1900), especially Chapters 3 and 5.’ Hence, he seemed to imply that it was Weyl who drew his attention to Schlesinger’s book, and this then started the whole development leading to the wave theory of the nonrelativistic hydrogen atom. We argue definitely against such conclusions. First, it cannot be assumed that Schrödinger involved Weyl in his problem of solving the nonrelativistic hydrogen equation before returning from the Christmas vacation.¹⁷⁰ Second, the detailed analysis of the short *Memorandum* on the relativistic hydrogen equation reveals that Schrödinger, from the very beginning of his concern with the hydrogen problem, had available the mathematical methods displayed in Schlesinger’s textbook on differential equations. These methods sufficed to solve both the relativistic and the nonrelativistic wave equations for the free hydrogen atom.¹⁷¹ Finally, Schrödinger had arrived at the solutions in both cases before Weyl took any great interest in his work.¹⁷²  
    Still the acknowledgment of essential assistance in dealing with the nonrelativistic hydrogen equation must be taken seriously. Its significance in the  

¹⁶⁹ We want to repeat at this point that Schrödinger nowhere in his notes or published papers on wave mechanics acknowledged the help of Peter Debye.  

¹⁷⁰ As we have discussed in detail, Schrödinger essentially started working on the nonrelativistic problem during the Christmas vacation in Arosa; however, he already possessed the outline of the mathematical solution (following the information in Schlesinger’s book on differential equations) when he first studied the relativistic hydrogen problem.  
    Of course, one cannot exclude in principle that Schrödinger had already asked Weyl for help during the early stages of his concern with the relativistic hydrogen atom; and that it was Weyl, who referred him to the mathematical methods contained in Schlesinger’s book. However, it appears unlikely that Schrödinger should have done so at such an early stage when he was not yet sure whether or not the whole idea of a wave equation would lead anywhere. Besides, why should he, after having obtained the expert’s [i.e., Weyl’s] advice on the solution of differential equations with eigenvalue solutions, complain of not knowing enough mathematics (as he did in the letter to Wien of 27 December 1925)?  

¹⁷¹ We seriously disagree with Helge Kragh’s statement: ‘Schrödinger was not able to find a solution, either in $N_1$ [i.e., the notes on “H-Atom, Eigenschwingungen”] or in the slightly later $N_2$ [i.e., the notebook “Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. I”]’ (Kragh, 1982, p. 181).  

¹⁷² It appears evident that Schrödinger was in possession of the first edition of Ludwig Schlesinger’s book of 1900—to which he referred in his first published paper—from his student days, and had taken it with him to Arosa where he began to compose *Notebook I*. (This evidence is confirmed by the fact that by 1922 there already existed a third edition of Schlesinger’s book, while Schrödinger—in the creative stage of wave mechanics—always referred to the first edition of 1900.)

context of the discovery of wave mechanics is not difficult to determine. It was for the formulation of the more rigorous mathematical details of the solution of the differential equation for the radial wave function, that Schrödinger consulted, in the last stages of formulating the content of the first publication on *‘Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem,’* his colleague Hermann Weyl, who was known to be an expert in the treatment of differential equations and eigenvalue problems.¹⁷³  
There existed quite a few mathematical questions of detail that had to be discussed on the way to solving the wave equations describing the free hydrogen atom or the hydrogen atom under the influence of constant electric and magnetic fields—the problems in which Schrödinger was mostly interested in January 1926. In any case, one must trace Weyl’s assistance in the progress of dealing with the mathematical methods of wave mechanics achieved after 8 January 1926, notably after the new programme had been introduced.  

Schrödinger’s programme not only applied to the free hydrogen atom but also to the case of the Zeeman effect in nonrelativistic approximation. (See the Notebook *‘Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. I,’* pp. 38–44.) There he used a different connection between the action function $S$ and the wave function $\psi$, i.e.,  

$$ S = iK \ln \psi, \quad K = \frac{h}{2\pi}. \tag{129'} $$  

He did not really carry out the necessary calculations of the Zeeman effect at this point. However, he succeeded essentially in solving other atomic problems, namely the linear oscillator in one and three dimensions (*Notebook I*, pp. 45–48), and the problem of the rotating and oscillating molecules (pp. 51–55). After a short sketch of the perturbation theory in the framework of wave mechanics (pp. 56–57), Schrödinger concluded *Notebook I* by an improved treatment of the Stark effect. Since these topics were not presented in his first publication on the new theory, we shall postpone a detailed analysis to later sections.  

**Quantization as a Variational Principle**  

On 29 January 1926 Erwin Schrödinger wrote a letter to Arnold Sommerfeld, the first after many months.¹⁷⁴ *‘It has been so very long since I have given you any news of me,’* he began, *‘that I must now write quickly. Otherwise you might write me after having looked at my quantum paper, which I sent to Geheimrat Wien for the *Annalen* requesting him to show it to you before [passing it on to the journal]’* (Schrödinger to Sommerfeld, 29 January 1926).  

¹⁷³ Weyl had been a student of David Hilbert (the founder of the modern theory of eigenvalue problems), and had dealt with the theory of linear differential equations involving singularities soon after his doctoral dissertation (Weyl, 1909).  
¹⁷⁴ The previous letter in the Schrödinger–Sommerfeld correspondence was from the summer of 1925: Schrödinger to Sommerfeld, 21 July 1925.

III.3 The Nonrelativistic Hydrogen Equation 487

What Schrödinger called the quantum paper (*Quantenarbeit*) was his first communication on ‘*Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem*’ (‘Quantization as an Eigenvalue Problem’), which he had submitted a few days earlier, namely on 26 January, to Willy Wien. He had already announced the paper to Wien several weeks earlier—see Schrödinger’s letter to Wien, 8 January 1926—and he had worked on finishing and polishing the material for nearly three weeks, obtaining here and there a little help from his Zurich colleagues.$^{175}$ The basic content of the paper is restricted to one question: to the nonrelativistic hydrogen problem, or the Kepler problem of one electron in the Coulomb field of an atomic nucleus. Schrödinger selected this problem from the bulk of problems that he had been treating with the wave equation approach in the course of the previous month (see his notebook on ‘*Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. I*’ discussed above) for two reasons: first, the hydrogen problem represented the starting point of his concern with matter waves; and second, he had worked out the mathematics completely and could use the solution to demonstrate the power of the new method.

The new method, which Schrödinger displayed in his paper, not only presented suitable practical tools for solving problems in atomic theory. More importantly, it provided a new foundation of the quantum theory of atomic structure, about which Schrödinger wrote to Sommerfeld: ‘Of course, I am anxiously awaiting your judgment more than anybody else’s, as to whether you *share* the *very* high expectations which I associate with the derivation of the quantum conditions from Hamilton’s principle’ (Schrödinger to Sommerfeld, 29 January 1926). That is, Schrödinger hoped to be able to remove the arbitrariness of the quantum conditions of the old quantum theory of atomic structure; he claimed that he could derive them from a deeper, more fundamental principle, a kind of new Hamiltonian principle, which he had obtained by connecting the Hamiltonian principle of classical dynamics with the idea of the matter wave equation. In other words, he argued that the undulatory features of mechanical systems might give rise to the occurrence of quantum conditions in atomic systems. He placed the same argument at the top of the publication. He wrote: ‘In this paper I wish to consider, first, the simplest case of the hydrogen atom (nonrelativistic and unperturbed), and show that the customary quantum conditions can be replaced by another postulate, in which the notion of “whole numbers”, merely as such, is not introduced.’ He explained further: ‘Rather when the integralness does appear, it arises in the same natural way as it does in the case of the *node-numbers* of a vibrating string. The new conception is capable of generalization, and strikes, I believe, very deeply at the true nature of the quantum rules’ (Schrödinger, 1926c, p. 361, English translation, p. 1).

Schrödinger devoted nearly the entire Section 1—the largest part of his paper (Schrödinger, 1926c, pp. 361–370)—to producing the desired ‘derivation’ of

(See our above discussion on p. 433.)
