quantum numbers in the case of the nonrelativistic hydrogen atom. He demonstrated, repeating the steps of the notebook on ‘*Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. I*,’ how to establish the variational problem for a general quantum-dynamical problem. In classical physics—and the old quantum theory—that problem was described by Hamilton’s partial differential equation,

$$H\left(q, \frac{\partial S}{\partial q}\right) = E, \qquad (146)$$

with $H$ denoting the Hamiltonian function depending on the position variables $q$, the momentum variables $p = \partial S/\partial q$ and $E$ the energy value of the system. Schrödinger further assumed that a solution of Eq. (146) existed, in which $S$ could be given by a sum of functions each depending only on one variable $q$. He then replaced the classical function $S$ by a new function $\psi$ via the relation

$$S = K \ln \psi, \qquad (147)$$

where the constant $K$ had the dimension of an action. He noticed further that Eq. (146), if expressed in terms of the new function $\psi$, assumed the particular shape: ‘quadratic form of $\psi$ and its first derivatives equated to zero,’ as long as the relativistic mass dependence was neglected (Schrödinger, 1926c, pp. 361–362).$^{176}$ Instead of attacking the equation directly, he now proposed a different solution. He wrote: ‘We seek a function $\psi$, such that for any arbitrary variation of it the integral of the said quadratic form, taken over the whole co-ordinate space, is stationary, $\psi$ being everywhere real, single-valued, finite and continuously differentiable up to the second order.’ Finally he stressed in italics: ‘*The quantum conditions are replaced by this variational problem*’ (Schrödinger, 1926c, p. 362).

The replacement of the Hamiltonian differential equation by the variational problem involving the space function $\psi$ appears to be an enormous step, both conceptually and mathematically. Certainly, from the point of view of logic, the connection is a rather natural one; after all, Eq. (146) itself followed from a variational principle, i.e., its solution also solved the extremum problem of dynamics. In this sense one must understand the assertion of Debye, in the Zurich colloquium reported earlier, that all important fundamental theories of physics might be cast in the form of a variational principle.$^{177}$ However, in mechanics, one was dealing thus far with the variation of the *time integral* over the Lagrange function, while Schrödinger’s reformulation led to a variational principle of a space integral. This shift in the nature of the problem originated from the earlier

$^{176}$ In the nonrelativistic limit the momentum variables always entered the Hamiltonian function $H$ quadratically. Replacing $S$ by $\psi$, the squares, $(\partial S/\partial q)^2$, turned into $(K^2/\psi^2)(\partial\psi/\partial q)^2$.

$^{177}$ The fact mentioned by Debye was well known among physicists at that time. For example, Max Planck had discussed the most famous of all variational principles in his article ‘*Das Prinzip der kleinsten Wirkung*’ (‘The Principle of Least Action’) in a popular presentation of physics (for the Volume *Physik* of the series *Die Kultur der Gegenwart*); and he had demonstrated in this article how the principle was valid in mechanics, electrodynamics, electron theory and relativity theory (Planck, 1915e). Planck had also drawn attention to the role played by the principle of least action in quantum theory (Planck, 1910b).

III.3  The Nonrelativistic Hydrogen Equation  
489  

ideas conceived by Schrödinger in applying Louis de Broglie’s matter waves. Notably, the replacement of electron orbits by standing matter waves introduced a function of space only, i.e., the time-independent wave amplitude $\psi$. The whole process appeared to be completely natural and straightforward to Schrödinger who had been, from his student days, familiar with the connection between differential equations for vibrations in continuum mechanics and variational principles, a connection which he now could take over literally into atomic theory. Having available a suitable candidate, Eq. (138), for the wave equation of the hydrogen atom, he could instantly formulate *the* variational principle from which the equation followed.  

In detail, he noticed that Eq. (146) gave rise, with the transformation (147), to the quadratic form  

$$F(x, y, z) = \left(\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial z}\right)^2 - \frac{2m_e}{K^2}\left(E + \frac{e^2}{r}\right)\psi^2 \tag{148}$$  

in the case of the nonrelativistic hydrogen problem, expressed in Cartesian co-ordinates. ($r$ denotes the radial variable, i.e., $\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}$.) This quadratic form had to be inserted into the variational problem  

$$\delta J = \delta \iiint F(x, y, z) \, dx \, dy \, dz = 0. \tag{149}$$  

Schrödinger took over the evaluation of the variation from his notebook (see Eqs. (135) and (136) above). If the surface integral, extended over an infinitely distant closed surface, provided no contribution, i.e.,  

$$\int \left( \delta\psi \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial n} \right) df = 0, \tag{150}$$  

—which implied a condition for the behaviour of $\psi$, respectively its normal derivative, for large $r$-values—then the variational principle possessed, as an Eulerian equation, the wave equation (138). The solution of this equation, with $\psi$ fulfilling the conditions mentioned above, thus also satisfied the variational principle given by Eqs. (148) and (149).  

Equation (138) represented, of course, the second-order differential equation for the matter wave function $\psi$, which Schrödinger had considered, from the previous December, as the candidate for the description of the nonrelativistic hydrogen atom. He had discovered that it possessed a very peculiar property: acceptable solutions seemed to exist merely for selected values of the energy $E$. From the equivalence of the variational principle and the differential equation, he was confident of being able to show ‘that $\psi$ can be so chosen for *all positive*, but only for a *discrete set of negative* values of $E$. That is, the above-mentioned variational problem has a discrete and a continuous spectrum of eigenvalues’ (Schrödinger, 1926c, p. 362).<sup>178</sup> This property appeared to be very desirable from  

<sup>178</sup>We have taken the English translation, p. 2, except that we have replaced ‘proper values’ by the now conventional ‘eigenvalues’.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0131 -->

490 Chapter III The Creation of Wave Mechanics

the point of view of the physical interpretation, as 'the discrete spectrum corresponds to the Balmer terms and the continuous [spectrum] to the energies of the hyperbolic orbits' (Schrödinger, 1926c, p. 362).

The connection between a variational principle of the type of Eq. (149), with $F$ a quadratic form of $\psi$ and its first derivatives (such as given by Eq. (148)), had been established many years earlier by the Göttingen mathematician David Hilbert. In his theory of linear integral equations, Hilbert had developed a systematic analysis of the eigenvalue spectrum of quadratic forms $F$ (Hilbert, 1904a, b; 1905; 1906a, b; 1910).<sup>179</sup> He had also been interested in obtaining a particular example, having simultaneously a discrete and a continuous spectrum, which could describe the physical situation of an atomic spectrum, but he had not been successful at that time. Schrödinger's form, Eq. (148), devised for the nonrelativistic hydrogen problem, now seemed to fulfill Hilbert's old dream. It might be taken as a sign of historical continuity that Hermann Weyl, a brilliant student of Hilbert in the old days, assisted Schrödinger nearly twenty years later in the mathematical evaluation of the problem.

**Discrete and Continuous Eigenvalues of the Nonrelativistic Hydrogen Equation**

The essential virtue of the discussion of nonrelativistic hydrogen problem in Schrödinger's first *Annalen* paper over the previous notes—contained in the notebook '*Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. I*'—lies in the fact that Schrödinger presented there a complete investigation of the mathematical questions. In clarifying the details of these questions, Hermann Weyl became active, hence Schrödinger felt that he 'owed deepest thanks to Hermann Weyl' as he acknowledged in his paper ('*zu größtem Dank verpflichtet*,' p. 363, footnote 1).

For the purpose of dealing with Eq. (138), Schrödinger introduced the polar co-ordinates, $r, \theta$ and $\phi$. He assumed, then, that $\psi$ might be written 'as the *product* of three functions, each only for $r, \theta$ or $\phi$' (Schrödinger, 1926c, p. 363). 'The method is sufficiently well known,' he claimed (*loc. cit.*). Indeed, Schrödinger had learned, more than fifteen years earlier, in the physical seminar on treating the problem of electromagnetic radiation, that the very same procedure applied to the wave equation<sup>180</sup>

$$\Delta \psi + q^2 \psi = 0, \qquad (151)$$

<sup>179</sup> For more detailed aspects of Hilbert's theory of linear integral equations, see Volume 3, Section I.2.

<sup>180</sup> See the notebook '*Phys. Seminar*' filed on AHQP Microfilm No. 39, Section 1. Equation (151) was solved by the *Ansatz* $\psi = P_n(\theta, \phi) \cdot R$, yielding the equation

$$\frac{d^2 R}{dr^2} + \frac{2}{r} \frac{dR}{dr} + \left( q^2 - \frac{n(n+1)}{r^2} \right) R = 0$$

for the radical part of the wave function.

Schrödinger emphasized: ‘The limitation of \(n\) to integral values is *necessary* so that the dependence [of the surface harmonic] on the polar angles may be single-valued’ (Schrödinger, 1926c, p. 363).

In the case of Eq. (138), Schrödinger obtained for the \(r\)-dependent part of \(\psi\), which he called \(\chi\), the ordinary second-order differential equation

\[
\frac{d^2\chi}{dr^2} + \frac{2}{r} \frac{d\chi}{dr} + \left( \frac{2m_e E}{K^2} + \frac{2m_e e^2}{K^2 r} - \frac{n(n+1)}{r^2} \right) \chi = 0, \qquad (152)
\]

with \(n = 0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots\).

Evidently, Eq. (152) possessed the same mathematical structure as the first matter-wave equation, Eq. (41), which he had considered months earlier for the relativistic hydrogen problem. The standard procedure for solving this equation was displayed in Schlesinger’s textbook on differential equations, and Schrödinger simply copied the relevant pages in his paper (Schrödinger, 1926c, pp. 363–367). The first step consisted of studying the singularities of Eq. (152) in the complex \(r\)-plane, namely at the points \(r = 0\) and \(r = \infty\). The variational principle demanded solutions that were finite and unique in the whole configuration space, i.e., for all real, non-negative \(r\). Schrödinger now claimed: ‘The equation has *in general* no integral which remains finite at *both* end points; such an integral exists only for certain special values of the constants in the equation. It is now a question of defining these special values.’ He emphasized subsequently: ‘This is the *jumping-off point* of the whole investigation’ (Schrödinger, 1926c, pp. 363–364).

Closely following *Schlesinger*, Chapter Three, Schrödinger investigated first the singular point \(r = 0\). The integral of Eq. (152) could be assumed to have the form

\[
\chi = r^\alpha U(r), \qquad (153)
\]

where the exponent \(\alpha\) is a positive root of the so-called ‘indicial’ equation (‘*determiniernde Fundamentalgleichung*’)

\[
\rho(\rho - 1) + 2\rho - n(n+1) = 0 \qquad (154)
\]

associated with Eq. (152). Obviously,

\[
\alpha = n. \qquad (155)
\]

The function $U$ was in that case simply given by the residue at this pole (see our discussion of the notebook, p. 473), and $\chi$ became
$$\chi = f\left(r \frac{\sqrt{-2m_e E}}{K}\right), \quad (163)$$

Evidently, the solution (163) remained finite for all real, non-negative $r$ and vanished exponentially for large $r$, that satisfy the surface condition Eq. (150). Schrödinger summarized the situation with the words: ‘For $E$ negative, our variational problem has solutions if, and only if, $E$ satisfies condition [(160)]. Only values smaller than $l$ (and there is always at least one such at our disposal) can be given to the integer $n$, which denotes the order of the surface harmonic appearing in the equation. The part of the solution depending on $r$ is given by [Eq. (163)]’ (Schrödinger, 1926c, p. 370; English translation, p.7). And since the surface harmonic of degree $n$ involved ($2n + 1$) constants, also ‘the discovered solution has exactly $2n + 1$ arbitrary constants for any possible $(n, l)$ combination, and therefore for a prescribed value of $l$ has $l^2$ arbitrary constants’ (*loc. cit.*, p. 370).$^{183}$

Of the remaining mathematical questions, Schrödinger did not deal with the problem of the completeness of the whole system of eigenfunctions which solved the hydrogen equation. He simply argued: ‘From experience of similar cases, it may be supposed that no eigenvalue has escaped us’ (*loc. cit.*, p. 370). On the other hand, he completed the discussion of the surface integral condition, Eq. (150): in the case of positive energy values, the eigenfunctions describing the continuous spectrum of the atom satisfied the condition only if $\delta\psi$ either vanished at infinity or approached a constant value, independent of the direction.$^{184}$

The interpretation of the results thus achieved in terms of the old Bohr-Sommerfeld theory of atomic structure presented no particular problem. Schrödinger noted: ‘The well-known Bohr energy-levels, corresponding to the Balmer terms, are obtained, if to the constant $K$, introduced into [Eq. (147)] for reasons of dimensions, we give the value

$$
K = \frac{h}{2\pi},
$$
[(164)]

from which comes

$$
-E_l = \frac{2\pi^2 m_e e^4}{h^2 l^2},
$$
[(165)]

(Schrödinger, 1926c, p. 371). Thus, the following relation existed between the integral numbers arising in the above treatment of the hydrogen atom as a variational problem on the one hand, and the quantum numbers of the old theory on the other. Schrödinger wrote: ‘Our $l$ is the principal quantum number. $n + 1$ is analogous to the azimuthal quantum number. The splitting up of this number through a closer definition of the surface harmonic can be compared with the resolution of the azimuthal quantum into an “equatorial” and a “polar” quantum’ (Schrödinger, 1926c, p. 371; English translation, p. 8).<sup>185</sup>
In the new theory, of course, the numbers had their own interpretation. They defined, in particular, the system of node lines on the sphere. Thus, for example, the analogue of the old radial quantum number, $l - n - 1$, fixed the number of ‘node spheres’; that is, the function $f(x)$, given by Eq. (163a), possessed roots at exactly $l - n - 1$ values of the radial variable $r$. The positive energy solutions, corresponding to the hyperbolic orbits in the old quantum theory, exhibited infinitely many oscillations and therefore could be associated with infinitely many node spheres or an infinite radial quantum number. Finally, the reciprocal of the factor multiplying $r$ in the expression for $x$—see Eq. (163)—determined somehow the extension of the hydrogen atom; it could be related to the semi-axes of Sommerfeld’s quantized Kepler ellipses, $a_l$, by<sup>186</sup>

$$
\frac{K}{\sqrt{-2m_e E}} = \frac{h^2 l}{4\pi^2 m_e e^2} = \frac{a_l}{l}.
$$
(166)

## **III.4 Sources of Undulatory Mechanics**

Schrödinger introduced a collection of his pioneering papers on wave mechanics, published as *Abhandlungen zur Wellenmechanik* about a year later, by saying:

> Referring to these papers ... a young lady friend recently remarked to the author: “When you began this work you had no idea that anything so clever would come out of it, had you?” This remark, with which I wholeheartedly agreed (with due qualification of the flattering adjective), may serve to call attention to the fact that the papers now combined in one volume were originally written *one by one* at different times. The results of the later sections were largely unknown to the writer of the earlier ones. Consequently, the material has unfortunately not always been set forth in as orderly and as systematic a way as might be desired, and further, the papers exhibit a gradual development of ideas. (Schrödinger, 1927d; English translation, 1928b, p. v)

This statement characterized rather accurately the procedure taken by Schrödinger to establish his theory of wave mechanics, which he described immediately afterwards—i.e., in September 1926—as ‘based on the very interesting and fundamental researches of L. de Broglie on what he called “phase waves” (“*ondes de phase*”) and thought to be associated with the motion of material points,’ however, unlike de Broglie’s theory, determined by ‘the point of view that material points consist of, or are nothing but, wave systems’ (Schrödinger, 1926i, p. 1049). The first step towards wave, or rather undulatory, mechanics—as the author used to call it in the beginning—consisted of setting up the wave equation for the hydrogen atom and solving it in the nonrelativistic approximation, as we have outlined in some detail in the last two sections. We have also drawn attention to the fact that Schrödinger, before finishing the composition of his first paper on the new theory, had gone on to discuss problems in his notebook ‘*Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. I*’ which he would present only in later papers, especially the Stark effect of hydrogen spectral lines. In addition, the same notebook, which we had found to be largely written prior to the paper ‘*Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem. I*’, contains sections on other quantum-theoretical problems, such as the linear oscillator and the rotator; that is, Schrödinger had begun, well before the end of January 1926, with the task of extending the wave equation method to a variety of systems. What was still lacking, however, was a general method of deriving suitable wave equations describing arbitrary atomic systems. To achieve that goal, the author had to deepen the ideas and

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0138 -->

### III.4 Sources of Undulatory Mechanics
497

foundations of his theory. He would do so in his second communication, ‘*Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem. (Zweite Mitteilung)*’ (Schrödinger, 1926d), in which he arrived at a definite prescription for translating mechanical systems into ‘undulatory’ mechanical systems, based on an analogy to the well-known relation of geometrical optics to wave optics. We shall discuss in this section the essential ideas and elements which entered Schrödinger’s path to a complete undulatory theory of quantum mechanical systems.

### Preliminary Arguments Given in the First Paper

In discussing, in the previous section, the contents of Schrödinger’s first paper on the new quantum theory, we have omitted Section 3 dealing with some general remarks on the nature of the wave function $\psi$ associated with an atomic system. Schrödinger opened the section by stating:

> It is, of course, strongly suggested that we should try to connect the function $\psi$ with some *vibration process* in the atom, which would more nearly approach reality than the electronic orbits, the real existence of which is being very much questioned today. I originally intended to found the new quantum conditions in this more intuitive manner, but finally gave them the above neutral mathematical form, because it brings more clearly to light what is really essential. (Schrödinger, 1926c, p. 372; English translation, p. 9)

Evidently, he had the desire not to present in the first publication any ‘intuitive,’ or even speculative, idea concerning the interpretation of the vibration process, but rather to restrict himself to the mathematical example of the hydrogen calculation, whose success—at least in the nonrelativistic approximation—was secured from the very beginning. The following statement by Schrödinger does support this desire, as he remarked: ‘I do not wish to discuss further the possible representations of the vibration process, before more complicated cases have been calculated successfully from the new standpoint. It is not decided that the results will merely re-echo those of the usual quantum theory’ (Schrödinger, 1926c, p. 372; English translation, p. 9). In that respect he quoted the relativistic Kepler problem which led in his approach to half-integral quantum numbers, in contrast to Arnold Sommerfeld’s treatment ten years earlier.

On the other hand, Schrödinger wished to emphasize as well—and this is the only place in his first paper where he did so—the direct origin of his approach from Louis de Broglie’s idea of matter waves and his own subsequent application of the latter to Einstein’s gas theory. He further stressed the essential difference of his own treatment from that of de Broglie, that is, his use of phase waves as standing eigenvibrations of atomic systems, analogous to the eigenvibrations in classical problems of electrodynamics and elasticity theory. ‘The above reflections on the atom [i.e., the treatment of the hydrogen atom with the wave equation],’ he claimed, ‘could have been represented as a generalization from those on the gas model’ (Schrödinger, 1926c, p. 373; English translation, p. 9).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0139 -->

498 Chapter III The Creation of Wave Mechanics

In the gas model treatment of December 1925—see the discussion in Section III.2—Schrödinger had calculated the energy of *n* gas molecules of mass *m* in a volume *V* by assuming the existence of standing phase waves of wavelength λ (= *h*/*p*, with *p* the momentum of the molecules). In principle, he had followed exactly the same procedure in the hydrogen case, except that he had to introduce there a wave equation and solve it with certain boundary conditions. The difference in dealing with the hydrogen problem resulted from the fact that in this situation he had not available a natural choice of the volume *V*; hence, he could not restrict himself to a purely geometrical consideration. We recall (from Section III.2) that in the gas theory he had emphasized an interpretation of the result—i.e., the Einstein gas theory—not in the sense of following from a new, unusual type of statistical behaviour of the gas molecules, but rather as being the consequence of a superposition of matter waves. He connected a similar interpretation with the new wave equation approach to the hydrogen problem, as he explained in the last part of his paper, especially for the origin of atomic spectra.

For that purpose, Schrödinger started from the expression he had given earlier for the wave function associated with a given negative energy-state of the (bound) hydrogen atom, namely,

$$\psi = P_n(\theta, \phi) \cdot f\left( r \frac{\sqrt{-2mE}}{h/2\pi} \right), \tag{167}$$

with

$$f(x) = x^n \exp(-x) \sum_{k=0}^{l-n-1} \frac{(-2x)^k}{k!} \binom{l+n}{l-n-1-k}. \tag{167a}$$

He argued: ‘If we take the separate functions [i.e., Eq. (167a) for a given discrete energy *E*], multiplied by a surface harmonic of order *n* [i.e., $P_n(\theta, \phi)$], as the description of the eigenvibration process, then the quantity *E* must have something to do with the related *frequency*’ (Schrödinger, 1926c, p. 373; English translation, p. 9).

In the usual vibration problems the quantity corresponding to the energy state *E* of the system was proportional to the square of a frequency. Referring to the situation of the hydrogen atom, Schrödinger continued, ‘such a statement... would lead to *imaginary* frequencies for the *negative E*-values’ (Schrödinger, 1926c, p. 373; English translation, p. 9). In addition, he knew from experience—or ‘instinct’ (‘*Gefühl*’), as he called it—that the energy involved in atomic emission and absorption processes had to be proportional to the frequency rather than to its square. He explained this fact—an old difficulty of the dynamical theory of spectra, indeed^187—in the following way: ‘There has been *no natural zero level*

^187 The difficulty caused by the quadratic dependence of the eigenvalues of the (second-order) wave equation and the frequency of the vibration process, which seemed to be inconsistent with the description of spectral lines of atomic systems, had already been noticed earlier. (See our Volume 1, Section II.2, especially p. 177.) For example, Walther Ritz had introduced, to secure a linear relationship between the energy terms of atoms and the frequency of the emitted spectral lines, his elementary magnet model of atoms (Ritz, 1908a).

Or, in mathematical language, this would be expressed as

$$
\nu = C'\sqrt{C + E} = C'\sqrt{C} + \frac{C'}{2\sqrt{C}} E + \dots, \tag{168}
$$

where $C'$ denotes another constant and the dots refer to higher-order terms in $E$, which become increasingly small due to the large value of the constant $C$.¹⁸⁹
Schrödinger then claimed that the additive constant $C$ thus inserted into the wave equation ‘has another very appreciable advantage,’ because ‘*it permits an understanding of the Bohr frequency condition*’ (*loc. cit.* p. 374; English translation, p. 10). According to the latter, the emission (and absorption) frequencies of atoms are proportional to energy differences. Evidently, the same followed from Eq. (168), provided one neglected the higher-order terms. Further, by choosing a large constant $C$, the eigenfrequencies of the atom are all very large when compared with the emission frequencies, hence different eigenfrequencies are very close and ‘the emission frequencies appear . . . as deep “difference tones” of the eigenvibrations themselves.’ Schrödinger concluded that the process of emitting light waves in transitions between energy states of the atom can easily be imagined in the new theory, namely, ‘the light-wave is causally related to the *beats*, which necessarily arise at each point of space during the transition; and . . . the frequency of the light is defined by the number of times per second the intensity maximum of the beat-process repeats itself’ (Schrödinger, 1926c, p. 374; English translation, p. 10).
This undulatory interpretation of the atomic transition process satisfied Schrödinger very much. He found it ‘much more congenial (*um vieles sympathischer*) . . . than to think of a jumping electron,’ because: ‘The changing of the

vibration form can take place continuously in space and time, and it can readily last as long as the emission process lasts empirically’ (Schrödinger, 1926c, p. 375; English translation, pp. 10–11). The same interpretation, he pointed out, would also be consistent with Willy Wien’s experiments of the decay-time of the luminescence of canal rays, which provided empirical information on the duration of the emission process (Wien, 1919, 1921, 1924). Finally, it accounted for an old observation, whose explanation had presented considerable difficulties in the old quantum theory.  
The difficulty had been addressed recently by Niels Bohr, Hendrik Kramers and John Slater who, referring to the original experiments of Johannes Stark on the influence of electric fields on spectral lines (Stark, 1913b), mentioned:

> In these experiments the emitting atoms move with large velocities, and the time intervals in which they pass between two points where the intensity of the electric field differs very much, are only a small fraction of the mean time of duration of the stationary states connected with the investigated spectral lines. Nevertheless Stark found that, except for a Doppler effect of the usual kind, the radiation from the moving atoms was influenced by the electrical field at any point of the path in the same way as the radiation from resting atoms subject to the constant action of the field at this point. (Bohr, Kramers and Slater, 1924, p. 796)

While previous authors had called for the ‘assumption of a new type of energy in the atom’ (Försterling, 1922, p. 392),^{190} Bohr, Kramers and Slater had claimed:

> It is clear that Stark’s results are in conformity with the picture adopted in this paper. In fact, during the passing of the atoms through the field, the motion in the stationary states changes in a continuous way, and in consequence also the virtual harmonic oscillators corresponding with the possible transitions. The effect of the virtual radiation field originating from the moving atoms will therefore not be different from that which would occur if the atoms along their whole path had moved in a field of constant intensity, at any rate if—as in Stark’s experiments—the radiation originating from other parts of their paths is prevented from reaching those parts of the apparatus on which the observation of the phenomenon depends. (Bohr, Kramers and Slater, 1924, p. 796)

The observed phenomena could easily be explained on the undulatory theory as well, since ‘if during this transition [between two stationary states] the atom is placed for a comparatively short time in an electric field which alters the eigenfrequencies, then the beat frequencies are immediately changed sympathetically, and for just as long as the field operates’ (Schrödinger, 1926c, p. 375; English translation, p. 11). Although Schrödinger had been sympathetic to the

[^190]: The situation had been analyzed before by Karl Försterling (1885–1960), who had argued that the observations—Stark had always seen the line-splitting due to the electric field—‘prove that for the emission the instantaneous state of the atom is decisive,’ hence ‘the most obvious assumption would be this: an electron continuously transfers, in a transition from the initial to the final orbit [in the atom], its energy to the ether’ (Försterling, 1922, p. 391). The latter assumption, however, led to a contradiction with the then accepted principles of Bohr’s theory (Försterling, 1922, pp. 391–392).

radiation theory of Bohr, Kramers and Slater—and still retained some sympathy for it after its refutation by the experiments of Hans Geiger and Walther Bothe and of Arthur Holly Compton<sup>191</sup>—he definitely preferred his own new interpretation. It allowed him to remain within the conventional space-time description of physics, a description which Bohr and his associates had discarded from the very beginning. (See Bohr, Kramers and Slater, 1924, p. 790.) Still he knew that he had to develop his theory in much greater detail. ‘Let us not forget, however, while rejoicing about these things coming closer to the human understanding,’ he concluded, ‘that the idea of only *one* eigenvibration being excited whenever the atom does not radiate ... is very far removed from the *natural* picture of a vibrating system’ (Schrödinger, 1926c, p. 375; English translation, p. 11). A macroscopic system, indeed, would exhibit in principle a *pot-pourri* of eigenvibrations. And yet, the assumption of a multitude of eigenvibrations emitted by an atomic system would not contradict experience, as long as one made the additional assumption that an atom in the ground state vibrates only with *one* eigenfrequency. Given this assumption, the fact that an atom in the ground state does not radiate follows immediately from the absence of beats, which arise only if at least two eigenfrequencies interfere.

While these and similar features seemed to be in perfect agreement with observation, Schrödinger also mentioned a possible difficulty of the proposed undulatory interpretation of atomic phenomena, namely the ‘*approximate* form (after expansion of the square root [in Eq. (168)], from which the Bohr frequency condition itself seems to obtain the nature of an approximation’ (Schrödinger, 1926c, p. 374; English translation, p. 10). Schrödinger, however, claimed this difficulty to be just an apparent one, promising: ‘It is wholly avoided when the *relativistic* theory is developed and makes a profounder insight possible’ (Schrödinger, 1926c, *l.c.*, English translation, p. 10). Actually, he knew from his previous treatment of the relativistic hydrogen theory—see Sections III.2 and III.3 above, and also Eq. (80a)—that the constant $C$ ‘is naturally very intimately connected with the rest-energy of the electron’ (Schrödinger, 1926c, p. 374; English translation, p. 10).<sup>192</sup>

Unlike Schrödinger, Arnold Sommerfeld, the old master of atomic structure with whom he had exchanged letters, was not satisfied by such arguments. After having seen the submitted paper ‘*Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem. I*’, he immediately pointed out to Schrödinger: ‘Up to p. 13 [of the manuscript] I completely agree with you, but from then onwards I become obstinate. For the moment I am not yet inclined to take your ideas to mean physical reality. The combination principle—or Einstein’s equation—I consider to be a sacred object. In your theory, it arises only by the fact that in the difference tone the unknown

constant *C* of p. 13 should cancel; this appears to me quite improper with respect to such a fundamental law of nature. You admittedly promise to improve on the situation in the relativistic treatment; until then, however, I oppose the undulatory interpretation as denoting reality’ (Sommerfeld to Schrödinger, 3 February 1926).
Sommerfeld further criticized another aspect in Schrödinger’s theory in the same letter. He wrote: ‘The difference of the points of departure between your and Heisenberg’s approaches is peculiar in the light of the same results [derived from both approaches]. Heisenberg starts from the epistemological postulate not to put more into the theory than can be observed. You put in all kinds of possible high frequency processes, node lines and spherical harmonics. After our epistemological knowledge has been sharpened by relativity theory, the large, unobservable ballast in your presentation also seems to me to be suspicious for the time being’ (Sommerfeld to Schrödinger, 3 February 1926).
While he had to accept, for the time being, Sommerfeld’s critique of his derivation of the frequency relation, Eq. (168), Schrödinger vigorously rejected the second accusation. He wrote: ‘However, I must protest, with due and full respect for epistemology, that I *put into* the theory so many, possibly unnecessary assumptions. Node lines, spherical harmonics, etc., this all is yet inevitably contained in the equation of vibration, exactly as the electron orbits with their loops, rotations of the perihelion are contained in the fundamental equations of mechanics. I really do not put in now anything else but the equation ν = *E*/*h*. And even this equation is already prefabricated by the Hamiltonian theory’ (Schrödinger to Sommerfeld, 20 February 1926).
In the same letter to Sommerfeld he announced: ‘In the next days I shall send to *Geheimrat* [Willy] Wien a second communication for the *Annalen*, and I shall ask him again to show it to you before submitting it for printing—I would just like to have the stamp “received” on it because of the many parallel works now existing in this field. The memoir contains mainly the general foundation of the theory, as I imagine it; then a few simple examples, though not yet the Stark effect; the latter I have just calculated yesterday’ (Schrödinger to Sommerfeld, 20 February 1926).
Before we turn to the content of Schrödinger’s second paper, and in particular to his preparatory notes, we shall recapitulate certain aspects of the work of Louis de Broglie, whose idea of matter waves had provided the initial stimulus for Schrödinger’s departure.

Louis de Broglie’s Mechanical–Optical Analogy

In a paper entitled ‘*Rayonnement noir et quanta de lumière*’ (‘Blackbody Radiation and Light-Quanta’), which he submitted in January 1922, Louis de Broglie tried to establish several results of the theory of blackbody radiation ‘without any reference to electrodynamics’ (‘*sans aucune intervention de ‘l’électromagnétisme*’, L. de Broglie, 1922b, p. 422). In particular, he assumed Einstein’s light-quantum hypothesis i.e., he considered blackbody radiation ‘as a gas consisting of light-

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0144 -->

III.4 Sources of Undulatory Mechanics
503

atoms having the energy $W = h\nu'$ (L. de Broglie, 1922b, p. 422). However, he also associated with each light-atom a small finite rest-mass $m_0$, given by the equation
$$ W = m_0 c^2 \sqrt{1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}}, \tag{169} $$
where the velocity $v$ of light-atoms should be infinitely close to $c$, the limiting velocity in relativity theory.$^{193}$
The first paper on light-quanta provided the entrance to a theory of matter which Louis de Broglie developed over the following three years. He first showed how the interference phenomena of light could be explained on the light-quantum theory if one assumed the existence of 'agglomeration of light-atoms' (L. de Broglie, 1922c, p. 813). In the fall of 1923, he went an essential step forward: quantum theory, he claimed, demanded that each particle of proper or rest-mass $m_0$ should be accompanied by 'a simple periodical phenomenon of frequency $\nu_0$, such that
$$ h\nu_0 = m_0 c^2 \tag{[(170)]} $$
with $c$ always denoting the limiting velocity in relativity theory and $h$ Planck's constant' (L. de Broglie, 1923a, p. 507).
In the observation of a particle moving with velocity $v$, de Broglie argued further, two frequencies occurred, namely,
$$ \nu = \frac{\nu_0}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}, \tag{171} $$
and
$$ \nu_1 = \nu_0 \sqrt{1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}}. \tag{172} $$
He connected the latter with a 'periodic phenomenon within the moving particle' ('phénomène périodique interne du mobile,' L. de Broglie, 1923a, p. 507), which he called 'a fictive wave associated with the motion of the particle' (L. de Broglie, 1923a, p. 508), because it propagated with velocity $c^2/v$ or faster than $c$. He also found that between the two periodic phenomena, with frequency $\nu$ and $\nu_1$, respectively, there always existed an 'agreement of phase' (L. de Broglie, 1923a, p. 508), which gave rise, in the case of an electron moving on a circular orbit in an atom, to the condition
$$ \frac{m_0 v^2}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}} T_r = nh, \tag{173} $$

---
$^{193}$ De Broglie stated explicitly in his paper: 'But for the light-atom $m_0$ should be infinitely small and $\beta$ [= $v/c$] infinitely close to 1, such that $m_0/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$ assumes a definite value $m$' (L. de Broglie, 1922b, p. 422, footnote 1). Later, in his thesis, de Broglie concluded that $m_0$ should be less than $10^{-44}$ g (L. de Broglie, 1925, p. 79).

with $\omega$ denoting the angular frequency and $a$ the radius of the circular orbit. In the next paper, de Broglie spoke of the periodic phenomenon associated with a particle of (rest) mass $m_0$ and velocity $v$ as the ‘phase wave,’ having a ‘group velocity’ $v$, a (phase) velocity $c^2/v$ and a frequency $\nu$ (L. de Broglie, 1923b, pp. 548–549).$^{194}$ Finally, he showed in a third paper how the statistical behaviour of gas atoms might be suitably described by the new phase wave theory (L. de Broglie, 1923c). Especially he concluded: ‘The rays of the phase wave coincide with the trajectories which are dynamically possible’ (L. de Broglie, 1923c, p. 632). That is: ‘Effectively, the rays may be calculated as in a medium of variable dispersion with the help of Fermat’s principle, which is formulated there as [with $V$ the phase velocity]

$$\delta \int \frac{\nu ds}{V} = \delta \int \frac{m_0 v}{h\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}} ds = 0; \tag{[(175)]}$$

hence the principle of least action in the formulation of Maupertuis determines the trajectories by the equation

$$\delta \int m_0 c^2 \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}} - \sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2} \right) dt = \delta \int \frac{m_0 v}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}} ds = 0. \tag{[(176)]}$$

The fundamental point which unites the two great principles of geometrical optics and dynamics is thus presented in full clarity’ (L. de Broglie, 1923c, p. 632). The mechanical-optical analogy, which is expressed by the agreement of the description of the particle trajectories (or their associated phase wave rays) by the Fermat and Maupertuis principles, respectively, constituted the essential result of de Broglie’s new theory.$^{195}$ It makes sure that the particle associated with a phase wave showed deviation from classical dynamics, in agreement with quantum theory. De Broglie even claimed: ‘Dynamics must undergo the same

evolution that optics has undergone when undulations took the place of purely geometrical optics’ (L. de Broglie, 1923d, p. 540). Still he did not want to give up the tradition of point or particle dynamics completely and turn to a pure wave description of matter, as we may derive from the report ‘*La nouvelle dynamique des quanta*’ (‘The New Quantum [Particle] Dynamics’), which he presented to the fifth Solvay Conference on Physics at Brussels in October 1927.$^{196}$

In this report he stressed the following features and results of his theory (L. de Broglie, 1928, pp. 105–109):
(i) A material point at rest consists of a centre with a periodic phenomenon of frequency $\nu_0$ around it, i.e., there exists a stationary wave of the form

$$u(x_0, y_0, z_0, t_0) = f(x_0, y_0, z_0) \cdot \cos(2\pi\nu_0 t_0). \tag{177}$$

(ii) In a different Galileian frame, $x, y, z, t$, having velocity $v$ relative to the rest frame of the particle, the phase wave assumes the frequency $\nu$, Eq. (171), and propagates with velocity $V$,

$$V = \frac{c^2}{v}. \tag{178}$$

(iii) Between the velocity $V$ and the frequency of the phase wave an interesting relation exists insofar as one may ‘define indeed an index of refraction $[n]$ in empty space for the waves of the material point having frequency $\nu_0$, according to the dispersion law

$$n = \frac{c}{V} = \sqrt{1 - \frac{\nu_0^2}{\nu^2}}, \quad [(179)]$$

(L. de Broglie, 1928, p. 106).
(iv) The dispersion law, Eq. (179), allows one to define a group velocity for the phase waves, which happens to be identical with the velocity $v$ of the material point, since the equation

$$\frac{1}{v} = d\left(\frac{\nu}{V}\right) / d\nu = \frac{1}{c} \frac{d(n\nu)}{d\nu} \tag{180}$$

is satisfied.
(v) The frequencies $\nu_0$ and $\nu$ are given by the quantum theory, i.e., by Eq. (170) and the equation

$$W = h\nu, \tag{181}$$

where $W$ denotes the energy of the moving mass point.

$$
n = \sqrt{\left(1 - \frac{F}{h\nu}\right)^2 - \frac{\nu_0^2}{\nu^2}}. \tag{182}
$$  

(vii) The quantum condition for periodic systems,  

$$
\oint p \, dq = kh \qquad (k\ \text{integer}) \tag{183}
$$  

(with $p$ and $q$ denoting momentum and position variables), have the following straightforward interpretation in de Broglie’s new quantum dynamics: ‘The phenomena of quantum stability seem therefore to be analogous to the resonance phenomena, and the occurrence of integer numbers must also be considered as natural as it is in the theory of strings and vibrating plates’ (L. de Broglie, 1928, p. 108).  

At the same time, Louis de Broglie indicated two points in which he considered his theory as not yet satisfactory or complete. First, the resonance interpretation ‘does not constitute more than just a first approximation’ (L. de Broglie, 1928, p. 108). Secondly: ‘A real theory of atomic structure of matter should ... *incorporate* the particles in the wave phenomenon by taking into account solutions with singularities in the equations of propagation’ (L. de Broglie, 1928, p. 122). That is, he wished to stick to the assumption ‘that the material point occupies a position which is well defined in space’; hence ‘the amplitude $f$ [given in Eq. (177)] should exhibit a singularity or at least have an anomalously high value in a very small region’ (L. de Broglie, 1928, pp. 108–109).  

Evidently, the singularity of which de Broglie spoke above had not yet shown up in his theory of phase waves of matter; all that counted so far was the phase. However, de Broglie hoped to be able to develop the theory further in a way that the singular amplitude also played an essential role. This development would imply the use of a wave equation, similar to those which Schrödinger used in his approach from November 1925. A decisive difference existed between the programme of Louis de Broglie and that of Schrödinger; the latter demanded that his wave amplitude $\psi$ represented a continuous function, exhibiting no singular behaviour anywhere. In addition, Schrödinger would establish a wave theory of matter, dissolving material points in undulatory systems. He achieved essential progress with his programme at the same time as de Broglie’s programme stagnated. His progress made use of the mechanical-optical analogy developed a hundred years earlier by William Rowan Hamilton in Dublin.  

**Hamilton’s Optical–Mechanical Analogy**  

On 3 December 1824, a lengthy memoir entitled ‘Theory of Systems of Rays’ was read at the Royal Irish Academy in Dublin. In it, the author, William Rowan Hamilton (1805–1865), then a student of Trinity College, Dublin, attempted—as

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0148 -->

III.4  Sources of Undulatory Mechanics
507

he summarized nearly four years later in a *Conclusion* to the published paper—'to establish general principles respecting the systems of rays produced by the ordinary reflexion of light, at any mirror or combination of mirrors, shaped and placed in any manner whatsoever; and to shew that the mathematical properties of such a system may all be deduced by analytic methods from the form of *one characteristic function*: as, in the application of analysis to geometry, the properties of a plane curve, or a curved surface, may all be decided by uniform methods from the form of the function which characterises its equations' (Hamilton, 1828, p. 174).<sup>197</sup>

In order to study the behaviour of rays of light subdued to reflection, Hamilton introduced at an early stage—in Section I of his memoir—a kind of 'principle of least action'. In particular, he derived an equation in the case of reflection of a light ray by a plane mirror connecting the distances from the mirror, $\rho$ and $\rho'$, of points on the incident and the reflected ray, respectively,

$$\delta\rho + \delta\rho' = 0; \qquad (184)$$

that is, the actual path of the reflected ray is determined by a minimum principle. Hamilton commented: 'This equation [(184)] is called the *Principle of Least Action*, because it expresses that if the co-ordinates of point of incidence were to receive any infinitely small variations consistent with the nature of the mirror, the bent path $(\rho + \rho')$ would have its variation nothing; and if light be a material substance, moving with a velocity unaltered by reflection, this bent path $(\rho + \rho')$ measures what in mechanics is called the *Action*, from the one assumed point to the other. Laplace has deduced the formula [(184)], together with analogous formulae for ordinary and extraordinary refraction, by supposing light to consist of particles of matter, moving with certain determined velocities, and subject only to forces which are insensible at sensible distances. The manner in which I have deduced it, is independent of any hypothesis about the nature or the velocity of light; but I shall continue to call it, from analogy, the principle of least action' (Hamilton, 1828, p. 82).

The above statement is the first indication in Hamilton's work of the analogy between mechanical—or dynamical, as they were then called—laws and the laws of optics. At that time, unlike twenty years earlier when Pierre Simon de Laplace (1749–1827) expounded his corpuscular theory of refraction, the undulatory theory of light had made great advances such that it could nearly be considered *the* established view.<sup>198</sup> Still Hamilton had not yet clearly fixed his opinion in

<sup>198</sup> The revival of the undulatory theory of light began in the year 1800, with the work of the English physicist Thomas Young (1773–1829); he, in particular, demonstrated the superiority of the wave theory to explain the phenomena of reflection and refraction simultaneously (Young, 1800). Laplace, in his memoir of 1808, especially proposed a theory of the refraction of the extraordinary ray in doubly-refracting crystals. Young immediately attacked Laplace's theory, claiming: 'A solution might be deduced upon the Huygensian principles, from the simplest possible supposition, that of a medium more easily compressible in one direction than in any direction perpendicular to it, as if

favour of the latter, but rather kept an open mind when he extended the optical principle *analogous to the principle of least action* to more complex mirror systems reflecting light rays. He then found the relation

$$\sum (\rho) = \text{constant.} \tag{185}$$

Or, in the more general case of the different refractive power $n$ of the media through which the rays are passed, the equation

$$\sum (n\rho) = \text{constant} \tag{186}$$

was satisfied for all surfaces cutting the reflected ray perpendicularly.$^{199}$ Hamilton continued:

> In the systems also, produced by atmospheric and by extraordinary refraction, there are analogous surfaces possessing remarkable properties, which render it desirable that we should agree upon a name by which we may denote them. Since then in mechanics the sum obtained by adding the several elements of the path of a particle, multiplied each by the velocity with which it is described, is called the *Action* of the particle; and since if light be a material substance its velocity in un-crystallized mediums is proportional to the refractive power, and is not altered by reflection: I shall call the surfaces [(185) or (186)] the *surfaces of constant action*; intending only to express a remarkable analogy, and not assuming any hypothesis about the nature or velocity of light. (Hamilton, 1828, p. 87)$^{200}$

All that Hamilton had to assume to carry out his treatment of optical systems involving mirrors, were ‘rays’, i.e., the lines along which light propagated, or ‘systems of rays’. These rays he now described analytically by equations connecting three co-ordinates, e.g., the co-ordinates of the point from which the ray

***

it consisted of an infinite number of parallel plates connected by a substance somewhat less elastic’ (Young, *Quarterly Review*, January 1809; quoted from Whittaker, 1951, pp. 104–105). A detailed investigation, however, was provided by Etienne-Louis Malus (1775–1812) in his essay

III.4 Sources of Undulatory Mechanics 509

emanates.$^{201}$ For each system of rays he observed a 'characteristic function' to exist, i.e., a function $V$ depending on the co-ordinates, $x, y, z$, such that the differential quotients yielded the cosines $\alpha, \beta$ and $\gamma$ of the angles which the ray passing through a given point $x, y, z$ made with the axes:

$$\frac{\partial V}{\partial x} = \alpha, \quad \frac{\partial V}{\partial y} = \beta, \quad \frac{\partial V}{\partial z} = \gamma. \tag{187}$$

The properties of any particular ray system, he concluded,

> may all be deduced by analytic reasonings from the form of the function ($V$); and it is the method of making this deduction, together with the calculation of the *characteristic function* ($V$) for each particular system, that appears to me to be the most complete and simple definition that can be given, of the *Application of analysis to optics*, . . . by which means optics acquires, as it seems to me, an uniformity and simplicity in which it has been hitherto deficient'. (Hamilton, 1828, p. 90)

Hamilton finally showed that the characteristic function satisfied, at least in the case of mirror reflections, the second-order differential equation

$$\left( \frac{\partial V}{\partial x} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial V}{\partial y} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial V}{\partial z} \right)^2 = 1. \tag{188}$$

In later papers Hamilton generalized and simplified his original approach to other optical systems involving straight and curved rays, ordinary and extraordinary rays (the latter existing in double-refracting crystals).$^{202}$ The essential results of his general theory of systems of rays may be summarized in the following:

(i) There exists an action integral for systems of rays, which can be identified with the characteristic function $V$. It is actually a function of six—not three, as indicated above—variables, say $x_0, y_0, z_0$ and $x_1, y_1, z_1$, where both triples denote points of the ray.

(ii) If one adopts the undulatory theory—which Hamilton did, later on—the action integral can be shown to be (up to a constant) equal to the time of propagation of the ray between the two points, i.e.,

$$V(x_0, y_0, z_0; x_1, y_1, z_1) = t_1 - t_0. \tag{189}$$

III.4 Sources of Undulatory Mechanics 511

so he now claimed, to reformulate the fundamental laws of dynamics; thus the actual motion of a mass point in a field of forces, e.g., is found to be governed by equations that are the analogues of those determining the propagation of the rays of light. The particular extension of the optical methods led the author to a new 'General Method in Dynamics,' the Hamiltonian scheme, which is based on Hamilton's variational principle of least action, the characteristic or principal function, and Hamilton's (canonical) equations of motion.$^{205}$

Hamilton's variational principle in dynamics assumed the form

$$\delta V = \delta \int_{t_0}^{t_1} L \, dt = 0, \tag{192}$$

where the letter $V$ has been kept to denote the analogy to the characteristic function in optics and $L$ denotes the well-known Lagrangean function (i.e., the difference between the kinetic energy and the potential energy $U$). For a single point particle of mass $m$, Eq. (192) becomes equal to

$$\delta V = \delta \int_{P_0}^{P_1} \sqrt{2m(E - U)} \, ds = 0, \tag{193}$$

where $E$ denotes the total energy and the integral extends between two fixed space points, $P_0$ and $P_1$, where $P_0$ is assumed at time $t_0$ and $P_1$ at time $t_1$. If one compares this form of the variational principle to Pierre de Fermat's principle of the shortest path of light rays, which is also Hamilton's principle of optics, namely,

$$\delta \int_{P_0}^{P_1} \frac{n}{c} \, ds = 0, \tag{194}$$

it is possible to derive an optical-mechanical analogy between the phase velocity of optical waves $u$ and a particular expression in particle dynamics, notably$^{206}$

$$u = \frac{c}{n} \leftrightarrow \frac{\text{constant}}{\sqrt{2m(E - U)}}. \tag{195}$$

Further analogies exist between the mechanical momentum components of the particle, $p_x$, $p_y$ and $p_z$, and the differential quotients of the characteristic function, $\partial V / \partial x$, $\partial V / \partial y$ and $\partial V / \partial z$, in the optical theory.

This optical-mechanical analogy, although having been treated in detail in Hamilton's papers, did not receive much attention in the following decades of

$^{206}$ The analogy (195) may be called 'Hamilton's optical-mechanical analogy'. (See, e.g., Jammer, 1966, p. 237.)

512 Chapter III The Creation of Wave Mechanics

the nineteenth century. Several reasons for this neglect can be given. One basked in the brilliance with which Carl Gustav Jacobi (1804–1851) in Germany elaborated on the dynamical theory of Hamilton. Forgetting completely about the origin of the scheme from optical considerations, he started from the Eulerian differential equations for the (Hamilton) variational principle, the Lagrangean equations of motion, which assumed in Hamilton’s dynamical theory the form.

$$\frac{dp_{\alpha}}{dt} = \frac{\partial H}{\partial q_{\alpha}} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{dq_{\alpha}}{dt} = -\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_{\alpha}}, \quad (196)$$

where $H$—later called the Hamiltonian function or simply the Hamiltonian—is equal to the total energy of a system expressed as a function of its dynamical variables, the position co-ordinates $q_{\alpha}$ and the canonically conjugate momenta $p_{\alpha}$. Jacobi then investigated the question of what were the most general (canonical) substitutions which leave the ‘canonical’ equations (196) unchanged. He arrived at the result that, provided the equations held for one set of variables, $p_{\alpha}^0$ and $q_{\alpha}^0$, this remained so for any set of variables, $p_{\alpha}^1$ and $q_{\alpha}^1$, obtained from the former ones with the help of a function $\Omega(q_{\alpha}^0, q_{\alpha}^1)$ which is differentiable in its variables, $q_{\alpha}^0$ and $q_{\alpha}^1$, and satisfies the equations

$$\frac{\partial \Omega}{\partial q_{\alpha}^0} = -p_{\alpha}^0 \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{\partial \Omega}{\partial q_{\alpha}^1} = p_{\alpha}^1. \quad (197)$$

Hamilton had obtained exactly the same equations for his characteristic function $V$, hence Jacobi identified both functions, $V$ and $\Omega$. Further, he studied the most general solutions of Hamilton’s differential equation for the function $V$, i.e.,

$$H\left( q_{\alpha}^0, \frac{\partial V}{\partial q_{\alpha}^0} \right) = E \quad (198a)$$

or

$$H\left( q_{\alpha}^1, \frac{\partial V}{\partial q_{\alpha}^1} \right) = E, \quad (198b)$$

developing an elegant and systematic method of integration.$^{207}$
In the formulation of the dynamical theory by Jacobi, any reminiscence of the optical origin of Hamilton’s theory had been suppressed. The power of the mathematical methods of Jacobi—which allowed a wide range of dynamical problems to be dealt with—persuaded most physicists in the later nineteenth century that he indeed had exhausted the physical content of Hamilton’s scheme.

$^{207}$Jacobi’s theory is contained in his *Vorlesungen über Dynamik*, which he gave in the winter semester of 1842–1843 and which were edited posthumously by Alfred Clebsch (Jacobi, 1866).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0154 -->

III.4 Sources of Undulatory Mechanics
513

In addition, one should remind oneself of the fact that Hamilton never did connect any deeper significance to the analogy between the optical and the mechanical schemes. He contented himself with, first, having found a general method of treating optical systems (rays of light), and second, with casting Lagrange’s dynamics in an elegant form by the introduction of a suitable characteristic function. He had certainly not the slightest desire to expound the idea that the physical phenomena described by dynamics should be interpreted as undulatory motions, an idea which was proposed several decades later by Baron Nicolai von Dellinghausen in Estonia.

Dellinghausen, in his book *Grundzüge einer Vibrationstheorie der Natur* (1872) and later publications, defined matter as a general substrate common to all bodies, the substances being invariable and imponderable and subdued to continuous motion; these motions he considered to be oscillations which propagate like waves; when these waves meet at particular space points and produce standing oscillations, they represent observable bodies.<sup>208</sup> Dellinghausen summarized his views in the following sentences:

*The phenomena of nature are phenomena of motion. In this statement is contained the unity of natural philosophy (‘Naturerkenntnis’). The variety of phenomena rests on the diversity of motions which can originate and also disappear. Only energy is imperishable .... Now the final goal of natural philosophy should indeed consist in this: not only to establish the equivalence of the transmutations [of motions], but also—as has already been done in the undulatory theory of light—to recognize the nature of motions in the bodies. Science is, however, still quite far away from this goal, not the least due to the variety of phenomena; further, the task defined above can be carried out only with the help of mathematics.* (Dellinghausen, quoted after Rosenberger, 1890, pp. 590–591)

And then he added the prophetic sentences:

*One can now predict with safety the decline of the atomistic view .... Future scientists will ... give up atomism and turn to that doctrine which can, without inferring artificial auxiliary assumptions, without atoms, forces and imponderabilities, still perform the task which atomic theory has failed to solve for 3,000 years. This doctrine is, however, the pure kinetic theory of nature, as has been displayed in this paper .... The immediate task of natural philosophy consists, however, in repeating what we have stated in words in this paper in terms of mathematical equations.* (Dellinghausen, quoted after Rosenberger, 1890, p. 591)

What a difference of attitude can be seen by comparing what Hamilton and Dellinghausen had done or claimed. While the Irish astronomer had worked out,

<sup>208</sup> Dellinghausen considered also the ether to be constituted by the same imponderable substrate. A more detailed discussion of his views may be found in Ferdinand Rosenberger’s *Geschichte der Physik, 3. Teil* (Rosenberger, 1890, pp. 586–591). A shorter account has been given by Max Jammer, who also reported that Dellinghausen studied physics at various universities (Dorpat, Leipzig, Heidelberg) before returning to his Baltic estate (Jammer, 1966, p. 241).

earlier in the century, the optical-mechanical analogy as a purely mathematical scheme, useful for practical calculations of optical or dynamical systems, the Baltic Baron had expounded, towards the end of the century, a complete undulatory interpretation of all physical phenomena without ever getting on to any mathematical equation.²⁰⁹  

### Relations Between Wave and Geometrical Optics  

During the nineteenth century the wave description of light became firmly established.²¹⁰ Physicists began to develop detailed models of the ether, which should describe the properties of the propagation of light waves. On the other hand, a decisive breakthrough in the understanding of the nature of light was achieved by James Clerk Maxwell who demonstrated, on the basis of his electrodynamical theory, that light was nothing other than electromagnetic waves (Maxwell, 1862a), and finally completed by Heinrich Hertz who created experimentally electromagnetic waves with the same properties as light waves possess except for the larger wavelength (Hertz, 1888a, b). Clearly, after that optics was reduced to representing an application of electrodynamical theory.  
Towards the end of the nineteenth century interest in a detailed understanding of optical instruments increased immensely, as it was, e.g., at that time when the new science of bacteriology demanded the use of a new generation of microscopes. In those days Ernst Abbe (1840–1905) in Jena developed his theory of optical resolution. But Abbe and his colleagues did not know of Hamilton’s previous work on optical rays which could have easily been extended to provide the corrections that wave phenomena imposed on the known laws of geometrical optics. Even people, who did refer to Hamilton’s work, referred—strangely enough—only to his dynamical theory and seemed to have forgotten entirely about the optical origin of this theory.²¹¹  

²⁰⁹ Of course, by the time Dellinghausen had written his books and pamphlets, physical science had progressed tremendously. Major steps had been achieved in the conservation of energy, the electromagnetic theory of light, and the kinetic theory of matter. All that Dellinghausen attempted to do—and so far only expressed in words and programmes—was to adapt the above developments into his unified kinetic doctrine of undulations.  
²¹⁰ One of the first decisive contributions came from Hamilton who, in his third supplement on systems of rays (of 1837), applied the variational principle to two-axial crystals and discovered the existence of a double—internal and external—conical refraction. This prediction was made on the basis of Augustin Fresnel’s wave surfaces—i.e., an undulatory concept—and was experimentally proved to be correct in 1833 (the year after the submission of the third communication) by Hamilton’s Irish colleague Humphrey Lloyd; this proof could be considered a triumph of undulatory theory. (For details, see: Whittaker, 1951, p. 122.)  
²¹¹ Felix Klein, in Germany, one of the advocates of Hamilton’s optical theory, recalled in this context: “In England, though, Hamilton’s [optical] theory has always been known, and the English writings have reached Germany. I refer in this context to various papers of Maxwell, in which W [i.e., the characteristic function of Hamilton] has been calculated for special, simple cases; in particular, however, [I also refer] to the *Treatise on Natural Philosophy* of [William] Thomson and [Peter Guthrie] Tait, which first appeared in 1867 and contains a full presentation of Hamilton’s procedure, with respect to its significance for general mechanics. This *Treatise* was translated into German in 1871 at the suggestion of [Hermann von] Helmholtz’ (Klein, 1926, p. 198).

# III.4 Sources of Undulatory Mechanics  
515

One such person was Heinrich Bruns who in 1895 presented the theory of what he called the eiconal.²¹² In particular, Bruns tried to establish a general description of the formation of the optical image by optical systems which he considered within the framework of geometrical optics. He obtained the following main result: ‘Each special image is completely characterized by a definite image function depending on four variables, for which I shall use—in order to have a short expression—the notion “*Eikonal*” (“eiconal”)’ (Bruns, 1895, p. 329). He further observed:

> The eiconal is, and this may be considered to be its main property, the generating function for the equations of a contact transformation connecting each of the quadruples of quantities that are necessary to define the two conjugate rays σ and Σ [i.e., the original ray and the final ray in the image]. Hence the contact transformation replaces the collinear relation, taken as the first approximation [in describing the transformation of the light ray]. (Bruns, 1895, p. 329)

The interesting point in the introduction to Bruns’ memoir is, of course, the reference to Hamilton. Bruns described it by saying:

> It may perhaps not be superfluous to illustrate the role played by the eiconal in the geometrical theory of the astigmatic path of rays by comparing it with another field of applied mathematics. In the presentation of analytical mechanics, one generally attributes a preferred role to those problems which satisfy the Hamiltonian principle. There is good reason for this preference, since the validity of Hamilton’s *Ansatz* permits one to treat all features, shared by the envisaged class of problems, together in a unified way. Now a quite similar role, as Hamilton’s concept in mechanics, the eiconal concept plays in the—admittedly much more narrow—field of geometrical optics: it provides the simplest mathematical formulation for the treatment of general features [of ray paths]. (Bruns, 1895, p. 329)²¹³

Klein’s claim that Thomson and Tait presented the origin of Hamilton’s dynamics from his theory of light rays is perhaps a little overstated. In the *Treatise*, Sections 321–328 deal with Hamilton’s variational principle and the scheme developed from it by Hamilton and Jacobi; only in Section 325 do Thomson and Tait refer to Hamilton’s theory of systems of rays as ‘one of the many applications of the general principle, made by Hamilton’ (Thomson and Tait, German translation, 1871, p. 273: ‘*eine der vielen Anwendungen der allgemeinen Prinzips, welche Hamilton machte*’) without going into any details.

---
²¹² Heinrich Bruns, born in Berlin on 4 September 1848, was professor of mathematics in Berlin (1876), before he became (in 1882) professor of astronomy and director of the observatory at the University of Leipzig. He worked on potential theory, the three-body problem, geometrical optics and stellar statistics. Bruns died on 23 September 1919 in Leipzig.

²¹³ Bruns stated, however, that for special problems occurring in practical optics the old computational methods might still be useful and necessary; he concluded, in particular: ‘I consider it to be probable, exactly on the basis of the developments given below [in the paper], that one cannot succeed at all, with the usually suggested elementary methods, in finding a practically useful, purely analytic or algebraic replacement for the above-mentioned numerical methods, even if one occasionally hits upon in the literature on lengthy developments by which authors claim to have overcome these difficulties’ (Bruns, 1895, pp. 329–330).

516

Chapter III The Creation of Wave Mechanics

As he had said above, Bruns described a given ray by four variables: the co-ordinates $x = h$ and $y = k$ in the fundamental plane of the system, given by $z = 0$, and the direction cosines $p$ and $q$. Then he introduced, to characterize a transformation of an initial ray (denoted by $h, k, p$ and $q$) into a final ray (denoted by $H, K, P$ and $Q$), the function $E$, depending on the four variables $h, k, P$ and $Q$ and having the properties

$$
np = \frac{\partial E}{\partial h}, \quad nq = \frac{\partial E}{\partial k},
$$

$$
NH = \frac{\partial E}{\partial P}, \quad NK = \frac{\partial E}{\partial Q},
$$

(199)

where $n$ and $N$ denoted the coefficients of refraction in the medium traversed by the initial ray and the final ray, respectively. It was exactly this type of function that he called ‘eiconals of the image considered’ (Bruns, 1895, p. 355).^{214} Keeping in mind that $p^2 + q^2 = 1$, the eiconal also satisfies the equation

$$
\left( \frac{\partial E}{\partial h} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial E}{\partial k} \right)^2 = n^2.
$$

(200)

The eiconals of Bruns’ theory have a very close relation to the characteristic function of Hamilton. Thus we note that Eqs. (199) and (200) are—with the proper specialization of Bruns in mind—identical to Hamilton’s equations (190) and (191). The two concepts of the characteristic function and of the eiconal can even be completely identified on account of Bruns’ derivation of the eiconal.^{215} He especially introduced the differential expression $dS$,

$$
dS = n (p \, dh + q \, dk) + N (H \, dP + K \, dQ)
$$

(201)

to describe a given ray transformation $(h, k, p, q) \rightarrow (H, K, P, Q)$ and showed that it was differentiable, the integration yielding the eiconal $E(h, k, P, Q)$. By exactly the same procedure, however, Hamilton’s function $V$ is obtained. Bruns in his paper on the eiconal had in mind to copy the corresponding steps in the dynamical theory of Hamilton and Jacobi; instead of achieving something new, he basically reproduced Hamilton’s initial optical theory. Thus we might argue that he would have saved some work, had he just consulted the optical papers of Hamilton. He could have obtained a hint to these papers at the *Naturforscherversammlung* held in Halle in 1891, from a lecture by the Göttingen mathematician Felix Klein, his former Leipzig colleague.

^{214} Equation (199) can be found in Bruns’ paper on p. 354 (see his Eqs. (59)).
^{215} See pp. 353 and 354 of Bruns’ paper.
