### III.4 Sources of Undulatory Mechanics

Klein had emphasized in his talk, entitled ‘*Über neuere Englische Arbeiten zur Mechanik*’ (‘On the New English Works on Mechanics’), the origin of Hamilton’s dynamical theory. In the shortened published version he wrote:

The fact seems to be completely unknown, although Hamilton has stated it at different places in his work, especially in his first memoir on systems of rays (1824), with sufficient clarity. Hamilton met with the concepts of the emission theory, according to which the determination of the light ray passing through an arbitrary inhomogeneous (though isotropic) medium is a special case of a usual mechanical problem dealing with the motion of a mass point; we may immediately add the remark that this specialization [of the mechanical problem] is not an essential one, that is, one rather may reduce, by implying higher-dimensional spaces, each mechanical problem to determining the path of a light ray in a suitable medium. And now *Hamilton’s discovery, according to which the integration of the differential equations of dynamics is related to the integration of a certain partial differential equation of first order*, simply rests on the fact that Hamilton, following the great physical movement of his time, embarked on deriving the results of geometrical optics, known on the basis of the emission theory, from the point of view of the undulation theory. Hamilton’s integration theory of the differential equations of dynamics is, in the first place, nothing other than a general analytic formulation of the well-known relation in physics between a *light ray* and a *light wave*. In the light of the thus given point of departure, one may understand the unnecessarily special form, in which Hamilton published his theory and which was then generalized by Jacobi. In investigating systems of rays, Hamilton first had in mind quite practical problems of instrument theory. Hence, he operated exclusively with light waves that are emitted from single *points*. Jacobi’s generalization then amounts to the fact *that one may use for the definition of the ray other arbitrary light waves as well*. Starting from special waves, one constructs in optical theory the general ones—as is well known—with the help of the so-called Huygens’ principle; this construction represents an exact [physical] equivalent for the analytical process, by which one obtains in the theory of partial differential equations of first order the general solution by starting from any [particular] “complete” solution. (Klein, 1892, pp. 35–36).

Klein’s enthusiastic appraisal of the optical origin of the dynamical theory of Hamilton and Jacobi did not represent the historical facts in all details; especially, there is, in the introduction of the optical method, no clear reference to the undulatory theory of light. Hamilton began, as we have mentioned above, very cautiously, avoiding any hypothesis about the nature of light.\(^{216}\) However, his theory of rays could easily be translated into the wave language. For example, Edmund Whittaker presented, in his textbook on *Analytical Dynamics*, a detailed treatment along these lines (Whittaker, 1904, Section 125).
As the point of departure of the wave interpretation of Hamilton’s scheme one may take Christiaan Huygens’ principle of constructing the wavefront of light at time \( t_1 \) from the wavefront of light at time \( t_0 \); according to this principle,

---
\(^{216}\) We have already mentioned in Footnote 211 that F. Klein, obviously knowing about the undulatory formulation of Hamilton’s optical theory, saw it expressed in writing, where an unprepared reader may have had difficulty in recognizing it.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0159 -->

518 & Chapter III The Creation of Wave Mechanics \\

each point of the original wavefront should be considered as the source of a secondary wavelet, and the resulting wavefront (at time $t_1$) is obtained by taking the secondary wavefronts together (Huygens, 1690). Hamilton had noticed especially that the time of propagation of a light ray passing from a space point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ to a space point $(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ depended only on the six co-ordinates, and he had thus introduced his characteristic function $V$—see Eq. (189). If one now calls the direction cosines of the normals to the original wavefront (at $t_0$) and of the final wavefront (at $t_1$) at the space points $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ and $(x_1, y_1, z_1)$, respectively, $\alpha_0, \beta_0, \gamma_0$ and $\alpha_1, \beta_1, \gamma_1$—these normals are, of course, just the rays of Hamilton’s initial theory of 1824—then one finds that $V$ satisfies the following equations,

$$
\frac{1}{\alpha_0} \frac{\partial V}{\partial x_0} = \frac{1}{\beta_0} \frac{\partial V}{\partial y_0} = \frac{1}{\gamma_0} \frac{\partial V}{\partial z_0} \tag{202a}
$$

and

$$
\frac{1}{\alpha_1} \frac{\partial V}{\partial x_1} = \frac{1}{\beta_1} \frac{\partial V}{\partial y_1} = \frac{1}{\gamma_1} \frac{\partial V}{\partial z_1} \tag{202b}
$$

Obviously, these equations correspond to Eqs. (190) of Hamilton’s original theory. On introducing the coefficients of refraction, $n_0$ and $n_1$ at the points $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ and $(x_1, y_1, z_1)$, respectively, the differential $dV$ assumes the form

$$
dV = n_1(\alpha_1 dx_1 + \beta_1 dy_1 + \gamma_1 dz_1) - n_0(\alpha_0 dx_0 + \beta_0 dy_0 + \gamma_0 dz_0) \tag{203}
$$

If one further writes

$$
V = W \cdot \Delta t \tag{204}
$$

and assumes $\Delta t$ $(= t_1 - t_0)$ to have a small value, then one immediately derives Hamilton’s (canonical) equations as

$$
\begin{cases}
\frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{\partial H}{\partial \xi}, \quad \frac{dy}{dt} = \frac{\partial H}{\partial \eta}, \quad \frac{dz}{dt} = \frac{\partial H}{\partial \zeta}, \\
\frac{d\xi}{dt} = -\frac{\partial H}{\partial x}, \quad \frac{d\eta}{dt} = -\frac{\partial H}{\partial y}, \quad \frac{d\zeta}{dt} = -\frac{\partial H}{\partial z},
\end{cases}
\tag{205}
$$

where $H$ denotes the (Hamilton) function

$$
H = \xi \dot{x} + \eta \dot{y} + \zeta \dot{z} - W \tag{206}
$$

and the momentum variables of the optical system are defined by

$$
\xi = n\alpha, \quad \eta = n\beta, \quad \zeta = n\gamma \tag{207}
$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0160 -->

III.4 Sources of Undulatory Mechanics                                                         519

The above procedure may be easily expressed in physical terms: The infinitesimal characteristic function $V$, Eq. (204), generates a contact transformation of the variables $x, y, z, \xi, \eta, \zeta$ into the infinitesimally neighbouring variables $x + \Delta x, y + \Delta y, z + \Delta z, \xi + \Delta \xi, \eta + \Delta \eta, \zeta + \Delta \zeta$, which in turn describes nothing other than the infinitesimal motion of a wavefront due to Huygens' principle. Evidently, *every Hamiltonian system can be interpreted as the motion of a wavefront in a suitably chosen medium*.

Although there exists the above-mentioned wave-like interpretation of Hamilton's theory of rays, one should not forget that the eiconal approach—such as taken originally by Hamilton himself and later rediscovered by Bruns—characterized by the eiconal equations, i.e.,

$$D(E) = \left( \frac{\partial E}{\partial x_0} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial E}{\partial y_0} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial E}{\partial z_0} \right)^2 = n_0^2, \qquad (208\text{a})$$

and

$$D'(E) = \left( \frac{\partial E}{\partial x_1} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial E}{\partial y_1} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial E}{\partial z_1} \right)^2 = n_1^2, \qquad (208\text{b})$$

does not provide a full undulatory description of optical systems. This was shown, for example, by Arnold Sommerfeld and J. Runge, who following 'an occasional oral remark of [Peter] Debye' were able to obtain the differential equation (208) 'by a limiting procedure from the differential equation of wave optics' (Sommerfeld and Runge, 1911, p. 290).

Sommerfeld and Runge proved Debye's claim by starting from the—for simplicity's sake—scalar wave equation

$$\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial z^2} + k^2 u = 0, \qquad (209)$$

where $u$ denoted the light amplitude (without the time factor $\exp(2\pi i \nu t)$!) describing either the electric or magnetic component and $k$ represented the wave number,

$$k = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}, \

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0161 -->

520 & Chapter III The Creation of Wave Mechanics

where $n(\alpha x + \beta y + \gamma z)$ [with $n$ the coefficient of refraction] denotes the path of light along the direction of propagation of the wave. Hence we put, considering the meaning of the eiconal as the path of light,

$$u = u_0 \exp\left( i \frac{k}{n} E \right). \quad [(212)]$$

We now attempt to determine [the eiconal] $E$ as a function of the space co-ordinates in such a way that this *Ansatz* satisfies approximately the wave equation, taking into account the magnitude $k$; further, we do not regard $u_0$ anymore as being strictly constant, but rather as a slowly varying space function which is noticeably constant only at a distance of the order of magnitude of the wavelength. (Sommerfeld and Runge, 1911, p. 291)

When inserting the *Ansatz* (212) into the wave equation (209), Sommerfeld and Runge found the equation

$$\left\{ n^2 - D(E) + \frac{in}{k} \Delta E + \frac{in}{u_0 k} (\text{grad } u_0, \text{grad } E) + \frac{n^2}{u_0 k^2} \Delta u_0 \right\} = 0. \quad (213)$$

It is immediately evident that in general the last terms in the curly brackets on the left-hand side of Eq. (213) may be dropped as $k^{-1}$ is a small quantity; then Bruns' eiconal equations (208) will be obtained. However, the situation is quite different when either $\Delta E$ or $\Delta u_0$ become very large.$^{217}$ The first case (large $\Delta E$), for example, occurred with systems having 'in the sense of geometrical optics a *focal plane* or, in particular, a *focal line* or a *focal point*' (Sommerfeld and Runge, 1911, p. 292). The second case turned up where geometrical shadow boundaries existed. Sommerfeld and Runge concluded: 'In both cases the laws of geometrical optics cease to provide a sufficient approximation, and diffraction phenomena begin to show up' (Sommerfeld and Runge, 1911, p. 292).

Based on these relations between geometrical and wave optics, a rather direct path seems to lead to Schrödinger's wave equation (137). Sommerfeld would sketch this path in his *Wellenmechanischer Ergänzungsband* (Sommerfeld, 1929, Section 1).$^{218}$ The idea is to start with the example of a mass point (of mass $m$) in the Hamiltonian scheme, where the equation

$$\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial x}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial y}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial z}\right)^2 = 2m(E - U) \quad (214)$$

holds between the derivatives of the characteristic function $S$ and the kinetic energy—which is the difference between the totel energy $E$ and the potential

---
$^{217}$According to Sommerfeld and Runge, Peter Debye had pointed out these special cases in which the eiconal equations (208) no longer provided a valid description. (See Sommerfeld and Runge, 1911, p. 292.)

$^{218}$Sommerfeld discussed the 'derivation' given below on pp. 3–7.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0162 -->

III.4 Sources of Undulatory Mechanics

521

energy $U$. Equation (214) evidently describes the purely mechanical situation, and the task arose of finding the appropriate equation in a suitable wave theory for the mass point.

In order to derive the desired equation, Sommerfeld turned to the second-order wave equation (209). He then made the transition from wave to ray optics by assuming very small wavelengths or very large wave numbers—see Eq. (210). Hence he was allowed to express the wave function through the *Ansatz* (See Eq. (212))

$$u = u_0 \exp\left(i \frac{k}{n} S\right), \tag{215}$$

where $u_0$ and $S$ meant slowly varying quantities; and, when inserted into Eq. (209), he found that $S$ satisfied the eiconal equation

$$\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial x}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial y}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial z}\right)^2 = n^2, \tag{216}$$

since terms proportional to $k^{-1}$ and $k^{-2}$ could be neglected. Thus a relation between the ray-optical description and the mechanical description of a mass point was established, provided the right-hand sides of Eqs. (214) and (216) were identified, or

$$n^2 = 2m(E - U). \tag{217}$$

To arrive at a genuine wave description, however, Sommerfeld had to go back to the wave equation of optics, i.e., Eq. (209), which he now reformulated slightly as

$$\Delta u + n^2 k_0^2 u = 0, \tag{218}$$

where

$$\Delta u = \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial z^2}, \tag{218a}$$

and the quantity $k_0$ was related to the wave number by

$$k_0 = \frac{k}{n}. \tag{218b}$$

On replacing the coefficient of refraction, $n$, by the mechanical quantity $2m \cdot (E - U)$, he finally obtained the equation

$$\Delta u + 2m(E - U)k_0^2 u = 0. \tag{219}$$

The above equation clearly has the same formal structure as Schrödinger’s wave equation (137). Both equations, moreover, become formally identical, if

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0163 -->

522 Chapter III The Creation of Wave Mechanics

one assigned to the constant $k_0$ the value$^{219}$

$$k_0 = \frac{2\pi}{h}. \tag{220}$$

Thus the Schrödinger equation for a mass point follows from a wave-like generalization of the dynamical equations that is analogous to the transition from the ray to the wave description in optics.$^{220}$

Schrödinger, to whom Sommerfeld had sent a copy of his *Wellenmechanischer Ergänzungsband* through the publisher, thanked Sommerfeld, assuring him:

> I shall study this volume very eagerly, and I cannot tell you how much new life it brings to me. I begin again to understand. Actually, I had ceased to understand.... Now I recognise in your book: he who has a desire to lead, in a clear presentation, up to the quantitative contact with experiment, leads in such a way that I can say he leads in paths that are familiar to me; but he illustrates them in a peculiar and ingenious way. (Schrödinger to Sommerfeld, 29 January 1929)

We do not know exactly whether Schrödinger had in mind, with the last remark, the outline of a derivation that Sommerfeld had offered for the wave equation; but in fact the above described way, although it might have appeared to be ‘in general familiar’ to Schrödinger, deviated considerably from the intuitive foundation which the latter gave to wave mechanics in his second paper.

### A Hertzian Formulation of General Relativity and the Mechanical–Optical Analogy

The first documented encounter of Schrödinger with the mechanical-optical analogy took place during his Vienna years; it occurred especially in extended notes on ‘*Tensoranalytische Mechanik*’ (‘Tensor-analytical Mechanics’), which are closely connected with a manuscript entitled ‘*Hertz’sche Mechanik und Einstein’sche Gravitationstheorie*’ (‘Hertzian Mechanics and Einstein’s Theory of Gravitation’) that was composed at about the same time.$^{221}$ Because of the, as we shall see crucial, importance of these notes written eight years earlier for the foundation of wave mechanics in the beginning of 1926, we shall go into some detail with the discussion of their contents.$^{222}$

***

(216)) and the characteristic function ($S$ has the dimension of an action in Eq. (214)).

III.4  Sources of Undulatory Mechanics  
523  

The reason for Schrödinger’s concern with a generalized formulation of mechanics in the late 1910s was provided by the impact which Einstein’s theory of general relativity made on him in those days.²²³ In a first attempt to understand more deeply the intimate connection between the concepts of energy, inertia and gravitation—as emerging from the new theory—Schrödinger recalled the mechanical scheme of Heinrich Hertz.²²⁴ Hertz had, more than two decades earlier, in a book entitled *Principien der Mechanik, in neuem Zusammenhange dargestellt* (*The Principles of Mechanics Presented in a New Form*) which was published shortly after his death, developed a systematic approach to dynamics whose particular feature consisted of an attempt to abolish the concept of force and to replace it by ‘the action of mass and motion, recognisable by our coarse senses’ (Hertz, 1894; English translation, p. 20). To carry out this idea mathematically, he had considered systems of particles subject to constraints or connections which can be expressed by linear differential forms; he had further proposed that the law of motion of these particles follows from a single postulate, the principle of the *straightest path*.  

Hertz’ book had been rather well known among the scientific community around the turn of the century, although few people had been able to do anything with it.²²⁵ In Vienna a particular interest had existed, and—as we have mentioned earlier—Paul Ehrenfest had devoted his doctoral thesis, under Ludwig Boltzmann, to the problem of generalizing Hertz’ mechanical system to deal with fluids (Ehrenfest, 1904).²²⁶ After the establishment of general relativity over a dozen years later, Schrödinger recognized ‘that in Einstein’s theory there has been created a phenomenology [of gravitation] of fascinating beauty, which will also  

²²³ We have discussed Schrödinger’s interest in General Relativity Theory and his own publications in this field in Chapter I, Section I.5.  

²²⁴ We assume here that the investigation contained in the three sections of the manuscript ‘Hertz’sche Mechanik und Einstein’sche Gravitationstheorie’ represent the beginning of Schrödinger’s concern with the problem of generalized mechanics. The three notebooks on tensor-analytical mechanics (*Notebooks I, II, III*) provide the next step in these endeavours. While the sequence of these unpublished texts follows naturally from their contents (see below), their precise dating is rather difficult. If we assume, as seems fairly obvious, that the three sections of the manuscript on Hertzian mechanics and gravitational theory had been devised more or less at the same time, a reference in Section 3 to Hermann Weyl’s *Raum-Zeit-Materie* (Weyl, 1918c) suggests that the manuscript was essentially composed in 1918. The same conclusion applies to the notebooks on tensor-analytical mechanics—there is also a reference to Weyl’s book in *Notebook II*—except they originated a little later.  

²²⁵ Hermann von Helmholtz, Hertz’ teacher and the inspirer of parts of Hertz’ mechanics, had remarked at the end of his preface to the book: ‘Admittedly, large difficulties will still have to be overcome in attempting to derive, from the foundations developed by Hertz, the description of the separate fields of physics. In its fullest context, however, Hertz’ presentation of the fundamental laws of mechanics is a book which must interest, to a high degree, any reader who enjoys a consequent system of dynamics displayed in an exceedingly complete and ingenious mathematical form. It is possible that this book will be of great heuristic value, as a guide in detecting new general types of forces in Nature’ (Helmholtz in Hertz, 1894; reprinted in Helmholtz, *Vorträge und Reden, Zweiter Band, 5. Auflage*, Braunschweig: Friedrich Vieweg & Sohn 1903, pp. 377–378).  

²²⁶ A discussion of the reception of Hertz’ book on the principles of mechanics by Boltzmann, and an analysis of Ehrenfest’s dissertation has been given by Martin J. Klein (Chapter 4 of M. J. Klein, 1970).

524  Chapter III  The Creation of Wave Mechanics

most probably turn out to be right’ (Schrödinger’s *Manuscript*, Section 1, p. 3). ‘This, however,’ he complained, ‘does not bring the fundamental empirical fact, on which this phenomenology is established, closer to our understanding for the time being’ (*loc. cit.*). The mechanics of Hertz, ‘a doctrine of a unique, intimate beauty’ (*loc. cit.*, p. 4), might help to obtain the desired understanding of the empirical fact—i.e., of the identity of the heavy and inert masses. Since in Hertz’ mechanics all forces were unreal and reduced to ‘fictitious forces *which all*—in an obvious way which does not arise by just formulating empirical facts—owe *their origin to the inertia of mass*, as has been concluded experimentally for gravitation,’ Schrödinger continued, ‘I have difficulty in not also assigning importance to *the* fact that *in both theories* [i.e., in Hertz’s mechanics and in Einstein’s theory of gravitation] *the “forces” occur in exactly the same mathematical dress, namely as the three-index symbols of Riemann and Christoffel*’ (Schrödinger, *Manuscript*, Section 1, p. 4). The mathematical justification for the similar description of forces in the two different approaches was, ‘that in both cases, i.e., in the case of Hertz’ as well as in the case of Einstein’s equations of motion, one is dealing with geodetic lines in a Riemannian continuum’ (*loc. cit.*, p. 5). Although Heinrich Hertz had not included in his treatment an ‘analogue of the field equations’ (‘*Analogon der Feldgleichungen*’), Schrödinger expected to be able to extend his predecessor’s scheme to apply also to gravitational and electromagnetic fields, because these—so argued Schrödinger—‘can be regarded as similar in principle to thermodynamic actions’ (*loc. cit.* p. 5).<sup>227</sup>

Schrödinger developed, in Section 2 of his manuscript, the mathematical relation between Hertz’ system of mechanics and Einstein’s theory of gravitation.<sup>228</sup> He used as the starting point the principle of least action,

$$
\delta \int_{t_0}^{t_1} 2\mathcal{T} \, dt = 0, \qquad (221)
$$

applied to a unit mass whose kinetic energy is given by the expression

$$
\mathcal{T} = \frac{1}{2}\left( \frac{ds}{dt} \right)^2, \qquad (222)
$$

and whose total energy $E$—the sum of the kinetic energy and the potential energy $U$—is a constant. The expression for $\mathcal{T}$ could be generalized immediately to an *arbitrary conservative* system, described by $n$ co-ordinates $q_1, q_2, \dots, q_n$, i.e.,

$$
2\mathcal{T} = \sum_{i,k=1}^{n} g_{ik}(q_1, \dots, q_n) \dot{q}_i \dot{q}_k. \qquad (223)
$$

---

<sup>227</sup> Schrödinger claimed that Hertz’ mechanics did apply to the ‘ponderomotoric actions exerted by hot bodies because of their intrinsic kinetic energy on other bodies’ (*Manuscript*, Section 1, p. 5); since these actions are of a type similar to the gravitation and electric fields, the latter should also be describable in Hertz’ mechanical scheme.

<sup>228</sup> Section 2 was written by Schrödinger on separate, numbered sheets. It was left unfinished.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0166 -->

III.4  Sources of Undulatory Mechanics                                                                                               525

The line element $ds$ had to be defined then by the equation

$$ ds^2 = 2 \mathcal{T} dt^2 = \sum_{i,k=1}^n dq_i dq_k. \quad (224) $$

Schrödinger noted: ‘That is, one introduces a general Riemannian metric in the co-ordinate space by the postulate: those line elements which are passed by the point of the system during the same period of time with the same kinetic energy are assumed to be *equal*; the time unit is provided by the time required for $\mathcal{T} = \frac{1}{2}$’ (Schrödinger, *Manuscript* on *Hertz’sche Mechanik und Einstein’sche Gravitations-theorie*, Section 2, sheet 2). With this metric, Schrödinger concluded the following: ‘The geometry of the motion is then quite generally determined by the equation

$$ \left[ \delta \int_{P_0}^{P_1} \sqrt{2 \mathcal{T}} ds = \delta \int_{P_0}^{P_1} \sqrt{2(E - U)} ds = 0. \right] \quad (225) $$

The orbits are the extremal curves of the action integral in the corresponding non-Euclidean space $R_n$. Although the measure does *not*, the action integral [Eq. (225)] still depends on the parameter $E$, which is the total energy. From an arbitrary point [in the $n$-dimensional space] $P_0$ to another arbitrary point $P_1$ still lead $\infty^1$ path orbits; hence we have altogether $\infty^{1+2n-2} = \infty^{2n-1}$ of them, as it should be’ (*loc. cit.*).

The transition time depended, for fixed space points, $P_0$ and $P_1$, on the total energy alone and was given by the integral

$$ t = \int_{P_0}^{P_1} \frac{ds}{\sqrt{2(E - U)}}, \quad (226) $$

which Schrödinger called the ‘chronometer integral’. Since the time differential $dt$ remained invariant under co-ordinate transformations, the velocity variables $\dot{q}_i$ constituted the contravariant components of a vector, whose covariant components were—with all masses being put equal to unity (which can always be achieved by a suitable transformation of variables),

$$ p_i = \frac{\partial \mathcal{T}}{\partial \dot{q}_i} = g_{ik} \dot{q}_k. \quad (227) $$

In Eq. (227), and in the following equations, one has always to sum over double indices.$^{229}$ Hence the invariant $2 \mathcal{T}$, Eq. (223), could likewise be written as

$$ 2 \mathcal{T} = g_{ik} \dot{q}_i \dot{q}_k = p_k \dot{q}_k = g^{ik} p_i p_k, \quad (228) $$

$^{229}$ Schrödinger used the sum convention which Einstein had introduced in General Relativity Theory; he did not, however, follow the notation in this theory systematically; e.g., he did not raise the indices in the case of contravariant components.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0167 -->

526 Chapter III The Creation of Wave Mechanics

with $g^{ik}$ representing the contravariant components of the fundamental metric tensor $g_{ik}$.

Having introduced the above concepts and definitions, Schrödinger then turned to the construction of a geometrical description of the paths. For that purpose he defined the direction vector **R**, having the contravariant components $R^i ( = \dot{q}_i / \sqrt{2\mathcal{T}})$ and the covariant components $R_i ( = p_i / \sqrt{2\mathcal{T}})$—at least in the case of holonomic systems (i.e., according to Hertz, systems which possess the same number of degrees of freedom in finite and infinitely small dimensions)—which satisfy the equations

$$R^i R_i = g^{ik} R_i R_k = g_{ik} R^i R^k = 1 . \tag{229}$$

Evidently, these equations correspond to the relations between the direction cosines in a three-dimensional Euclidean space. Schrödinger further defined the angle between two such vectors, **R** and **S**, through the equation,

$$\cos(\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{S}) = R_i S^i . \tag{230}$$

The product on the right-hand side assumes values $\leq 1$, since the metric in $q$-space is positive definite. Two direction vectors were called perpendicular if the product $R_i S^i$ is zero. A hyperplane in the $n$-dimensional place could be defined by the equation

$$f(q_1, q_2, \dots, q_n) = C, \tag{231}$$

where $C$ denotes an arbitrary constant. For any point $P$ in the plane, the gradient, $\partial f / \partial q_i$, is perpendicular to the plane. In its direction the strongest change of the function occurs, namely,

$$\psi \, ds = \sqrt{g^{ik} \frac{\partial f}{\partial q_i} \frac{\partial f}{\partial q_k}} \, ds, \tag{232}$$

along the line element of the trajectory. Also, for any ensemble of hypersurfaces given by Eq. (231) with a variable $C$, i.e.,

$$f = C, \quad f = C + dC, \quad \dots \tag{233}$$

the increase, $dC$, of $f$ on a line element $ds'$ is larger than the value given by Eq. (232), if $ds'$ is not orthogonal to the hypersurface. Consequently, the line integral

$$\int_{(C_0)}^{(C_1)} \psi \, ds = C_1 - C_0 \tag{234}$$

assumes, on *all orthogonal trajectories* between the surfaces defined by $C_0$ and $C_1$, the same value which is a *minimum value*.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0168 -->

527

**III.4 Sources of Undulatory Mechanics**

When Schrödinger applied these geometrical results to dynamical systems—which had to be conservative and holonomic (in the sense of Heinrich Hertz)—defined by the integral (225), he found

$$\psi = \sqrt{2(E - U)}, \tag{235}$$

or

$$\psi^2 = g^{ik} \frac{\partial f}{\partial q_i} \frac{\partial f}{\partial q_k} = 2(E - U). \tag{235'}$$

He noted in particular: 'The orthogonal trajectories constitute a *field of extremum paths* for the line integral in question,' and that Eq. (235') 'is nothing else but Hamilton's partial differential equation (multiplied by the factor 2) in that form which one usually takes for conservative systems, i.e., when [the potential] $U$ does not depend explicitly on the time' (*Manuscript*, sheet 7). The differential equations for the trajectories of the mechanical system thus were obtained, according to Schrödinger, by putting their direction cosines equal to those of the orthogonal trajectories of the plane (231), yielding the equations

$$\sqrt{2(E - U)} g^{ik} \frac{dq_k}{ds} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial q_i} = p_i. \tag{236}$$

'This constitutes the *first set of Jacobian equations of motion*,' Schrödinger concluded (*loc. cit.*).

In the geometrical interpretation, any dynamically possible orbit can be considered as a member of a field of trajectories belonging to an ensemble of hypersurfaces $f = C$ satisfying the partial differential equations (236). These equations demand that the gradient of $f$ is given by the space-dependent function $\sqrt{2(E - U)}$. Hence Schrödinger suggested the following construction for a given dynamical problem defined by the variational principle, Eq. (221), and a given total energy $E$: Take any surface

$$\phi = 0, \tag{237}$$

and proceed on its normal trajectories (to every point $P_0$) by the infinitesimally small distance $\delta s$,

$$\delta s = \frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{2(E - U)}}, \tag{238}$$

with $\epsilon$ an infinitesimally small constant. The space points thus obtained make up a surface

$$f = C_0 + \epsilon, \tag{239}$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0169 -->

528 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Chapter III &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The Creation of Wave Mechanics

provided

$$f = C_0 \qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad (240)$$

defines the same surface as Eq. (237). ‘By repeating sufficiently often this procedure of establishing the perpendicular line and by connecting the end points by a new surface, actually on both banks [sides] of the $\phi$-surface—most preferably by always using the same constant $\varepsilon$—one now is *really* able to derive from it a quite determined ensemble of surfaces, which will also have to be represented in the form

$$f^* = C^*; \qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad [(241)]$$

and which must constitute, *if our problem has a solution at all*, the *only* solution’ (Schrödinger, *Manuscript*, sheet 8).$^{230}$

In Section 3 of the manuscript on Hertzian mechanics and Einstein’s theory of gravitation, Schrödinger finally established the description of forces with the help of the Riemann–Christoffel three-index symbols. He especially set out to show how any (conservative and holonomic) dynamical system can be described by the equation of motion,

$$\frac{d^2 q_l}{ds^2} + \begin{Bmatrix} \mu \nu \\ l \end{Bmatrix} \frac{dq_\mu}{ds} \frac{dq_\nu}{ds} = 0, \qquad\qquad\qquad (242)$$

where the curly bracket expression denotes the Riemann–Christoffel symbol,

$$\begin{Bmatrix} \mu \nu \\ l \end{Bmatrix} = \frac{1}{2} g^{kl} \left[ \frac{\partial g_{\mu k}}{\partial q_\nu} + \frac{\partial g_{\mu k}}{\partial q_\mu} - \frac{\partial g_{\mu \nu}}{\partial q_k} \right], \qquad\qquad (242\text{a})$$

and one has again to sum over double indices. In the case of non-vanishing potential energy, the additional term

$$-\left( g^{kl} - \frac{dq_l}{ds} \frac{dq_k}{ds} \right) \frac{\partial \ln \sqrt{E - U}}{\partial q_k}$$

may be removed, according to Heinrich Hertz’ ideas, by introducing further degrees of freedom. That is, the potential energy $U$ may appear to be ‘caused by the fact that the original system is just *a part of a larger system* having extra degrees of freedom. The potential energy of the partial system would be given by the equation

$$U = g^{\alpha \beta} c_{\alpha} c_{\beta}, \qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad (243)$$

$^{230}$ In an unfinished part of Section 2 of the manuscript, Schrödinger started to outline how the second, integrated form of Jacobi’s equations of motion might be obtained.

III.4 Sources of Undulatory Mechanics 529

where $c_{\alpha}$ and $c_{\beta}$ represent the velocity co-ordinates of these extra degrees of freedom, and $g^{\alpha\beta}$ is the appropriately enlarged metric tensor.

While Schrödinger concentrated in his manuscript on the relationship between general relativity theory and the usual mechanics, notably in the form suggested by Heinrich Hertz, he discussed the general structure of dynamics in his three notebooks on tensor-analytical mechanics. In many respects, these notebooks can be considered as an immediate continuation of the just discussed manuscript.$^{231}$ He began *Notebook I* with a summary of the results which he had found in the *Manuscript*, in particular with the introduction of the metric tensor in the definition of the kinetic energy, Eq. (223); a derivation of the equations of motion from the principle of least action, Eq. (221); and finally, the construction of the trajectories for a given hypersurface $f = C$. He then proved two further points:

(i) If $f$ depended, besides $C$, on $s - 1$ other independent parameters, $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \dots, \alpha_{s-1}$, then one can derive $s - 1$ trajectories perpendicular to $C$ satisfying the equations

$$\eta_1 = \frac{\partial f}{\partial \alpha_1}, \quad \eta_2 = \frac{\partial f}{\partial \alpha_2}, \quad \dots, \quad \eta_{s-1} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial \alpha_{s-1}}. \quad (244)$$

(ii) The derivative, $\partial f / \partial E$ provides the 'chronometer-integral' $\int_{P_0}^{P_1} ds / \sqrt{2(E - U)}$ along the trajectory from $P_0$ to $P_1$.

In the remaining part of the notebook Schrödinger dealt with Hertz' principle of the straightest path and Gauss' principle of minimum constraint.$^{232}$

Schrödinger opened the second notebook on *Tensoranalytische Mechanik* by investigating the curvature of mechanical trajectories at a given point, before he returned to a renewed discussion of Hertz' and Gauss' mechanical principles, now from the point of view of Hermann Weyl's generalization of the Riemannian geometry.$^{233}$ Schrödinger then elaborated on a dynamical description along the lines of Hertz in the rest of *Notebook II* and the first part of *Notebook III*.$^{234}$ The second part of the last notebook, however, consists of notes on what Schrödinger called 'Analogien zur Optik' ('Analogies to Optics'). These sections

Chapter III   The Creation of Wave Mechanics

reveal Schrödinger’s particular mechanical-optical analogy, that is, his version of the connection between the mechanical scheme of Hamilton and Jacobi and a systematic treatment of optical systems. 

In establishing the connection between Hertz’ mechanics and Einstein’s theory of gravitation, Schrödinger had already noticed the fact that the two theories actually dealt with rather different concepts. Einstein’s theory in particular involved fields, while Hertz spoke exclusively about particles and their orbits. Nevertheless, Schrödinger had encountered no difficulties in establishing a formal relation between the conceptually so-different theories, a relation, which he found to provide a deeper insight into the structure of both theories. In the mechanical-optical analogy Schrödinger now explicitly addressed the common features as well as the differences between point mechanics on the one hand, and ray or wave optics on the other. 

Schrödinger started out by emphasizing the analogy between the two variational principles, i.e., the Maupertuis principle of least action in mechanics, i.e.,

$$\delta \int_{t_1}^{t_2} 2\mathcal{T} dt = 0, \qquad (245)$$

and Fermat’s principle in optics, i.e.,

$$\delta t = \delta \int \frac{ds}{q} = 0, \qquad (246)$$

where $q$ denotes a velocity—in wave optics the phase velocity.$^{235}$ In order to obtain the left-hand side of Eq. (245), he observed that the kinetic energy could be expressed as a quadratic form in the velocity components of the mechanical system, Eq. (223). By inserting the expression for the line element, Eq. (224), he found

$$2\mathcal{T} dt = \left( \frac{ds}{dt} \right)^2 dt = \frac{ds}{dt} ds = \sqrt{2\mathcal{T}} ds. \qquad (247)$$

Evidently, the kinetic energy of a conservative system—and Schrödinger had in mind only such systems—could be written as $E - U$, with $E$ denoting the total energy and $U$ the potential energy depending only on the co-ordinates $q_i$. Since, after the replacement of the $t$-integration in the Maupertuis principle by the $s$-integration, both integrals take the same form, two analogies follow:

(i) The mechanical expression $\sqrt{2(E - U)}$ corresponds to the inverse of the optical velocity, $1/q$.
(ii) The kinetic energy, $\frac{1}{2}(ds/dt)^2$, corresponds to the inverse square of the optical velocity. 

‘It is important,’ Schrödinger concluded, ‘that an analogy exists between radiation

Schrödinger then turned to the optical integral in Eq. (246), finding that it could be written as a function $t(x_0, y_0, z_0, x, y, z)$, such that for a fixed point $P_0$ (where $P_0$ has the space co-ordinates $x_0, y_0, z_0$) the equation

$$t(x_0, y_0, z_0, x, y, z) = \text{constant}, \quad (248)$$

defines the surfaces of light propagation and the equations

$$\frac{\partial t}{\partial x} = \frac{1}{q} \frac{dx}{ds}, \quad \frac{\partial t}{\partial y} = \frac{1}{q} \frac{dy}{ds} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{\partial t}{\partial z} = \frac{1}{q} \frac{dz}{ds} \quad (249)$$

define the orthogonal trajectories to these surfaces, which at the same time represent minimum paths. Obviously, $t$ satisfied the differential equation

$$\left( \frac{\partial t}{\partial x} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial t}{\partial y} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial t}{\partial z} \right)^2 = \frac{1}{q^2}, \quad (250)$$

which corresponded, as Schrödinger realized, to Hamilton’s partial differential equation. He further observed that a function $\bar{t}(x, y, z, \alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_3)$, depending on the three parameters $\alpha_1, \alpha_2$ and $\alpha_3$, would solve the differential equation (250), provided a first-order partial differential equation, i.e.,

$$F \left( \frac{\partial \bar{t}}{\partial \alpha_1}, \frac{\partial \bar{t}}{\partial \alpha_2}, \frac{\partial \bar{t}}{\partial \alpha_3} \right) = 0, \quad (251)$$

held as well.

The direct translation of these optical results to the mechanical situation led to the introduction of a function $S$, the analogue of the optical function $t$,

$$S = S(q_i, q_i^0) = \int_{P_0}^P \sqrt{2(E - U)} \, ds, \quad (252)$$

where the path of integration extends from the point $P_0$ (with the co-ordinates $q_i^0$) to point $P$ (with co-ordinates $q_i$).$^{236}$ The equation, corresponding to the

or

$$\delta \int \sqrt{(E - U)} \, ds = 0,$$

which are equivalent to ours if one redefines the co-ordinates $q_i$ and $q_i^0$ appropriately. We have chosen consistently the definition which Schrödinger used in early 1926 (in his second memoir on wave mechanics: Schrödinger, 1926d).

532 Chapter III The Creation of Wave Mechanics

optical equation (250), evidently was

$$g^{il} \frac{\partial S}{\partial q_l} \frac{\partial S}{\partial q_i} = 2(E - U).$$ (253)

By a proper variation of $S$, the Lagrangian equation of motion,

$$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial q_i} - \frac{d}{dt} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{q}_i} = 0,$$ (254)

followed, where $\mathcal{L}$ denoted the Lagrangian function

$$\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{T} - U = \frac{1}{2} g_{ik} \dot{q}_i \dot{q}_k - U,$$ (254a)

i.e., the difference between the kinetic energy $\mathcal{T}$ (a quadratic function of the $\dot{q}_i$ or the momenta $p_i$) and the potential energy (a function of the position variables $q_i$ only).
Schrödinger closed the third notebook on tensor-analytical mechanics with a section on thermodynamics. In this field he also sketched how relations analogous to the optical ones could be established.
The study of Schrödinger’s notes on Hertz’ mechanics and Einstein’s theory of gravitation and of the three notebooks on tensor-analytical mechanics reveals that Schrödinger had already become acquainted in 1918 with ideas which he would use heavily years later: the analogy of the fundamental dynamical equations and the fundamental equation describing light propagation in optical media. Therefore, when he was about to lay the foundations of wave or undulatory mechanics, he needed little, if any, stimulus from special literature or colleagues; rather, he must be considered as completely independent and self-supporting with respect to the tools of mathematics and physics. That is, the essential step he had to undertake consisted of going back to his old notes and notebooks and copying from them the derivations and formulae, adapting them to his present needs. This general situation, however, did not prevent Schrödinger from referring once in a while in his published papers to the literature, in order to support the presentation: thus, for example, he quoted the section on Hamilton’s characteristic function in Edmund Whittaker’s textbook on analytical dynamics (see Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 489, footnote 3) for the eiconal approximation of wave optics. These references enabled him to skip the lengthy derivations which he had earlier gone through in his own detailed notes. The familiarity with the mathematical and physical aspects of the mechanical-optical analogy also permitted Schrödinger to proceed rapidly with his programme. In spite of being mainly concerned with applications of his wave mechanical scheme, he submitted, less than a month after the paper ‘Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem. (Erste Mitteilung),’ another paper, ‘Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem. (Zweite Mitteilung),’ which contained the foundations of undulatory mechanics.

III.5 Foundations of Undulatory Mechanics

# III.5 Foundations of Undulatory Mechanics

533

In Section 3 of his first publication on ‘*Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem*’, Schrödinger had indicated the possibility that the wave function of the hydrogen atom might be interpreted as some ‘*vibration process* in the atom, which would more nearly approach reality than electronic orbits’ and had added that he had ‘originally intended to found the new quantum conditions in this more intuitive manner’ (Schrödinger, 1926c, p. 372; English translation, p. 9). However, in the paper he had restricted himself to a ‘neutral mathematical formulation,’ i.e., he had replaced the mechanical Hamilton–Jacobi equation (146) of the system via the mathematical substitution (147) by the wave equation (137). Four weeks later he was really ready to present publicly the ‘more intuitive’ formulation, and he wrote right away in the introduction to his second paper on quantization as an eigenvalue problem:

> Before we go on to consider the problem of eigenvalues for further special systems, let us throw more light on the *general* correspondence which exists between the Hamilton–Jacobi differential equation of a mechanical problem and the “allied” *wave equation*, i.e., equation [(137)] of Part I in the case of the Kepler problem. So far we have only briefly described this correspondence on its external analytic side by the transformation [(147)], which is in itself unintelligible, and by the equally incomprehensible transition from the *equating to zero* of a certain expression to the postulation that the *space integral* of the said expression shall be *stationary*. (Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 489; English translation, p. 13)

Schrödinger now did *not* want ‘to pursue further this procedure’, which ‘was only intended to give a provisional, quick survey of the external connection between the wave equation and the Hamilton–Jacobi equation’ (Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 489; English translation, p. 13, footnote 1).

Although Schrödinger thus gave up his belief in the general value of his earlier ‘derivation’ of the wave equation—e.g., he noticed that ‘$\psi$ is not actually the action function of a definite motion in the relation stated in [(147)] of Part I’—he still held that ‘the connection between the wave equation and the variation problem is of course very real,’ since ‘the integrand of the stationary integral [see Eqs. (148) and (149)] is the Lagrange function for the wave process’ (Schrödinger, 1926d; English translation, p. 13, footnote 1). That is, he spoke in his second communication, or Part II, definitely about a wave process in the atom, which he was about to explain and define in some detail in the paper. Hence, it is this publication that finally established the foundations and the definite outlines of what was later called ‘wave mechanics’.237

The progress in the foundation and formulation of undulatory mechanics, presented by Schrödinger in the second communication, resulted from a deepened pursuit of the mechanical-optical analogy, which we have discussed in the

previous section. As well as this he tried to answer some of the questions that had been asked by his closest correspondents, namely by Arnold Sommerfeld and Willy Wien in Munich. Finally, the author treated, in the same publication, further examples of quantum systems by his undulatory approach.

## First Response from Munich$^{238}$

During the crucial period when wave mechanics was created, Schrödinger had a regular correspondence with his Munich colleagues, the experimentalist Willy Wien and the theoretician Arnold Sommerfeld. Wien, with his request to obtain manuscripts from Zurich for the *Annalen der Physik* (of which he was an editor), had stimulated Schrödinger to send his completed papers to Munich. Schrödinger asked Wien, before submitting the manuscripts for printing, to show them to Sommerfeld, whom he regarded as a kind of referee in theoretical questions. Wien did so, and both he and Sommerfeld were the first physicists to respond to the new theory of atomic systems. Thus, Wien wrote on 6 February, after receiving the first communication on '*Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem*' (Schrödinger, 1926c) on 27 January 1926: 'Your paper, which I have passed on—following your request—to Sommerfeld, has raised great interest here. Of course, it is not yet possible to oversee all consequences. I just want to address here two points which have not yet become clear to me' (Wien to Schrödinger, 6 February 1926).

Wien's first question was: 'In the case of absorption the high frequencies must also be in some way subject to absorption, or do you assume that these frequencies are not absorbed at all?' (Wien to Schrödinger, 6 February 1926). Evidently, Wien continued, the usual absorption process in atoms applied only to Schrödinger's beat frequencies (which represented the real discrete line frequencies); but one expected that an absorption of the beat frequencies affected in some way the original (term) frequencies as well, in spite of the fact that 'their direct absorption is evidently, however, still not observed' (Wien to Schrödinger, 6 February 1926).

Wien's second question touched on an even more crucial point in the new theory. 'How would one derive blackbody radiation in your theory?' he asked, and added the further question: 'The physical significance of the constant $h$ has not become clear to me,' and finally: 'How does it come that the equipartition theorem of energy to the degrees of freedom does not apply to your eigenvibrations?' (Wien to Schrödinger, 6 February 1926).

In spite of these serious questions which had to be answered satisfactorily, Wien received Schrödinger's theory quite favourably, as he found it to possess

III.5 Foundations of Undulatory Mechanics

535

‘the great advantage that one can also treat in it time changes of [quantum] states.’ Therefore he closed his letter by encouraging Schrödinger with the words: ‘In any case, I congratulate you on your achievement and wish you good luck with all my heart. Perhaps one will now succeed in attacking the quantum problem which up to now seemed to be so hopeless’ (Wien to Schrödinger, 6 February 1926).

Wien, who had been educated in the school of Hermann von Helmholtz both as an experimentalist *and* as a theoretician—he had actually obtained his doctorate, his *Habilitation* and his Nobel prize through theoretical work—had in the past decades become disillusioned with the progress of the quantum and atomic theories. He had retired increasingly to special experimental studies, for example, to those on radiation damping, i.e., measuring the decay-time of the luminescence of hydrogen canal rays (Wien, 1919, 1921, 1924). On the other hand, the most recent theoretical approaches—such as pursued in Copenhagen and Göttingen in particular—claimed to give up essential features of what Wien considered to be a decent theory, i.e., the usual space-time description of atomic phenomena including also a description of the continuous time change of atomic states, which seemed to follow from the radiation-damping experiments. Schrödinger’s undulatory theory offered new hope in that respect, as it promised to re-establish the good old theoretical description of atomic phenomena; hence, it raised Wien’s expectation for a solution of the ‘hopeless-looking quantum problem’.

Schrödinger thought about Wien’s questions for a while. After two weeks he finally answered: ‘Thank you very much for your amiable letter of 6 February and forgive me, please, that I have not yet replied to it’ (Schrödinger to Wien, 22 February 1926). The reason was that he, Schrödinger, was extremely busy with developing consequences from the undulatory theory which provided new, satisfactory results every day. After a happy outbreak of joy about the successes—Schrödinger called it ‘fancy’ (‘*Schwärmerei*’)—he turned to Wien’s questions, admitting: ‘With all that you will really laugh at me, because for the moment I am sorry that I can answer them, important as they are, only very partially’ (Schrödinger to Wien, 22 February 1926). Concerning the absorption of high frequencies—or their emission—he expressed the opinion that ‘both, emission as well as absorption, are somehow *principally* connected with the *co-operation* of two different fundamental frequencies’ (Schrödinger to Wien, 22 February 1926). How this occurred physically, Schrödinger argued, depended on the nature of the coupling of the vibrations of the electrons in the atom—described by the wave function $\psi$—with the electromagnetic field which was still unknown. With respect to the mathematical representation of the actually observed frequencies, however, just the simplest procedure was necessary, namely just taking differences of the frequencies of the $\psi$-vibrations; moreover, this procedure corresponded naturally to the empirical combination principle of atomic spectral lines. The pure vibration frequencies did in fact escape physical observation, ‘but it may lie in its nature that, drastically speaking, a single, purely harmonic vibration cannot put the ether into motion’ (Schrödinger to Wien, 22 February 1926).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0177 -->

536  
**Chapter III The Creation of Wave Mechanics**

Schrödinger then discussed the problem of the physical interpretation of the constant $h$ in his theory. He wrote:

> I believe this will become *rather* clear in my present formulation—today I am sending you a second communication. The waves in the phase space are something real in a sense, and the constant $h$ universally determines their frequencies or their wavelengths. It therefore enters as in the optical situation; after one had dealt for some time with geometrical optics—and had then anticipated with great certainty undulatory optics and applied the latter—suddenly, through [Augustin] Fresnel’s measurement of the velocity of light, the *real* frequency of all these waves had been fixed by this *single* constant. The analogue to Fresnel’s measurement would be the measurement and interpretation of the spectrum of blackbody radiation—only the further path of the theory did not turn out to be so smooth and simple. (Schrödinger to Wien, 22 February 1926, p. 2)

The equipartition theorem did not seem to work in the new theory either, as Schrödinger rather expected: ‘The laws of interaction (coupling equations) between the $\psi$-vibrations and the electromagnetic field will simultaneously have to yield the correct statistical behaviour of radiation and of the material system (i.e., the $\psi$-vibrations) as well’ (Schrödinger to Wien, 22 February 1926, p. 2). At the same time he warned: ‘One should of course not interpret the $\psi$-vibrations as processes in the old mechanics; on the contrary, the latter has, in my opinion, rather been dissolved in the vibrations’; hence, in trying to establish the coupling equations one may have to change some concepts, and Schrödinger suggested that ‘*perhaps* the *field* will have to undergo a similar metamorphosis as mechanics’ (Schrödinger to Wien, 22 February 1926).<sup>239</sup>

Wien had, at Schrödinger’s request, first passed the paper on ‘*Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem*’ to Sommerfeld before submitting it for printing in the *Annalen*. Almost simultaneously Schrödinger resumed his correspondence with Sommerfeld that had stayed in abeyance since July 1925; in a letter dated 29 January 1926 he explained the contents of his paper in a few words. He then mentioned the preliminary results from the calculations of further examples, such as the linear oscillator, the rotator and the force-free motion of a mass point; and he raised the still unsolved problem of how to evaluate in his theory the intensity and polarization of spectral lines. Finally, he turned to a difficulty that had bothered him for a long time. He wrote:

> I am worrying about the relativistic Kepler problem. I am not *sure* that what I say in the paper is true, namely that the co-motion of the nucleus is essential for the *new* treatment. Even less do I want to reiterate my remark that it might perhaps already be so with the old treatment [i.e., in the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory of the hydrogen atom]; hence, I would request you to ignore this remark if you think it is nonsense. (Schrödinger to Sommerfeld, 29 January 1926)

<sup>239</sup> At this point, Schrödinger referred to the attempts of ‘Born and Heisenberg,’ meaning the treatment of electromagnetic fields in matrix mechanics by Born and Jordan (1925b) and by Born, Heisenberg and Jordan (1926). We have discussed these items in Volume 3, Sections II.5 and IV.2.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0178 -->

III.5 Foundations of Undulatory Mechanics  
537  

Ultimately he added, a little in despair:  

> And yet, for me only the co-motion of the nucleus can provide help; otherwise one gets half-integral quanta, in contrast to experience. These partial quanta come exactly from the *n(n + 1)* of the spherical harmonics which, on the other hand, is a welcome result. (Schrödinger to Sommerfeld, 29 January 1926)  

Sommerfeld was thrilled by the news. On 3 February 1926 he answered:  

> What you write, in the paper as well as in the letter, is indeed terribly interesting. My personal opinion on the integral number mysticism must remain silent; also my personal convenience. (Sommerfeld to Schrödinger, 3 February 1926)  

With respect to the latter he told Schrödinger that he was just about to prepare for a visit to London, where he wanted to present his usual views on atomic structure, when like a ‘thunderclap’ (‘*Donnerschlag*’) he was hit by the content of Schrödinger’s manuscript.²⁴⁰ Sommerfeld suggested:  

> It is my impression that your method is a substitute for the new quantum mechanics of Heisenberg, Born and Dirac (R[oyal] Soc[iety] Proc[eedings] 1925); in particular, a simplified method, so-to-speak, an analytic resolvent of the algebraic problem stated there, *because your results fully agree with theirs*. (Sommerfeld to Schrödinger, 3 February 1926)  

By this identity of results he meant those obtained for the oscillator and the rotator, which Schrödinger had reported to him in the previous letter.  
Even the result on the relativistic hydrogen atom involving the half-integral quantum numbers—which bothered Schrödinger so much—Sommerfeld found perfectly reasonable. He had just recently discovered, together with his student Albrecht Unsöld, that ‘a quantum labelling of the type found in alkaline atoms is strongly demanded by experiment in this case’ (Sommerfeld to Schrödinger, 3 February 1926). To illustrate the situation further, he enclosed with his letter a copy of a paper ‘*Über das Spektrum des Wasserstoffs*’ (‘On the Spectrum of Hydrogen’) which he was about to submit to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, adding the remark:  

> Pauli, who has done numerous calculations on the new quantum mechanical scheme (Stark effect, Balmer series), had trouble with the fine structure. He will also receive a copy of my manuscript and will then probably summon the courage to change the quantum labelling. I suppose that he will arrive at the same result as you. (Sommerfeld to Schrödinger, 3 February 1926)²⁴¹

3 February 1926).<sup>245</sup> With respect to the motion of the nucleus that had been suggested by Schrödinger as a possible cure for the unsatisfactory relativistic hydrogen result, Sommerfeld claimed that it would not give too large an effect, arguing: 'This has been shown by [Charles Galton] Darwin (see p. 421 of my book [Sommerfeld, 1924d]). Since I consider your vibration treatment an improvement on the mechanical one, I must also assume that in your case the nuclear motion is not essential. Therefore, I have crossed out your corresponding remark on p. 12 [of the manuscript on *Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem. I*], as you have suggested' (Schrödinger to Sommerfeld, 3 February 1926).<sup>246</sup>

Finally, Sommerfeld asked the question: 'Does there exist, perhaps, an analogy between your formulation of the variational principle and the vibrating rectangle of Ritz, which led him to the Ritz formula? Nobody remembers anymore this intricate construction, but perhaps you will restore to it some respectability' (Sommerfeld to Schrödinger, 3 February 1926).

Walther Ritz (1878–1909)<sup>247</sup> had tried, in his Göttingen doctoral thesis of 1902, to derive the series formulae for line spectra from the vibration of two-dimensional figures, especially those of a plane square $F$, to which he associated a particular potential energy $\Phi^2$, with

$$\Phi = \iint_F \Delta' w \cdot f \, dx' \, dy'. \qquad (255)$$

The expression $\Delta'w$ was the differential term

$$\Delta'w = \frac{\partial^2 w}{\partial x'^2} + \frac{\partial^2 w}{\partial y'^2}, \qquad (255a)$$

where $w$ denoted the (small) distortion perpendicular to the plane $F$. For the function $f$ Ritz took

$$f = v|x - x'| \cdot |y - y'|, \qquad (255b)$$

with $v$ a constant. (See, e.g., Ritz, 1903, especially pp. 276–278.)<sup>248</sup> Ritz had

***

<sup>245</sup> This question of Sommerfeld's referred to the vibrations associated with the terms of the hydrogen atom; it was connected, of course, with Wien's question which we have mentioned earlier.

<sup>246</sup> Sommerfeld referred to a paper by the British physicist Charles Galton Darwin (1887-1962), who had found that the co-motion of the nucleus in the hydrogen atom resulted in a correction of the Rydberg constant; in addition, a small additive term of the order $\alpha^2 m_e / M$ ($\alpha = 2\pi e^2 / hc$)—with $m_e$ and $e$ the mass and the charge of the electron and $M$ the mass of the hydrogen nucleus—resulted which was very small indeed (Darwin, 1920).

<sup>247</sup> A short biography of Walther Ritz may be found in Volume 1, p. 166.

<sup>248</sup> Ritz' theory of spectral lines has been discussed, e.g., by Sigeko Nisio in his paper 'From Balmer to the Combination Principle' (Nisio, 1966).

540 Chapter III The Creation of Wave Mechanics

further assumed that a Hamiltonian principle was valid, that is, the relation,

$$\int_{t_0}^{t_1} dt \iint_F \left[ \frac{1}{2} \rho \left( \frac{\partial w}{\partial t} \right)^2 - \Phi^2 \right] dx' dy' = \text{minimum} \qquad (256)$$

held, where $\frac{1}{2} \rho (\partial w/\partial t)^2$ denoted the kinetic energy ($\rho$ the density) of the vibrating square. From this principle then followed the differential equation of motion,

$$\rho \frac{\partial^{10} w}{\partial t^2 \partial x^4 \partial y^4} + 32v^2 \Delta \Delta w = 0, \qquad (257)$$

with $\Delta w$ representing the second-order differential expression

$$\Delta w = \frac{\partial^2 w}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 w}{\partial y^2}. \qquad (257a)$$

Equation (257) had to be solved under the boundary conditions,

$$\frac{\partial w}{\partial n} = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial n} = 0, \qquad (258)$$

where $\partial/\partial n$ meant the differentiation in the normal direction to the boundary line of square.
Ritz finally found that Eqs. (257) and (258) yielded as the only solution

$$w = A \sin(\nu t + C) \sin\left( m + \frac{1}{2} \right) \frac{\pi x}{a} \cdot \sin\left( n + \frac{1}{2} \right) \frac{\pi y}{a}, \qquad (259)$$

containing the arbitrary constants $A$ and $C$ and depending on the integral numbers $m, n = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \dots$ ($2a$ was the length of the side of the square). For the frequency he obtained the formula,

$$\pm \nu = N \left[ \frac{1}{(m + \frac{1}{2})^2} + \frac{1}{(n + \frac{1}{2})^2} \right], \qquad (260)$$

with

$$N = \sqrt{\frac{32}{\rho}} \cdot \frac{a^2 v}{\pi^2}. \qquad (260a)$$

This frequency formula he had then compared with the empirical hydrogen formula, i.e.,

$$\pm \nu = 109675.0 \left[ \frac{1}{n^2} - \frac{1}{m^2} \right]. \qquad (261)$$

III.5 Foundations of Undulatory Mechanics 541

Evidently both equations were nearly the same, since the constant \(N\) could be adjusted to the Rydberg constant in Eq. (261). Ritz had further shown that by a slight change of the *Ansatz* for the potential energy, i.e., by putting
\[
\Phi = v \iint_F dx' dy' \left(|x - x'| - \frac{|x - x'|^2}{2a}\right) \left(|y - y'| - \frac{|y - y'|^2}{2a}\right) \nabla' w, \tag{255'}
\]
with
\[
\Delta' w = \frac{\partial^2 w}{\partial x'^2} - \frac{\partial^2 w}{\partial y'^2}, \tag{255a'}
\]
one could indeed reproduce Eq. (261), the Balmer formula for the hydrogen atom. Finally, Ritz had also been able to reproduce the series spectra of other elements, such as those of alkaline atoms. He had proudly concluded: 'The attempt to extend the theory of the hydrogen spectrum to other elements hence leads to a remarkable agreement with experience. The formula derived from the theory surpasses considerably the one so far obtained with respect to accuracy, especially for low-term numbers' (Ritz, 1903, p. 309).\(^{249}\)
Ritz had admitted: 'Although these results now speak in favour of the fertility of the fundamental assumption of the theory, the expansions given here demonstrate that the special *Ansätze* and interpretations which go beyond the general mathematical foundation are still very arbitrary, as it lies in the nature of the problem with the present [limited] status of our knowledge. I intended to bring closer to an understanding the mathematical side of the problem, the only one accessible for the moment .... The advantage of the [electromagnetic] theory of the emission of light in its present form, as compared to the theory discussed above, is its simplicity. However, as long as that simpler picture fails to describe the spectral lines, it must be left undecided as to which of the two conceptions will turn out to be simpler in the light of the *entirety* of phenomena' (Ritz, 1903, pp. 309–310).
Schrödinger, on Sommerfeld's suggestion, studied Ritz' work in February 1926.\(^{250}\) He replied two weeks later: 'With a shiver, I looked up the Ritz vibrations of the rectangle, but also of course with admiration. I do not believe that

with further constants \(A, \mu, b, c, \ldots\). This formula allowed the establishment of certain quantitative relations between different series and the prediction of new series of a given element.

this attempt had anything to do with the present one’ (Schrödinger to Sommerfeld,  
20 February 1926, sheet 2). He saw the main difference in this:

> Unfortunately, Ritz always attempted to represent the *line* frequencies; he believed that he had to derive eigenvalues of the form $1/n^2 - 1/m^2$, while one is dealing with the *term* values $1/n^2$. This fact of course, must, complicate the situation enormously. The most peculiar, great and eternal discovery of Ritz, the combination principle, was then still too new to be grasped in its entirety, even by the author himself. Twenty-three years later one is admittedly in an easier position. (Schrödinger to Sommerfeld, 20 February 1926)

Ritz’ considerations, especially his square-plate model of the atom, did not help Schrödinger in understanding the wave equation approach. Meanwhile, he had been able to ponder a little more on what the atomic vibrations meant. Schrödinger obtained some help in trying to answer Sommerfeld’s question on the damping of the $\psi$-vibrations: obviously these vibrations *per se* could neither be emitted nor absorbed.$^{251}$ He wrote to Sommerfeld:

> The $\psi$-vibrations are naturally not electromagnetic vibrations in the old sense. Between them some *coupling* must exist, corresponding to the coupling between the vectors of the electromagnetic field and the four-dimensional current in the Maxwell–Lorentz equations. In our case the $\psi$-vibrations correspond to the four-dimensional current, that is, the four-dimensional current must be replaced by something that is derived from the function $\psi$, say the four-dimensional gradient of $\psi$. But all this is my fantasy; in reality, I have not yet thought about it thoroughly. (Schrödinger to Sommerfeld, 20 February 1926, sheets 1–2)

Sommerfeld’s letter of 3 February did indeed stimulate Schrödinger in many respects. On the one hand, he agreed with Sommerfeld’s cautious warning in assuming a simple physical reality of the $\psi$-waves. He wrote back: ‘By the way, my general presentation still approaches your wishes on a second point, namely with respect to the “physical reality of the $\psi$-vibrations”. Since $\psi$ in general depends on many more than three variables, the immediate interpretation as vibrations in the three-dimensional space is made difficult in any desirable manner’ (Schrödinger to Sommerfeld, 20 February 1926, sheet 2). He also thanked Sommerfeld for the ‘correction of the point: the co-motion of the nucleus.’ He confessed:

> I have not yet looked up Darwin’s paper myself, but I am now convinced that for the *point mechanics* everything is alright. For wave mechanics there is still a difficulty *there* [i.e., in the nucleus], because in it such a prominent role is played by the point $r = 0$. In the close vicinity of the nucleus not only does the co-motion of the nucleus enter strongly, but the entire relativistic mechanics of the electron becomes doubtful due to large accelerations; the *magnetic* interactions come into play, etc. (Schrödinger to Sommerfeld, 20 February 1926, sheet 2)

$^{251}$ Sommerfeld’s question was, of course, related to Wien’s as to whether one could observe an absorption of the term frequencies.

III.5  Foundations of Undulatory Mechanics 543

On the other hand, he protested—as we have reported earlier (in Section 4)—against Sommerfeld’s accusation that he, unlike Heisenberg, ‘*had put* so many, possibly unnecessary, assumptions *into* the theory’ (‘*so sehr viel möglicherweise Unnötiges in die Theorie hineinstecke*’).

Schrödinger enclosed two addenda in his letter, a treatment of the relativistic electron in a magnetic field and a discussion of a ‘beautiful, simple “perturbation theory,” which is certainly known to mathematicians, but which has pleased me very much, because at one stroke it brings a host of problems into the analytical reach of the new theory’.^252

He closed his letter with the remarks: ‘Thank you again, highly revered professor, for your kind interest, and for a hundred-fold direct and indirect assistance which I owe to you’ (Schrödinger to Sommerfeld, 20 February 1926).

### Preparations for the Second Communication

In searching for the origin and genesis of the second communication on *Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem*, we must refer to two entries in Schrödinger’s manuscripts from early 1926; both are entitled ‘*Für die zweite Mitteilung*’ (‘For the Second Communication’) and are placed at the beginning of the notebooks on *Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. II* and *Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. III*, respectively.^253 We shall now analyse the content of the relevant section in *Notebook II*, and also compare the results to those contained in Schrödinger’s earlier studies on the mechanical-optical analogy. He wrote:

> First the somewhat dark connection between the Hamiltonian differential equation (1) [i.e. our Eq. (146)] and the wave equation (5) [our Eq. (137)] must be clarified. This connection is not new at all; it was, in principle, already known to Hamilton and formed the starting point of Hamilton’s theory, since Hamilton’s variational principle has to be considered as *Fermat’s principle* for a certain wave propagation in configuration space, and the partial differential equation of Hamilton as *Huygens’ principle* for exactly this wave propagation. Equation (5) [i.e., Eq. (137)] is nothing but—or better, just a possible—wave equation for exactly this wave process. These things are generally known, but perhaps I should recall them at this point. (*Notebook II*, p. 1)^254

^252 We shall discuss the first item below, the second in the next chapter.

^253 These notebooks, henceforth called *Notebook II* and *Notebook III*, have been filed on AHQP Microfilm No. 40, Sections 6 and 7, respectively. They were clearly composed after the notebook *Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. I*, which we have dated from late December 1925 to the middle of January 1926. The title of the first section of *Notebook II*, mentioned above, indicates that the notebook was started after Schrödinger had decided on the material which he wanted to put into the first communication. Whether this was before he wrote up the latter paper, or after that, is difficult to decide. Since Schrödinger was a fast writer, it does not matter much anyway. Certainly, *Notebook II* does not contain any material used for the first communication. *Notebook III* was written in February 1926, perhaps with some parts added in March; this material went into the second and later communications on wave mechanics.

^254 In order to illustrate common knowledge on the relation of Hamilton’s dynamics to wave optics, Schrödinger referred to the treatment in Whittaker’s book—which we have discussed earlier (in the previous section).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0185 -->

544 Chapter III The Creation of Wave Mechanics

In recalling the mechanical-optical relations, Schrödinger proceeded more or less as in his old notebook on tensor-analytical mechanics of 1918.²⁵⁵ He wrote in the notebook on *Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. II*:

It is sufficient for the moment to consider the simple case of a mass point with mass ½, which moves in an arbitrary stationary field of force, whose potential function may be given by $V(x, y, z)$. Then Hamilton's partial differential equation, in a form which no longer contains the time variable, reads

$$ \left( \frac{\partial W}{\partial x} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial W}{\partial y} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial W}{\partial z} \right)^2 = E - V, \quad [(262)] $$

with $E$ the total energy. This is now, as is easily recognized, the *differential equation for the wave surfaces* of a wave process with the *space* (but not direction!) dependent velocity of propagation const./$\sqrt{E - V}$. That is, if $W$ is a solution of this equation . [(262)], and if therefore $W$ plus an arbitrary constant also satisfies the equation, then the ensemble

$$ W = \text{const.} = C \quad [(263)] $$

constitutes a system of possible wave surfaces for this process. (*Notebook II*, pp. 1–2)²⁵⁶

The remaining pages of the new notebook summarize exactly the results of the older one, except that he used, in early 1926, the language of wave theory consistently. Schrödinger therefore selected an arbitrary wave plane and showed how one had to construct neighbouring wave planes by observing the relation

$$ |\text{grad } W| = \sqrt{E - V}. \quad (264) $$

This meant that, starting from a given surface $W = C$ (with $C$ denoting a constant), the surface $W = C + dC$ was obtained by drawing, on any point of the $C$-surface, the normal line and taking on these normal lines *in one direction*

²⁵⁵ We do not consider it to be accidental that Schrödinger kept these notes all his life; they were important to him, and we can be sure that he used them at the time when he worked on the foundation of wave mechanics.

²⁵⁶ The fact that Schrödinger drew on his knowledge of the mechanical-optical analogy from his old notes, rather than from the literature, is evident. For example, Whittaker does not discuss the steps in detail in his book—the relevant chapter is quoted by Schrödinger in his second communication (Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 489, footnote 3). On the other hand, the line of argument presented in *Notebook II* follows exactly from that given in the notebook on *Tensoranalytische Mechanik III* (and presented by us in the last section).

We should mention that in our present notation, we have changed slightly the notation which Schrödinger gave in *Notebook II* by using the letter $W$ instead of $S$ for the characteristic function. This is in agreement with the later publication (Schrödinger, 1926d), in which Schrödinger also took a mass point of mass 1 rather than mass 1/2, hence the factor 2 appears on the right-hand side of Eq. (262). On the other hand, in the notebook on tensor-analytical mechanics he assumed the mass 1/2, hence the corresponding formulae in *Tensoranalytische Mechanik. III* and *Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. II* agree completely.

III.5 Foundations of Undulatory Mechanics 545

the distances $dC/\sqrt{E - V}$; then the surface characterized by $C + dC$ was found in the configuration space—which is the three-dimensional space $(x, y, z)$ in the case of the single mass point—by connecting the end points on the normal lines. Schrödinger interpreted the whole procedure with the words: ‘We may also say that we construct around each point of [the surface $W = $] $C$ a sphere of radius $dC/\sqrt{E - V}$, and associate with the ensembles of spheres the parameter values $C \pm dC$’ (*Notebook II*, p. 2).$^{257}$ This construction of the wave surfaces in the configuration space, $C(x, y, z)$, was evidently consistent with Hamilton’s differential equation (262), that is, the curves $C$ and $C \pm dC$ satisfied this equation. Further, Schrödinger noticed that it ‘is identical with Huygens’ principle [of wave optics]’ and that ‘the orthogonal trajectories of the ensemble [of surfaces $W = C(x, y, z)$] are the extremum paths of Hamilton’s variational principle in the time-independent form of Maupertuis,’ i.e., ‘they are possible orbits of the mass point for the given energy $E$’ (*Notebook II*, p. 3).

Schrödinger claimed that the extension to an arbitrary mechanical system was straightforward, and added: ‘In that case one is then eventually dealing with a wave process in a many-dimensional space’ (*Notebook II*, p. 3). He further stated that the equation

$$\Delta\psi + \text{const. } (E - V)\psi = 0 \tag{265}$$

described, in fact, the wave motion demanded by the above construction. In Eq. (265) $\psi$ denoted the wave function and the time dependence, which was originally contained in a wave equation, had already been removed by the *Ansatz* that the process occurs with a *given frequency*, on which the velocity of propagation might depend.$^{258}$ In the mechanical theory, described by Eq. (262), the elimination of the time variable was achieved by restricting oneself to the motion of a mass point of a *given energy* on which, of course, the velocity of the particle depends. Schrödinger concluded: ‘These observations suggest an association of the $E$-values with the *frequencies* of the wave process’ (*Notebook II*, p. 3).$^{259}$

***

$^{257}$ Evidently, one envelope of spheres corresponded to the wave surface in the plus direction (i.e., $W = C + dC$), while the other corresponded to the wave surface in the minus direction (i.e., $W = C - dC$). See the construction in the notebook *Tensoranalytische Mechanik III*, which we have mentioned earlier.

$^{258}$ Perhaps we should draw attention to the fact of how much the ideas, which guided Schrödinger in the notes of 1918 on general relativity and tensor-analytical mechanics, harmonized with the ideas on the atomic vibrations which he developed in late 1925 and early 1926. The old ideas were developed in order to understand the then new theory of gravitation, to isolate the significance of the concept of time, and simultaneously to provide a time-independent form of the equations. The undulatory description of stationary states of atoms demanded exactly the same theoretical treatment, leading to the replacement of propagating waves by standing waves. This replacement was, of course, physically the most important step from de Broglie’s matter waves to Schrödinger’s undulatory description of atomic processes.

$^{259}$ Schrödinger implied, without mentioning it explicitly, that the association of $E$-values and frequencies also existed in the more general case of several mass points.
