III.5 Foundations of Undulatory Mechanics 575

only on the position co-ordinates $q_k$ of the mechanical system)

$$\text{div grad } \psi + \frac{8\pi^2}{h^2} (h\nu - V)\psi = 0, \tag{319}$$

or, when the ‘frequency’ $\nu$ was replaced by the ‘energy’ $E$ via Planck’s equation (293),

$$\text{div grad } \psi + \frac{8\pi^2}{h^2} (E - V)\psi = 0. \tag{320}$$

With the undulatory description of atomic systems—on the basis of the wave equation (315) or (320)—replacing the usual mechanical description, a serious difficulty threatened to arise, ‘on account of the multitude of solutions that such an equation possesses’ (Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 510; English translation, p. 28). For the purposes of describing quantum phenomena the situation looked even worse, because previously in the old quantum theory of atomic structure one had already had to restrict the manifold of solutions of the classical dynamical theory by the so-called quantum conditions; hence ‘it seems to be a bad beginning for a new attempt in this direction if the number of possible solutions has been *increased* rather than diminished’ (Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 511; English translation, p. 28).$^{296}$

Fortunately, however, the actual examples of the undulatory theory that Schrödinger had already considered up to now with the help of Eq. (320) showed no such unphysical variety of solutions. On the contrary, the equation ‘*carries within itself the quantum conditions*’ (*loc. cit.*), as he had noticed earlier. That is: ‘It distinguishes in certain cases, and indeed in those where experience demands it, *of itself*, certain frequencies or energy levels as those which alone are possible for stationary processes, without any further assumption, other than the almost obvious demand that, as a physical quantity, the function $\psi$ must be single-valued, finite, and continuous throughout configuration space’ (Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 511; English translation, p. 28). In the case of a one-body problem—as, for example, the nonrelativistic hydrogen atom treated in the first communication—the energy levels could be determined by a much simpler method than in the previous quantum theory of atomic structure. Instead of operating in two steps—(i) the definition of all dynamically possible paths; and (ii) discarding the greater part of these solutions and selecting a few paths by quantum conditions—one defined quantum states in the new theory ‘*at once* as the *eigenvalues* of Eq. (315), which *carries in itself its natural boundary condition*’ (Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 512; English translation, p. 29).

***

$^{296}$The fact that the classical Hamilton–Jacobi equation also possessed, like the above wave equation, a continuous infinity of solutions had a different interpretation in physics: any complete solution of it provided a complete solution for the orbits of the mechanical system; a different, and complete, solution of the Hamilton–Jacobi equation then described the very *same* motion.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0217 -->

# 576 Chapter III  The Creation of Wave Mechanics

Schrödinger did not exclude the possibility that for more general dynamical systems further conditions might be required; however, he definitely expected that these would ‘no longer be of such a strange and incomprehensible nature as the previous “quantum conditions”’, but rather ‘will be of the type that we are accustomed to find in physics with a partial differential equation as initial or boundary conditions’ (Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 511; English translation, p. 28).

As Schrödinger emphasized, the undulatory mechanics thus allowed one to simplify the solution of problems of atomic dynamics considerably beyond the previous methods. Earlier one had to integrate the equations of motion of a given problem, then select a solution by the quantum conditions, and finally determine the energy states. The use of the Hamilton–Jacobi methods—invoked by Schwarzschild, Epstein and Sommerfeld—had already simplified the evaluation: a real calculation of all possible orbits was avoided and the complex momentum integral was directly obtained, from which then the energy states could be derived. In undulatory mechanics one immediately attempts to get the energy states; one may begin first by solving the wave equation without the boundary and the continuity conditions, and soon find that applying the latter simplifies the solution enormously—as Schrödinger had shown, for example, in the case of the non-relativistic hydrogen equation, where the general solution for the wave function, Eqs. (153) and (157), was then reduced to the very simple form, Eq. (163).

Moreover, it did not seem impossible that more direct methods for calculating the energy eigenvalues existed or would come to exist in the future. These methods, Schrödinger wrote, should work especially in the case of the low-order eigenvalues, which were of special interest for spectroscopy and atomic physics. In conclusion, Schrödinger said:

> From the idea, definitely outlined, that every problem of eigenvalues allows itself to be treated as one of maxima or minima without reference to the differential equation, it appears to me very probable that direct methods will be found for the calculation, at least approximately, of the eigenvalues, as soon as *urgent* need arises. At least it should be possible to test in individual cases whether the eigenvalues, *known* numerically to all desired accuracy through spectroscopy, *satisfy* the problem or not. (Schrödinger, 1926d, 513; English translation, p. 29)²⁹⁷

To decide this and similar problems and to complete the establishment of the new theory, he had to treat further examples of microscopic quantum systems, which he would amply do in the following weeks and months.

***

²⁹⁷ It is interesting to remark at this point that, several months earlier, Max Born in Göttingen had contemplated a similar abbreviation of the computational methods in matrix mechanics, in order to obtain directly the energy eigenvalues of quantum mechanical systems—just as Schrödinger had done—but without immediate success. (See the three-man paper: Born, Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926, p. 581.)

# Chapter IV
## Early Response and Applications

### Introduction

In a letter (dated 20 February 1926) to Arnold Sommerfeld, Schrödinger, for the first time, used the name ‘*Wellenmechanik*’ (wave mechanics), in order to characterize his new theory compared with (classical) point mechanics. He also reported in the same letter on recent progress in applying wave mechanics. He wrote:

> At the moment I am proceeding along the line of least resistance, and am doing what I can. The most pleasant outcome is that the Stark effect turns out to be the same as that of Epstein—the opposite result would have been disastrous. Because, without the action of a magnetic field and without relativity everything follows nearly automatically, and one can hardly think of a change anymore. (Schrödinger to Sommerfeld, 20 February 1926)

The information given in the above-mentioned letter, plus the results which Schrödinger presented in a previous letter (Schrödinger to Sommerfeld, 29 January 1926)—about the linear oscillator, the rotator and the free mass point—provided evidence of the first successes of the wave mechanical scheme to problems apart from the nonrelativistic hydrogen atom. These fundamental applications were made by Schrödinger more or less during the same period in which he established the foundations of his method. He then published the results in the second and third communications on *Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem* (Schrödinger, 1926d, f). The last paper mentioned was only completed at the beginning of May, although Schrödinger had most of the results available by the end of February 1926, as is evident from examining the notebooks *Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. I, II, and III.* The reason for the delayed submission lay in the fact that Schrödinger, in between the second and third communications, concentrated on showing the equivalence of his own wave mechanical method and the quantum mechanical method of Max Born, Paul Dirac, Werner Heisenberg and Pascual Jordan in evaluating the energy states of atomic systems. While we shall discuss this particular work and related efforts in a later section (Section IV.3), we summarize the earliest applications of wave mechanics in Section IV.1.

The first physicists who reacted to Schrödinger’s new atomic theory were naturally Willy Wien and Arnold Sommerfeld, with whom he regularly corresponded during the time he created and confirmed wave mechanics. As soon as the papers were published, however—i.e., from the middle of March 1926 onwards—people started to respond to the new theory. Several senior physicists, notably

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0219 -->

578 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

Max Planck, Albert Einstein and Hendrik Lorentz, immediately. wrote letters to Schrödinger in which they congratulated him on his achievement and asked further questions about the theory. These letters provided Schrödinger with great encouragement to continue along the lines he had developed, as we shall show in Section IV.2.

One of the most enthusiastic responses came from Schrödinger’s younger colleague and Viennese countryman Wolfgang Pauli. Pauli, having already been informed about the new forthcoming theory (prior to publication) in early February 1926 by Sommerfeld, seized on the first publication (Schrödinger, 1926c) soon after it appeared in print. A few weeks later Pauli demonstrated, in a letter to Pascual Jordan in Göttingen, that the wave mechanical method (which appeared to be so different from the Göttingen quantum mechanics), yielded nevertheless the same energy eigenvalues for atomic systems (Pauli to Jordan, 12 April 1926). Schrödinger himself had arrived at exactly the same conclusion nearly four weeks earlier, and his paper establishing the formal equivalence proof—‘*Über das Verhältnis der Heisenberg-Born-Jordanschen Quantenmechanik zu der meinen*’ (Schrödinger, 1926e)—was already in print. Schrödinger’s and Pauli’s result, which will be analysed in Section IV.3, not only pleased those who disliked the methods of matrix mechanics and similar schemes (such as the one developed by Paul Dirac in Cambridge), but also stimulated many theoreticians in Europe and America to attack old and new quantum-theoretical problems with the help of Schrödinger’s wave mechanics (Section IV.4).

Thus in the spring of 1926 physicists found that a new, successful description of atomic systems and processes existed in two, widely differing formulations—as far as their origin and mathematical tools were concerned. Schrödinger, in particular, had arrived at wave mechanics by bypassing—to a large extent—the broad road leading from Bohr’s theory of atomic constitution of 1913, over the correspondence principle and the so-called dispersion-theoretic approach to quantum mechanics. By applying a few peculiar and original ideas, he had expanded the matter wave hypothesis of Louis de Broglie into a detailed dynamical, perfectly operating scheme, which apparently allowed him to avoid many of the quantum concepts that had been employed in the previous decade. Did his theory also provide a completely new insight into the nature of quantum phenomena? Did it perhaps allow him to drop the assumption of quantum jumps, that had been so difficult for physicists to accept for a quarter of a century? Now, in the summer of 1926, Schrödinger suggested that the answer to these questions was affirmative. On the other hand, the advocates of quantum mechanics seriously objected. The debate on the physical interpretation of the new quantum theory, which was opened in the summer of 1926, would continue vigorously for more than a year. For most of the participants in the debate it would be decided (in late 1927) against Schrödinger’s hopes and suggestions. The details of the debate will constitute the central content of the next volume. Here, in Section IV.5, we will just be able to enter into the preliminaries of this important development.

IV.1 The Scheme Starts to Work 579

# **IV.1 The Scheme Starts to Work**

In his letter of 29 January 1926 to Sommerfeld, Schrödinger, after referring to his first communication (on the hydrogen atom), mentioned: ‘I have since translated a few further mechanical problems into the new conceptual scheme. As far as my mathematical methods suffice, everything develops in the nicest way; and it is still *not* a stereotype of the old quantum rules, but differs from it in characteristic points.’ He then explained in a few sentences the results: (i) on the linear oscillator; (ii) on the rotator in three dimensions; and (iii) on the free motion of a mass point. Finally, he stated the problems that had to be treated next in the new theory, i.e., ‘besides the evaluation of important special cases—like the Stark effect, the Zeeman effect and the relativistic Kepler motion—the establishment of a rule for the intensity and polarization which must replace the correspondence principle’ (Schrödinger to Sommerfeld, 29 January 1926). He had already begun the investigation of parts of these problems and would complete and publish them in the following months. The results constituted the first tests and confirmation of the theory of wave mechanics, which had originally been derived for the specific case of calculating the energy states of the hydrogen atom.

## **The Discovery of ‘Hilbert’s Mathematics’**

In the earliest discussion of a quantum-theoretical problem different from the hydrogen atom (without or with electric and magnetic fields) i.e., that of the linear oscillator in the notebook on *Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. I*, Schrödinger quoted a method given in the book on *Methoden der mathematischen Physik* by Richard Courant and David Hilbert (1924). In his notes, Schrödinger especially attempted to treat the linear oscillator of mass $m$ and frequency $\nu$, described by the wave equation

$$\frac{d^2\psi}{dq^2} + (a - bq^2)\psi = 0, \tag{1}$$

with $q$ denoting the elongation and $a$ and $b$ constant expressions, i.e.,

$$a = \frac{2mE}{K^2} \tag{1a}$$

and

$$b = \frac{4\pi^2\nu^2m^2}{K^2}. \tag{1b}$$

($E$ and $K$ were the energy and the quantum-theoretical constant $h/2\pi$,

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0221 -->

580 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Chapter IV &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Early Response and Applications

respectively.)$^1$ He first introduced the transformation of the variable $q$ to $x$,

$$q^2 = x, \qquad (2)$$

by which Eq. (1) became what he called a Laplace equation, namely,$^2$

$$\frac{d^2\psi}{dx^2} + \frac{1}{2x} \frac{d\psi}{dx} + \left( \frac{a}{4x} - \frac{b}{4} \right) \psi = 0. \qquad (3)$$

Similarly, in the treatment of the nonrelativistic hydrogen atom—which we have discussed in Section III.3—the eigenvalue condition (derived from the uniqueness of the solution) now became$^3$

$$\frac{a}{\sqrt{b}} = 2n + 1, \quad n = 0, 1, 2, \dots \qquad (4)$$

On this result Schrödinger commented: ‘One may instead also transform Eq. (1) such that

$$q \sqrt[4]{b} = z; \qquad [(5)]$$

$^1$ See *Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. I*, p. 45.
$^2$ Equation (3) is indeed a special case of the equation
$$x \frac{d^2u}{dx^2} + (\delta_0 x + \delta_1) \frac{du}{dx} + (\varepsilon_0 x + \varepsilon_1)u = 0,$$
given in the textbook of Ludwig Schlesinger on differential equations (Schlesinger, 1900, p. 192). We have especially $\delta_0 = 0, \delta_1 = \frac{1}{2}, \varepsilon_0 = -b/4$, and $\varepsilon_1 = a/4$.

$^3$ Equation (4) evidently corresponds to the condition that the exponents $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ in the integral solution of Eq. (3)—which has the same structure as the one given by Eq. (156) in Section III.3—assumes an integral value. The exponents $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ are the following expressions:

$$\alpha_1 = \frac{\varepsilon_1 + \delta_1 c_1}{c_1 - c_2}, \quad \alpha_2 = \frac{\varepsilon_1 + \delta_1 c_2}{c_2 - c_1},$$

with $c_1 = \sqrt{b/4}$ and $c_2 = -\sqrt{b/4}$. Hence $\alpha_1 = \frac{1}{4}(a/\sqrt{b} + 1), \alpha_2 = -\frac{1}{4}(a/\sqrt{b} - 1)$. Now the condition for an integral value for $\alpha_1 - 1$—see the nonrelativistic hydrogen case—would yield

$$\frac{1}{4} \frac{a}{\sqrt{b}} - \frac{3}{4} = \text{integral number}, \quad (*)$$

or

$$\frac{a}{\sqrt{b}} = 1, 5, 9, \dots,$$

which is in disagreement with Eq. (4). The difficulty, however, is enhanced by noticing that an additional condition for the uniqueness of the solution, namely that the sum $\alpha_1 + \alpha_2$ should assume an integral value, obviously cannot be satisfied—the unique result is $\frac{1}{2}$. The puzzle will be resolved by reminding oneself of transformation (2). Since the exponent for the variable $q$ is twice the one for the variable $x$, the condition is

$$2\alpha_1 - 1 = \frac{1}{2} \frac{a}{\sqrt{b}} - \frac{1}{2} = \text{integer},$$

rather than Eq. (*). This then leads indeed to Eq. (4).

This can easily be brought into the form (see *Courant–Hilbert*, p. 261):

$$ \frac{d^2 \psi}{dz^2} + (1 - z^2)\psi + \lambda \psi = 0. \qquad [(7)] $$

This possesses as eigenvalues

and as eigenfunctions the Hermitean orthogonal functions:

Thus it agrees with my calculation.' (*Notebook I*, p. 45).
The hint to Eq. (7) and its treatment in the book of Courant and Hilbert, and the observation that its solution agreed with the one obtained for Eq. (3) along the lines of Schlesinger’s book, occurred to Schrödinger immediately after he had achieved the complete solution of the nonrelativistic hydrogen atom in his *Notebook I*. Schrödinger then discussed, at that stage of the development, in a little more detail the nature of eigenfunctions associated with specific atomic systems. He clearly found, by using the information from *Courant–Hilbert*: ‘For the linear oscillator one thus obtains the Hermitean orthogonal functions [as eigenfunctions]’ (*Notebook I*, p. 45).
Because of the similarity of the wave equation for the harmonic oscillator (if expressed in the form of Eq. (3)), and that for the radial wave equation of the (non-)relativistic Kepler problem, i.e.,

$$ \frac{d^2 U}{dr^2} + \frac{(2\alpha + 1)}{r} \frac{dU}{dr} + \left( \frac{2m_e E}{K^2} + \frac{2m_e e^2}{K^2} \frac{1}{r} \right) U = 0, \qquad (11) $$

he also proposed to apply the same technique of solution to the latter; however, he did not get anywhere with it. (See *Notebook I*, p. 46.) He was more successful

582

in the case of the spatial oscillator; its eigenfunctions could be considered as ‘a generalization of the Hermitean polynomials’ (*Notebook I*, p. 48). Finally, he turned to the rotator, arriving at encouraging results which he mentioned in his letter to Sommerfeld of 29 January 1926.

Making use of Courant–Hilbert’s *Methoden der mathematischen Physik*, instead of Schlesinger’s *Einführung in die Theorie der Differentialgleichungen*, therefore enabled Schrödinger to extend greatly the range of application of the wave mechanical scheme. Evidently, he began to consult this book in detail shortly after completing his first communication on the hydrogen atom, i.e., in the last week of January 1926. One may speculate that Hermann Weyl, who helped Schrödinger in straightening out the solution of the equation for the hydrogen atom, had directed Schrödinger’s attention to *Courant–Hilbert*. An even more suitable person appears to have been Erwin Fues, the new assistant at the theoretical physics institute of the University of Zurich.⁴

Fues had just arrived from Stuttgart. The *Courant–Hilbert* was certainly known in Stuttgart, since Paul Ewald—the head of the physics institute—had published a detailed review in the *Naturwissenschaften* issue of 1 May 1925. He wrote, in particular:

A perfect example of a book, which attempts the goal of acquainting the physicist with the methods of modern mathematics, is that by Courant and Hilbert: *Methoden der mathematischen Physik* (I). It indeed provides the physicist the opportunity to grasp the spirit of the purposeful, uniform mathematical method in a particularly important field which can be characterized by the key words: *eigenvalues* and *eigenfunctions*. In physics, as is well known, these problems—whose extensions have been defined in the widest sense—lead to the consideration of vibrations of every kind: of systems of discrete mass parts, of strings, of membranes, of plates and rods, electromagnetic and acoustic vibrations. . . . In terms of mathematics, one deals, depending on the formulation, either with the solution of certain partial differential equations with boundary conditions or with the solution of variational problems. The necessity of satisfying the boundary and initial conditions leads to the problem of expanding arbitrary functions in terms of the eigenfunctions for the domain, which implies the important problem of expansions in terms of trigonometric series or the series of spherical harmonics, Bessel functions, etc. (Ewald, 1925, p. 385)

The above characterization of the contents of *Methoden der mathematischen Physik* must strike anyone who studies the programme of Schrödinger in developing wave mechanics. In particular, all the steps, which Schrödinger had undertaken in early 1926, seem to demand the application of the methods displayed in *Courant–Hilbert*, although apparently he was not aware of it.⁵ In any case,

584  Chapter IV  Early Response and Applications

# The Oscillator in Wave Mechanics

The most important content of undulatory or wave mechanics could be expressed in the form of the general, second-order differential equation,

$$div \ grad \ \psi + \frac{8\pi^2}{h^2}(E - V)\psi = 0, \tag{12}$$

for the wave function $\psi$ describing atomic systems of arbitrarily many degrees of freedom. Equation (12) took on a well-defined shape, if the potential energy $V$ of the system was given as a function of, say, its $f$ position and $f$ momentum or velocity co-ordinates. The differential operation ‘div grad’ had to be interpreted as operating in a $f$-dimensional Riemannian space, with the line element

$$ds^2 = 2\bar{T}(q_k, \dot{q}_k) \ dt^2, \tag{13}$$

where $\bar{T}$ denoted the kinetic energy of the system when expressed as a function of the position and velocity co-ordinates, $q_k$ and $\dot{q}_k$, $k = 1, \dots, f$.

In figuring out the applications of wave mechanics beyond the nonrelativistic hydrogen problem, Schrödinger, after several unsuccessful attempts with the relativistic Kepler problem and the hydrogen atom in a magnetic field, soon alighted on the problem of the linear oscillator.$^7$ This problem had played a distinguished role in the history of quantum theory, because it was the quantization of the linear oscillator that provided the starting point for the entire theory. Schrödinger also knew that the result of any new treatment of the oscillator had to coincide more or less with the one presented by Max Planck as early as December 1900; it had especially to yield the famous, repeatedly substantiated blackbody radiation law. Whether this result would be obtained by the wave mechanical method could not be considered as being obvious; hence, even the solution of a problem as simple as the one-dimensional linear oscillator provided a crucial test of the new scheme, in which the quantization was not imposed directly but rather followed via applying boundary and uniqueness conditions on the wave function satisfying Eq. (12) in that special case.

Evidently, in the case of the one-dimensional linear oscillator, the kinetic energy $\bar{T}$ could be written as

$$\bar{T} = \frac{1}{2}\dot{q}^2, \tag{14}$$

provided the single position co-ordinate $q$ was chosen to be the elongation times the square-root of the oscillating mass. From Eq. (13) it then followed immediately

***

I*’ on page 45, after the successful solution of the nonrelativistic hydrogen equation and another unsuccessful discussion on the Zeeman effect of hydrogen.

$$ \text{div grad } \psi = \frac{d^2\psi}{dq^2}. $$  
(16)  
Further, the potential energy $V$ depended only on the position variable $q$ and the oscillator frequency $\nu_0$, that is,  
$$ V(q) = 2\pi^2 \nu_0^2 q^2. $$  
(17)  
On inserting Eqs. (16) and (17) into Eq. (12), Schrödinger arrived at the equation  
$$ \frac{d^2\psi}{dq^2} + (a - bq^2)\psi = 0, $$

with

to describe the one-dimensional linear oscillator in wave mechanics.

(1) into the Laplacean equation (3), which had basically the same form as the one describing the Kepler problem; he then wrote down the solution along the lines which had worked before in the case of the nonrelativistic hydrogen atom. He immediately added that the very same solution followed from another, rather different path, if one transformed Eq. (1) into the differential equation for the Hermitean orthogonal functions, referring at this point to Courant and Hilbert’s *Methoden der mathematischen Physik*, as we have mentioned earlier. In the published paper, i.e., the second communication ‘Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem,’ he suppressed the first step and presented only the solution according to Courant and Hilbert (Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 515). However, at a later point in his paper, Schrödinger recalled his original solution in a footnote, in which

Chapter IV  Early Response and Applications

he wrote: ‘Moreover, the *one*-dimensional oscillator leads to the same equation [i.e., a Laplacean equation similar to the one for the hydrogen atom] if $q^2$ be taken as variable. I originally solved the problem directly in *that* way. For the hint that it was a question of Hermite polynomials, I have to thank *Herr* E. Fues’ (Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 518, footnote 1; English translation, p. 33, footnote 1).⁸

The ‘equation for Hermitean polynomials’ mentioned by Schrödinger was of course

$$
\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} + (1 - x^2)y + \lambda y = 0, \qquad (18)
$$

an equation quoted in *Courant-Hilbert* (on p. 261, the page quoted by Schrödinger in *Notebook I*, p. 45, and in the paper, p. 515), together with its complete set of continuous and (in the entire region $-\infty \leqslant q \leqslant +\infty$) finite solutions, $y(x)$, the Hermitean orthogonal functions $\exp(-x^2/2)H_n(x)$, each of which is associated with one of the proper eigenvalues $\lambda = 0, 2, 4, 6, \dots$ (see Courant and Hilbert, 1924, *loc. cit.*). The wave equation (1) for the one-dimensional linear oscillator assumed the form of Eq. (18) after a transformation of the position co-ordinate, namely

$$
x = q \sqrt[4]{b}. \qquad (19)
$$

Then Schrödinger obtained the new equation

$$
\frac{d^2\psi}{dx^2} + (1 - x^2)\psi + \left( \frac{a}{\sqrt{b}} - 1 \right) \psi = 0, \qquad (20)
$$

which implied the condition for the eigenvalues:

$$
\lambda = \left( \frac{a}{\sqrt{b}} - 1 \right) = 0, 2, 4, 6, \dots, \qquad (21)
$$

or

$$
\frac{a}{\sqrt{b}} = 1, 3, 5, \dots, (2n + 1). \qquad (22)
$$

Schrödinger, in his published paper, also immediately copied from the book the general formula for the Hermitean polynomials, i.e.,

$$ H_n(x) = (-1)^n \exp(x^2) \frac{d^n \exp(-x^2)}{dx^n} \tag{23} $$

(see Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 515, Eq. (27), and *Courant–Hilbert*, 1924, p. 76, Eq. (59)), and the equations for the first five polynomials, i.e.,

$$ \left. \begin{aligned} H_0(x) = 1, & \qquad H_1(x) = 2x, \\ H_2(x) = 4x^2 - 2, & \qquad H_3(x) = 8x^3 - 12x, \\ H_4(x) = 16x^4 - 48x^2 + 12 \end{aligned} \right\} \tag{24} $$

(see Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 515, Eqs. (27'')), and *Courant–Hilbert*, 1924, p. 76, Eqs. (63)).

All that he had to do after that step, in order to find the eigenvalues of the one-dimensional linear oscillator in wave mechanics, was to insert the expressions (1a) and (1b) into Eq. (22). This yielded the result

$$ E_n = \frac{(2n + 1)}{2} h \nu_0, \qquad n = 0, 1, 2, \dots, \tag{25} $$

whereupon Schröd

588 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

additional terms as caused by the thermal expansion. Then in the old quantum theory it followed that ‘the “allowed” energy values of the total system are no longer *linear* but rather *quadratic* functions of the quantum numbers’ (Schrödinger, 1926k, p. 317). With the tacit assumption of a similar conclusion arising in the wave mechanical treatment of the solid body, he now concluded that the effect of the additional term $\frac{1}{2} h \nu_0$ would not disappear, even when only the difference of the energy states was considered. Similarly, he argued that in the case of the band spectra of molecules the ‘zero-point energy’ entered.$^9$

Of course, the agreement of the result for the energy eigenvalues of the one-dimensional linear oscillator with the existing empirical tests satisfied Schrödinger immensely. However, he was still more ambitious, because his solution of the wave equation (20) still contained additional information in the wave functions $\psi_n$, which were given by the expressions

$$\psi_n(q) = \exp\left(-\frac{2\pi^2 \nu_0 q^2}{h}\right) H_n\left(2\pi q \sqrt{\frac{\nu_0}{h}}\right), \quad n = 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots \qquad (26)$$

as functions of the position variable $q$. From the explicit formulae, given in *Courant–Hilbert* for Hermite polynomials, $H_n(x)$, he could derive several conclusions, if he evaluated them numerically.$^{10}$ This he did in a set of notes, entitled ‘Oszillatorschwingungen’ (‘Oscillator Vibrations’);$^{11}$ he especially calculated the roots, maxima and minima of several polynomials, finding: ‘Consideration [of Eqs. (24)] shows that the first function [i.e., $\psi_0(q)$] is a *Gaussian error-curve*; the second vanishes at the origin and for $x [= 2\pi q \sqrt{\nu_0/h}]$ positive corresponds to a “Maxwell distribution of velocities” in two dimensions, and is continued in the manner of an odd function for $x$ negative. The third function is even, is negative at the origin, and has two symmetrical zeros at $\pm 1/\sqrt{2}$, etc. The curves can easily be sketched roughly and it is seen that the roots of consecutive polynomials *separate* one another. From [Eq. (26)] it is also seen that the characteristic points of the eigenfunctions, such as half-width (for $n = 0$), zeros, and maxima, are, as regards order of magnitude, within the range of the classical vibration of the oscillator’ (Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 516; English translation, p. 32).

Schrödinger found the classical amplitude of the $n$th vibration to be

$$q_n = \frac{\sqrt{E_n}}{2\pi \nu_0} = \frac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\frac{h}{\nu_0}} \sqrt{\frac{2n+1}{2}}. \qquad (27)$$

He wrote down this equation without substantiating the above claim in the second communication of February 1926. Several months later, however, Schrödinger presented full details in a note entitled ‘*Der stetige Übergang von der Mikro*’

In the note he especially demonstrated *in concreto* the transition to macroscopic mechanics, by showing that a *group* of eigenvibrations of *high* order-number $n$ (“quantum number”) and of relatively small order-number differences (“quantum number differences”) may represent a “particle”, which is executing the “motion”, expected from the usual mechanics, i.e. oscillating with the frequency $\nu_0$ (Schrödinger, 1926g, p. 665; English translation, p. 42).

To prove the case, Schrödinger formed the following expression,

$$\psi = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \left(\frac{A}{2}\right)^n \frac{\psi_n}{n!}, \tag{28}$$

which corresponded to a sum of normalized oscillator eigenfunctions with the coefficients $A^n(2^n n!)^{-1/2}$. This expression exhibits a strong, narrow maximum at the order number

$$n = \frac{A^2}{2}. \tag{29}$$

After the summation was performed—with the help of an equation in *Courant–Hilbert* (Eq. (58) on p. 76)—a wave function resulted, whose real part had the form

$$\psi = \exp\left[\frac{A^2}{4} - \frac{1}{2}(x - A \cos 2\pi\nu_0 t)^2\right] \tag{30}$$
$$\times \cos\left[\pi\nu_0 t + (A \sin 2\pi\nu_0 t) \cdot \left(x - \frac{A}{2} \cos 2\pi\nu_0 t\right)\right].$$

The first factor on the right-hand side represents a tall, narrow ‘hump’ of the shape of a Gaussian error-curve, having a width of the order of magnitude of unity and being centred at time $t$ at the position

$$x = A \cos 2\pi\nu_0 t. \tag{31}$$

This hump now oscillates like a classical oscillating mass-point with the energy

$$E = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{dq}{dt}\right)^2 + 2\pi\nu_0^2 q^2 \tag{32}$$

and an amplitude$^{12}$

$$a = \frac{A}{2\pi} \sqrt{\frac{h}{\nu_0}}. \tag{33}$$

$^{12}$The amplitude of the position variable $q$ ($=\sqrt{m}$ times the elongation) can be obtained from the amplitude $A$ of the $x$-vibration with the help of Eqs. (19) and (1b).

$$E = 2\pi^2 a^2 \nu_0^2 = \frac{A^2}{2} h\nu_0. \tag{34}$$

On inserting relation (29), Schrödinger found:

$$E = nh\nu_0, \tag{35}$$

i.e., the quantum energy of the wave function with the average order number $n$ of the original wave group. 'The "correspondence" is thus complete in this respect also,' he concluded (Schrödinger, 1926g, p. 666; English translation, p. 43).$^{13}$

While the classical amplitude could be given a quantum-theoretical analogue, Schrödinger failed to interpret other properties of the eigenfunctions in wave mechanics, such as the exact positions of the turning points in the graphs of eigenfunctions. ### Several Degrees of Freedom and Degeneracy

In Section 3.1 of the second publication, Schrödinger also discussed the extension of the linear oscillator problem to several degrees of freedom. He considered two situations, namely, the case in which the mechanical eigenfrequencies belonging to the individual degrees of freedom are all different, and the case in which they are not. In the first, non-degenerate case, the extension of the one-dimensional oscillator treatment was straightforward, and Schrödinger summarized the essential points in the following statements: '$\psi$ [i.e., the wave function of the oscillator system of many non-degenerate degrees of freedom] is taken as the *product* of functions, each of a single co-ordinate, and the problem splits up into just as many separate problems of the type treated above [in the one-dimensional situation] as there are co-ordinates present. The eigenfunctions are products of Hermite orthogonal functions, and the eigenvalues of the whole problem appear as sums of those separate problems, taken in every possible combination. No eigenvalue (for the whole system) is multiple, if we presume that there is no rational relation between the $\nu_0$-values' (Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 518; English translation, p. 33).

Schrödinger knew, of course, that in nature oscillator problems occurred which did not correspond to the non-degenerate case. Certainly, these also had to be treated in wave mechanics, but proper care had to be applied, as in the solutions difficulties of uniqueness might show up. Thus: 'Multiple eigenvalues appear and the "separation" [of the co-ordinates in the sense of the old quantum theory] can certainly be effected in other co-ordinates, e.g. in the case of the isotropic, space oscillator in spherical polars' (Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 518; English translation, p. 33).

In his published paper, Schrödinger did not display such a treatment of the spatial oscillator in spherical co-ordinates; there he restricted himself to the following hint in a footnote: 'We are led thus to an equation in [the radial variable] *r*, which may be treated by the method shown in the Kepler problem of Part I' (Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 518; English translation, footnote 1 on p. 33). In his notebook on *'Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. I'* however, he wrote down the solution in detail (on pp. 47–48). In particular, the spatial oscillator was described by the second-order differential equation for the radial wave function $\psi$,

$$ \frac{d^2\psi}{dr^2} + \frac{2}{r} \frac{d\psi}{dr} + \left( a - br^2 - \frac{n(n + 1)}{r^2} \right) \psi = 0, \quad n = 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots \quad (36) $$

On replacing $r^2$ by the new variable $z$, Schrödinger transformed Eq. (36) into a Laplace equation, similar to the one occurring in the nonrelativistic Kepler

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0233 -->

592 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Chapter IV &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Early Response and Applications

problem. Its unique and final solution required either one of the following conditions to be satisfied,

$$ \frac{a}{\sqrt{b}} = 4l - 2 - 1, \quad l = 0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots, \qquad (37a) $$

or

$$ \frac{a}{\sqrt{b}} = 4l + 2n + 1, \quad l = 0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots \qquad (37b) $$

Schrödinger finally added three comments: (i) ‘Hence, essentially [we obtain] the same as previously.’ (ii) ‘Of course, one can also treat this in [co-ordinates] $x, y$ and $z$ instead of $r, \theta$ and $\phi$.’ (iii) ‘Evidently, in all these cases one is dealing with a generalization of Hermite polynomials’ (*Notebook I*, p. 48).$^{15}$ The fact that the eigenvalues of the spatial, degenerate oscillator in wave mechanics do not depend upon the particular method of treatment—i.e., whether one solved a wave equation in spherical or in Cartesian co-ordinates—led Schrödinger to the general conclusion: ‘The eigenvalues that we get, however, are certainly in each case exactly the same, at least insofar as we are able to prove the “completeness” of a system of eigenfunctions, obtained in *one* way’ (Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 518; English translation, p. 33). This situation, with respect to the eigenvalues obtained from wave mechanics, resembled the one for the energy states in the old quantum theory because of the Sommerfeld–Epstein quantum conditions. Still, in the undulatory treatment a—as Schrödinger said—‘not unwelcome’ (‘*nicht unerfreulicher*’) difference could be observed with respect to another difficulty of the previous quantum theory of atomic systems. In the latter, it was possible to connect the same energy values with various, completely deviating paths or orbits. Also, in the wave mechanical treatment of degenerate systems different methods of solution—say, in the case of the nonrelativistic hydrogen problem either the use of spherical coordinates or of parabolic co-ordinates—do result in quite different systems of eigenfunctions; but, due to the linearity of the wave problem and the completeness of the systems of eigenfunctions, one is always able to express a given eigenfunction of one system by a linear combination of eigenfunctions—Schrödinger called this ‘*lineares Aggregat*’ (‘linear aggregate’)—of the other systems. He stressed: ‘A *possible state of vibration* is not just the single *eigenvibration* [of a given system of eigenfunctions], but an arbitrary, finite or infinite, *linear aggregate* of such vibrations’ (Schrödinger,

$^{15}$ We should mention that Schrödinger, in his notebook, also carried out a calculation which proved the second claim in footnote 1 on page 518 of his second communication, namely: ‘The polynomial appearing in the Kepler problem [of Part I] is the $(2n + 1)$th differential quotient of the $(n + l)$th polynomial of Laguerre, as I subsequently found’ (Schrödinger, 1926d; English translation, p. 33, footnote 1).

Clearly, he defined with this statement a new concept of the state of an atomic system, a concept which he had already intuitively guessed a year earlier when speaking about 'higher harmonics of the orbits of series electrons' (Schrödinger to Sommerfeld, 7 March 1925), i.e., the situation where the atomic systems were characterized by a series of eigenfrequencies rather than by single electron orbits.¹⁶

### The Rotator and the Diatomic Molecule in Wave Mechanics

In the notebook on *'Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. I,'* Schrödinger discussed, immediately after the spatial oscillator, first Laguerre polynomials—according to *Courant-Hilbert*—and showed that the eigenfunction, $P(n, l)$, occurring in the solution of the nonrelativistic Kepler problem—see Eq. (163) in Section III.3—could be obtained by a derivation of the $(n + l)$th Laguerre polynomial, i.e.,

$$P(n, l) = f(r) = \frac{d^{(2n+1)}}{dr^{(2n+1)}} L_{n+l}(r). \quad (38)$$

(See *Notebook I*, pp. 49–50.) He then continued directly with a new problem, the *'Rotator mit freier Achse'* ('Rotator with Free Axis'), for which he formulated only the wave equation (p. 50) without presenting the solution. Finally, he discussed the problem of the *'Rotierendes und schwingendes Molekül'* ('Rotating and Vibrating Molecule'), which he displayed in quite some detail—starting with an outline of the two-dimensional problem (p. 51), then presenting the wave equation for the three-dimensional problem (p. 52) and giving its solution, including a discussion of suitable approximations (pp. 53–55). With these preparations, Schrödinger directly composed those parts of his second communication on *'Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem'* dealing with the application of wave mechanics to the rotator problem (i.e., Subsections 3.2, 3.3 and 3.4 of Schrödinger, 1926d).

Schrödinger started out with what he called 'the simplest conceivable example of vibration theory' (Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 519, English translation, p. 34): the rotator having an axis fixed in space. It corresponded, on the one hand, to a one-dimensional problem, hence the line element was, of course, Euclidean in the angle $\phi$. On the other hand, it involved no potential energy at all.¹⁷ Consequently the equation of vibration, or the wave equation, assumed the form,

$$\frac{1}{A} \frac{d^2\psi}{d\phi^2} + \frac{8\pi^2E}{h^2} \psi = 0, \quad (39)$$

where $A$ denoted the moment of inertia. Equation (39) evidently possessed the

¹⁶See our discussion in Section II.4.
¹⁷Because of this primitive simplicity, Schrödinger did not bother to treat the one-dimensional rotator in his preliminary notes.

solution

$$
\psi = \begin{cases}
\sin\left(\sqrt{\frac{8\pi^2EA}{h^2}}\phi\right), \\[1em]
\cos\left(\sqrt{\frac{8\pi^2EA}{h^2}}\phi\right).
\end{cases}
$$
(40)

The boundary condition, demanding the uniqueness and the continuity of the solution throughout the entire range of the angle $\phi$, led to the equation

$$
E_n = \frac{n^2h^2}{8\pi^2A},
$$
(41)

with $n$ assuming integral values$^{18}$

$$
n = 0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots
$$
(41a)

By Eq. (41) the energy values of the rotator were restricted to a discrete sequence, as was formerly the case through the quantization rule in the Bohr-Sommerfeld theory of the same system, which had been suggested—even before Bohr and Sommerfeld—by Paul Ehrenfest (Ehrenfest, 1913b). One had also tried to discuss physical examples of microscopic rotating systems; thus one associated energy differences from Eq. (41) with the band spectra or the specific heats of diatomic molecules, achieving rather mixed success.$^{19}$ Schrödinger now declared frankly: ‘No meaning, however, can be attached to the result of the application to band spectra . . . . It is a peculiar fact that our theory gives *another* result for the rotator with *free* axis. *And this is true in general*. It is not allowable in the applications of wave mechanics, to think of the freedom of movement of the system as being more strictly limited, in order to simplify calculation, than it *actually is*, even when we know from the integrals of the mechanical equations that in a single movement certain definite freedoms are not made use of’ (Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 520; English translation, pp. 34–35). Undulatory mechanics, i.e., the theory describing microscopic (mechanical) systems, deviated strongly from the usual mechanics insofar as properties of single paths, including their symmetry properties, did not play a role. Schrödinger emphasized: ‘A wave process fills the *whole* of the phase space. It is well known that even the *number* of the dimensions in which a wave process takes place is very significant’ (Schrödinger, *loc. cit.*; English translation, p. 35).

IV.1 The Scheme Starts to Work **595**

While a diatomic molecule could not, even in a weak approximation, be represented by a rigid rotator with *fixed* axis, a rigid rotator with *free* axis may be considered a suitably simplified model of the atomic system. Schrödinger discussed the model in Section 3.3 of his paper, where he used the two polar angles, $\theta$ and $\phi$, made by the line connecting the two nuclei (of the molecule), as position variables. In those variables and their canonically conjugate (angular) momenta, $p_{\theta}$ and $p_{\phi}$, the kinetic energy was expressed as

$$\mathcal{T} = \frac{1}{2A} \left( p_{\theta}^{2} + \frac{p_{\phi}^{2}}{\sin^{2} \theta} \right). \tag{42}$$

Equation (42) also described the kinetic energy of a point particle whose motion is constrained to a spherical surface. The Laplacean operator $\Delta$ in the fundamental equation (12), therefore, can be identified in this case with that part of the spatial Laplacean operator in spherical co-ordinates, $r, \theta$ and $\phi$, which depends only on the polar angles, i.e.,

$$\Delta = \frac{1}{\sin \theta} \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}\left( \sin \theta \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \right) + \frac{1}{\sin^{2} \theta} \frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial \phi^{2}}. \tag{43}$$

Finally, the wave equation for the rigid rotator with free axis becomes rather similar to Eq. (39), i.e.,

$$\frac{1}{A} \Delta \psi + \frac{8\pi^{2} E}{h^{2}} \psi = 0. \tag{44}$$

Due to the different structure of the Laplacean operator, however, the wave mechanical boundary conditions yielded the eigenvalue equation

$$\frac{8\pi^{2} A}{h^{2}} E = n(n+1), \tag{45}$$

with

$$n = 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots, \tag{45a}$$

or the energy levels

$$E_{n} = \frac{n(n+1)h^{2}}{8\pi^{2} A}, \quad n=0,1,2,3, \dots \tag{46}$$

Schrödinger realized immediately that the result, Eq. (46), deviated from *all* results of the old quantum theory. However, he also noticed that ‘various arguments from experiment . . . led to putting “half-integral” values for $n$ in formula

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0237 -->

596 | Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

[(41)]' (Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 521; English translation, p. 35). Indeed, the use of half-integral quantum numbers in the old quantum-theoretical rotator formula provided practically the same result as Eq. (46), because the identity

$$n(n + 1) = (n + \frac{1}{2})^2 - \frac{1}{4} \qquad (47)$$

reduced the discrepancy between the energy values given by Eqs. (41) and (46), respectively, to—in general—the small, additional term $\frac{1}{4}$. The practical identity of the wave mechanical result for the rotator with free axis, and the result derived from the old quantization rules with half-integral quantum numbers, could even be shown to be valid in the case of the short-wave bands as well, where electronic jumps resulted in different moments of inertia for the initial and final state of the molecule. For that purpose, Schrödinger discussed (in the last part—Section 3.4—of his second communication) a more realistic model of a diatomic molecule.

The full microscopic system describing a diatomic model possesses six degrees of freedom, associated with the two-body problem of masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ and their Cartesian position co-ordinates $x_1, y_1, z_1$ and $x_2, y_2, z_2$. Now a potential energy $V$ exists between the two masses, given by the expression

$$V = 2\pi^2 \nu_0^2 \mu (r - r_0)^2, \qquad (48)$$

with $r$ denoting their distance, i.e.,

$$r = \sqrt{(x_1 - x_2)^2 + (y_1 - y_2)^2 + (z_1 - z_2)^2}, \qquad (48a)$$

and $\mu$ the ‘resultant mass’, or,

$$\mu = \frac{m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}. \qquad (48b)$$

Evidently, the two mass points—representing essentially the nuclei of the two atoms—perform vibrations with frequency $\nu_0$, such that their connecting line remains fixed in space; $r_0$ is the minimum distance. In his preparatory notes (in *Notebook I*, p. 51), Schrödinger first simplified the problem by treating it in two dimensions, in order to find the structure of the solution quickly. He especially introduced—instead of the variables $x_1, y_1$ and $x_2, y_2$—the new variables

$$\left. \begin{aligned} x &= x_1 - x_2, & y &= y_1 - y_2, \\ \xi &= \frac{m_1 x_1 + m_2 x_2}{m_1 + m_2}, & \eta &= \frac{m_1 y_1 + m_2 y_2}{m_1 + m_2}. \end{aligned} \right\} \qquad (49)$$

He then obtained the following wave equation

$$\frac{1}{\mu} \left( \frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial y^2} \right) + \frac{1}{m_1 + m_2} \left( \frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial \xi^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial \eta^2} \right) + [a'' - b'(r - r_0)^2]\psi = 0, \qquad (50)$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0238 -->

with the constants  

$$a'' = \frac{8\pi^2 E}{h^2} \quad \text{and} \quad b' = \frac{16\pi^4 \nu_0^2 \mu}{h^2}. \tag{50a}$$  

To solve Eq. (50) he suggested the following *Ansatz* for the wave function,  

$$\psi = \psi_1(\xi, \eta) \cdot \psi_2(x, y), \tag{51}$$  

which is ‘separable’ in the two pairs of co-ordinates. Evidently, the wave equation satisfied by $\psi_1(\xi, \eta)$, namely,  

$$\frac{1}{m_1 + m_2} \left( \frac{\partial^2 \psi_1}{\partial \xi^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \psi_1}{\partial \eta^2} \right) + \text{const. } \psi_1 = 0, \tag{52}$$  

described a force-free motion of a microscopic mass point. Thus a constant solution $\psi_1(\xi, \eta)$, representing a mass point at rest, implied a zero value for the constant in Eq. (52), while other solutions, e.g.,  

$$\psi_1(\xi, \eta) = \frac{\sin(k \sqrt{\xi^2 + \eta^2})}{\sqrt{\xi^2 + \eta^2}} \tag{53}$$  

led to a finite value for the constant, say $8\pi E_t / h^2$. In the latter case, the whole molecule performed a translational motion with the positive translation energy $E_t$. In his notebook, Schrödinger simply added: ‘We draw this [result] into the constant $a''$’ (‘Wir ziehen das in die Konstante $a''$ hinein,’ *Notebook I*, p. 51).²⁰ That is, he indicated that one could restrict oneself to solving only the wave equation for $\psi_2(x, y)$, an equation having the same structure as Eq. (50), but involving a slightly different constant, $a'$, namely,  

$$a' = \frac{8\pi^2 (E - E_t)}{h^2}, \tag{54}$$  

instead of $a''$.  

In the case of the spatial problem, exactly the same type of separation, now in the two triples of co-ordinates, $x, y, z$ and $\xi, \eta, \zeta$, could be achieved. The equation for the wave function in the variables $\xi, \eta$ and $\zeta$ again described the

translational motion of the molecule with the positive kinetic energy $E_\mathrm{t}$.$^{21}$ The equation for the wave function $f(x, y, z)$ in the other variables, i.e.,

$$
\frac{1}{\mu} \left( \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z^2} \right) + [a' - b'(r - r_0)^2]f = 0, \tag{55}
$$

then was transformed by introducing the spherical co-ordinates, $r, \theta$ and $\phi$, instead of $x, y$ and $z$.$^{22}$ As in the case of the nonrelativistic hydrogen problem, discussed in Chapter III, an angle-dependent factor of the wave function could also be split off here, namely, a surface harmonic with eigenvalues $-n(n + 1)$. The remaining $r$-dependent function $\chi$ had to satisfy the wave equation

$$
\frac{\partial^2 \chi}{\partial \rho^2} \left[ \mu a' - \mu b' \rho^2 - \frac{n(n+1)}{(r_0 + \rho_0)^2} \right] \chi = 0, \tag{56}
$$

with

$$
\rho = r - r_0. \tag{56a}
$$

Schrödinger was not able to present a straightforward solution of Eq. (56). He realized, however, that it might be reformulated as

$$
\frac{\partial^2 \chi}{\partial \rho'^2} + \left( a - b \rho'^2 + \left[ \frac{\rho'}{r_0} \right] \right) \chi = 0, \tag{57}
$$

with $a$ and $b$ denoting slightly modified constants and $\rho' = \rho$ minus a small constant.$^{23}$ Hence, if terms of the order $\rho'/r_0$ and higher powers could be neglected, Eq. (57) possessed the same form as Eq. (1), i.e., the equation describing the one-dimensional linear oscillator. Solving this equation along the lines of the oscillator procedure yielded the following discrete energy eigenvalues:

$$
E = E_\mathrm{t} + \frac{n(n+1)h^2}{8\pi^2 A} \left( 1 - \frac{\mathscr{E}}{1 + 3\mathscr{E}} \right) + \frac{2l + 1}{2} h \nu_0 \sqrt{1 + 3\mathscr{E}}, \tag{58}
$$

with

$$
n, l = 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots, \tag{58a}
$$

$^{21}$Schrödinger remarked in his paper (on pp. 523–524) that the treatment of a system of molecules in a box led to discrete eigenvalues for $E_\mathrm{t}$, and finally to Albert Einstein’s gas theory, referring to his recent paper on that subject (Schrödinger, 1926b).

and $\mathcal{A}$ denoting the (small) quantity  

$$
\mathcal{A} = \frac{n(n + 1)h^2}{16\pi^2\nu_0^2 A^2} \tag{58b}
$$  

The moment of inertia, $A$, is defined as $\mu r_0^2$.  

Schrödinger added two comments to the result, Eq. (58). First, he observed that $\mathcal{A}$ denoted (in the old mechanical language) the square of the ratio of frequency of rotation to frequency of vibration ($\nu_0$), which was indeed—for not outrageously high (rotational quantum numbers) $n$—a small quantity. Consequently, the energy of the diatomic molecule consisted of three separate terms: translational ($E_t$), rotational (i.e., $n(n + 1)h^2/8\pi^2A$, if the $\mathcal{A}$-term was neglected), and vibrational (i.e., $(2l + 1)/2\ h\nu_0$, with the $\mathcal{A}$-correction neglected). Second, the suppression of the term $[\rho'/r_0]$—which allowed one to integrations Eq. (57)—could only be justified for small vibrational eigenvalues, i.e., small integers $l$, in which the eigenfunctions of the oscillator (see Figure 3) do not extend very far in $r$-space.  

In spite of the fact that the result, Eq. (58), very much resembled the one used previously in the analysis of molecular spectra, Schrödinger refused to compare his result with the data. The reason for his hesitation was that he had not yet taken into account deviations of the nuclear vibrations from the harmonic type—which would introduce further corrections besides those given by the $\mathcal{A}$-terms. He confined himself to having shown that  

> the intuitive idea of the *equilibrium configuration* of the nuclear system [in the molecule] retains its meaning in undulatory mechanics also, and . . . the manner in which it does so, provided that the wave amplitude $\psi$ is different from zero practically only in a small neighbourhood of the equilibrium configuration. (Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 526; English translation, p. 39)  

On the other hand, he claimed that the non-harmonic terms—necessary to complete the description of the diatomic molecules—could also be introduced in a wave mechanical treatment via the same method, which had been ‘selected skillfully by [Adolf] Kratzer for the classical mechanical treatment,’ if one made use of ‘the theory of *perturbation of eigenvalues and eigenfunctions*’ (Schrödinger, *loc. cit.*). He continued: ‘This “perturbation theory” is the complete counterpart of that of classical mechanics, except that it is simpler because in undulatory mechanics we are always in the domain of *linear* relations’ (Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 527; English translation, p. 40). Finally, in concluding the second communication, he announced an ‘important practical success . . . that the *Stark effect* of first order will be found to be really completely in accord with Epstein’s formula, which has become unimpeachable through the confirmation of experience’ (Schrödinger, *loc. cit.*).

Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

# Undulatory Perturbation Theory

Schrödinger introduced his third communication on ‘*Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem*,’ which he submitted in early May 1926, again via Wilhelm Wien in Munich, to *Annalen der Physik*, as follows:

> As has already been mentioned at the end of the preceding paper [i.e., Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 527], the available range of application of the eigenvalue theory can by comparatively elementary methods be considerably increased beyond the “directly soluble problems”; for, as one may figure out, the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions can readily be approximately determined for *such* boundary value problems as are sufficiently closely related to a directly soluble problem. In analogy with ordinary mechanics, let us call the method in question the *perturbation theory* for the eigenvalue problem. It is based upon the important *property of continuity* possessed by eigenvalues and eigenfunctions, principally, for our purpose, upon their *continuous* dependence on the *coefficients* of the differential equation, and less upon the extent of the domain and on the boundary conditions, since in our case the domain (“entire *q*-space”) and the boundary conditions (“remaining finite”) are generally the same for the unperturbed and perturbed problems. (Schrödinger, 1926f, p. 437; slightly revised English translation, p. 62)

Schrödinger’s first interest in the topic of ‘the perturbation theory for the eigenvalue problem,’ however, dates back to January 1926, immediately after the completion of communication No. I, and it can be documentarily fixed through an entry of one and a half pages in the notebook on ‘*Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. I*’.

As the first step Schrödinger wrote down what he called the ‘*totale Differentialgleichung*,’ i.e., the differential equation which can be integrated directly. He remarked: ‘We use it in the simple form, into which it can always be brought, i.e.,

$$ \frac{d^2u}{dx^2} + [E - f(x)]u = 0. \tag{59} $$

He continued further:

Now, let an eigenvalue $E_0$ of this equation be known, and let $u_0$ be an associated eigenfunction. Then we consider the [new] equation

$$ \frac{d^2u}{dx^2} + [E - f(x) - \lambda \phi(x)]u = 0. \tag{[(60)]} $$

We say, it may possess for an eigenvalue $E$,

$$ E = E_0 + \lambda \varepsilon \tag{[(61)]} $$

the eigenfunction $u$,

$$ u = u_0 + \lambda v. \tag{[(62)]} $$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0242 -->

IV.1 The Scheme Starts to Work 601

We introduce [Eqs. (61) and (62) into Eq. (60) and obtain]

$$ \frac{d^2 u_0}{dx^2} + \lambda \frac{d^2 v}{dx^2} + [E_0 + \lambda \varepsilon - f(x) - \lambda \phi(x)](u_0 + \lambda v) = 0, \quad [(63)] $$

[or]

$$ \frac{d^2 u_0}{dx^2} + [E_0 - f(x)] u_0 + \lambda \left\{ \frac{d^2 v}{dx^2} + (\varepsilon - \phi) u_0 + (E_0 - f) v \right\} = 0. \quad [(63')] $$

Hence $v$ should have to solve the *inhomogeneous* equation

$$ \frac{d^2 v}{dx^2} + (E_0 - f) v = (\phi - \varepsilon) u_0. \quad [(64)] $$

In general, this equation possesses, however, no solution at all for the *eigenvalue* [i.e., $E_0 + \lambda \varepsilon$], except for the sole case that the right-hand side [of Eq. (64)] is orthogonal to $u_0$, i.e., if [we have]

$$ \int (\phi - \varepsilon) u_0^2 \, dx = 0. \quad [(65)] $$

That is, we obtain

$$ \varepsilon = \frac{\int \phi u_0^2 \, dx}{\int u_0^2 \, dx} = \int \phi u_0^2 \, dx, \quad [(66)] $$

[the last equation being valid] if [the eigenfunction $u_0$ to Eq. (59)] is normalized.
*(Notebook I, pp. 56–57)*

Schrödinger then formulated the ‘Theorem: The perturbation of an eigenvalue is equal to the integral over the product of the “perturbation function” and the square of the unperturbed eigenfunction.’ He added: ‘By the way, the differential equation must be brought into the *self-adjoint form*,’ and commented on the whole result with the words: ‘So-to-speak: average value over the unperturbed motion’ (*Notebook I*, p. 57).

The immediate purpose of developing the perturbation theory in wave mechanics was—as Schrödinger mentioned several times in letters (e.g., Schrödinger to Sommerfeld, 20 February 1926) and the second communication (Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 527)—to treat the influence of a homogeneous (static) electric field on the energy states of a hydrogen atom or, more accurately, their differences. The wave equation for this problem, the so-called Stark effect, could in fact be

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0243 -->

602 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

brought into a form corresponding to Eq. (60), namely (see Schrödinger, 1926f, p. 459, Eq. (41)),

$$z \frac{d^2 u}{dz^2} + \frac{du}{dz} + \left[ \frac{Dz^2}{(2\sqrt{-A})^3} + E - f(z) \right] u = 0, \tag{67}$$

where the last term in the square bracket represents the potential energy of the free hydrogen atom, while the first term denotes the influence of the electric field. The coefficient, $D/(2\sqrt{-A})^3$, where $D$ and $A$ are given by the equations

$$D = \pm \frac{\pi^2 m_e e F}{h^2} \tag{68}$$

and

$$A = \frac{2\pi^2 m_e E}{h^2} \tag{69}$$

(with $m_e$ and $e$ denoting mass and electric charge of the electron and $h$ Planck’s constant), is for *not too large* electric field strength $F$ indeed a small quantity. Hence the perturbation treatment of Eq. (67) can be justified, and it finally yields the same result as Paul Sophus Epstein had obtained ten years earlier on the basis of the old quantum theory (Epstein, 1916c), a result perfectly in accord with the empirical data.

Although Schrödinger found the above result only after lengthy calculations, he had completed the first successful treatment of the Stark effect before the end of February 1926—even before the submission of his second communication, as we shall display in some detail below. At the same time, he also had available an extended version of the perturbation theory, which allowed another, different treatment of the same problem.$^{24}$ Hence, the main steps towards establishing the wave mechanical perturbation scheme were taken within a period of about a month including the last week of January and the first three weeks of February. The reason for this extremely fast progress—at the same time Schrödinger, besides presenting his lecture courses and performing other duties as a university professor during the on-going winter semester, also completed the foundations of wave mechanics (i.e., the first two sections of the second communication)—Schrödinger disclosed in a letter to Wien (of 22 February 1926) by referring to the ‘wonderful mathematics of Hilbert,’ and in the published papers (especially, Schrödinger, 1926d, f) by frequent quotations from pages of Courant and Hilbert’s *Methoden der mathematischen Physik*.

$^{24}$The main reason for concluding that Schrödinger had the perturbation theory and the Epstein formula for the Stark effect in hand *before* completing his second communication is as follows: the correct result for the Stark effect occurs on page 27 of the notebook on *‘Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. II’*, the extended perturbation theory on pp. 28–33 of the same notebook, while essential parts of the second communication—the ones dealing with the foundation of the wave mechanical scheme—occur only in the later notebook on *‘Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. III’*.

IV.1  The Scheme Starts to Work 603

The possibility of developing a perturbation theory for wave mechanics rests, as Schrödinger realized, on the continuity property of the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the wave equation which constitute the main concepts and tools of the scheme. In the book by Courant and Hilbert a detailed section, i.e., Section VI, §2.4, was devoted to this problem (see Courant and Hilbert, 1924, pp. 337–342). In particular, Courant and Hilbert considered a differential equation of the Sturm–Liouville type, namely,

$$L[y] + \lambda \rho y = 0, \qquad (70)$$

with

$$L[y] = (py')' - qy, \qquad (70a)$$

where $p$ and $q$ were functions of the independent variable $x$ and prime denoted the derivative with respect to $x$. Then they proved the theorem: ‘The $n$th eigenvalue of the differential equation $L[y] + \lambda \rho y = 0$ changes, for all boundary conditions considered, continuously with the coefficients of the differential equation [i.e., with the functions $p, q$ and $\rho$]’ (Courant and Hilbert, 1924, p. 338).²⁵

The eigenvalue problem of the Sturm–Liouville equation—we recognize that *all of Schrödinger’s wave equations, for example, Eq. (59), were of that type*—was treated in Sections V, §5.1 and V, §10.5 of the book (Courant and Hilbert, pp. 237–241; pp. 289–291). Equation (70) resulted, as the mathematicians wrote, from a generalization of the (classical) equation for an inhomogeneous string. The eigenfunctions, $y_i(x)$, of this equation therefore described eigenvibrations of the string with frequency $\nu = \sqrt{\lambda_i}$; and the eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ can be shown to form an ordered (positive) sequence, $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3 \ldots$, with each value occuring only once. Different eigenfunctions are orthogonal, i.e., satisfy the equation

$$\int_{0}^{\pi} \rho y_i y_k dx = 0 \qquad (i \neq k), \qquad (71)$$

and the entire sequence, $\sqrt{\rho} y_1, \sqrt{\rho} y_2, \sqrt{\rho} y_3 \ldots$, constitutes a complete orthogonal system of functions. Finally, in Section V, §10.2 (see Courant and Hilbert, 1924, pp. 276–279), Eq. (70) was altered by an additional term, namely,

$$L(y) + \lambda \rho y - \psi(x) = 0. \qquad (72)$$

The authors showed that for any eigenfunction, $y_i(x)$, of this new equation the relation

$$\int y_i(x) \psi(x) = 0 \qquad (73)$$

²⁵ The same evidently applied to associated eigenfunctions.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0245 -->

604 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Chapter IV &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Early Response and Applications

had to be valid, i.e., the inhomogeneous term $\psi(x)$ had to be orthogonal to *all* $y_i(x)$ solving Eq. (72). The orthogonality property was, as Schrödinger emphasized, ‘the starting point of the whole perturbation theory’ (‘*der springende Punkt der ganzen Störungstheorie*,’ Schrödinger, 1926f, p. 443). According to Courant and Hilbert, Eq. (72) might be interpreted as describing the vibrations of a string, on which an external force is imposed. Mechanically, condition (73) then means: ‘If the external force is in resonance with an eigenvibration, then and only then will there exist a stationary state, provided this force does not perform work in the system moving with the pure eigenvibration in question’ (Courant and Hilbert, 1924, p. 279).

In his published paper (i.e., in the third communication: Schrödinger, 1926f, p. 443), Schrödinger quoted the relevant pages of Courant and Hilbert’s book, including especially the above-mentioned orthogonality relation (73) and its physical interpretation. He further reformulated the results of the mathematicians in the language of wave mechanics. This led exactly to the steps described above from Eqs. (60) to (65).<sup>26</sup> Schrödinger would also copy (Schrödinger, 1926f, pp. 444–445) the derivation and result for the perturbation of the *k*th eigenfunction (of the perturbed Eq. (60)),

$$u_k^* = u_k + \lambda v_k \quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad (74)$$

(with $u_k$ the unperturbed eigenfunction solving Eq. (59)), namely,

$$v_k = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \gamma_{ki} u_i(x), \quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad (75)$$

with

$$\gamma_{ki} = \frac{\int \phi u_k u_i \, dx}{E_k - E_i}, \quad i \neq k, \quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad (75\text{a})$$

from *Methoden der mathematischen Physik*.<sup>27</sup>

**The Transcription of Epstein’s Calculation of the Stark Effect**

Schrödinger’s interest in applying the methods of undulatory mechanics to the problem of the Stark effect was awakened at a very early stage of the whole enterprise. On page 12 of the notebook ‘*Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. I*’—i.e., in the part that he composed during the first weeks of January, perhaps even before returning from the Arosa Christmas vacations to Zurich—he included in a

*Programm*, besides the problem of the action of a magnetic field on the atom, a second point, entitled ‘*E-Feld. Parabelkoordinaten. $\nu$-Spektrum*?’ (‘*E*-Field. Parabolic Co-ordinates. $\nu$-Spectrum?’). In carrying out this part of the programme, he introduced parabolic co-ordinates, i.e., the angle $\phi$ (around the axis given by the electric field $E$) and certain variables $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$, in which the wave equation for the hydrogen atom in the electric field could be separated—that is, written as triple of wave equations, each involving either $\phi$, $\lambda_1$ or $\lambda_2$. On the latter equations Schrödinger commented: ‘Seems to lead to Epstein’s quantum conditions, if one takes into account the homogeneous electric field’ (*Notebook I*, p. 14). But he was not sure about the result.

A little later in the notebook—i.e., after he had obtained the first complete solution of the nonrelativistic hydrogen atom (including eigenvalues and eigenfunctions) with the help of the techniques derived from Schlesinger’s book (see our discussion in Section III.3)—Schrödinger tried to treat the two equations for the parabolic co-ordinates $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ with exactly the same method; however, he did not proceed as far as finding the solution of the problem (see *Notebook I*, pp. 24–29). Towards the end of the notebook, he developed the first version of his perturbation theory (pp. 56–57, see our discussion above), upon which he launched a new attack on the Stark effect in the following pages (58–72). This first systematic treatment, though, did not quite lead to the desired result; hence, Schrödinger renewed his efforts on the Stark effect in the following notebook on ‘*Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. II*,’ pp. 24–27, and finally succeeded in confirming Paul Sophus Epstein’s formula on the basis of wave mechanics. Schrödinger presented a condensed and improved version of the calculation, summarizing all these efforts in §3 of his third communication (Schrödinger, 1926f, pp. 457–464).

The key to solving the eigenvalue problem for the hydrogen atom in a homogeneous electric field of strength $F$ in the $z$-direction, which is described by the wave equation

$$\Delta \psi + \frac{8\pi^2 m_{\mathrm{e}}}{h^2} \left( E + \frac{e^2}{r} - eFz \right) \psi = 0, \qquad (76)$$

—with $m_{\mathrm{e}}$, $e$ and $h$ denoting the mass and charge of the electron and Planck’s constant, respectively—consists of introducing—as Epstein had done a long time before (Epstein, 1916c)—parabolic co-ordinates into the problem. In the published paper, Schrödinger selected spatial parabolic co-ordinates defined by the equations

$$x = +\sqrt{\lambda_1\lambda_2} \cdot \cos \phi, \quad y = +\sqrt{\lambda_1\lambda_2} \cdot \sin \phi$$

and

$$z = \frac{1}{2}(\lambda_1 - \lambda_2), \qquad (77)$$

with $n$ an integral constant $(=0, 1, 2, 3, \dots)$; the coefficients $B$ and $D$ by

The solution of Eqs. (80) in the field-free case—i.e., in the absence of the Stark term $D\xi^2$—and for energy smaller than zero ($A < 0$, bound states), yielded the well-known Balmer term formula,

$$E = -\frac{2\pi^2 m_e e^4}{l^2 h^2}, \tag{85}$$

with the integral ‘principal quantum number’ $l$ given by the equation

$$l = k_1 + k_2 + n + 1. \tag{86}$$

The quantities $k_1$ and $k_2$ have to assume, like $n$, integral values, i.e.,

$$n, k_1, k_2 = 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots, \tag{86a}$$

For the purpose of obtaining the eigenfunctions of the (perturbation)-free nonrelativistic hydrogen atom, Schrödinger made use—in *Notebook I*, pp. 64 ff., as well as in the paper (1926f, pp. 460–461)—of the fact that Eqs. (80b) and (80c) could be brought into the different form

$$
\frac{d^2u}{d\eta^2} + \frac{n + 1}{\eta} \frac{du}{d\eta} + \left[ \frac{D\eta}{(2\sqrt{-A})^3} - \frac{1}{4} + \frac{B}{\sqrt{-A}} \frac{1}{\eta} \right] u = 0, \tag{87}
$$

if one replaced the wave functions $\Lambda$ by $u$, via the equation

$$
\Lambda = \xi^{n/2}u, \tag{87a}
$$

and the variable $\xi (= \lambda_1, \lambda_2)$ by the variable $\eta$, via the equation

$$
2\xi\sqrt{-A} = \eta. \tag{87b}
$$

In the case of zero electric field (no perturbation: $D = 0$), Eq. (87) turned out to be the equation satisfied by the $n$th derivative of the $(n + k)$th Laguerre polynomial, multiplied by $\exp(-\eta/2)$; hence the solutions were$^{32}$

$$
u_k(\eta) = \exp\left(-\frac{\eta}{2}\right) L_{n+k}^n(\eta), \tag{88a}
$$

where the corresponding eigenvalue was given by the equation

$$
\frac{B}{\sqrt{-A}} = \frac{n + 1}{2} + k, \qquad k = 0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots \tag{88b}
$$

In order to apply the perturbation theory described above, Eq. (87) must be taken *in a form which is self-adjoint*, hence it must be multiplied by the factor

given in *Courant–Hilbert* (1924, p. 78, Eq. (72)). He found by trial that $\exp(-x/2) L_{n+k}^n(x)$ satisfied the equation

The analogue to the old ‘equatorial quantum number’ in the new scheme was the number $n + 1$, and Schrödinger noticed happily: ‘The value zero for the *latter* is thus *automatically* excluded by wave mechanics, just as by Heisenberg’s mechanics’ (Schrödinger, 1926f, p. 463, English translation, p. 81). Indeed, in the old quantum theory, electron orbits passing through the nucleus (as connected to the equatorial quantum number zero) had to be arbitrarily excluded, while in the quantum mechanics developed by Heisenberg the exclusion happened automatically. With the reproduction of this result, Schrödinger’s Stark effect calculation could be considered as a complete success.$^{36}$

**Perturbation Theory for Many Degrees of Freedom**

The treatment of mechanical systems with the help of the mathematical method of small perturbations in celestial mechanics had been developed in the eighteenth century. One had discussed then, for example, the influence of other planets on the orbits of the earth and the moon. This theory of perturbed periodic systems had been perfected during the nineteenth century within the scheme of the Hamilton–Jacobi theory of multiply periodic systems, a theory which had been taken over around 1920 by physicists treating atomic and molecular systems (see, e.g., Bohr, 1918a, b: Born and Brody, 1921b; Born and Pauli, 1922). In the latter field it had led to certain successes and also to notable failures, as in the theory of the energy states of the helium atom (Kramers, 1923a; Born and Heisenberg, 1923b). After Werner Heisenberg had formulated the principles of quantum mechanics in July 1925 (Heisenberg, 1925c), he had established in the fall of 1925, along with Max Born and Pascual Jordan in the so-called three-man paper (Born, Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926) a systematic perturbation theory within the scheme of matrix mechanics. Born, Heisenberg and Jordan distinguished, in their paper, between the method applicable to systems having one degree of freedom (Chapter 1, §4) and the method valid for systems having several degrees of freedom, both in the case of no degeneracy (Chapter 2, §1) and of degeneracy (Chapter 2, §2). Further, they wrote down a general perturbation theory that could be used in the case of systems possessing arbitrarily many degrees of freedom, non-degenerate as well as degenerate ones, based on Hilbert’s theory of eigenvalues of Hermitean forms (in Chapter 3, §2).$^{37}$

---
$^{36}$Schrödinger referred to the recent papers by Wolfgang Pauli (1926a) and Niels Bohr (1925b), who had stressed this point in connection with matrix mechanic, stating: ‘This important and gratifying circumstance was already brought to light in Part I in counting the constants [Schrödinger, 1926c, p. 370], and also afterwards in §2 of Part I [p. 371] in connection with the azimuthal quantum number, through the non-existence of states of vibration corresponding to *pendulum orbits*; its full meaning, however, only fully dawned on me through the remarks of the two authors just quoted’ (Schrödinger, 1926f, p. 463; English translation, p. 81).

$^{37}$We have discussed the development of the matrix mechanical perturbation theory in Volume 3, Sections III.2 and III.5.
