IV.1    The Scheme Starts to Work
611

The three-man paper containing the first quantum mechanical perturbation theory appeared in print in February 1926, at the same time when Schrödinger established his perturbation theory in wave mechanics; the latter was founded mathematically on the theory of eigenvalues for differential equations with boundary conditions. Since the schemes of Born, Heisenberg and Jordan, on the one hand, and that of Schrödinger, on the other, possessed the same mathematical foundation—that had been supplied by the same person, David Hilbert—many analogies can be observed between the two perturbation theories. We shall, however, not focus on this particular aspect at this moment.

Schrödinger outlined an ‘*Erweiterung der Störungstheorie*’ (‘Generalization of Perturbation Theory’) in his notebook ‘*Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. II*’, and he later carried over this theory into his published paper (Schrödinger, 1926f). The extension concerned the occurrence of several independent position variables in the fundamental wave equation describing systems of several degrees of freedom. Although, in these cases, the perturbation scheme discussed in the foregoing (for one degree of freedom) still worked in principle—with the suitable replacement of the single variable $x$ by a finite, or even infinite, set of variables $x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots$—certain peculiarities and changes had to be observed. First: ‘The postulation “self-adjoint” [of the differential expression $L[y]$ in Eq. (70)] is *now* no longer unimportant, as the property cannot be generally gained by multiplication by a suitably chosen $f(x)$, as was the case with *one* variable. In the particular differential expression of wave mechanics, however, this is still the case, as it arises from a variation principle’ (Schrödinger, 1926f, p. 447; English translation, p. 69). Second, Eq. (70) could be regarded ‘as the formulation of the Sturm–Liouville eigenvalue problem in the case of several variables [$x$] also,’ and everything stated in the case of a single variable ‘about the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions, their orthogonality, normalisation, etc., as also *the whole perturbation theory there developed*—in short the whole of §1—*remains valid without change, when* all the eigenvalues are *simple* . . . . And only *one* thing does not remain valid, namely that they *must* be simple’ (Schrödinger, 1926f, p. 447; English translation, p. 69).

While from the mathematical point of view the occurrence of multiple eigenvalues had to be considered an exceptional event, it ‘*is the rule in applications*, on account of the especially simple and symmetrical structure of the differential expressions $L[y]$ (and the “boundary conditions”) which appear’ (Schrödinger, 1926f, p. 44

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0253 -->

612 &emsp; Chapter IV &ensp; Early Response and Applications

scheme of perturbation theory for systems having several degrees of freedom, whose unperturbed energy states are degenerate (see *Notebook II*, pp. 28–33, and Schrödinger, 1926f, pp. 448–457). Schrödinger started from the equation of motion

$$
L[y] + E\rho y - \lambda ry = 0, \tag{92}
$$

with $\lambda$ denoting a small parameter, $L[y]$ a second-order partial differential expression, and $\rho$ and $r$ functions of several independent variables. If the perturbation-free equation ($\lambda = 0$) possesses, for the eigenvalue $E_k$, not just a single but $\alpha$ linear independent eigenfunctions, $u_{k1}$, $u_{k2}, \dots, u_{k\alpha}$, as solutions, then $E_k$ is $\alpha$-fold degenerate. Each $u_{ki}$, $i = 1, 2, \dots, \alpha$, can be assumed to be orthogonal to every eigenfunction belonging to an eigenvalue different from $E_k$. The $u_{ki}$, however, need not be orthogonal to each other, although they can be transformed into an orthogonal, normalized system, i.e., made to satisfy the relations

$$
\int \rho(x) u_{ki}(x) u_{k'i'}(x) dx = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{for } (k, i) \neq (k', i'), \\ 1 & \text{for } k' = k, i' = i. \end{cases} \tag{93}
$$

($x$ represents a many-dimensional variable, and $\rho(x)$ the density function ensuring the self-adjointness of the differential equation.) There exists, of course, not only one suitable transformation establishing the orthogonal, normalized system (93), but infinitely many, which are connected by orthogonal transformations. The addition of the perturbation term $\lambda ry$ in general removes the degeneracy of some, or all, eigenvalues $E_k$. If so, the corresponding $E_k$ splits up in closely neighbouring eigenvalues,

$$
E_{kl}^* = E_k + \lambda \mathcal{E}_l, \quad l = 1, 2, 3, \dots, \alpha; \tag{94}
$$

That is, the $\alpha$-fold degeneracy will either be completely (if all $\mathcal{E}_l$ are different) or partially (if some $\mathcal{E}_l$ are identical) abolished. The new eigenfunctions are given by the equations

$$
u_{kl}^* = \sum_{i=1}^{\alpha} \kappa_{li} u_{ki}(x) + \lambda v_l(x), \tag{95}
$$

with the coefficients $\kappa_{li}$ denoting an orthogonal substitution. The interpretation of Eq. (95) is straightforward: one can establish by an orthogonal substitution unperturbed eigenfunctions $u_{kl}$, $l = 1, 2, \dots, \alpha$, which lie very close to the perturbed ones, namely to $u_{kl}^*$. Schrödinger commented: 'This particular specification of the *unperturbed* eigenfunctions, which is defined uniquely by the nature of the perturbation and may fittingly be designated as the "approximation of zero order" for the *perturbed* functions, will naturally *not* in general coincide with that definition of the unperturbed functions which we chanced to adopt to begin

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0254 -->

IV.1  The Scheme Starts to Work
613

with. Each group of the latter, belonging to a definite $\alpha$-fold eigenvalue $E_k$, will have first to be submitted to an orthogonal substitution, defined by the kind of perturbation, before it can serve as the starting-point, the "zeroth approximation," of a more exact definition of the perturbed eigenfunctions. *The determination of the orthogonal substitutions—one for each multiple eigenvalue—is the only essential new point* that arises because of the increased number of variables, or from the appearance of multiple eigenvalues' (Schrödinger, 1926f, pp. 449–450; revised English translation, p. 71). The extra task in wave mechanics had to be expected in analogy with the situation existing in the previous atomic mechanics, because it (i.e., the task) was 'the exact counterpart to the finding of an approximate separation system [of the Hamilton–Jacobi type] for the perturbed motion in the theory of conditionally periodic systems' (Schrödinger, 1926f, p. 450; English translation, p. 71).$^{38}$

By inserting the eigenvalues $E_{kl}^*$, Eqs. (94), and the eigenfunctions $u_{kl}^*$, Eqs. (95), into the wave equation (92), Schrödinger derived for the terms of first order in the perturbation parameter $\lambda$ the system of equations

$$L[v_l] + E_k \rho v_l = \sum_{i=1}^\alpha \kappa_{li}(r - \mathcal{E}_{li}\rho)u_{ki}. \qquad (96)$$

In order that this system 'have a solution at all, it is necessary and sufficient that its right-hand side should be orthogonal to *all* the eigenfunctions of the homogeneous equation [i.e., of Eq. (92) with $\lambda = 0$] belonging to $E_k$,' noted Schrödinger (1926f, p. 452; English translation, p. 73). This requirement yielded, if the normalization condition (93) was also taken into account, the following system of equations for the $\kappa_{lm}$,

$$\kappa_{lm} \mathcal{E}_l = \sum_{i=1}^\alpha \kappa_{li} \mathcal{E}_{mi}, \qquad l, m = 1, 2, 3, \dots, \alpha, \qquad (97)$$

where the coefficients $\mathcal{E}_{mi}$ were given by

$$\mathcal{E}_{mi} = \mathcal{E}_{im} = \int r u_{ki} u_{km} \, dx, \qquad i, m = 1, 2, 3, \dots, \alpha. \qquad (97a)$$

The system (97) possesses a non-trivial solution (i.e., non-zero $\kappa_{li}$) only if its determinant is zero, that is, the equation

$$\begin{vmatrix} \mathcal{E}_{11} - \mathcal{E}_l & \mathcal{E}_{12} & \cdots & \mathcal{E}_{1\alpha} \\ \mathcal{E}_{21} & \mathcal{E}_{22} - \mathcal{E}_l & \cdots & \mathcal{E}_{2\alpha} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \mathcal{E}_{\alpha 1} & \mathcal{E}_{\alpha 2} & \cdots & \mathcal{E}_{\alpha\alpha} - \mathcal{E}_l \end{vmatrix} = 0 \qquad (98)$$

$^{38}$The theory of such systems had been described, for instance, in Max Born’s *Vorlesungen über Atommechanik* (Born, 1925, §43), a book which Schrödinger had consulted earlier.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0255 -->

614
Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

is fulfilled. This equation, which Schrödinger—in analogy to the corresponding equation in the previous theory of multiply periodic systems—called the ‘secular equation,’ provided $\alpha$ real roots (determined up to a constant factor) and the $\alpha^2$ coefficients $\kappa_{li}$ constituting the orthogonal substitution for the unperturbed eigenfunctions. In case Eq. (98) yielded multiple roots as well, the perturbation term $\lambda ry$ in Eq. (92) failed to remove the degeneracy completely, at least in the approximation up to order $\lambda$; as a consequence, the system of eigenfunctions was not completely fixed by the perturbation.$^{39}$

With the orthogonal substitution in hand, the main task was achieved for the purpose of establishing the perturbation theory in the degenerate case. From now on the first-order calculation proceeds just like the non-degenerate case, yielding the perturbed eigenfunctions (95) including the terms $v_l(x)$,

$$v_l(x) = \sum_{k',i'} \gamma_{l,k',i'} u_{k'i'}(x), \tag{99}$$

where the coefficients $\gamma_{l,k'i'}$ are given by

$$\gamma_{l,k',i'} = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \frac{1}{E_k - E_{k'}} \sum_{i=1}^{\alpha} \kappa_{li} \int r u_{ki} u_{k'i'} dx & \text{for } k' \neq k, \\ 0 & \text{for } k' = k, \end{array} \right. \tag{99a}$$

$l = 1, 2, 3, \dots, \alpha.$

Note that the $k'$-summation on the right-hand side of Eq. (99) extends over infinitely many terms ($k' = 0, 1, 2, 3 \dots$), that is, all eigenfunctions $u_{k'i'}$ of the system come into play; for each fixed $k'$, on the other hand, only a finite number of $i'$-terms have to be included, namely those belonging to the degenerate energy eigenvalue $E_{k'}$. The eigenvalues $E_{kl}^*$ associated with these first-order eigenfunctions are determined by Eq. (94), with the $\mathscr{E}_l$ being obtained as roots of the determinantal equation (98).

Schrödinger did not develop—either in his notes or in his published paper—the general scheme of perturbation theory, say, in the same way as Born, Heisenberg and Jordan had done in the three-man paper. He rather suggested: ‘We succeed best in any special case if we do not use ready-made formulae, but go directly by the simple fundamental principles, which have been explained, perhaps too minutely, in the present paper’ (Schrödinger, 1926f, p. 456; English translation, p. 76). Evidently, his personal temperament rejected the systematic, bookkeeping approach which Max Born, in particular, had superimposed on matrix mechanics. However, he mentioned a particular difficulty that might arise in wave mechanics: Equation (92) loses the property of self-adjointness when the perturbation term contains derivatives; as a consequence, the roots of Eq. (98), and therefore also the energy eigenvalues, cease to be real (see Schrödinger, 1926f, p. 456).

$^{39}$Schrödinger did not investigate the situation of the multiple roots of Eq. (98) any further. He might have referred, however, to the situation in the old quantum theory (and classical mechanics), where one used higher-order approximations to solve the problem.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0256 -->

# IV.1 The Scheme Starts to Work

The newly developed scheme of perturbation theory could be applied to the problem of the Stark effect of hydrogen lines. Upon introducing the polar coordinates, $r, \theta$ and $\phi$, and replacing the radial variable by $\eta$ through the equation

$$\eta = 2r \sqrt{-\frac{8\pi^2 m_e E}{h^2}} = \frac{2r}{la_0} \tag{100}$$

the wave equation of this problem becomes

$$\Delta'\psi + \left(-\frac{1}{4} - g\eta \cos \theta + \frac{l}{\eta}\right)\psi = 0, \tag{101}$$

with the perturbation parameter $g$,

$$g = \frac{a_0^2 F l^3}{4e}. \tag{101a}$$

Evidently, $a_0$ denotes the Bohr radius of the unperturbed, non-excited hydrogen atom; $\Delta'$ is the Laplacean operator in the variables $\eta, \theta$ and $\phi$. In the zero-order approximation—i.e., in the perturbation-free case—Eq. (101) possesses the eigenvalues

$$l = 1, 2, 3, \dots, \tag{102}$$

and the eigenfunctions ($n < l$)

$$\psi_{lnm} = P_n^m(\cos \theta) \begin{cases} \cos(m\phi) \\ \sin(m\phi) \end{cases} \cdot \eta^n \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{\eta}{2}\right) \cdot L_{n+l}^{2n+1}(\eta). \tag{103}$$

These eigenfunctions can be normalized if multiplied by the factor

$$\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \sqrt{\frac{2n+1}{2}} \sqrt{\frac{(n-m)!}{(n+m)!}} \sqrt{\frac{(l-n-1)!}{[(n+l)!]^3}} \quad \text{for } m \neq 0,$$

or by the factor

$$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \sqrt{\frac{2n+1}{2}} \sqrt{\frac{(l-n-1)!}{[(n+l)!]^3}} \quad \text{for } m = 0.$$

In order to calculate the coefficients $\mathcal{E}_{im}$ of the 'secular equation' (98), one needs the perturbation function $r(x)$ of the self-adjoint version of Eq. (101). This $r(x)$ is not $-g\eta \cos \theta$, but $-g\eta^3 \cos \theta \sin \theta$. For a given $l$ and a given $m$, Schrödinger then obtained a set of $l-m$ equations, which have a non-trivial

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0257 -->

[blank page or OCR returned no text]

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0258 -->

IV.2 Response to Wave Mechanics I. The Early Phase 617

Evidently, the integer $k^*$, Eq. (105a), is equal to the difference $k_2 - k_1$ in the earlier calculation according to the method of separation of variables, Eq. (91). Like the previous difference, $k^*$ assumes the values $0, 1, 2, 3, \dots, (l - 1)$, and each $k^*$ possesses the multiplicity $l - |k^*|$. These results completed the evaluation of the energy states in the Stark effect up to first order in the perturbation parameter. In spite of the greater generality of the method devised for many degrees of freedom, Schrödinger concluded: 'On the whole, we must admit that in the present case the method of secular perturbations is considerably more troublesome than the direct application of a system of separation. I believe that this may also be true in other cases. In ordinary mechanics it is, as we know, usually quite the reverse' (Schrödinger, 1926f, p. 483; English translation, p. 96).

Such judgment notwithstanding, the establishment of the perturbation theory in wave mechanics, for systems involving several degrees of freedom and degenerate unperturbed eigenvalues, constituted a new triumph for Schrödinger's scheme. The path now seemed open to attack, with the same mathematical methods (of Courant and Hilbert) and on the basis of the same physical principles (of Schrödinger), more complicated problems of atomic and molecular theory.

## IV.2 Response to Wave Mechanics I. The Early Phase

The ideas and results of wave mechanics became known to the two Munich physicists, the experimentalist Wilhelm Wien and the theoretician Arnold Sommerfeld, prior to publication and they were the first to respond. Soon afterwards the news spread to Berlin, reaching two other correspondents of Schrödinger, namely Albert Einstein and Max Planck. Among the colleagues abroad, Hendrik Lorentz in Holland, who had obtained from Schrödinger advance copies of his papers, also became interested in wave mechanics. On the other hand, his Viennese countryman, Wolfgang Pauli in Hamburg, was already warned by Sommerfeld prior to any publication. Thus Sommerfeld wrote to Pauli in a letter: 'Here [i.e., in Munich] a manuscript by Schrödinger for the *Annalen* has arrived. Schrödinger seems to obtain exactly the same results as Heisenberg and you, but in a quite different, totally crazy way (*total verrückten Wege*), not [by] matrix algebra but [by solving] boundary value problems. Surely, something reasonable and final will, in some way or another, soon emerge from all that' (Sommerfeld to Pauli, 3 February 1926). About five weeks after the date of this letter, Schrödinger's first publication on the subject appeared in print (Schrödinger, 1926c), and a few weeks later Pauli wrote an important letter to Pascual Jordan in Göttingen, which he began by saying: 'Today I will ... rather tell you the results of some considerations of mine connected with Schrödinger's paper "*Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem*" which just appeared in the *Annalen der Physik*. I feel that this paper is to be counted among the most important recent publications. Please read it carefully and with devotion' (Pauli to Jordan, 12 April 1926; English translation: Van der Waerden, 1973, p. 278).

# Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

## Continuation of the Correspondence with Wilhelm Wien and Arnold Sommerfeld

After the submission of the first two communications on ‘*Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem*,’ the close relations between Munich and Zurich continued. Of course, contact with Wien had to be kept up automatically, because Schrödinger went on to write and send further papers on wave mechanics to the editor of *Annalen der Physik*. As a rule, he requested that Wien show the manuscripts to Sommerfeld first. But this formal, official business was not all: besides giving certain explanations concerning the contents of the papers, Schrödinger reported other important events to Wien, especially the further successes of the new theory and its propagation. Thus, for example, he wrote at the beginning of March 1926: ‘Hilbert is in Arosa and is said to feel well over there. On his return journey [to Göttingen] he will pass through Zurich; I hope then to gain his interest in the new theory’ (‘*Hilbert ist in Arosa und soll sich dort sehr wohl befinden. Auf der Rückreise kommt er durch Zürich, wobei ich hoffe, sein Interesse für die neue Quantentheorie zu gewinnen*,’ Schrödinger to Wien, 4 March 1926).
Certainly, Schrödinger looked forward excitedly to meeting the great mathematician from Göttingen, who was recovering at that time from pernicious anemia, a serious illness. The possibility of winning the founder of the mathematical tools of his theory, a man who was himself deeply interested in fundamental physical theory, over to wave mechanics offered quite favourable prospects. For the meeting with Hilbert, Schrödinger even had available a further important result, so-to-say, as a present: the equivalence of wave mechanics with the Born-Heisenberg-Jordan matrix scheme, again an outcome of the application of Hilbert’s mathematical methods. Although we do not actually know from the available documents whether Hilbert really made the stop in Zurich and met Schrödinger, or whether the latter had the opportunity to gain Hilbert’s support for wave mechanics, we know one thing for sure: Hilbert lectured in Göttingen during the winter semester of 1926/1927 ‘on the more recent development of quantum mechanics’ (‘*über die neuere Entwicklung der Quantenmechanik*,’ Hilbert, von Neumann and Nordheim, 1928, p. 1).
Later in March Schrödinger sent Wien the manuscript of the paper containing the demonstration of the equivalence of wave and matrix mechanics (on 17 March 1926); two days afterwards he commented on the results of the paper, upon which Wien replied promptly: ‘Your last essay I have sent immediately to the printing office, since Sommerfeld [to whom Schrödinger had requested that Wien show the paper beforehand] is still in England’ (Wien to Schrödinger, 21 March 1926). Wien wrote further: ‘It is highly astonishing and delightful to observe how fast the steps proceed; your new result, which establishes the mathematical bridge to the matrix theory, certainly does not leave any doubt about the fact that you have chosen the right path’ (Wien to Schrödinger, 21 March 1926). What Wien meant by ‘the right path’ may become evident from the following statement in the same letter. ‘For me it would now be extremely valuable,’ he wrote, ‘if it were

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0260 -->

# IV.2 Response to Wave Mechanics I. The Early Phase

possible to form an intuitive picture of the radiation process itself’ (Wien to Schrödinger, 21 March 1926).

So far, Wien was not, as he declared, happy with Schrödinger’s interpretation of the radiation process in the atoms. Especially, he had trouble in understanding ‘how beat vibrations can act like vibrations although one cannot observe the individual vibrations themselves that give rise to the beat vibrations’ (‘*wie Schwebungen als Schwingungen wirken können, wenn man die einzelnen Schwingungen selbst nicht beobachten kann, aus denen die Schwebungen entstehen*,’ Wien to Schrödinger, 21 March 1926). The experimentalist from Munich reminded his theoretical colleague of the fact that, e.g., no beat frequencies are received if too high frequencies are sent into a telephone, since none of the latter can be transmitted. Wien argued: ‘For the reception of beat vibrations a rectifying action is always required, thus a direct current becomes superimposed on the high frequency alternating current. The direct current then passes through the telephone, and the beat frequencies then cause periodic changes of the amplitudes of the direct current, and it is those one can hear’ (Wien to Schrödinger, 21 March 1926). On the other hand, Wien hoped that Schrödinger might soon come up with another explanation, by which ‘the curiosity of the physicists that is naturally directed especially towards such questions can soon be satisfied’ (*loc. cit.*). Although Schrödinger had no immediate answer to this question, he felt sure that he might find one in due time. In any case, he fully agreed with a characterization of his theory, which Wien gave in a later letter as follows:

> It can hardly be doubted any longer that you have solved the problem of atomic vibrations; and you have done so in a pleasant way, which is connected most closely with the classical theory: the whole quantum theory is now not so strange anymore as it was previously. Planck, with whom I spoke on the subject, was also enthusiastic about it and he shares this opinion fully. (Wien to Schrödinger, 13 May 1926)

Schrödinger accepted Wien’s correction of his picture about the reception of beat frequencies gratefully, as he said: ‘I might easily have used it on some occasion as a popular example, and I might then have received very unpleasant knocks on my fingers, namely if I’d presented it publicly’ (Schrödinger to Wien, 6 May 1926). However, he only modified his ideas slightly about the eigenfrequencies of the atoms due to the undulatory theory. In that, he was stimulated by a recent paper by the American physicist Robert Andrews Millikan in the *Annalen der Physik*, of which Wien had sent him, with his letter of 21 March, a reprint (Millikan, 1926). In this paper, Millikan reported on the observation of very short wavelength radiation of cosmic origin, and Wien had mentioned in his letter: ‘The wavelength estimated here must approach closely the domain of your frequencies’ (Wien to Schrödinger, 21 March 1926).

Schrödinger read Millikan’s paper carefully, had it presented in the Zurich *Kolloquium* of 5 May 1926, and then replied to Wien: ‘I believe that one must certainly keep in mind that these hard rays might have something to do with the

619

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0261 -->

620 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

enormously high frequencies which are calculated from the Einstein–Einstein relation [i.e., from $E = h\nu = mc^2$], if one inserts in it for $m$ the mass of the electron or even of the proton. Millikan estimates his hardest radiation to possess [a wavelength of] 0.00038 Å. The above formula gives, with the electron mass [inserted], about 0.02 Å. Half of it, namely 0.01 Å roughly corresponds to such an atomic eigenvibration [according to wave mechanics]. If the proton mass is inserted, the above formula yields roughly 0.00001 Å’ (Schrödinger to Wien, 6 May, 1926). Evidently, in no case was Millikan’s value really obtained, hence Schrödinger did not believe ‘that one is allowed to give up the postulate: the *single* eigenvibration does not radiate’ (*loc. cit.*). In his opinion, the task of explaining the origin of atomic radiation frequencies consisted of finding a suitable coupling between the scalar of the undulatory (matter) field and the electromagnetic field vector, such that two frequencies of an atom give rise to a purely harmonic electromagnetic wave. ‘The essential fact is: the interaction always occurs between the (at least) *three* objects mentioned, not between *two* of them,’ Schrödinger emphasized, immediately adding the question: ‘But how should one establish this?’ (Schrödinger to Wien, 6 May 1926).

In spite of the fact that Schrödinger had not yet found a reasonable model for making perceptible the coupling he had in mind, Wien was confident that he would eventually succeed, and he concluded in his next letter: ‘In any case, a great deal has been achieved by your solution, because the whole status of quantum theory had gradually become unbearable’ (Wien to Schrödinger, 13 May 1926). Schrödinger, for his part, felt ‘extremely happy that men like you and *Geheimrat* Planck share the good hopes for the path that I have chosen’ (‘*außerordentlich beglückt, daß gerade Männer wie Sie und Geheimrat Planck die guten Hoffnungen teilen, die ich in den eingeschlagenen Weg setze*,’ Schrödinger to Wien, 18 June 1926), because this positive attitude did not prevail in general. He remarked: ‘It seems presently that the conviction does not exist everywhere that one should welcome without reservation a renunciation of the fundamental discontinuities, *if* one can do so’ (*loc. cit.*). He further added that he had ‘always ardently hoped that this would be possible’ and that he ‘would have seized it with both hands’—as much as in the case of the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory—‘even if chance had not played the first (in view of de Broglie I should more correctly say the second) tip directly into my own hands’ (*loc. cit.*). He again thanked Wien most heartily, in particular for his ‘strong advocacy in favour of the classical theory’ (‘*starke Stellungnahme zugunsten der klassischen Physik*’), and added the remark: ‘It would be fine if one were allowed again to think in a clear and simple way instead of in terms of verdicts and commandments, rules and correspondence-like analogies—which certainly constituted an unavoidable and highly appreciable intermediate situation’ (Schrödinger to Wien, 18 June 1926).

Sommerfeld, although he did not share Wien’s antipathy towards the previous status of quantum theory, nevertheless followed Schrödinger’s work with extreme interest. He spread the news about wave mechanics not only by letters—e.g., to

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0262 -->

IV.2 Response to Wave Mechanics I. The Early Phase 621

Pauli, quoted earlier—but also in his public talks and lectures such as those he delivered in England in March 1926.<sup>42</sup> When a talk by Schrödinger was announced at the joint meeting of several south German sections plus Swiss members of the German Physical Society at Stuttgart, later in the spring of 1926, Sommerfeld planned to attend it with his students, as he wrote to Schrödinger on 27 April. Quickly the latter replied:

> I must immediately answer your kind letter of yesterday, because you make in some awful way your coming to Stuttgart dependent on my coming and lecturing there. This is awful because Ewald already grumbles terribly that I do *not* come. If he now finds out that it is my fault that you and your students won't come, then my relations with him will be spoilt forever. (Schrödinger to Sommerfeld, 28 April 1926)

Schrödinger then explained to Sommerfeld why he could not attend the Stuttgart meeting; namely, that the work on the scientific papers plus his duties at the university had put enormous stress on him, all the more so as he did not even have an assistant who could hold problem sessions for his—Schrödinger's—classes; consequently 'people [i.e., students] will certainly lose too much' ('*verlieren die Leute doch zu viel*') by his absence. In spite of such dark prospects, he wrote that Sommerfeld might have a good chance to see him soon. Schrödinger had practically accepted an invitation to speak in the Berlin *Kolloquium* in July on wave mechanics. 'However, there [in Berlin] the last available date is 9 July,' he reported, and added: 'Perhaps I could then proceed as follows. Provided that I can endure until that time and have promoted enough of the material of my lecture courses, I might close [my classes] a few days earlier and pass on my return [from Berlin] through Munich. (The official conclusion [of the summer semester at the University of Zurich] is on 17 July, though.) I would ardently love to talk and discuss with you' (Schrödinger to Sommerfeld, 28 April 1926).

Fortunately, Sommerfeld went to the Stuttgart meeting, where Erwin Fues also presented a talk on '*Das Eigenwertschwingungsspektrum zweiatomiger Moleküle in der Undulationsmechanik*,' ('The Eigenvalue Vibration Spectrum of a Diatomic Molecule in Undulatory Mechanics'), the first on the new theory in an official meeting.<sup>43</sup> A few weeks later, in July, Schrödinger actually went to Munich and lectured there on his theory before Sommerfeld and Wien. It was an important event for the new theory and led to further, even more important consequences, as we shall report later in this chapter.

# Letters to and from Berlin

The exchange of scientific ideas on the problems of statistical mechanics with two of the most eminent representatives of theoretical physics in Berlin, Max Planck and Albert Einstein—in this sequence—contributed crucially in 1925 to Schrödinger’s getting on to the path to wave mechanics.$^{44}$ After he had submitted the paper on ‘*Die Energiestufen des idealen einatomigen Gasmodells*’ (‘The Energy Levels of the Ideal Monatomic Gas Model’) at the beginning of December 1925, the connection with Berlin was interrupted for a while, hence the people there heard about the establishment of the new atomic theory later than their colleagues in Munich. Still, they learned about wave mechanics earlier than other scientific circles, and they did so through personal reports by Schrödinger. As a result, they had the opportunity of responding to his ideas very early.

As we have mentioned before, Einstein had presented Schrödinger’s paper, which the latter had sent him in December, early in 1926 to the Prussian Academy of Sciences (Schrödinger, 1926a). In this paper, Schrödinger had clarified his own ideas about the statistics of independent particles and their close connection with Einstein’s recent quantum theory of ideal gases.$^{45}$ These ideas had arisen in response to, and as a critical review of, Planck’s treatment of identical particles in quantum theory. Planck had sharpened his point of view in several papers at that time, and again in an article entitled ‘*Eine neue statistische Definition der Entropie*’ (‘A New Statistical Definition of Entropy’), which he submitted in late October 1925 to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Planck, 1925c). As soon as reprints of this paper were available, Planck sent a copy to Schrödinger. Schrödinger replied:

> Please accept many, albeit awfully delayed, thanks for kindly sending me your entropy paper in *Zeitschrift für Physik*. I must state first of all—as regards the first paragraph—that I feel the new formulation, which you have given in Eq. (1) to the concept of entropy, represents the clear, beautiful crowning of the conceptual development, and I am *completely* in agreement with it. [And] I wish to consider the objections which I have ever raised to be a comparatively totally subordinate question—from *my* point of view, I don’t know whether also from yours. (Schrödinger to Planck, 26 February 1926)$^{46}$

---

$^{44}$ See especially the events which we have reviewed in Sections III.1 and III.2.

$^{45}$ We have discussed these developments in detail in Section III.2.

$^{46}$ Planck’s definition of the entropy (given in Planck, 1925c, Eq. (1)) associates with the entropy expression $k \ln P$, where $k$ denoted Boltzmann’s constant and $P$ the number of those stationary (microscopic) states of the system in question whose energy does not exceed the amount $E$.

Schrödinger, in his letter to Planck, dated 26 February 1926, mentioned that he had nearly guessed this definition—even before seeing it in Planck’s paper—from a hint that Planck had written to him earlier. Among the ‘subordinate’ aspects of the problem, in which he still disagreed with Planck, Schrödinger emphasized the ‘arbitrariness in defining states of equal probability’ (‘*Willkür bei der Festsetzung der gleichwahrscheinlichen Zustände*’). He especially drew attention, in this context, to the difficulties connected with the degeneracy of atomic states, difficulties that could not be overcome by any entropy definition.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0264 -->

IV.2 Response to Wave Mechanics I. The Early Phase 623

In the second part of his letter, Schrödinger reported 'still quite briefly about a thing which has captured me completely for two months and which—I am already totally convinced about—possesses a quite extraordinary significance' (Schrödinger to Planck, 26 February 1926). He then formulated the 'thing' in the case of conservative systems of classical mechanics, since—as he wrote—the generalization to relativistic atomic systems and to systems in a magnetic field did not yet work. Let $\mathcal{T}(q, p)$ be the kinetic energy of this system (depending on position and momentum variables, $q$ and $p$), $V$ its potential energy, $\psi$ a function of the $q$'s (having the dimension of an action), $K$ a universal constant (also having the dimension of an action), and finally $d\tau$ the volume element of the configuration (i.e., the $q$-)space normalized by the square root of the determinant of $\mathcal{T}(q, p)$. If $\psi$ was now determined such that the 'Hamiltonian integral'

$$\int \left\{ K^2 \mathcal{T}\left(q, \frac{\partial\psi}{\partial q}\right) + \psi^2 V \right\} d\tau \qquad (107)$$

took on a stationary value, with the subsidiary condition

$$\int \psi^2 d\tau = 1 \qquad (107\mathrm{a})$$

being satisfied, then this variational problem possessed—as Schrödinger wrote to Planck—discrete solutions in certain cases, and the assertion could be made: 'The stationary values of the Hamiltonian integral [(107)] are the quantum values of the energy for the mechanical system under consideration, if one assigns to the constant $K$ the value $h/2\pi$' (Schrödinger to Planck, 26 February 1926). He concluded with the question: 'Isn't that rather remarkable?' ('*Ist das nicht sehr merkwürdig?*', *loc. cit.*).

After explaining to Planck the role of the boundary condition in the new approach to atomic problems, Schrödinger summarized the problems which he had solved so far; namely, the nonrelativistic hydrogen atom, the rigid rotator, the one-dimensional oscillator, the rotating and oscillating diatomic molecule and the Stark effect of first order of the hydrogen lines. Since the results of the calculations seemed to be very encouraging, he continued optimistically:

I do have the very boldest hopes that one would now succeed in constructing a harmonious quantum theory, free of all roughness, not in the sense that everything becomes continuously more discontinuous and represented more by integral numbers, but rather in the opposite sense: the beautiful classical methods [of second-order differential equations with boundary conditions] provide automatically all the integralness that is necessary; this is no mysticism of integral numbers (*keine Mystik in den ganzen Zahlen*) but just the same integral numbers, which we are used to since long as occurring in surface harmonics, Hermitean and Laguerre polynomials (the former for the oscillator, the latter for the hydrogen electron). (Schrödinger to Planck, 26 February 1926)$^{47}$

$^{47}$ At this point, Schrödinger added: 'Sommerfeld's comparison with the number mysticism of the Pythagoreans strikes the point *exactly*: the integral values in the atom arise for roughly the same reason as the higher harmonics of a vibrating string' (Schrödinger to Planck, 26 February 1926).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0265 -->

624
Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

After this enthusiastic report, Schrödinger added a word of caution: ‘I do not, of course, mean that now one can again explain everything by *ordinary mechanics*, that say these $\psi$-vibrations are mass vibrations in the sense of the usual mechanics. On the contrary: they or something similar seems to be at the basis of all mechanics and electrodynamics’ (Schrödinger to Planck, 26 February 1926). He concluded this highly informative letter with the words: ‘Please forgive me, highly revered *Herr Geheimrat*, the unsatisfactory aspect of this short presentation; I cannot report the things with much more clarity in a few pages’ (Schrödinger to Planck, 26 February 1926). Within a month, however, Schrödinger had available reprints or proof-sheets of his first two communications on ‘*Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem*’ (Schrödinger, 1926c, d); he immediately dispatched copies to Max Planck in Berlin. This started an exchange of several letters on wave mechanics between Planck and Schrödinger during the period between April and June 1926. Planck acknowledged the receipt of Schrödinger's paper in a postcard:

Many thanks for the reprint. I read your article the way an inquisitive child listens in suspense to the solution of a puzzle that he has been bothered about for a long time, and I am delighted with the beauties that are evident to the eye, but I have to study it much more closely and in detail to be able to grasp it completely. Besides, I find it extremely congenial that such a prominent role is played by the action function $W$. I have always been convinced that its significance in physics was still far from exhausted. There is just one little blemish that I would have been glad to see removed. Old Jacobi would have been a little annoyed, despite all his interest, over the alteration of his name. Can it still be changed? (Planck to Schrödinger, 2 April 1926)$^{48}$

Planck's extremely positive reception of wave mechanics also affected Albert Einstein, who wrote a letter two weeks later. He started by saying: ‘Professor Planck pointed your theory out to me with well justified enthusiasm and I studied it too, with the greatest interest’ (Einstein to Schrödinger, 16 April 1926).$^{49}$ He then quickly mentioned a difficulty that had occurred to him while reading Schrödinger's paper. Referring to the addition property of energies in two un-

Then follow four letters by Schrödinger and three further pieces by Planck in time sequence, the last letter by Schrödinger being dated 4 July 1927. The next set is devoted to the Einstein–Schrödinger correspondence (six letters and postcards from Einstein, dated from 16 April 1926 to 22 December 1950; ten letters by Schrödinger, dated from 23 April 1926 to 18 November 1950). The last set is devoted to the Lorentz–Schrödinger correspondence (two letters from Lorentz, dated 27 May and 19 June 1926, one letter by Schrödinger dated 6 June 1926). These letters have been excellently translated into English by Martin J. Klein and published in 1967 as *Albert Einstein, Erwin Schrödinger, Max Planck, H. A. Lorentz: Letters on Wave Mechanics*. It is a pity that the selection does not include the correspondence with Wilhelm Wien and Arnold Sommerfeld, the most important source of information for the genesis of wave mechanics, of which we have made ample use in the previous sections.

coupled systems, he remarked: ‘I do not, however, understand how your equation

$$\text{div grad } \phi + \frac{E^2}{h^2(E - \Phi)} \phi = 0 \qquad [(108)]$$

is to express this property’ (*loc. cit.*, English translation, p. 23).$^{50}$ In order to cure the difficulty, Einstein proposed to take ‘another equation that would satisfy this condition:

$$\text{div grad } \phi + \frac{E - \Phi}{h^2} \phi = 0.' \qquad [(109)]$$

For two uncoupled systems, described by wave functions $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$, energies $E_1$ and $E_2$ and potentials $\Phi_1$ and $\Phi_2$, evidently the equation

$$\text{div grad}(\phi_1 \phi_2) + \frac{(E_1 + E_2) - (\Phi_1 + \Phi_2)}{h^2} (\phi_1 \phi_2) = 0 \qquad [(110)]$$

held. Einstein concluded: ‘I have tried in vain a relationship of this sort for your equation. It also seems to me that the equation ought to have such a structure that the integration constant of the energy does not appear in it; this also holds for the equation I have constructed, but despite that I have not been able to assign a physical significance to it, a matter on which I have not reflected sufficiently’ (Einstein to Schrödinger, 16 April 1924; English translation, p. 24). In spite of that difficulty, Einstein wrote in the margin of his letter the sentence: ‘The idea of your article shows real genius’ (‘*Der Gedanke Ihrer Arbeit zeugt von ächter Genialität!*’).

Six days after his letter, Einstein sent a postcard in which he admitted that he had misread Schrödinger’s first article. He wrote: ‘You really based your considerations on the equation [(109)] which satisfies the addition theorem for independent systems. Thus my letter was superfluous’ (Einstein to Schrödinger, 22 April 1926; English translation, p. 25).

Schrödinger held a different opinion about Einstein’s first reaction on wave mechanics. Thus he answered in a letter, written *before* receiving Einstein’s postcard: ‘My sincere thanks for your extremely kind letter of the 16th. Your approval and Planck’s mean more to me than that of half the world. Besides, the whole thing would certainly not have originated yet, and perhaps never would have, (I mean, not from me), if I had not had the importance of de Broglie’s ideas really brought home to me by your second paper on gas degeneracy’ (Schrödinger to Einstein, 23 April 1926; English translation, p. 26).

**With respect to Einstein’s question Schrödinger continued:**

The objection in your last letter makes me even happier. It is based on an error in memory. The equation [(108)] is *not* mine, as a matter of fact, but my equation really runs *exactly* like the one that you constructed free hand from the two requirements of the "additivity" of the quantum levels and the non-appearance of the absolute value of the energy: Eq. [(109)]. Your basic requirements *are* therefore fulfilled. I am, moreover, very grateful for this error in memory because it was through your remark that I first became consciously aware of an important property of the formal apparatus [namely, of the additivity of energy of uncoupled systems]. Besides, one’s confidence in a formulation always increases if one—and especially if *you*—construct the same thing afresh from a few fundamental requirements.
(Schrödinger to Einstein, 23 April 1926; English translation, pp. 26–27)

Einstein acknowledged Schrödinger’s answer quickly. He wrote back: ‘I am convinced that you have made a decisive advance with your formulation of the quantum condition, just as I am equally convinced that the Heisenberg–Born route is off the track. The same condition of additivity is *not* satisfied in their method’ (Einstein to Schrödinger, 26 April 1923; English translation, p. 28).^51 Two days after Einstein wrote the letter, Werner Heisenberg presented the Göttingen quantum mechanics at the Berlin *Kolloquium*, providing Einstein more detailed information about this theory. He faced a critical Einstein, who had already concerned himself with what he called the ‘Heisenberg–Born scheme’ (see Einstein to Ehrenfest, 12 February 1926) for some time. The particular point concerning whether or not the additivity property was lacking in the matrix mechanical treatment of cavity radiation, Heisenberg could not finally answer, since even Pascual Jordan—who had been responsible for this section (Chapter 4, Section 3 of the three-man paper: Born, Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926)—was not able to do so at that time.^51

More frequently than with Einstein

ger to Planck, 8 April 1926; English translation, p. 5). Thus he enclosed a sheet of paper on which he indicated the relative intensities of the Stark components of the hydrogen lines following from wave mechanics. It seemed, he said, that the calculation was successful, since the results including selection rules for the ‘azimuthal quantum numbers’ and the existence of some very weak components came out in agreement with experiment. He concluded his report on wave mechanics by saying: ‘I am now calculating [the intensities of the hydrogen lines] $H_\alpha, H_\beta, H_\gamma$. The calculations are unfortunately terribly difficult to see through and I cannot manage to bring them into a simpler form’ (Schrödinger to Planck, 8 April 1926; English translation, p. 5).

Schrödinger continued to keep Planck informed about the latest progress of wave mechanics by sending him reprints—or proof-sheets—of his papers. Upon receiving a copy of another communication on Schrödinger’s theory (probably Schrödinger, 1926e), Planck thanked his colleague again. He wrote:

You can imagine the interest and enthusiasm with which I plunge into the study of these epoch-making works, although I now make very slow headway penetrating into this peculiar train of thought. In connection with that I have high hopes of the beneficial influence of a certain amount of familiarity which in time facilitates the use of new concepts and ideas, as I have often found already. (Planck to Schrödinger, 24 May 1926; English translation, p. 6)

Besides repeating his appraisal of Schrödinger’s ideas, Planck had something else to say. He wrote: ‘But what especially delights me, and the reason for my really writing you today, is the joyful hope that we may soon have the opportunity to hear you and to talk to you here’ (*loc. cit.*). Schrödinger had already been invited to Berlin sometime earlier to present a talk at a meeting of the (German) Physical Society. Planck had discussed with Eduard Grüneisen, then President of the Berlin Section, and now mentioned in his letter the possibility of having Schrödinger’s visit during the summer semester, i.e., before the end of July. Hence he wrote enthusiastically: ‘Let me tell you explicitly how much pleasure all of the physicists here would have in having you yourself present your new theory and coming into contact with your ideas. And don’t be afraid that we will make too many demands on you and tire you out’ (Planck to Schrödinger, 24 May 1926; English translation, p. 6). Life in a big city like Berlin, he pointed out, is freer and more independent, and one can retire to one’s own leisure and work without being disturbed by anybody, much easier than in a smaller place. Finally, Planck expressed ‘just one selfish request,’ namely that Schrödinger might not come before 11 July: ‘Because in the beginning of July I have to go to Bonn for a few lectures and I would be sad if I missed your visit here as a result’ (Planck to Schrödinger, 24 May 1926; English translation, p. 7).

On Planck’s suggestion Schrödinger answered promptly, stating: ‘Your kind and extremely gracious letter of 24th . . . now has finally decided me to accept the attractive invitation for this semester, however things may go’ (Schrödinger to Planck, 31 May 1926; English translation, p. 8). The question of the date of

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0269 -->

628 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

Schrödinger’s visit still caused some problems: Grüneisen, on the one hand, did not wish to postpone the meeting after 9 July, while Schrödinger could not come to Berlin before the end of June, because an international meeting of physicists—including Arnold Sommerfeld and Otto Stern from Germany and Paul Langevin and Pierre Weiss from France—had been scheduled to take place in Zurich from 21 to 26 June. Another question that Schrödinger asked Planck was related to the kind of audience to which he should address his lecture in Berlin. He wrote:

> Should I think more of the fact that you and Einstein and Laue are in the audience—a thought without which I should feel uneasy—or should I direct myself more to those gentlemen who are further removed from theoretical work? . . . Naturally I can do both, if there is the opportunity, one in a general meeting and the other in a more restricted colloquium. (Schrödinger to Planck, 31 May 1926; English translation, p. 9)

Planck did not let Schrödinger wait long before he had solved these questions. ‘My colleague Grüneisen . . . suggests July 16th . . . . I should just like to join him in this,’ he replied, and said that such a date suited the interested physicists in Berlin well except Grüneisen, who would be away then (Planck to Schrödinger, 4 June 1926; English translation, p. 12). Schrödinger’s talk, on the other hand, was expected to be on the level of ‘students in the upper classes who, therefore, have already had mechanics and geometrical optics, but who have not yet advanced into the higher realms; to whom, therefore, the Hamilton–Jacobi differential equation . . . signifies . . . not by any means something to be taken for granted’; hence Schrödinger should give ‘a general survey of the fundamentals for the purpose of orientation without much calculation and without many individual problems’ (Planck to Schrödinger, 4 June 1926; English translation, p. 13). He went on to say: ‘Perhaps it would be easier and more natural for you to carry this out, if on the other day, Saturday morning the 17th of July, you were to give a second lecture in our Colloquium, aimed at more special matters with supplements and continuations of the lines of thought you will have described at the more general meeting’ (Planck, loc. cit.).

Planck also invited Schrödinger to stay at his house during the Berlin visit, as ‘my wife and I would be especially happy if you would stay with us,’ promising him to ‘have the opportunity to withdraw and occupy yourself as you see fit’ (Planck to Schrödinger, 4 June 1926; English translation, p. 12). Schrödinger accepted the dates of the lectures as well as the invitation to Planck’s home ‘with the utmost pleasure’. He wrote back: ‘The words with which you offer me your house as a “place of refuge from Berlin” express a boundless, thoughtful, concerned kindness that has truly touched me’ (Schrödinger to Planck, 11 June 1926; English translation, p. 15). He hoped to be able, despite his end-of-semester fatigue, to ‘give as much as I possibly can, both in and outside the “official” hours, to the gentlemen in Berlin who are so friendly as to be interested in my work’; and he would like, ‘from a purely selfish standpoint . . . to make full and intensive use of the opportunity to discuss the things that have held me completely

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0270 -->

captured for months, with a number of the most distinguished scientists with the widest variety of research interests’ (Schrödinger to Planck, 11 June 1926; English translation, pp. 15–16). Schrödinger finally announced—after mentioning in his letter some recent results on an application of wave mechanics to dispersion theory—that he would like to arrive in Berlin on the evening of 15 July 1926.

In a letter dated 15 June, Planck confirmed the arrangements of the lectures to the Physical Society (on 16 July 1926) and to the Berlin *Kolloquium* (on 17 July 1926). He wrote further: ‘On the evening of the 17th I hope to have several colleagues and you at our home,’ indicating that he planned to have a party at his house, where Schrödinger might meet and discuss more privately with some of the eminent Berlin physicists. As Planck had expected, Schrödinger’s visit including his talk on ‘Grundlagen einer auf Wellenlehre begründeten Atomistik’ (‘Foundation of an Atomic Theory Based on the Wave Approach’) before the Physical Society and the Colloquium lecture were very successful.⁵³ The acquaintance with Berlin and the physics community there would contribute to the invitation to Schrödinger, within less than a year, to take up the chair of theoretical physics at the University of Berlin as the successor to Max Planck.

### Some Penetrating Questions by Hendrik Lorentz

In his letter of 31 May 1926 to Planck, Schrödinger mentioned: ‘Today I received a very kind and very interesting letter of 13 closely written pages from H. A. Lorentz which I still have to study in detail, of course. He raises a good many interesting questions; however, he does not reject it at all, on the whole, but still appears to be very critical (Schrödinger to Planck, *loc. cit*.; English translation, p. 9)’. The letter he referred to came from Haarlem, and the Dutch physicist and grand old master of theory started it with the following remarks:

I am finally getting around to answering your letter and to thanking you very much for kindly sending me the proof sheets of your three articles [i.e., Schrödinger, 1926c, d, e], all of which I have in fact received. Reading these has been a real pleasure to me. Of course the time for a final judgment has not come yet, and there are still many difficulties, it seems to me, about which I shall get to speak immediately. But even if it should turn out that a satisfactory solution cannot be reached in this way, one would still admire the sagacity that shows forth from your considerations, and one would still venture to hope that your efforts will contribute in a fundamental way to penetrating these mysterious matters.’ (Lorentz to Schrödinger, 27 May 1926; English translation, p. 43)

Lorentz, whom Schrödinger knew personally from attending, two years earlier, the fourth Solvay Conference on Physics in Brussels, had received advance copies of the first two communications on *Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem* (Schrödinger, 1926c, d) and of the subsequent paper establishing the relation

⁵³ In the absence of Grüneisen, Walther Nernst chaired the session (see *Verhandlungen der Deutschen Physikalischen Gesellschaft* (3) 7, 36, 1926).

between wave mechanics and the quantum mechanics of Heisenberg, Born and Jordan (Schrödinger, 1926e). He now felt obliged and inclined to give his views on the new theory, and as usual he did so in quite some detail after analysing the content of the papers rather thoroughly.$^{54}$ Lorentz immediately realized that many of Schrödinger’s ideas and their presentation appealed to him quite a lot, and that the whole work, even if it ultimately did not provide a fully satisfactory solution of the quantum problem, exhibited a fundamental depth of thought.

The first point which attracted Lorentz was that Schrödinger had shown, in the third paper, how to calculate the matrices of the Göttingen physicists. He—Lorentz—knew that the Göttingen physicists had taken major steps towards the solution of the quantum problem, but he did not really like matrices, the main mathematical tool of Born, Heisenberg and Jordan, which in his opinion possessed less ‘intuitive clarity’. Lorentz then continued:

> There is another point in addition where your methods seem to me to be superior. Experiment acquaints us with situations in which an atom persists in one of its stationary states for a certain time, and we often have to deal with quite definite transitions from one such state to another. Therefore we need to be able to represent these stationary states, every individual one of them, and to investigate them theoretically. Now a matrix is the summary of all possible transitions and it cannot at all be analyzed into pieces. In your theory, on the other hand, each of the states corresponding to the various eigenvalues $E$ plays its own role. (Lorentz to Schrödinger, 27 May 1926; English translation, p. 44)$^{55}$

After this appraisal of the general structure of Schrödinger’s new atomic theory, Lorentz listed seven comments on specific points of theory, showing his understanding and simultaneously raising some criticism. The first two concerned the introduction of the kinetic velocity $u$ which, in the case of the hydrogen atom (or the electron in a Kepler orbit), was given by the equation

$$u = \sqrt{\frac{2}{m_{\text{e}}} \left( E + \frac{e^2}{r} \right)}, \tag{111}$$

and of the phase velocity $w$ of the matter waves through the relation

$$\frac{1}{u} = \frac{d}{d\nu} \left( \frac{\nu}{w} \right), \tag{112}$$

$^{54}$ Ten years earlier, Lorentz had rendered a similar service to another important theory, i.e., Einstein’s General Relativity Theory. Unlike the situation in wave mechanics, however, Lorentz had been informed about the preliminary steps of the earlier theory through his correspondence with Albert Einstein. He had then analyzed the new theory and even contributed two papers on specific aspects. (For a discussion, see, e.g., Mehra, 1973a, Section 6.1.)

$^{55}$ As Schrödinger had pointed out several times, Lorentz’ opinion that one could consider single states of atomic systems in wave mechanics was not quite justified. But it was certainly possible to deal in principle with single eigenfunctions solving the differential equation for a given system. These eigenfunctions, however, did not really correspond to the description of stationary states in the sense of Niels Bohr’s old theory.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0272 -->

IV.2 Response to Wave Mechanics I. The Early Phase 631

where $E, m_e$ and $e$ denoted the energy, mass and electric charge of the electron, respectively, and $\nu$ denoted the frequency of the matter wave. Equations (111) and (112) yielded an equation for the frequency, namely

$$\nu = \frac{1}{h} \left( E + \frac{e^2}{r} + \text{const.} \right), \tag{113}$$

which Lorentz reformulated as

$$\nu = \frac{1}{h}(E_0 + E), \tag{113a}$$

with $E_0$ a constant independent of $E$ and the position variables. When Eq. (113a) was used to describe the stationary states of Bohr's atomic theory—so said Lorentz in his fifth comment—then the atomic radiation frequencies

$$\nu_i - \nu_k = \frac{1}{h}(E_i - E_k), \tag{114}$$

might be interpreted either as beat frequencies or as combination frequencies. The first interpretation did not seem to be very attractive to Lorentz, because: 'No instrument (resonator, grating) whose operation is completely determined by linear equations would respond to these beats as it would to vibrations of frequency $\nu_1 - \nu_2$ [i.e., the difference of the frequencies of two vibrations causing the beats]' (Lorentz to Schrödinger, 27 May 1926; English translation, p. 49). While the beat interpretation thus implied the existence of 'obscure processes,' the one by combination tones did not. However, in order to explain the origin of combination frequencies, Lorentz knew, 'it is necessary that the fundamental equation [describing the system] be non-linear' (*loc. cit.*).

Lorentz now tried to construct a simple model, in which the fundamental equation contained squares of the wave function $\psi$, without really getting the desired frequencies: instead, he arrived at the combination frequencies $\nu_1 + \nu_2$ and $2\nu_1 - \nu_2$, when starting from two coupled systems with vibration frequencies $\nu_1$ and $\nu_2$. Still, he was not particularly worried about the result, since one could pursue this kind of game further until one had found the right combination frequencies. But he did not feel too comfortable with such a procedure anyway, and wrote:

> What I do not like very much about this interpretation of radiation as produced by sum and difference oscillations is that the radiation is considered to be something . . . that depends on terms in the fundamental equations that one even neglects in first approximations (in deriving the wave equation). Is it not really much simpler to hold onto Bohr's stationary states and then perhaps to assume that a Planck oscillator of frequency $(\nu_2 - \nu_1)$ is present, (the atom could turn into one), and finally that this absorbs the energy $h(\nu_2 - \nu_1)$ in a quantum jump $2 \rightarrow 1$ and then it calmly radiates? (Lorentz to Schrödinger, 27 May 1926; English translation, p. 51)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0273 -->

632 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

Indeed, Lorentz still felt that Niels Bohr’s proposal of relating the frequency of atomic radiation to energy differences had simplified the understanding over explanations prior to 1913, in which sum and difference oscillations had played a major role (Comment 6 in: Lorentz to Schrödinger, 27 May 1926; English translation, pp. 51–52). Moreover, he observed a difficulty with the energy relationships, when combination vibrations are again taken to provide the real basis of the wave mechanical description of atomic radiation (Comment 7, *loc. cit.*, pp. 52–53). To demonstrate this point, he assumed the stationary states to be associated in the wave theory with the energy values

$$E_0 + E_1, E_0 + E_2, E_0 + E_3, \dots, \qquad (115)$$

where $E_1, E_2, E_3, \dots$ denote Bohr’s negative energy values of the bound electron. He called this choice ‘the simplest thing’ (Lorentz, *loc. cit.*, p. 52). Now, if one wanted to obtain from the ground state ($E_0 + E_1$) the third Bohr state ($E_0 + E_3$), and have radiation corresponding to the transition from the third to the second Bohr state ($E_0 + E_2$) emitted, the necessary energy to achieve the process would be

$$E_0 + E_2 + E_0 + E_3 - E_0 - E_1 = E_0 + E_2 + E_3 - E_1, \qquad (116)$$

which could hardly be reconciled with the observed values following from electronic collisions, namely $E_3 - E_1$. Lorentz did not know any way out of this difficulty—i.e., no choice different from (115) worked for arbitrary cases—and concluded:

> One can feel that it is unsatisfactory in Bohr’s theory that the frequencies emitted are completely distinct from the frequencies of the periodic motions that really take place. It is fine that in your theory both kinds of frequencies are brought into a much simpler connection with each other, (namely $\nu_{\text{emitted}} = \nu_2 - \nu_1$, where $\nu_1$ and $\nu_2$ are “internal” frequencies); nevertheless it is not easy to understand this connection. (Lorentz to Schrödinger, 27 May 1926; English translation, p. 53)

Schrödinger’s answer to these sets of questions was rather short. He replied: ‘The most important [consideration] seems to me to be this: one should *not* set the *individual* proper oscillations [eigenoscillations] of the wave theory in parallel with the *individual* stationary orbits of Bohr theory. For if one does that the transition from micromechanics to macromechanics by means of the correspondence principle is absolutely impossible’ (Schrödinger to Lorentz, 6 June 1926; English translation, p. 59). In the case of large quantum numbers the individual Bohr orbits are built of many eigenoscillations that are closely adjacent to one another. Schrödinger did not associate a definite energy with any individual eigenoscillation; he argued: ‘The *only* property of the individual eigenoscillation that has anything to do with energy is its *frequency*, I believe’ (Schrödinger, *loc. cit.*, p. 60). With respect to Lorentz’ discussion of the beat and superposition

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0274 -->

IV.2 Response to Wave Mechanics I. The Early Phase

633

mechanisms, he declared that so far he had not thought too much about details. He wrote: ‘I was so extremely happy, first of all, to have arrived at a picture in which at least something or other really takes place with that frequency which we observe in the emitted light that, with the rushing breath of a hunted fugitive, I fell upon that something in the form it immediately offered itself, namely as the amplitudes periodically rising and falling with the beat frequency . . . . Between the *alternatives* of beats or difference tones, however, I obviously declare myself for the latter’ (Schrödinger to Lorentz, 6 June 1926; English translation, p. 61). In a word, Schrödinger was simply happy to have escaped what he called ‘the *monstrous* frequency discrepancy in the Bohr model’ (*loc. cit.*).

In another set of remarks presented in the above-mentioned letter, Lorentz concerned himself with the description of a particle in wave mechanics (see Comments 3 and 4 of his letter dated 27 May 1926, pp. 47–49). He wrote: ‘Your conjecture that the transformation which our dynamics will have to undergo will be similar to the transition from ray optics to wave optics sounds very tempting, but I have some doubts about it’ (*loc. cit.*, p. 47). The main difficulty seemed to him to be the representation of an electron by a wave packet moving with group velocity, since—so he argued—‘a wave packet can never stay together and remain confined to a small volume in the long run’ (Lorentz, *loc. cit.*). Even without dispersion any wave packet would spread more and more in the transverse direction, while dispersion pulls it apart in the direction of propagation. Lorentz, therefore, declared: ‘Because of this unavoidable blurring a wave packet does not seem to me to be very suitable for representing things to which we want to ascribe a rather permanent individual existence’ (Lorentz, *loc. cit.*, p. 47).

To give an example of such blurring, Lorentz proposed looking at the case of the electron in the hydrogen atom. Lorentz argued that according to Schrödinger’s own testimony (in the second communication), its main wavelength was comparable to the Bohr orbits, hence the wave packet could not stay together.$^{56}$ Even if this dissipation of wave packets was to be tolerated for the description of electrons in atoms, a very serious disadvantage would arise by using the wave picture of the electron in accounting for the phenomena of photoelectricity and the emission of electrons from heated metals, where the particle properties appear quite clearly. Lorentz wrote:

> If one wants to imagine that electrons are not always little planets that circulate about the nucleus, and if one can accomplish something by such an idea, then I have nothing against it. But if we take a wave packet as model of the electron, then

$^{56}$ Lorentz admitted that one might think of using a large value for the energy (close to $m_e c^2$), hence $\nu$ would assume—in agreement with Eq. (113a)—an arbitrarily high frequency; but this would not result in a small wavelength $\lambda$, as the latter was given by the equation

$$\lambda^{-1} = \frac{1}{h} \sqrt{2m_e\left(E + \frac{e^2}{r}\right)},$$

in which only $(E + e^2/r)$ occurred and not $(E + e^2/r + \text{const.})$.

Schrödinger's answer to these objections, connected with the interpretation of electrons by wave packets, was simply the following. He wrote to Lorentz:

> Allow me to send you . . . a copy of a short note in which something is carried through for the simple case of the oscillator which is also an urgent requirement for all more complicated cases, where however it encounters great computational difficulties . . . . It is a question of really establishing the wave groups (or wave packets) which mediate the transition to macroscopic mechanics when one goes to large quantum numbers. (Schrödinger to Lorentz, 6 June 1926; English translation, pp. 58–59)

He emphasized that 'the text of the note was written *before* I received your letter,' and that it provides evidence of 'how much I too was concerned about the "staying together" of these wave packets' (*loc. cit.*, p. 59).

Schrödinger had entitled his note '*Der stetige Übergang von der Mikro- zur Makromechanik*' ('The Continuous Transition from Micro- to Macro-Mechanics') and submitted it to *Naturwissenschaften*, where it appeared in the issue of 9 July 1926 (Schrödinger, 1926g). We have already discussed—in Section III.5—most parts of this note, especially those dealing with the system of eigenfunctions of the one-dimensional harmonic oscillator and the construction of wave packets in that case. The essential point of the note in relation to Lorentz' problem is treated in the last part (Schrödinger, 1926g, pp. 665–666). Schrödinger investigated there the structure of the wave packet that he obtained from a special superposition of eigenfunctions of the oscillator of frequency $\nu_0$, having ordering numbers close to a high integral (quantum) number $n$, such that simultaneously $n \gg A$, with $A \gg 1$ an arbitrarily selected number, i.e.,

$$
\psi = \exp \left[ \frac{A^2}{4} - \frac{1}{2} (x - A \cos 2\pi \nu_0 t)^2 \right] \cdot \cos \left[ \pi \nu_0 t + (A \sin 2\pi \nu_0 t) \cdot \left( x - \frac{A}{2} \cos 2\pi \nu_0 t \right) \right]. \quad (117)
$$

The time behaviour of the wave packet (117) is determined by two factors. First, the exponential function describes a narrow hump having the shape of a Gaussian error curve placed at the position $A \cos 2\pi\nu_0t$, which oscillates according to the classical law of motion. Second, the cosine function assumes in general a small

Schrödinger noted: ‘The *number* and *breadth* of the “furrows” or “wavelets” within the particle [i.e., the shape which the second factor superimposes on the narrow hump described by the first factor] vary with the time. The wavelets are most *numerous* and *narrowest* when passing through the centre \(x = 0\); they become *completely smoothed* out at the turning points \(x = \pm A’\)’ (Schrödinger, 1926g, p. 666; English translation, p. 43).
As the main result of the calculation, Schrödinger concluded the following: ‘The entire extension of the wave group (“density of the particle”) remains, however, always the same . . . . [Hence] *our wave group always remains compact, and does not spread out into larger regions as time goes on, as we were accustomed to make it do, for example, in optics*’ (Schrödinger, 1926f, p. 666; English translation, p. 44). Schrödinger admitted that this result, obtained for the simple example of the one-dimensional oscillator, need not have any relevance for the actual situation in atoms, although he also argued that in the special case of a (non-degenerate?) three-dimensional oscillator the situation remained the same.
He further hoped, as he wrote to Lorentz, ‘that this is so, in any event for all those cases where ordinary mechanics speaks of *quasi-periodic* motion,’ and that the only difficulties which might finally remain—i.e., the only dissipating wave packets that possibly will occur—are those ‘of the completely *free* electron in a complete field-free space’ (Schrödinger to Lorentz, 6 June 1926; English translation, p. 59). He thus suggested the following picture of a bundle of cathode rays: ‘The bundle has a certain “granular” structure, in just the same way that many phenomena have made this seem plausible for a bundle of light-rays, where in *both* cases neither a pure wave description nor a pure particle description exactly reaches the truth, but rather something in between that we have not yet adequately achieved’ (Schrödinger, *loc. cit.*).
Thus, in his note on the transition from atomic to ordinary mechanics, Schrödinger foresaw that ‘[non-dissipating] wave groups can be constructed which move round highly quantized Kepler ellipses and are the representation by wave mechanics of the hydrogen electron’ (Schrödinger, 1926g, p. 666; English translation, p. 44). Only the greater technical difficulties had prevented him—so he thought—from proving this assertion. Lorentz, on the other hand, did not get discouraged by the difficulties. As he explained in a subsequent letter, he attacked the problem by asking the slightly different question: ‘If one *assumes* that there are wave groups that remain permanently confined to a small volume, can one then prove that they have to move in a field of force exactly as an electron would [especially in the atom]?’ (Lorentz to Schrödinger, 19 June 1926; English translation, p. 70). In a detailed calculation which he reported in the letter, he showed that the wave packet associated with a high quantum number orbit (in the classical theory)—of the sort that Schrödinger had discussed in the case of the oscillator—did not indeed remain compact.58 Therefore, it appeared to be very likely, Lorentz

After reviewing the undulatory treatment of the hydrogen atom in his own way—he used six points to characterize the safe results as well as the remaining difficulties (see Lorentz to Schrödinger, *loc. cit.*, pp. 72–74)—Lorentz admitted that Schrödinger had taken an ‘important step’ forward. He concluded:

> Nevertheless, if we have to give up wave packets and with them one of the basic ideas of your theory, the transformation of classical mechanics into wave mechanics, something would be lost that would have been very beautiful. I should be very pleased if you could find a way out of this. (Lorentz to Schrödinger, 19 June 1926; English translation, pp. 74–75)

Lorentz had indeed, with his penetrating questions, probed into the heart of wave mechanics. Schrödinger would struggle with these questions for some time and reach at least partial answers on his route to the completion of the new atomic theory.

**IV.3 Formal Equivalence of Wave Mechanics and the Quantum Mechanics of Born, Heisenberg, Jordan and Dirac**

In his reminiscences on the history of quantum theory, Hartmut Kallmann—a former Berlin physicist who had witnessed a good part of its development—recalled the events in 1926 as seen from the Berlin perspective:

> Two memoirs appeared, which added to the confusion, the famous papers by Schrödinger on wave mechanics and by Heisenberg, Born and Jordan on quantum mechanics. When a colloquium was held on this topic at the University of Berlin, not 20 [as usually did] but 200 physicists attended; people just were crammed into the hall when the theories of Schrödinger and Heisenberg were treated. After the report, Einstein rose and said: “Now listen! Up to now we had no exact quantum theory, and today we suddenly have two of them.” He continued: “You will agree with me that these two theories exclude one another. Which theory is the correct one? Perhaps neither of them is correct!” At this moment—and I shall never forget it—Gordon (of the Klein–Gordon equation) stood up and said: “I have just arrived from Zurich. Pauli has proved that both theories are identical.” He went to the blackboard and demonstrated the proof for us. This was a wonderful moment to see that [there were] two theories, apparently based on totally different fundamental ideas, [which] nevertheless both described nature accurately. I feel this was the birthday of the modern quantum theory. (Kallmann, 1966, p. 498)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0278 -->

IV.3 Formal Equivalence of Wave Mechanics 
637

Certainly some details in Kallmann’s recollection sound a bit apocryphal if the historical time schedule of events is considered in detail. First, the lecture on the two theories at the Berlin *Kolloquium* could not have been held before the publication of Erwin Schrödinger’s first paper on wave mechanics (i.e., of Schrödinger, 1926c) in late March or early April 1926. Second, by that time *several* papers on the approach of Born, Heisenberg and Jordan had already appeared, notably the pioneering paper by Werner Heisenberg (1925c) in September 1925, the paper by Max Born and Pascual Jordan introducing the matrix methods (Born and Jordan, 1925b) in late November or early December 1925, and the extended three-man paper by Born, Heisenberg and Jordan in February 1926 (Born, Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926). Third, Albert Einstein had been aware of the Göttingen approach to quantum mechanics from September 1925; on seeing the first paper of the series (Heisenberg, 1925c), Einstein had written to his friend Paul Ehrenfest: ‘Heisenberg has laid a big quantum egg’ (‘*Heisenberg hat ein großes Quantenei gelegt*,’ Einstein to Ehrenfest, 20 September 1925). Einstein had also continued to be interested in ‘the Heisenberg–Born scheme’—as he called it—and had concluded, after a study of recent work (Born, Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926), in a letter again to Ehrenfest: ‘More and more I tend to the opinion that the idea, in spite of all the admiration for it, is wrong’ (Einstein to Ehrenfest, 12 February 1926). In support of his opinion he had emphasized the problems of zero-point energy and the size of fluctuations in the matrix mechanical treatment of cavity radiation.59 Hence Einstein’s knowledge of the Göttingen branch of the new quantum theory was pretty old in the spring of 1926, and he had already arrived at a somewhat critical attitude towards it when he came across Schrödinger’s wave mechanics. Finally, it is true that Wolfgang Pauli proved the equivalence of both schemes, of matrix mechanics and wave mechanics, at the beginning of April 1926; however, at that time he resided not in Zurich but in Hamburg. Hence, it is most likely that Walter Gordon brought the news about Pauli’s equivalence proof from Hamburg rather than from Zurich, the more so since he—Gordon—was also in Hamburg in the spring of 1926.60

In spite of these wrong details, Kallmann’s general impression provides a correct picture of the situation and his conclusion must be taken seriously: the proof that the two so different-looking schemes, the quantum mechanics of the Göttingen school and of Dirac in Cambridge and the wave mechanics of Schrödinger, were equivalent as far as important results were concerned indeed inaugurated something like the birth of modern quantum theory. That is, after the twin birth of two new atomic theories in July 1925 and January 1926, respectively, a new

We would like, however, to exclude this possibility because by that time Schrödinger’s own paper containing the equivalence had appeared (i.e., Schrödinger, 1926e, published in the first half of May).
