**First Hints of a Relation of Wave Mechanics to Quantum Mechanics**  

On seeing the manuscript of Schrödinger's first communication on *Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem*, Arnold Sommerfeld wrote to Schrödinger: 'My first impression is this. Your method is a substitute for the new quantum mechanics of Heisenberg, Born and Dirac (*Proc. Roy. Soc.* 1925), in particular a simplified one—so-to-say an analytical resolvent of the algebraic problem posed there [i.e., in quantum mechanics]' (Sommerfeld to Schrödinger, 3 February 1926). Sommerfeld was deeply impressed by the new, so-completely different atomic theory, and he immediately thought of connecting it to the quantum mechanical scheme developed earlier. Obviously, he mentioned this to his experimental colleague Wilhelm Wien, who soon emphasized the same point in his own letter to Schrödinger. Wien reported: 'Sommerfeld thinks that your theory agrees with that of Heisenberg and Born. Since I do not know the latter, I cannot judge it' (Wien to Schrödinger, 6 February 1926).  

Schrödinger, stimulated by the remarks of Sommerfeld and Wien soon undertook the 'Untersuchung des Zusammenhanges mit Born und Heysenberg [sic]' ('Investigation of the Connection with Born and Heisenberg'), as he wrote on the first page of his notebook 'Eigenwertproblem des Atoms. III'.<sup>61</sup> He considered a mechanical system, described by the classical Hamiltonian $H$,  

$$H = f(q)p^2 + V(q), \tag{118}$$  

or the variational problem  

$$\delta J = \delta \int \left[ f\cdot \left(\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial q}\right)^2 - \frac{1}{K^2}(E - V)\psi^2 \right] dq = 0 \tag{119}$$  

in the undulatory mechanics. (The $p$ and $q$ denoted the momentum and position variables, and $K$ the constant $h/2\pi$.) He then expanded the wave function $\psi$ into a Fourier series, i.e.,  

$$\psi = \sum_{\alpha=-\infty}^{+\infty} c_{\alpha} \exp(2\pi i \alpha q). \tag{120}$$  

<sup>61</sup> See AHQP Microfilm No. 40, Section 7, p. 1.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0280 -->

IV.3 Formal Equivalence of Wave Mechanics & 639

By inserting the expressions for $(\partial \psi / \partial q)^2$ and $\psi^2$ following from the *Ansatz*, namely,

$$\left(\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial q}\right)^2 = -4\pi^2 \sum_{\gamma=-\infty}^{+\infty} \exp(2\pi i \gamma q) \sum_{\alpha=-\infty}^{+\infty} \alpha(\gamma - \alpha) c_{\alpha} c_{\gamma-\alpha}, \tag{121a}$$

and

$$\psi^2 = \sum_{\gamma=-\infty}^{+\infty} \exp(2\pi i \gamma q) \sum_{\alpha=-\infty}^{+\infty} c_{\alpha} c_{\gamma-\alpha}, \tag{121b}$$

he found, in the special case with $f(q) = 1$ and zero potential, $V = 0$, the action function

$$J = \sum_{\alpha} \left( 4\pi^2 \alpha^2 - \frac{E}{K^2} \right) c_{\alpha} c_{-\alpha}. \tag{122}$$

Having performed these steps, he turned to the discussion of the problem in matrix mechanics, observing: 'According to Born I had to proceed in *such a way that* [the Hamiltonian] $H_{kl} = \sum_{i} p_{ki} p_{il}$ [and] *to transform* [the quadratic form] $\sum H_{kl} x_{k} x_{l}$ *to principal axes*'. He noted finally: 'I cannot do anything with that' (*Notebook III*, p. 1).

Schrödinger's inability to do something in order to establish a relation between the wave mechanical scheme and the matrix mechanics remained during the following weeks. Thus he wrote on 22 February 1926 as the fourth point of a long letter to Wien:

> Relation to Heisenberg. I am convinced, along with *Geheimrat* Sommerfeld, that an intimate relation exists. It must, however, lie rather deeply, because Weil [*sic*], who has studied Heisenberg's theory very thoroughly and has developed it further himself, says upon reading the first manuscript that he is unable to find the connection. Consequently, I have given up looking any further myself. This I have done the more happily since the matrix calculus was already unbearable to me long before I even distantly thought of my theory (. . . *Und das umso lieber als, mir der Matrizenkalkül unerträglich war lange bevor ich an meine Theorie auch nur entfernt dachte*). [He quickly added:] I want to say with all that, that it is not the preference for my own child which now makes me interested in nothing else. *Now* I firmly hope, of course, that the matrix method, after its valuable results have been absorbed by the eigenvalue theory, will disappear again. I believe I am being honest with myself, if I state: I would wish this, with no less fervour, to be the case if the eigenvalue theory had originated from a Mr. Schultze. Because the mere thought makes me shudder, if I later had to present the matrix calculus to a young student as describing the true nature of the atom. (Schrödinger to Wien, 22 February 1926)

As he reported to Wien, Schrödinger had indeed given up thinking about the relation for a while, because in his *Notebook III* on the eigenvalue problem he

developed (after page 1) only those items which he published in the second communication, and also some detailed calculations on the Stark effect of the hydrogen atom which he would publish even later. Even at that time, when he submitted the second communication (on 23 February 1926), he had not proceeded any further. In this second communication he wrote in a conciliatory tone:

> I would not like to proceed without mentioning here the fact that at the present time an attempt is being prosecuted by Heisenberg, Born, Jordan and other distinguished researchers [in a footnote Paul Dirac was explicitly mentioned], to remove the quantum difficulties, which already has yielded such noteworthy success that it can hardly be doubted that it contains at least a part of the truth. In its *tendency*, Heisenberg’s attempt stands very near the present one .... In its method it is totally different that I have not yet succeeded in finding the connecting link. [Schrödinger, however, speculated:] I am distinctly hopeful that these two advances will not fight against one another, but on the contrary, just because of the extraordinary difference between the starting points and methods, that they will supplement one another and that the one will make progress where the other fails. (Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 513; slightly revised English translation, pp. 29–30)

Actually, Schrödinger assumed that the strength of Heisenberg’s scheme lay in the fact that

> it promises to give the *line-intensities*, a question that we have not approached yet at all [by the undulatory method], [while the advantage of our own method consists] in the guiding physical point of view, which creates a bridge between the macroscopic and the microscopic mechanical processes, and which makes intelligible the outwardly different modes of treatment which they demand. (Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 514; English translation, p. 30)

The situation did not change for at least one more week; in a letter, dated 4 March 1926, Schrödinger asked Wien to include some corrections to the second communication, but did not report any news on the problem of relating the two theories. However, two weeks later a radical change had occurred: on 18 March Wien received a completely finished and polished article from Schrödinger, entitled ‘*Über das Verhältnis der Heisenberg–Born–Jordanschen Quantenmechanik zu der meinen*’ (‘On the Relation between the Heisenberg–Born–Jordan Quantum Mechanics and My Own’), which was intended to be published in the *Annalen der Physik*. A day later Schrödinger commented in a letter to Wien: ‘The day before yesterday I again sent you a quantum manuscript, and now for security I let this letter follow in addition, especially since it is very possible that you are not in Munich presently’ (Schrödinger to Wien, 19 March 1926).

Schrödinger had used the first few weeks of the semester vacations rather profitably. He wrote to Wien:

> The hope which I expressed in point 4 of my letter of 22 February has been fulfilled much earlier than I thought. The relationship [of my theory] to Heisenberg’s has now been completely clarified, and this in the sense that anyone who does not want

also must not calculate with matrices, since both representations are—from the purely mathematical point of view—totally equivalent. From the physical point of view, though, my representation seems to me to be considerably more satisfactory and expandable (*ausbaufähiger*), because one is guided by intuition. Also, the fact that I succeeded from the point of view of undulatory mechanics in revealing the relation [to Heisenberg’s theory], while Weyl—with whose mathematical knowledge and ability I cannot [even] remotely compare—did not manage it from the matrix point of view, speaks *a posteriori* in favour of the superiority of my theory and of the much better prospect it also provides as far as the mathematical methods are concerned. (Schrödinger to Wien, 19 March 1926)

Wien reacted to Schrödinger’s announcement with enthusiasm, and wrote back: ‘Your new result, which at least provides the mathematical bridge to the matrix theory, certainly no longer leaves any doubt that you are proceeding on the right path’ (Wien to Schrödinger, 21 March 1926).

Schrödinger outlined his view on the problem of establishing a relationship with what he abbreviated as ‘Heisenberg’s quantum mechanics’ (meaning the matrix theory of Born, Heisenberg and Jordan) in the introduction of the new paper as follows:

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Considering the extraordinary differences between the starting-points and the concepts of Heisenberg’s quantum mechanics and of the theory which has been designated “undulatory” or “physical” mechanics, and has lately been described here [i.e., in the papers: Schrödinger, 1926c and 1926d, published in the *Annalen der Physik*], it is very strange that these two new theories agree *with one another* with regard to the known facts even where they differ from the old quantum theory....⁶² That is really very remarkable, because starting-points, presentations, methods, and in fact the whole mathematical apparatus, seem fundamentally different. Above all, however, the departure from classical mechanics in the two theories seems to occur in diametrically opposite directions. In Heisenberg’s work the classical continuous variables are replaced by systems of discrete numerical quantities (matrices) which depend on a pair of integral indices, and are defined by *algebraic* equations. The authors themselves [i.e., Born, Heisenberg and Jordan (1926, p. 879)] describe the theory as a “true theory of a discontinuum”. On the other hand, wave mechanics shows just the reverse tendency; it is a step from the classical point-mechanics towards a *continuum theory*. (Schrödinger, 1926e, pp. 734–735; English translation, p. 45)

Indeed, one could hardly imagine a bigger antagonism than that existing between the undulatory mechanics, in which a ‘continuous *field-like* process in configuration space . . . governed by a single *partial* differential equation’ replaces the finite number of differential equations plus the quantum conditions describing a system of finitely many variables in the ‘classical quantum theory’, on the one hand, and, on the other hand, the Göttingen approach which ‘connects the

solution of a problem in quantum mechanics with the solution of a system of an infinite number of algebraic equations, in which the unknowns—infinite matrices—are allied to the classical position- and momentum-co-ordinates of the mechanical system, and functions of these, and obey peculiar *calculating rules'* (Schrödinger, 1926e, p. 735; English translation, pp. 45–46).

In order to establish a relation between the two schemes, Schrödinger planned to proceed in two steps. First, he showed how

> to each function of the position- and momentum-co-ordinates there may be related a matrix in such a manner, that these matrices, *in every case, satisfy* the formal calculating rule of Born and Heisenberg. [He emphasized:] This relation of matrices to functions is *general*; it takes no account of the *special* mechanical system considered, but is the same for all mechanical systems . . . . However, the relation is still *indefinite* to a great extent. It arises, namely, from the *auxiliary introduction* of an *arbitrary* complete orthogonal system of functions having for domain *entire configuration space* [i.e., the full *q*-space]. (Schrödinger, 1926e, pp. 735–736; English translation, p. 46)

As a second step, Schrödinger showed:

> The *special* system of algebraic equations, which, in a *special* case, connects the *matrices* of the position and momentum co-ordinates with the *matrix* of the Hamilton function, and which the authors [i.e., Born, Heisenberg and Jordan] call “equations of motion”, will be completely solved by assigning the auxiliary role to a *definite* orthogonal system, namely, to the system of *eigenfunctions* of that partial differential equation which forms the basis of my wave mechanics. The solution of the natural *boundary-value problem* of this differential equation is *completely equivalent* to the solution of Heisenberg’s algebraic problem. (Schrödinger, 1926e, p. 736, English translation, p. 46)

The entire demonstration thus resulted, as Schrödinger pointed out, in the conclusion:

> From the formal mathematical standpoint, one might well speak of the *identity* of the two theories . . . . [Especially,] all Heisenberg’s matrix elements, which may interest us from the surmise that they define “transition probabilities” or “line-intensities”, can be actually evaluated by *differentiation and quadrature*, as soon as the *boundary value problem* is solved. [Wave mechanics even had, so Schrödinger claimed, the advantage of providing] these matrix elements, or quantities that are closely related to them . . . the perfectly clear significance of amplitudes of the partial oscillations of the atom’s electric moment, [thus making] the intensity and polarisation of the emitted light intelligible *on the basis of the Maxwell–Lorentz theory*. (Schrödinger, 1926e, p. 735; English translation, pp. 46–47)

<center><b>A Paper by Lanczos on the Field-like Representation of Quantum Mechanics</b></center>

The last issue of *Zeitschrift für Physik*, Volume 35, which was dated 26 February and appeared in print in early March, contained an article by Kornel (Cornelius)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0284 -->

IV.3 Formal Equivalence of Wave Mechanics
643

Lanczos entitled *'Über eine feldmäßige Darstellung der neuen Quantenmechanik'* ('On a Field-like Representation of the New Quantum Mechanics,' Lanczos, 1926a). Lanczos pointed out in his paper the 'closest connection' ('*engsten Zusammenhang*') that existed between the matrix mechanics of Heisenberg, Born and Jordan and the theory of integral equations. He stated in particular: 'The equations of motion and also the quantum condition can be written down in the form of integral equations. Thus a continuum interpretation arises, which has to be compared to the discontinuum interpretation [of Born, Heisenberg and Jordan] as having equal rights, since there exists a unique relation between the two' (Lanczos, 1926a, p. 812). He further claimed: 'As far as the fundamental interpretation of the theory is concerned, the formulation in terms of integral equations possesses the advantage of being in immediate harmony with the usual field-like conceptions of physics' (Lanczos, 1926a, p. 812).

What had Kornel (or Cornelius, as he would call himself in later years) Lanczos, then assistant at the Institute for Theoretical Physics of the University of Frankfurt achieved?^63^ He started in his paper by considering the central quantity in the theory of integral equations, namely the so-called 'kernel-function' $K(s, \sigma)$ depending on two points ($s$ and $\sigma$) of some co-ordinate space (of arbitrarily many dimensions). With a given symmetrical kernel one can then associate a system of eigenfunctions, $\phi^i(s)$, $i = 1, 2, 3, \dots$, each solving the integral equation

$$\phi(s) = \lambda \int K(s, \sigma) \phi(\sigma) \, d\sigma,$$ (123)

with a particular eigenvalue $\lambda_i$. The system of eigenfunctions is orthogonal and normalized, i.e., satisfies the equations

$$\int \phi^i(s) \phi^k(s) \, ds = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{for } i = k, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise;} \end{cases}$$ (124)

and it is complete, because any given, at least piecewise continuous kernel function $f(s, \sigma)$ may be expanded in terms of the $\phi^i(s)$ as

$$f(s, \sigma) = \sum a_i(\sigma) \phi^i(s).$$ (125)

The coefficients $a_i(\sigma)$ and Eq. (125) depend on the variables $\sigma$ only; they might be expanded themselves in terms of the eigenfunctions $\phi^k(\sigma)$. This yields altogether

$$f(s, \sigma) = \sum_{i,k} a_{ik} \phi^i(s) \phi^k(\sigma),$$ (126)

^63^ We have introduced Lanczos, his biography and his contributions in some detail in Volume 3, Section V.2. Here we only recapitulate the essential contents of his first paper of 1926 and emphasize its connection with wave mechanics.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0285 -->

644 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

i.e., an expansion of $f(s, \sigma)$ in products of two eigenfunctions with coefficients $a_{ik}$ that constitute in general an infinite quadratic matrix **a**. Lanczos concluded:

> The matrix **a** must then be regarded as a complete representation of the function $f(s, \sigma)$, since for a given [set of elements] $a_{ik}$ the function $f(s, \sigma)$ may be established in the sense of the formula [(126)]. On the other hand, the function $f(s, \sigma)$ can also be considered as a representation of the matrix **a**, since one can immediately obtain from it, by integration according to the formula
>
> $[a_{ik} = \int f(s, \sigma)\phi^{i}(s)\phi^{k}(\phi)\ ds\ d\sigma]$ (127)]
>
> the elements of the matrix. (Lanczos, 1926a, p. 813)

Because of this equivalence of the mathematical representation, either by matrices or by kernels of a linear integral equation, Lanczos derived—for every matrix equation that Max Born and Pascual Jordan had proposed earlier on the basis of Werner Heisenberg’s quantum mechanical scheme (see Born and Jordan, 1925b, the only paper which was available to Lanczos)—the corresponding integral equation. He especially defined quantities which replaced, in the theory of integral equations, such concepts as the diagonal sum of a matrix, the product of two matrices and the differentiation of a matrix with respect to a parameter or to the time variable. In the last case, Lanczos found the equivalent equation to be

$$\dot{f}(s, \sigma) = (Kf - fK)(s, \sigma),$$ (128)

where the quantity $Kf(s, \sigma)$ denotes the integral,

$$Kf(s, \sigma) = \int K(s, \tau)f(\tau, s)\ d\tau,$$ (128a)

and the dot the ‘time’-variation, defined as $\partial/\partial(2\pi i t)$ rather than as $\partial/\partial t$. Evidently, Eq. (128) constituted the integral-equation analogue to the matrix equation,

$$\dot{\text{f}} = \frac{2\pi i}{h} (\text{Hf} - \text{fH}),$$ (128’)

where $\text{H}$ is the Hamiltonian matrix of the quantum system under consideration. Hence, if Lanczos wrote instead of his fundamental symmetrical kernel $K(s, \sigma)$—see Eq. (128)—the likewise symmetrical kernel $H(s, \sigma)$,

$$H(s, \sigma) = \frac{1}{h} K(s, \sigma),$$ (129)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0287 -->

646  
**Chapter IV Early Response and Applications**

Lanczos further noticed that the eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ of his fundamental integral equation (123) were related to the diagonal elements $W_i$ of the Hamiltonian matrix ($H_{ik}$) as

$$\frac{1}{\lambda_i} = \frac{W_i}{h}, \tag{133}$$

and that the equations of motion (131) would follow from a variational principle,

$$\delta I = \delta \int [pKq - qpK - H(p, q)](s, \sigma) ds = 0. \tag{134}$$

He finally concluded:

> Because of the mutual unique relation existing between the matrices and the kernel functions used in our representation, it does not matter at all for the formal treatment of the [quantum mechanical] problems, whether one writes down the fundamental equations in the form of integral equations—as we have done here—or whether one starts immediately from the constituent coefficients and applies the matrix equations. Depending on the nature of the mathematical problem one might preferably choose one or the other representation. (Lanczos, 1926a, p. 819)

While from the mathematical point of view both representations were thus equivalent, this was not so for the physical interpretation. Thus Lanczos noticed a difference between matrix mechanics and the integral equation representation insofar as, in the latter, besides the eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian (essentially those of the kernel function $K$) also the orthogonal set of eigenfunctions occurs explicitly. The question now arose: Did the eigenfunctions have any physical significance? If so, then Lanczos concluded that only the full kernel $K(s, \sigma)$ described a given quantum mechanical problem completely and not just the set of eigenvalues $\lambda_i$. The complete knowledge of $K(s, \sigma)$, on the other hand, implied the advantage that the quantum condition, Eq. (132), reduced to an identity, i.e., it did not have to be assumed in addition to the dynamical integral equations. After pointing to some relation between the new formalism and the theory of general relativity, Lanczos finally emphasized certain difficulties in visualizing the kernel functions. In this context he mentioned that, e.g., the functions $p(s, \sigma)$ and $q(s, \sigma)$, representing the momentum and position variables, denoted the *entirety* of possible states of any given system; a ‘quantum state’, on the other hand—which could be visualized according to the old quantum theory as a closed trajectory—was described by an integral of these variables multiplied by a particular eigenfunction, for example, by

$$p_i(s) = \int p(s, \sigma)\phi^i(\sigma) d\sigma. \tag{135}$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0288 -->

IV.3 Formal Equivalence of Wave Mechanics 647

Hence, essentially the eigenfunctions characterized the quantum states of atomic systems in Lanczos’ theory.

The above reformulation of the Göttingen matrix mechanics involved many surprising aspects, the foremost being perhaps the fact that it was Lanczos, previously not known as a contributor to atomic theory, who proposed it. How did he come to consider the problem at all, and how did he arrive at the particular mathematical methods of the theory of integral equations? The second question can be answered more readily.<sup>64</sup> Back in the autumn of 1924, when Lanczos was investigating the problem of weak fields in general relativity theory, he had suggested a method of solving the corresponding equations of gravitation by treating an integral equation of the Fredholm type, i.e.,

$$\phi_{ik}(s) - \lambda \int \phi^{mn}(\sigma) K_{mn}(\sigma, s)_{ik} ds = f_{ik}(s), \qquad (136)$$

where the $f_{ik}(s)$ are given functions and the kernel $K_{mn}(\sigma, s)_{ik}$ represents a kind of Green’s function, an extension of Green’s function occurring in the problems of classical potential theory. Lanczos had also added the following remark-in-proof of his paper:

> In writing this paper, I have unfortunately not sufficiently taken into account the already existing mathematical literature. Therefore, at this point I want to allude to the fact that Hilbert had already applied, in his fundamental memoirs on integral equations—which have been assembled in a volume by the Teubner Publishing Company in 1912—the “Green’s tensor” for solving simultaneous differential equations ([Hilbert, 1912c], pp. 206–215; see also the book by Courant and Hilbert: *Methoden der mathematischen Physik I*, p. 316, Springer 1924, which provides a particularly useful review of the theory of integral equations). (Lanczos, 1925a, p. 124, footnote 1)

The discovery of the mathematical literature, notably the work of David Hilbert and the book by Courant and Hilbert, had then played a decisive role in the following papers by Lanczos: ‘Zum Problem der Ätherstrahlung in einer räumlich geschlossenen Welt’ (‘On the Problem of Ether Radiation in a Spatially Closed World,’ Lanczos, 1925b) and ‘Stationäre Elektronenbahnen und die Methode der Eigenfunktionen’ (‘Stationary Electron Orbits and the Method of Eigenfunctions,’ Lanczos, 1925c), in which he discussed—for the first time in his professional career—problems of quantum theory. In these papers, he especially used the method of eigenfunctions in order to describe radiation in the universe and its

---

<sup>64</sup> The question as to why Lanczos became interested in atomic theory, we have tried to answer in Volume 3, Section V.2. The main reasons were that he had earlier studied the problem of the nature of radiation in several papers, and that his position at Frankfurt demanded some acquaintance with the problems of modern atomic theory besides those of relativity theory, to which Lanczos had previously devoted his full attention.

interaction with the motion of electrons in atoms. He then arrived at the conclusion
that the ether in a spatially closed universe exhibited eigenvibrations connected
with a system of eigenfunctions which could not be observed, however; the
frequencies of the electrons in Bohr orbits should coincide with the eigenfrequen-
cies of those ‘standing ether waves’, but the coupling of ether waves to the electron
motion had to be zero; the emitted atomic frequencies, on the other hand, resulted
from the perturbation caused by the electrons when not moving on Bohr orbits
in the atoms.
    Lanczos had written in May 1925: ‘On account of this conception it therefore
appears that the solution of the quantum problem [i.e., of the Bohr orbits and
of atomic radiation] falls back on the knowledge of a general Hamiltonian
principle, which at present lies hidden deeply in the darkness, and on its connec-
tion with the eigenfunctions. On the other hand, we must not consider it to be
excluded that, by a closer pursuit of the wide-ranging “method of eigenfunctions”,
even without explicit use of a Hamiltonian principle, new light might be thrown
on still further details’ (Lanczos, 1925c, p. 141).
    Six months later, after Heisenberg had introduced fundamentally new ideas
into quantum theory, Lanczos was able to provide such a pursuit of the ‘far-ranging
method of eigenfunctions’, by applying it to reformulate the matrix theory of
Born and Jordan in the language of integral equations and their eigenfunctions,
thus deriving many remarkable insights in the new quantum mechanics.
    Lanczos’ paper appeared—as we have mentioned earlier—at the beginning of
March 1926, exactly at the moment when Schrödinger became stuck with the
problem of demonstrating the relationship of wave mechanics to the Born-
Heisenberg–Jordan matrix theory. Since Schrödinger followed the literature on
quantum mechanics carefully—being fully aware of the parallel work in the field
of a new atomic theory—he also discovered the original investigation of the—quite
unknown—Frankfurt physicist. In his later paper on the equivalence problem,
he cited it in the last section dealing—among other things—with ideas on the
coupling between the dynamical processes in the atom—i.e., essentially the matter
waves—and the electromagnetic field. Schrödinger then mentioned explicitly in
a footnote that Lanczos had expressed similar ideas ‘in an interesting note that
has just appeared’ and referred to the published paper (Lanczos, 1926a). He then
stated: ‘This note [of Lanczos] is also valuable as showing that Heisenberg’s
atomic dynamics is capable of a continuous interpretation as well,’ and added
immediately: ‘However, Lanczos’ work has fewer points of contact with the
present work than at first it was thought to have. The determination of his formal
system, which was provisionally left quite indefinite, is *not* to be sought by
following the idea that in some way the symmetrical nucleus [i.e., the “kernel
function”] $K(s, \sigma)$ of Lanczos can be identified with the *Green’s function* of our
wave equation.... For this Green’s function, if it exists, has the quantum levels
themselves as eigenvalues. On the other hand, it is required that Lanczos’ function
should have the *reciprocals* of the quantum levels as eigenvalues’ (Schrödinger,
1926e, p. 754, footnote 1; English translation, p. 60).

when applied to any arbitrary function of the $q$'s, *reproduces* the function, i.e., this operator gives *identity*. This simple fact will be reflected in the domain of matrices as Heisenberg's commutation rule. (Schrödinger, 1926e, p. 737; slightly revised English translation, p. 47)

The above-mentioned starting point of Schrödinger's demonstration reminds one of the corresponding starting point of Max Born's translation—in July 1925—of Heisenberg's new quantization rule into matrix language. At that time the replacement of the equation
$$
h = 2\pi m \sum_{\tau=-\infty}^{+\infty} \left[ |q(n + \tau, n)|^2 \omega(n + \tau, n) - |q(n, n - \tau)|^2 \omega(n, n - \tau) \right] \tag{138}
$$
(i.e., essentially of Eq. (16) of Heisenberg, 1925c), by the equation (of Born),
$$
\sum_k \left[ p(n, k)q(k, n) - q(n, k)p(k, n) \right] = \frac{h}{2\pi i}, \tag{139}
$$
had led to the matrix relation, Eq. (132') (see Born and Jordan, 1925b, p. 871, Eq. (38)), and thus to the whole matrix scheme of quantum mechanics. While Lanczos, in his recent paper, had explicitly introduced the 'unit kernel,' $E(s, \sigma)$, in order to transcribe the matrix equation (132') as the integral equation (132), Schrödinger now observed that the replacement of the momentum variable $p$ by essentially the operator
$$
p = K \frac{\partial}{\partial q}, \quad \left( K = \frac{h}{2\pi i} \right), \tag{140}
$$
a procedure that he had already followed in the first attempt to derive the hydrogen wave equation (see Schrödinger, 1926c, p. 362, Eq. (5)), led to an automatic satisfaction of the Born–Heisenberg–Jordan quantum condition.$^{65}$

This important observation provided a strong stimulus to try an attempt at 'a systematic construction' of a simple operator formalism that would replace the matrix scheme of the Göttingen physicists. In presenting this attempt, Schrödinger followed to some extent the detailed steps which had been taken earlier by Born and Jordan when building up matrix mechanics.$^{66}$

The first point which he noticed was the following: in constructing the operator corresponding to a function of the position and momentum variables, $q_k$ and $p_k$, one must take care of the commutation rule (132') and, therefore, prescribe a

IV.3 Formal Equivalence of Wave Mechanics
651

‘function-symbol written in a definite way,’ which he called a ‘well-arranged’ or ‘well-ordered function symbol’ (Schrödinger, 1926e, pp. 737–738; English translation p. 47). For example, Schrödinger associated with a function of the type,

$$F(q_k, p_k) = f(q_1, \dots, q_n) p_r p_s p_t g(q_1, \dots, q_n) p_{r'} h(q_1, \dots, q_n) p_{r''} p_{s''} \dots, \tag{141}$$

the well-ordered function-symbol

$$[F, .] = f(q, \dots, q_n) K^3 \frac{\partial^3}{\partial q_r \partial q_s \partial q_t} g(q_1, \dots, q_n)$$
$$\times K \frac{\partial}{\partial q_{r'}} h(q_1, \dots, q_n) K^2 \frac{\partial^2}{\partial q_{r''} \partial q_{s''}} \dots \tag{141'}$$

The operator $[F, .]$ may be applied to any function $u$ of the position variables alone, and the same can be done with a product operator $[GF, .]$—which is defined such that first $F$ is applied to $u$, and then $G$ to the resulting function. Because of the commutation rule, Schrödinger observed in general that

$$[GF, .] \neq [FG, .]. \tag{142}$$

With the ‘well-ordered function-symbol’ following the same relations as the corresponding matrix symbol, Schrödinger proceeded to establish detailed operator expressions for the important matrix expressions of quantum mechanics. For that purpose he assumed that his operators acted on a complete orthogonal function system defined in the entire $x$-space (where $x$ denotes the $n$ co-ordinates $q_1, \dots, q_n$),

$$u_1(x)\sqrt{\rho(x)}, \quad u_2(x)\sqrt{\rho(x)}, \quad u_3(x)\sqrt{\rho(x)}, \quad \dots, \tag{143}$$

with each function $u_i(x)$ vanishing fast enough at infinite $x$.^67 He then associated with the operator (141) the matrix of coefficients $F^{kl}$ by the relation

$$F^{kl} = \int \rho(x) u_k(x) [F, u_l(x)] \, dx, \tag{144}$$

which he expressed verbally as: ‘A matrix element is computed by *multiplying* the function of the orthogonal system [(143)] denoted by the *row-index* (whereby we always understand $u_i$, not $u_i\sqrt{\rho}$) by the “density function” $\rho$, and by the result arising from using our operator on the orthogonal function corresponding to the *column-index*, and then by *integrating* the whole over the domain’ (Schrödinger, 1926e, p. 739; English translation, pp. 48–49). The entire procedure, Eq. (144),

^67 Despite the claim that Lanczos’ theory had little in common with his own, Schrödinger in this procedure very much followed the footsteps of Lanczos.

652 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Chapter IV &nbsp;Early Response and Applications

represented nothing else other than that which Lanczos had said earlier in his equation (127). But Schrödinger now went ahead and demonstrated explicitly how his ‘matrices’ $F^{kl}$ indeed obeyed the matrix relations of Born, Heisenberg and Jordan.

First of all, the definition contained in Eq. (144) obeyed the rule of matrix multiplication, i.e.,$^{68}$

$$(FG)^{km} = \sum_l F^{kl}G^{lm}. \tag{145}$$

Similarly, Schrödinger established the matrix mechanical rules for the (partial) differentiation of a (matrix) variable with respect to the position or momentum variable, namely,

$$\left[\frac{\partial F}{\partial q_l}, \cdot\right] = \frac{1}{K} [p_l F - F p_l, \cdot], \tag{146a}$$

or

$$\left[\frac{\partial F}{\partial p_l}, \cdot\right] = \frac{1}{K} [F q_l - q_l F, \cdot]. \tag{146b}$$

The crucial point in the entire demonstration of equivalence between the matrix and the wave mechanics now had to do with the solution of the equations of motion. In matrix form the latter read

$$\left(\frac{\partial q_l}{dt}\right)^{ik} = \left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_l}\right)^{ik}, \tag{147a}$$

$^{68}$ To prove Eq. (145)—on pp. 739 and 740 of his paper—Schrödinger used what he called the ‘revolved’ (‘umgewälzte’) operator, i.e., the one ($[\bar{F}, \cdot]$) obtained from $[F, \cdot]$, Eq. (141), after integrating by parts, such that the operator finally acts on $\rho(x)u_k(x)$ instead of on $u_l(x)$. In performing the ‘revolving’ procedure, one should observe that the order of factors in the product (141) interchanges. Finally, one obtains

$$F^{kl} = \int u_l(x)[\bar{F}, \rho(x)u_k(x)] dx,$$

and the matrix product becomes indeed

$$\sum_l F^{kl}G^{lm} = \int [\bar{F}, \rho(x)u_k(x)][G, u_m(x)] dx = \int \rho(x)u_k(x)[FG, u_m(x)] dx,$$

on using the completeness relation.

IV.3 Formal Equivalence of Wave Mechanics 653

and

$$\left(\frac{dp_l}{dt}\right)^{ik} = -\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial q_l}\right)^{ik}, \qquad (147b)$$

with a suitably symmetrized Hamiltonian diagonal matrix ($H^{ik}$).$^{69}$ Since the time derivative of the matrix element $q^{ik}$ reproduced the matrix element multiplied by the factor $2\pi i(\nu_i - \nu_k)$, Eqs. (147) assumed the form

$$(\nu_i - \nu_k)q_l^{ik} = \frac{1}{h}(Hq_l - q_lH), \qquad (148a)$$

and

$$(\nu_i - \nu_k)p_l^{ik} = \frac{1}{h}(Hp_l - p_lH). \qquad (148b)$$

Schrödinger made two essential claims:

1. The Eqs. [(148)] will in general be satisfied if we choose as the orthogonal system the *eigenfunctions* of the natural boundary value problem of the following partial differential equation

$$-[H, \psi] + E\psi = 0. \qquad [(149)]$$

$\psi$ is the unknown function of $q_1, q_2, \dots, q_n$; $E$ is the eigenvalue parameter.... The quantities $\nu_i$ are found to be equal to the eigenvalues $E_i$ divided by $h$. ($H^{kl}$ becomes a diagonal matrix, with $H^{kk} = E_k$.
2. If the symmetricalising of the function $H$ has been effected *in a suitable way*—the process of symmetricalising, in my opinion, has not hitherto been defined uniquely—then [Eq. (149)] *is identical with the wave equation which is the basis of my wave mechanics*. (Schrödinger, 1926e, pp. 745–746; English translation, p. 54)

The use of the eigenfunctions of the differential equation (149) as the complete system $u_i(x)$ for the operator formalism obviously led to the following matrix elements $H^{kl}$,

$$H^{kl} = E_l \int \rho(x) u_k(x) u_l(x) dx = \begin{cases} E_l & \text{for } l = k, \\ 0 & \text{for } l \neq k. \end{cases} \qquad (150)$$

If inserted into the right-hand side of Eq. (148a), one obtains $((E_i - E_k)/h)q_l^{ik}$; consequently the transition frequency indeed assumes the value $(E_i - E_k)/h$, as has been asserted by Claim 1.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0295 -->

654 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

In order to prove the remaining, most important, Claim 2, Schrödinger recalled the derivation of his wave equation from the classical problem described by the Hamiltonian $H$,
$$H = \mathscr{T}(q_k, p_k) + V(q_k), \tag{151}$$
where the kinetic energy $\mathscr{T}$ is supposed to be a quadratic form of the momentum variables $p_k$ and the potential $V$ depends only on the position variables $q_k$. In his first communication, he had proceeded by calling upon the variational principle
$$0 = \delta J_1 = \delta \int \left\{ \frac{h^2}{4\pi^2} \mathscr{T}\left(q_k, \frac{\partial\psi}{\partial q_k}\right) + \psi^2 V(q_k) \right\} \Delta_p^{-1/2} dx, \tag{152}$$
supplemented by the subsidiary condition
$$J_2 = \int \psi^2 \Delta_p^{-1/2} dx = 1. \tag{152a}$$
($\Delta_p$ denoted the discriminant of the quadratic form $\mathscr{T}$.)$^{70}$ When he carried out the variation in the following way,
$$0 = \frac{1}{2} (\delta J_1 - E \delta J_2) = \int \left[ - \frac{h^2}{8\pi^2} \sum_k \frac{\partial}{\partial q_k} \left( \Delta_p^{-1/2} \frac{\partial \mathscr{T}}{\partial p_k} \right) + (V - E) \Delta_p^{-1/2} \psi \right] \delta \psi dx, \tag{153}$$
the Eulerian equation,
$$\frac{h^2}{8\pi^2} \Delta_p^{1/2} \sum_k \frac{\partial}{\partial q_k} \left( \Delta_p^{-1/2} \frac{\partial \mathscr{T}}{\partial p_k} \right) - V\psi + E\psi = 0, \tag{154}$$
followed immediately. By referring to the relation
$$\mathscr{T}(q_k, p_k) = \frac{1}{2} \sum_k p_k \frac{\partial \mathscr{T}(q_k, p_k)}{\partial p_k}, \tag{155}$$
which is valid for a quadratic form in the $p_k$, and by observing the relation (140), this equation transformed into Eq. (149). Schrödinger concluded triumphantly: 'Hence the solution of the whole system of matrix equations of Heisenberg, Born, and Jordan is reduced to the natural boundary value problem of a linear partial differential equation. If we have solved the boundary value problem, then by the use of Eq. [(144)] we can calculate by differentiations and quadratures every matrix element we are interested in' (Schrödinger, 1926e, p. 749; English translation, p. 56).$^{71}$

Although he had confined himself to a nonrelativistic problem in atomic physics in which no external magnetic field occurred, he doubted ‘scarcely that the complete parallel between the two new quantum theories will stand when this generalisation is obtained’ (*loc. cit.*, p. 750; English translation, p. 57).⁷²

### A Letter by Wolfgang Pauli

Schrödinger wrote to Sommerfeld on 18 April 1926: ‘With Pauli I have exchanged a couple of letters. He really is a phenomenal person. How he has discovered everything again? In a tenth of the time which I needed for it!’ He evidently referred with these words to the recent news that he had received from Wolfgang Pauli, especially to what the latter called a ‘complete clarification of the connection of Schrödinger’s theory and quantum mechanics’ (‘*die Verbindung von Schrödinger mit der Quantenmechanik vollständig klargestellt*,’ Pauli to Wentzel, 8 May 1926).⁷³

Pauli obtained this clarification during a visit in the spring of 1926 to Copenhagen, where he had gone to discuss the burning problems of atomic physics in those days.⁷⁴

Pauli arrived during the Easter holidays and had the opportunity of seeing two visitors, namely Llewellyn Thomas and Friedrich Hund (from Göttingen), at his accommodation, before he met Bohr himself.⁷⁵ Within a few days in Copenhagen he not only enjoyed the company of physicists and the relaxed atmosphere at Bohr’s Institute—where he was finally completely converted to

---

⁷²Schrödinger was also aware of the fact that he had worked on the proof of equivalence only with discrete eigenfunctions; however, he argued that in the presence of a continuous spectrum the conclusions would not be changed essentially.

⁷³It seems that ‘the couple of letters’ mentioned by Schrödinger, as being exchanged between him and Pauli immediately before 18 April, have not been preserved. In the Pauli *Scientific Correspondence*, only a letter from Pauli to Schrödinger dated later (i.e., on 24 May 1926) is available.

⁷⁴During the previous months, Pauli had carried on a regular correspondence with Niels Bohr and Hendrik Kramers, debating in particular the problem of the electron’s intrinsic angular momentum or spin, a concept which had been introduced by George Uhlenbeck and Samuel Goudsmit from Leyden in a note submitted in November 1925 to *Naturwissenschaften* (Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, 1925). Bohr had supported the idea, while Pauli had heavily criticized it. In February 1926, Llewellyn Hilleth Thomas, a visitor from England at Bohr’s Institute, had removed a major obstacle to the spin concept by removing the still existing factor 2 which so far had destroyed agreement of theory and data (Thomas, 1926a). After some further resistance, Pauli finally accepted the spin hypothesis (Pauli to Bohr, 12 March 1926).

For a detailed account of the spin debate we refer to Volume 3, Chapter V.

⁷⁵Before Pauli came to Copenhagen, Bohr had written: ‘Kramers has just left for the Easter vacation, hence I reply to the letter you sent him. We will all be very happy to see you again and to discuss [with you] the many different, open problems. Miss Schultz [i.e., Bohr’s secretary] has telephoned Mrs. Schack’s Pension, where [Ralph] Fowler stayed and where Thomas and Hund are now staying, and she has reserved a room for you. It is available from Sunday, April 4. I shall not be in town for the Easter holidays, but I shall be back on Tuesday or Wednesday’ (Bohr to Pauli, 31 March 1926).

Apparently, the letter from Pauli to Kramers mentioned by Bohr has not been preserved—it is not contained in the published *Scientific Correspondence*—although a previous letter from Pauli to Kramers exists where he stated: ‘I shall write later on about my trip to Copenhagen’ (Pauli to Kramers, 12 March 1926).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0297 -->

656 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Chapter IV &nbsp; Early Response and Applications

the correctness of Thomas' spin calculation—he also seized the opportunity of propagating the news about Schrödinger's new **undulatory atomic theory**. As Bohr reported to Heisenberg: 'He [Pauli] is fascinated by the just published paper by Schrödinger, and has been able to prove that Schrödinger's scheme leads to results which agree with those obtained from your quantum mechanics' (Bohr to Heisenberg, 10 April 1926).

Two days later, on 12 April 1926, Pauli formulated the result for his considerations in a detailed letter addressed to Pascual Jordan in Göttingen.⁷⁶ He wrote:

> Today I want to write neither about my *Handbuch* article nor about multiple quanta. I will rather tell you the results of some considerations of mine connected with Schrödinger's paper "*Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem*" which just appeared in the *Annalen der Physik*. I feel that this paper is to be counted among the most important recent publications. Please read it carefully and with devotion. (Pauli to Jordan, 12 April 1926; English translation, p. 278)

This solemn beginning and the other facts mentioned in the letter reveal the following. Pauli, whom we know had been 'pre-warned' by Arnold Sommerfeld of the forthcoming publication by Schrödinger containing a '**totally crazy method**' which nevertheless made it possible to reproduce many results of quantum mechanics (see Sommerfeld to Pauli, 3 February 1926), had watched out for the appearance of the paper in print.⁷⁷ As soon as the issue of *Annalen der Physik* in question was published, he jumped at it, and 'at once asked myself how his [Schrödinger's] results are connected with those of the Göttingen mechanics' (Pauli to Jordan, 12 April 1926). This reaction by Pauli must not be considered as very surprising. Schrödinger, in his paper (Schrödinger, 1926c), had just solved the problem of the hydrogen atom in wave mechanics, which Pauli himself had treated successfully a little earlier with the matrix methods of quantum mechanics. Pauli was also very impressed by the fact that the results in both cases agreed so perfectly, in spite of the very different fundamental ideas and mathematical methods of the two schemes. Clearly, it seemed to him most natural to assume that there existed some relation connecting the Born-Heisenberg-Jordan theory and the Schrödinger theory, and he set out to provide this relation in the following weeks. He wrote to Jordan:

> I think I now have completely clarified this connection. I have found that the energy values resulting from Schrödinger's approach are always the same as those of the Göttingen mechanics, and that from Schrödinger's functions $ψ$, which describe the eigenvibrations, one can in a quite simple and general way construct matrices

Perhaps his method is not that crazy' ('*Ihre Mitteilung über die Arbeit von Schrödinger hat mich sehr interessiert. Vielleicht ist sein Weg doch nicht so verrückt*, Pauli to Sommerfeld, 9 February 1926).

# IV.3 Formal Equivalence of Wave Mechanics
657

satisfying the equations of the Göttingen mechanics. Thus at the same time a rather deep connection between the Göttingen mechanics and the Einstein–de Broglie radiation field is established. (Pauli to Jordan, 12 April 1926; English translation, p. 278)

Pauli’s procedure of establishing the relation between the two theories consisted of two parts. In the letter, he first provided his own, simplified presentation of the steps leading to Schrödinger’s fundamental wave equation; in a second part he wrote down several expressions of the undulatory theory which possessed the structure and properties of the matrices used by the Göttingen physicists.

In part one of his demonstration, where he presented Schrödinger’s theory ‘styled a little differently’ (Pauli to Jordan, 12 April 1926), Pauli started from the relativistic equations valid for momentum $G$ and energy $E$ of a mass point, having the rest-mass $m_0$ and moving with the velocity $v$, i.e.,

$$G = \frac{m_0 v}{\sqrt{1 - v^2 / c^2}} \quad \text{and} \quad E = \frac{m_0 c^2}{\sqrt{1 - v^2 / c^2}}. \tag{156}$$

According to Louis de Broglie, one associated with this mass point a vibration process of frequency $\nu$ and wavelength $\lambda$ in a relativistically invariant way, namely,

$$\nu = \frac{E}{h} \quad \text{and} \quad \lambda = \frac{h}{|G|}. \tag{157}$$

Since the phase velocity of the vibration process was given by

$$\lambda \nu = \frac{E}{|G|}, \tag{158}$$

de Broglie’s phase wave satisfied—due to Schrödinger—the wave equation

$$\Delta \psi - \frac{G^2}{E^2} \frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial t^2} = 0, \tag{159}$$

with $\psi$ denoting the wave amplitude. In the case that the mass point moves in a potential $E_{\text{pot}}$—such that the potential depends only on the position co-ordinates $x, y, z$—the wave equation could be written as$^{78}$

$$\Delta \psi - \frac{[E - E_{\text{pot}}(x, y, z)]^2 - m_0^2 c^4}{c^2 E^2} \frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial t^2} = 0. \tag{160}$$

***

$^{78}$ Equation (160) is obtained from Eq. (159) by taking into account the relation between momentum $G$ and energy $E$, i.e., $E^2 - c^2 G^2 = m_0^2 c^4$, where the left-hand side must be replaced in the presence of a potential by $(E - E_{\text{pot}})^2 - c^2 G^2$. In the latter case, the phase velocity of de Broglie’s wave depended on the space point.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0299 -->

658 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

Pauli now formulated Schrödinger’s *Ansatz* as follows: ‘A quantum state of the system with energy $E$ is only possible if a standing de Broglie-wave without spatial singularities, depending on $t$ like a sine function with frequency $\nu = E/h$, can exist in accordance with Eq. [(160)]’ (Pauli to Jordan, 12 April 1926, English translation, p. 279). That is, one had to write $\psi$ as

$$ \psi = \bar{\psi} \exp\left( 2\pi i \frac{E}{h} t \right), \qquad (161) $$

and derive from Eq. (160) the time-independent wave equation

$$ \Delta \bar{\psi} + \frac{(E - E_{\text{pot}})^2 - m_0^2 c^4}{c^2 K'^2} \bar{\psi} = 0 \qquad (162) $$

with $K' = h/2\pi$. (We have replaced Pauli’s $K$ here by $K'$, as it differed from Schrödinger’s $K$, Eq. (140) above.) Equation (162) then represented an eigenvalue problem for the energy $E (=h\nu)$ of the electron wave, and the radiation emitted from the atomic system—consisting of Schrödinger’s example of the electron in the Coulomb potential of a hydrogen nucleus—corresponded to ‘difference oscillations of the de Broglie radiation.’ Equation (162) was not yet identical with Schrödinger’s wave equation; but the latter was easily obtained from it when one replaced the (relativistic) energy $E$ by the nonrelativistic expression $\bar{E}$, defined as

$$ \bar{E} = E - m_0 c^2. \qquad (163) $$

This finally yielded the equation,

$$ \Delta \bar{\psi} + \frac{2m_0}{K'^2} (\bar{E} - E_{\text{pot}}) \bar{\psi} = 0, \qquad (164) $$

that could be found in Schrödinger’s first communication (see Schrödinger, 1926c, Eq. (5) on p. 362—note that $K'^2 = -K^2$).

Upon writing Eq. (164), Pauli added a comment. As he wrote to Jordan, he had learned from Oskar Klein—whom he had met during the Easter visit to Copenhagen—that ‘the difference between the general quantum theory of periodical systems [i.e., the old quantum theory of the atom] and Schrödinger’s quantum mechanics based upon Eq. [(164)] is, from the point of view of the de Broglie-radiation, the same as the difference between geometrical optics and wave optics’ (Pauli to Jordan, *loc. cit.*, p. 280). Since for small wavelengths the wave function $\bar{\psi}$ might be written as $\exp(i(S/K'))$, with $S$ denoting the characteristic function in the Hamilton–Jacobi scheme of classical dynamics, it followed that ‘$\bar{\psi}$ becomes a univalued function only if the moduli of periodicity of $S/K'$ are integral multiples of $2\pi$’ which ‘leads to the usual condition $\int p \, dq = nh$’ (*loc. cit.*). Pauli

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0300 -->

IV.3 Formal Equivalence of Wave Mechanics

659

concluded that Schrödinger's wave equation (164), therefore, had to be used especially in those cases where $S/K'$ is not large in general.$^{79}$

While the first half of the discussion just provided a simplified introduction to Schrödinger's wave theory, Pauli turned in the second half to his 'own contribution, namely the connection with Göttingen mechanics,' which he provided—'for the sake of simplicity,' as he wrote—for a one-dimensional problem in Cartesian co-ordinates.$^{80}$ Then the Schrödinger wave equation,

$$ \frac{d^2\psi}{dx^2} + \frac{2m_0}{K'^2} [E - E_{\text{pot}}(x)]\psi = 0, \tag{165} $$

($\psi$ taken without the bar, $x$ the single position co-ordinate), possessed solutions only for discrete eigenvalues of the (nonrelativistic) energy parameter $E$, i.e., $E_1, E_2, \dots$ The corresponding eigenfunctions, $\psi_1, \psi_2, \dots$, formed a complete, orthogonal and normalized set, i.e., they satisfied the equations

$$ \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \psi_n \psi_m dx = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{for } n \neq m, \\ 1 & \text{for } n = m, \end{cases} \tag{166} $$

and any arbitrary, sufficiently continuous function of $x$ could be expanded in a series with respect to the $\psi_n$.

Pauli then developed his main result in the following sentences:

Now one considers in particular the expansion of $x\psi_n$:

$$ \left. \begin{aligned} x\psi_n(x) &= \sum_m x_{nm} \psi_m(x); \\ x_{nm} &= \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} x \psi_n \psi_m dx. \end{aligned} \right\rbrace \tag{167} $$

One also puts

$$ \left. \begin{aligned} (p_x)_{nm} &= iK' \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{\partial \psi_n}{\partial x} \psi_m dx; \\ iK' \frac{\partial \psi_n}{\partial x} &= \sum_m (p_x)_{nm} \psi_m(x), \end{aligned} \right\rbrace \tag{168} $$

---

$^{79}$ Evidently, the remark by Oskar Klein, reported by Pauli, reproduced Schrödinger's earlier considerations along the same lines which Schrödinger had described in his second communication (see our discussion in Section III.4). Schrödinger's paper, although submitted in February 1926, was not in general available to physicists when Pauli wrote the letter to Jordan on 12 April 1926; it appeared, however, shortly afterwards.

$^{80}$ Pauli claimed that the demonstration given below could also be extended to three-dimensional examples including even gyroscopic terms, i.e., the electron spin. (See Pauli's letter to Jordan, 12 April 1926; English translation,

660 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

$(i = \text{imaginary unit}, K' = h/2\pi)$. Now if $x_{nm} = x_{mn}$ is real, $(p_x)_{nm} = -(p_x)_{mn}$ is purely imaginary. It can be shown without difficulty, that the matrices for $x$ and $p_x$ [i.e., the assembly of coefficients $x_{nm}$ and $(p_x)_{nm}$] thus defined satisfy the equations of the Göttingen mechanics. Namely,

$$p_x x - x p_x = \frac{h}{2\pi i} 1, \quad \text{and} \quad H = \frac{1}{2m_0} p_x^2 + E_{\text{pot}}(x),$$

with $H$ representing the diagonal Hamiltonian matrix whose elements $E_n$ provide the energy eigenvalues]. From the rule of multiplication it follows that the matrix belonging to any function $F(x)$ of $x$ is just given by [the coefficients]

$$F_{nm} = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} F(x) \psi_n \psi_m \, dx. \quad \text{[(169)]}$$

I shall not write out the calculations in detail; you will be able to verify the assertion easily. (Pauli to Jordan, 12 April 1926; English translation, pp. 280–281)

On having established the central relations between matrix and wave mechanics, Pauli was able to reproduce the matrix mechanical results on the oscillator and rotator ‘according to Schrödinger’—including the Hönl–Kronig formulae for the intensity of Zeeman components—as ‘easy consequences of the properties of the spherical harmonics.’ He further reported in his letter to Jordan:

> Perturbation theory can be carried over completely into the new theory, and the same thing holds for the transformation to principal axes, which in general is necessary if degenerations (multiple eigenvalues) are cancelled by external fields of force. At the moment I am occupying myself with the calculation of the transition probabilities in hydrogen from the eigenfunctions calculated by Schrödinger. For the Balmer lines finite rational expressions seem to come out. For the continuous spectrum the situation is more complicated: the exact mathematical formulation is not yet quite clear to me. (Pauli to Jordan, *loc. cit.*, p. 281)

Finally, he turned to the physical interpretation of the results, saying a few words about the significance of his Eqs. (167) and (168). Pauli noticed especially that, in passing from the time-dependent Eq. (160) to the time-independent Eq. (164), a phase $\delta_n$ associated with each energy eigenvalue $E_n$ had been suppressed. Therefore, any given matrix element $x_{nm}$ of the quantum mechanical scheme should not only contain the time-dependent phase factor $\exp[(2\pi i/h) (E_n - E_m) t]$—as Born, Heisenberg and Jordan had pointed out earlier—but also another one that depended on the time. Pauli argued: ‘In principle, in the Göttingen theory as well as in de Broglie’s statement of the quantum problem, no description of the electron in the atom in space and time is given’ (Pauli to Jordan, *loc. cit.*,

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0302 -->

IV.3 Formal Equivalence of Wave Mechanics  
661  

pp. 281–282).⁸¹ He concluded:  

The problem of the asymptotic linkage [of the new theory] with the usual pictures in space and time for the limiting case of large quantum numbers remains unsolved. Yet it is a definite progress to be able to see the problems [of atomic theory] from two different sides [i.e., from matrix mechanics and wave mechanics]. It seems that one also sees now, how from the point of view of quantum mechanics the contradistinction between “point” and “set of waves” fades away in favour of something more general. (Pauli to Jordan, 12 April 1926; *loc. cit.*, p. 282)  

**Pauli, Lanczos’ Field-like Formulation and the Born–Wiener Approach**  

The central, most original part of Pauli’s letter (reported above) invites several comments, which throw light especially on the way Pauli arrived at his crucial conclusions contained in Eqs. (167), (168) and (169). Admittedly, he had shown himself to be ‘a phenomenal person’—as Schrödinger called him—on many previous occasions; and he had displayed, more than once, incredible speed in arriving at quite subtle conclusions, which took others months or even years to find. Still every success, especially very quick success, must possess certain definite roots that have to be uncovered if one wishes to draw a true picture of the scientific development.  

In the case of Pauli’s demonstration of equivalence between the matrix and the wave mechanical schemes, it seems necessary to back up a bit and recall the problems which concerned him in the first few months of 1926. Among these problems the treatment of atomic structure within the Göttingen quantum mechanics and the debate concerning the spin hypothesis stood out. Pauli did not work on these problems alone but carried on a detailed discussion of them with Werner Heisenberg mostly through correspondence between Hamburg and Göttingen.⁸² One of the main mathematical difficulties constituted the calculation of atomic energy terms because it required the use of angular variables. The matrix description failed to cover these continuously growing variables. In early January 1926, however, Heisenberg wrote to Pauli about some progress on that question. He proposed to introduce the angle $\phi$ in a two-dimensional problem, described by the Cartesian position variables $x$ and $y$—both representable as matrices—formally by the equation  

$$
\phi = \arctan \frac{y}{x} \, .
$$  

(170)  

⁸¹ The situation in de Broglie’s theory is that, as Pauli clearly recognized, outside the validity of geometrical optics one cannot construct rays of matter waves. Indeed, Louis de Broglie never did go beyond this approximation, while Schrödinger explicitly abandoned it for his own description of atomic dynamics.  

⁸² Pauli’s *Scientific Correspondence* during this period contains four letters, three written by Heisenberg and one from Pauli to Heisenberg. Further letters, especially those of Pauli, seem to have been lost.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0303 -->

662 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

Then he added the remark: ‘That this quantity [if interpreted classically] cannot be expanded in a Fourier series, does not matter due to a more recent paper by Born and Wiener’ (Heisenberg to Pauli, 7 January 1926). With the defining relation (170) in hand, he developed a quantum-theoretical formalism of action and angle variables, whose application allowed one to compute, e.g., the energy states of the relativistic hydrogen atom including the effects arising from the existence of an intrinsic angular momentum of the electron.<sup>83</sup>

The reason for the procedure was the following. Heisenberg, on returning to Göttingen from his Christmas vacation in the early days of 1926, found in his mail a manuscript sent by his professor, Max Born, who was then in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Born had developed, with the mathematician Norbert Wiener of M.I.T., what they called ‘*Eine neue Formulierung der Quantengesetze für periodische und nicht periodische Vorgänge*’ (‘A New Formulation of the Laws of Quantization of Periodic and Aperiodic Phenomena’) and submitted papers to *M.I.T. Journal of Mathematics and Physics* and *Zeitschrift für Physik*, respectively (Born and Wiener, 1926a, b).<sup>84</sup> The crucial step in the work of Born and Wiener constituted a replacement of quantum-theoretical matrices, say the position matrix $(q_{mn})$, by the integral operators in the time variable $t$, defined as

$$q \equiv q(t) = \lim_{\tau\rightarrow\infty} \frac{1}{2\tau} \int_{-\tau}^{+\tau} q(t, s) ds \ldots, \tag{171}$$

where the ‘kernel function’ $q(t, s)$ was given by the double sum

$$q(t, s) = \sum_{m,n} q_{m,n} \exp\left[ \frac{2\pi i}{h} (W_m t - W_n s)\right], \tag{171a}$$

with $W_m$ and $W_n$ denoting the diagonal elements of the Hamiltonian matrix of the system under investigation. Born and Wiener claimed that the operator $q$, when applied on a continuous function $x(s)$, would provide a quantum-theoretical description even in those cases where a matrix representation $(q_{mn})$ did not exist. Hence one might hope to reformulate position variables like angles in multiply periodic systems in terms of operators.

A central role in the Born–Wiener scheme was played by the operator $D$, the time derivative $d/dt$, which the authors found to satisfy the quantum mechanical relation

$$\dot{q} = Dq - qD. \tag{172}$$

***

<sup>83</sup> The story of this extension of matrix mechanics has been described in Volume 3, Section V.4.

<sup>84</sup> The German version of the paper was received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* on 5 January 1926. Born had sent an extra copy of the paper to Heisenberg, who returned to Göttingen on 6 January 1926.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0304 -->

IV.3 Formal Equivalence of Wave Mechanics
663

Evidently, this equation could be replaced by the equivalent one,

$$ \dot{q} = \frac{2\pi i}{h} ( Wq - qW), \tag{172'} $$

hence $D$ represented, up to the factor $2\pi i / h$, the generalized Hamiltonian matrix or the Hamiltonian operator $H$. By applying the operator formalism, in which all operators were considered as functions of time $t$ and the differential operator $D$, to the harmonic oscillator problem, Born and Wiener obtained the same solutions as in the matrix scheme. For the problem of uniform, straight-line motion of a mass point—a problem that could not be treated in the matrix theory—they found essentially the classical result, with the quantum conditions providing no extra constraints in this case.

Heisenberg wrote to Pauli on 14 January 1926: ‘Herewith I send you the paper by Born and Wiener, and a similar one by Lanczos, for discussion on Wednesday.’ He had been invited to present a popular talk on 19 January at the Bowling Club of Stade, not far from Hamburg, and looked forward to meeting Pauli the following day in Hamburg, where he planned to stop on his return to Göttingen. The two friends did indeed get together on the 20th, and they discussed the burning physical problems of quantum mechanics, including a formulation of the cyclical variables, i.e., of action and angle variables. Both Heisenberg and Pauli continued to work on the last-mentioned topic afterwards, with Heisenberg sticking rather closely to the Born–Wiener theory. Pauli, on the other hand, regarded the operator formalism unnecessarily complicated and mathematically ‘erudite’. Therefore he invented an alternative calculus, which could be employed in problems of atomic theory.

In Pauli’s calculus, the functions $q(t, W)$ represented the main elements which corresponded to the column sums of the matrices used in matrix mechanics. Pauli reported to Heisenberg: ‘It is essential that the quantities $q(t, W)$ be taken to be continuous functions of the energy $W$, as soon as one deals with aperiodic quantities as well as the periodic ones. … The rules for the multiplication of two rational functions, or of infinite power series, of $t$ and $W$ are now of such type that they contain, when applied to expressions like $\exp(2\pi i \nu t)$, the former matrix multiplication as special cases. The introduction of “operators”, at any rate, is totally superfluous for many purposes’ (Pauli to Heisenberg, 31 January 1926).

Pauli’s operator calculus was based on the commutation rule

$$ Wt - tW = \frac{h}{2\pi i} 1, \tag{173} $$

which followed immediately from the Born–Wiener equation (172’), on introducing $t$ for the operator $q$. Pauli also introduced the special exponential function

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0305 -->

664
Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

$\underline{\text{exp}}[f(\alpha)t]$, given by the equation

$$\underline{\text{exp}}[f(\alpha)t] = \sum_{p=0}^{\infty} \frac{[f(\alpha)]^p t^p}{p!}, \tag{174}$$

with

$$\alpha = \frac{2\pi i}{h} W, \tag{174a}$$

and defined the quantity

$$x(W, t) = \sum_{\tau} x_{\tau}(W) \underline{\text{exp}}[2\pi i \nu_{\tau}(W) t], \tag{175}$$

which evidently corresponded in the matrix theory to a column sum (over $\tau$ positive and negative). The multiplication of two such quantities, $x(W, t)$ and $y(W, t)$, then yielded the result

$$xy(W, t) = \sum_{\tau} (xy)_{\tau}(W) \underline{\text{exp}}[2\pi i \nu_{\tau}(W) t], \tag{176}$$

with coefficients

$$(xy)_{\tau}(W) = \sum_{\sigma} x_{\sigma}(W) y_{\tau-\sigma}(W - h\nu_{\sigma}(W)). \tag{176a}$$

On the basis of the new formalism, Pauli succeeded in deriving the fundamental formulae of the action-angle theory in quantum mechanics, including the commutation relation

$$Jw - wJ = \frac{h}{2\pi i} 1, \tag{177}$$

for the action variable $J$ and the angle $w$.<sup>85</sup>

What, one may ask, distinguished the calculus of Pauli from the operator methods of Born and Wiener? The main difference lay in the fact that in the latter operators occurred which depended on two time-like variables $t$ and $s$, as compared with the situation in Pauli's theory, where only one time variable entered the functions $x(W, t)$ and, in addition, the specially ordered exponential $\underline{\text{exp}}[2\pi i \nu_{\tau}(W)t]$.<sup>86</sup> Hence Pauli succeeded not only in avoiding the mathematically

(See Born and Wiener, 1926b, p. 177, Eq. (10).)

IV.3 Formal Equivalence of Wave Mechanics 665

perhaps questionable limiting operation on the right-hand side of Eq. (171); he also could drop the integration procedure (over the variable $s$) and forget about the ‘kernel function’, which had been used by Born and Wiener to define the operators. Pauli noticed that the same type of kernel functions seemed to show up in the paper by Cornelius Lanczos that had been brought to his attention by Heisenberg. Actually, the basic operator Eq. (171) of Born and Wiener represented a particular form of the integral equations, on which Lanczos had built his field-like representation of matrices, expressed by the equations

$$f(s, \sigma) = \sum_{i,k} a_{ik}\phi^i(s)\phi^k(\sigma), \tag{126}$$

and

$$a_{ik} = \int f(s, \sigma)\phi^i(s)\phi^k(\sigma) ds d\sigma, \tag{127}$$

which allowed him to translate matrices into kernel functions and *vice versa*. These equations now exhibited a great similarity to Pauli’s relations connecting matrices and wave functions, i.e.,

$$x\psi_i(x) = \sum_k x_{ik}\psi_k(x), \tag{167}$$

and

$$x_{ik} = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} x\psi_i(x)\psi_k(x) dx. \tag{169'}$$

The essential difference between Eq. (169)’ and Eq. (127) consists only in the fact that Pauli wrote down a relation in which the integration must be performed only over one variable, while Lanczos needed a two-fold integration over the space variables $s$ and $\sigma$. The replacement of Eq. (127) by Eq. (169’), therefore, hints at a similar simplification of Lanczos’ equation which Pauli had performed earlier by replacing the Born–Wiener operator $q$, Eq. (171), through the continuous function $q(W, t)$, Eq. (175). This time the simplification appeared to be an even more obvious one.

In January 1926, Pauli had declared the operator formalism to be a ‘superfluous’ complication that had to be ‘left behind’. Now, in April 1926, he judged the forerunner of his formalism, by which he established the equivalence between wave and matrix mechanics, with the following words:

> As regards Lanczos, my considerations have only very few points of contact with his ideas. He considers a problem for which the eigenvalues are the reciprocal energy values, whereas here [i.e., in Schrödinger’s theory] the eigenvalues are just the energy

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0307 -->

666  
Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

values. In his [Lanczos’] exposition certain functions depending, like Green’s functions, on two points, play an essential role; such functions are not used here. On the whole I feel that Lanczos’ approach has not much value. (Pauli to Jordan, 12 April 1926; English translation, p. 281)

Thus Pauli criticized two points in Lanczos’ approach: first, the use of kernel functions instead of simple functions depending on one (basically physical) variable; and, second, the fact that the eigenvalues appeared to be reciprocals of those in wave mechanics. One may answer that the first criticism does not exclude that Lanczos’ relation (127) provided the key idea to Pauli in writing down his relation, Eq. (169), one of the two basic equations of the equivalence proof. The second criticism, however, is found to be unjustified; it simply rests on an inaccurate study of Lanczos’ paper.

It may be considered a remarkable fact that Schrödinger, in referring to Lanczos’ work, made exactly the same mistaken statement about the inverse eigenvalues. Still, both Viennese physicists, Schrödinger and Pauli, were wrong at the same point. Lanczos based his formulation on the theory of linear integral equations by Hilbert. Hilbert had considered, more than twenty years earlier, equations of the type

$$
\phi(x) - \lambda \int K(x, y) \phi(y) \, dy = 0. \qquad (178)
$$

This equation possesses eigenfunctions $\phi_i(x)$, each of which belong to a definite eigenvalue $\lambda_i$, $i = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$. (The eigenvalues could be discrete or continuous.) Schrödinger’s wave equation, on the other hand, i.e.,

$$
-\Delta\psi + V\psi = E\psi, \qquad (179)
$$

corresponded to an integral equation

$$
\psi(x) - \frac{1}{E} \int K(x, y) \psi(y) \, dy = 0. \qquad (180)
$$

That is, Hilbert’s eigenvalue $\lambda_i$ did indeed represent Schrödinger’s reciprocal eigenvalue, or

$$
\lambda_i = \frac{1}{E_i}. \qquad (181)
$$

Clearly enough, Lanczos had pointed out the reciprocity of the energy eigenvalues of the physical theory and of the eigenvalues of integral equations in his paper, where he had also given the correct definition of $\lambda_i$. (See Lanczos, 1926a, p. 816, Eqs. (21) and (18).)<sup>87</sup>

---
<sup>87</sup> B. L. van der Waerden, in his analysis of Pauli’s letter on the equivalence proof, has drawn attention to the misunderstanding by Pauli and Schrödinger (Van der Waerden, 1973, pp. 283–285).

IV.3  Formal Equivalence of Wave Mechanics
667

From the situation described here one can derive the following conclusion: Pauli, in his desire—should we say, obsession—to free quantum mechanics from—in his opinion—unnecessary complications, occasionally shot beyond the goal and even claimed erroneously that others had made mistakes. He rejected, for example, the elaborate matrix methods in the Born–Heisenberg–Jordan paper, especially the principal axes transformation theory.$^{88}$ He also considered the operator methods of Born and Wiener as an outcome of ‘mathematical learning’, declaring them to be related to his $q(W, t)$-formalism ‘like the theory of the principal axes transformations is to your [i.e., Heisenberg’s] matrix calculus’ (Pauli to Heisenberg, 31 January 1926). Apparently, he put Lanczos’ methods into the category of the principal axes transformations, although they made it possible to establish a one-to-one relation between the matrix mechanical and the wave mechanical equations and he himself had, in his own proof, more or less copied the ideas of the other. Pauli just did not like ‘kernal functions’, neither the ones of Lanczos nor those of Born and Wiener. He believed that Born and Wiener loved bombastic mathematical methods, and that a kind of ‘*Göttingen Hochmut*’ (‘arrogance’) had prevented them from discovering wave mechanics themselves.$^{89}$ If the facts are properly evaluated, however, one must admit that Pauli overstated the case to the extent that even he was wrong. The ideas that led to the discovery of matrix and wave mechanics, respectively, were very different from each other. This difference prevented, e.g., Born and Wiener in late 1925 from discovering wave mechanics themselves; they rather stopped half way, because they could not free themselves from the idea that quantum mechanics involved an essential element of discontinuity. Lanczos, on the other hand, went quite a bit further; in his case it was the fundamental goal which he connected with the integral equation approach, namely the hope of involving a ‘world kernel’ in his theory, that prevented him from writing down the formula which corresponded to the Schrödinger equation to the hydrogen atom.$^{90}$

Nearly half a century later, in September 1972, Bartel Leendert van der Waerden put the record straight in a public talk, when he analysed the contents of Pauli’s letter to Jordan and especially corrected the error of judgment about Lanczos’ work. (See Van der Waerden, 1973.) After his presentation, Van der Waerden asked Lanczos, who also participated in the meeting: ‘Did you know all this to which I have referred in my paper? Were you aware of these connections?’ Lanczos replied:

> You are absolutely right. You rehabilitated my work. Pauli was a vicious man . . . . Anything which didn’t agree with his ideas was wrong, and anything was right only

$^{90}$ Lanczos’ ‘world kernel’ was connected with a Hamiltonian for the entire universe. According to the ideas which he had developed earlier, the universe was responsible for the particular behaviour of the microscopic quantum systems. (See Volume 3, Section IV.2.)
