if he made it, if he discovered it, which is alright for such a great man . . . . I certainly was aware of these connections, . . . the weakness was that I didn’t specify the kernel functions and the special [eigen]functions.
At that time, you know, after the matrix mechanics, it looked as if you couldn’t do anything with the continuum . . . . Everything is discontinuous in the matrices. Now I was very much interested at that time in integral equations, and actually the integral equation which I used was not the Schrödinger equation, but the inverse equation . . . . And that is the reason why the energies actually come in with a reciprocal, so that the Green’s function which I had is basically the Schrödinger equation with the source of a delta function. If you have a source, and that source happens to be a delta function, then this function does have a physical significance, whereas it looks after Pauli’s criticism that it has no physical significance. But it does have a physical significance. (Lanczos in Van der Waerden, 1973, p. 287)

Upon Van der Waerden’s question: ‘Yes, but after you had read Schrödinger’s paper, did you realize that this was the case?’ Lanczos said: ‘Afterwards, it was too trivial . . . . I mean, it was no longer of interest, because Schrödinger came along and he did it. As it often happens, it is the second man who hits the nail on the head and not the first one’ (Lanczos, *loc. cit.*).

Lanczos certainly did not discover wave mechanics, nor did Born and Wiener. But all three contributed their share in establishing the equivalence of matrix and wave mechanics. Pauli, who had not discovered the scheme of wave mechanics either, was probably quite unfair—‘vicious,’ as Lanczos called him—when he accused these colleagues; after all, their prior work had helped him to make a valid contribution to the whole field.

### A Combination of Schrödinger’s and Lanczos’ Theory

In the previous parts of this section, we have shown how little the established quantum physicists thought of the contribution of Cornelius Lanczos, a younger colleague essentially unknown to them. The first physicist to appreciate his work fully was Carl Eckart from Pasadena, another newcomer, who contributed (at the end of May 1926) a paper to the *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences* entitled ‘The Solution of the Problem of the Simple Oscillator by a Combination of the Schrödinger and the Lanczos Theories’ (Eckart, 1926a).
Carl Henry Eckart was born on 4 May 1902 in St. Louis, Missouri. After studying first (from 1919 to 1923) at Washington University in his hometown, he joined Princeton University in 1923 and earned his doctorate (in 1925) under Karl T. Compton, the older brother of Arthur Holly Compton. From Princeton he also submitted (in August 1924) an interesting note on ‘The Wave Theory of the Compton Efect’ to *Physical Review* (Eckart, 1924). This paper had been stimulated by an English publication of Louis de Broglie in the *Philosophical Magazine* entitled ‘A Tentative Theory of Light Quanta’ (L. de Broglie, 1924a). De Broglie had explained in that paper his interpretation of light as particles having an extraordinarily small mass $m_0$ and energy $hv_0$, connected with a phase

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0310 -->

IV.3 Formal Equivalence of Wave Mechanics 669

wave of frequency $\nu$ ($=\nu_0/\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}$, with velocity $v$ very close to $c$). Eckart later recalled the origin of that paper: ‘Someone called my attention [to de Broglie’s papers], and I read them in the Palmer Library [of Princeton University]. It must have been in the Spring of 1924, because I spent the summer of 1924 in St. Louis, and there wrote a paper on a wave explanation of the Compton effect which was discussed with Frank Bubb and [George Eric MacDonnell] Jauncey’ (Eckart, AHQP Interview, p. 10). Bubb even added a note to the paper of the graduate student Eckart, in which he pointed out the ‘very interesting similarity between the recent theory of de Broglie and the present theory,’ that had ‘developed in conversations with Mr. Eckart,’ and in which he summarized the content as: ‘Both these views essentially regard the frequency of radiation as the time component of a vector whose properties are very similar to those of the covariant energy-momentum vector of a particle. The puzzling questions which arise through the quantum theory’s peculiar use of the frequency . . . do not leave one perfectly satisfied with our ordinary conception of frequency . . . . It seems likely that a proper generalization of the frequency will either answer or remove the questions just now tormenting us so’ (Bubb, note added to Eckart, 1924, pp. 595–596).

In his paper, Eckart interpreted the Compton effect as being caused by the changing curvature of space near gravitating matter, i.e., the electron. The equation thus obtained for the frequency difference of the radiation before (point A) and after (point B) passing through the non-static gravitational field,

$$ \nu_B - \nu_A = \text{const.} \int_A^B \frac{\partial g_{ij}}{\partial t} \frac{dx^i}{da} \frac{dx^j}{da} da \quad (182) $$

(with $g_{ij}$ the fundamental matrix tensor), showed a striking similarity to that derived by Arthur Compton on the basis of the light-quantum hypothesis, namely,

$$ h\nu_B - h\nu_A = m_e c^2 - \frac{m_e c^2}{\sqrt{1 - v_e^2/c^2}} \quad (182') $$

(with $m_e$ and $v_e$ denoting the mass and velocity of the scattering electron).$^{91}$ The theory ‘was an endeavor to construct a formal “geometric optics” theory to carry de Broglie’s ideas further. My enthusiasm for this was so great that I listed this as a project for a National Research Fellowship in 1925,’ Eckart recalled later (Eckart, AHQP Interview, p. 10). He indeed obtained the fellowship and went, in 1925, to the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena. Paul Sophus Epstein, the theoretician there, listened to the newcomer’s proposal and remarked: ‘That’s fine. How do you propose to begin?’ (Eckart, AHQP Interview, p. 11). Since Eckart did not have any idea and did not receive any further encouragement when he presented Louis de Broglie’s work in the Caltech Colloquium, he dropped the topic.

$^{91}$ Eckart derived a covariant formalism, including equations for the momentum of radiation—with each equation corresponding to one in Compton’s light-quantum theory.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0311 -->

670 &emsp; Chapter IV &emsp; Early Response and Applications

Towards the end of his paper on the Compton effect, Eckart had referred to the radiation theory of Niels Bohr, Hendrik Kramers and John Slater—which unlike his own paper—relegated ‘the wave to a subordinate position’ (Eckart, 1924, p. 595). Although it would be disproved in the following year, the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory of radiation exerted—via Kramers’ dispersion theory and its extensions—a certain influence on the path to the new quantum theory which Heisenberg proposed in the summer of 1925. Max Born and Pascual Jordan then proposed the matrix formulation of this theory. As Eckart recalled: ‘I was not greatly attracted to this [scheme], but in the late winter of early 1926 Born came to Pasadena and his lucid lectures aroused my interest’ (Eckart, AHQP Interview, p. 11).

Born had earlier, while staying at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology together with Norbert Wiener, developed the operator calculus of quantum mechanics. Eckart recalled: ‘The interpretation of the commutator law for $p$ and $q$ as [being] identical with the differentiation operator was very strongly emphasized in his lectures. The result was that I spent the spring of 1926 working rather intensively with this operator formulation, and was completely familiar with what is now known as the Schrödinger operator (the energy operator) before Schrödinger’s papers appeared in Pasadena’ (Eckart, AHQP Interview, p. 12).

The differentiation operator form of the ‘commutator’ law for a particle of mass $\mu$, referred to above, was

$$
\frac{h}{2\pi i} = \mu[\dot{q}q - q\dot{q}], \qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad (183)
$$

where the time derivative of the position operator $q$ could be replaced by the operator product difference, i.e.,

$$
\dot{q} = Dq - qD, \quad \text{with} \quad D = \frac{d}{dt}, \qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad (184)
$$

and the operator $D$ constituted, up to a factor $2\pi i/h$, the energy operator. (See Born and Wiener, 1926b, pp. 177–183.)

Born and Wiener had treated (by their operator method) the problems of the one-dimensional harmonic oscillator and of the uniform straight-line motion of a mass point, arriving in the latter case at a formula which involved, besides the known classical term, another term which had the order of magnitude of the de Broglie wavelength $h/\sqrt{2\mu W}$ (with $\sqrt{2\mu W}$ denoting the momentum of the particle). They had not paid any attention to that particular point and neglected it, since it was small for large energies; thus, they had failed to establish a relation to the phase wave theory. The same happened to Eckart, who recalled later: ‘It never occurred to me, for reasons very obscure—which I can’t begin to recapture—to associate this [theory of Born and Wiener] with my earlier interest in the de Broglie idea . . . It perhaps does indicate the weakness of the whole operator idea as it was originated by [Oliver] Heaviside. The operator calculus certainly cannot

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0312 -->

# IV.3 Formal Equivalence of Wave Mechanics

671

be completely divorced from things the operators act on' (Eckart, AHQP Interview, p. 12).
Then, however, the papers of Lanczos and Schrödinger, published in March 1926 (Lanczos, 1926a; Schrödinger, 1926c), helped to solve the problem in the following sense: 'The Lanczos quantum theory requires a set of orthogonal functions, by means of which the matrices of Born and Jordan are to be determined. . . . Schrödinger has published a quantum principle which leads directly to a set of orthogonal functions . . . . If these are interpreted as the functions entering into the Lanczos theory, the matrices of the Born–Jordan theory are readily obtained' (Eckart, 1926a, p. 473).<sup>92</sup>
The problem which Eckart attacked in his paper—submitted in late May 1926 to the *Proceeding of the National Academy of Sciences*—was, as he put it himself, 'to show, in a purely formal way, that the Schrödinger equation *must be the basis for the Born, Jordan and Heisenberg matrix calculus*' (Eckart, 1926a, p. 473). He found: 'This is most readily accomplished by using the Lanczos modification of the latter' (Eckart, *loc. cit.*). For a first demonstration he selected the problem of the linear oscillator. He recalled later: 'The paper [by Schrödinger] contained the solution of the hydrogen atom. It did not contain the simple oscillator. So, having gone over the solution to the simple oscillator problem in the Heisenberg version many times, I immediately tried to do it in the Schrödinger version and was blocked by the Hermite equation, which is deceptively simple . . . after you have learned enough about differential equations which I had not at that time' (Eckart, AHQP Interview, p. 13). Since he did not know how to continue, Eckart asked his colleague Fritz Zwicky for help after writing down the equation on the blackboard. Zwicky could not give the solution either, but fortunately Epstein stood near them and listened to the problem. As Eckart recalled: 'He went into his office, came back and handed me a copy of his dissertation. I opened it and found the whole theory of the Hermite polynomials neatly worked out, and quite promptly applied it to the simple oscillator problem' (Eckart, AHQP Interview, p. 13).
In his paper, Eckart started from the classical Hamilton–Jacobi equation of the oscillating point having mass $\mu$, frequency $\omega/2\pi$ and energy $W$,

$$\frac{1}{2\mu} \left( \frac{dS}{dx} \right)^2 + \frac{1}{2} \mu \omega^2 x^2 - W = 0, \qquad (185)$$

which he turned into the analogous equation according to Schrödinger,

$$- \frac{1}{2\mu} \frac{h^2}{4\pi^2} \frac{d^2\psi}{dx^2} + \left\{ \frac{1}{2} \mu \omega^2 x^2 - W \right\} \psi = 0, \qquad (186)$$

<sup>92</sup> Later Eckart recalled that he learned of Lanczos’ paper (Lanczos, 1926a) shortly after seeing the first communication by Schrödinger (1926c); and that his impression was that ‘Lanczos essentially converted the Schrödinger equation into an integral equation’ (Eckart, AHQP Interview, p. 12). Actually, this recollection does not describe the order of publication of the two papers, as Schrödinger’s appeared in print about two weeks after Lanczos’; also, Lanczos did convert the matrix equations into integral equations, and not Schrödinger’s wave equation, as the latter did not exist at the time of submission of Lanczos’ paper.

by substituting

$$S = \frac{h}{2\pi} \ln \psi \qquad \text{(187)}$$

and solving the associated extremum problem (i.e., $\delta \int \psi^2 G dx = 0$). Eckart, referring to the Munich dissertation of Paul Sophus Epstein, remarked: ‘The solution of this equation [(186)] has been discussed by P. S. Epstein and leads to parabolic cylinder functions’ (Eckart, 1926a, p. 474).

For this purpose the new variable $u$,

$$x = (h / 4\pi\mu\omega)^{1/2} u, \qquad \text{(188)}$$

must be introduced into Eq. (186), which then assumes the form

$$\frac{d^2\psi}{du^2} - \left\{ \frac{u^2}{4} - \frac{2\pi W}{h\omega} \right\} W = 0. \qquad \text{(189)}$$

Evidently, the *Ansatz*

$$u = \exp\left\{\pm\frac{u^2}{4}\right\} f_\pm(u) \qquad \text{(190)}$$

makes it possible to simplify this equation further to

$$\frac{d^2 f_\pm}{du^2} \mp \frac{df_\pm}{du} \pm \left\{ \frac{2\pi W}{h\omega} - \frac{1}{2} \right\} f_\pm = 0. \qquad \text{(191)}$$

Only for integral values of the curly expression do the solutions $f_\pm$ become finite polynomials $f_n(u)$; then the orthogonal eigenfunctions are

$$\psi_n = \sqrt{n!} \sqrt[4]{\frac{2\mu\omega}{h}} \exp\left(-\frac{u^2}{4}\right) f_n(u), \qquad \text{(192)}$$

with

$$f_0 = 0, \quad f_1 = u, \quad \text{etc.}, \qquad \text{(192a)}$$

and the energy eigenvalues

$$W_n = (n + \frac{1}{2}) \frac{h\omega}{2\pi}. \qquad \text{(193)}$$

From the paper by Born and Wiener, Eckart knew the equations of motion to be given by the operator equations

$$ \dot{X} = \frac{1}{\mu} P = DX - XD, \qquad (194\mathrm{a}) $$

and

$$ \dot{P} = -\mu \omega^2 X = DP - PD, \qquad (194\mathrm{b}) $$

with the position operator $X$ and the momentum operator $P$. Further, $X$ and $P$ satisfy the commutation relation,

$$ PX - XP = \frac{h}{2\pi i}. \qquad (195) $$

Eckart emphasized: 'The essential mathematical point of this paper is to show that the condition [(195)] may be replaced by the requirements

$$ x = \frac{1}{\psi_n(x)} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} X(x, \xi) \psi_n(\xi) \, d\xi, \qquad [(196\mathrm{a})] $$

$$ \frac{2\pi i W_n}{h} = \frac{1}{\psi_n(x)} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} D(x, \xi) \psi_n(\xi) \, d\xi, \qquad [(196\mathrm{b})] $$

(Eckart, 1926a, p. 475). The quantities $D(x, \xi)$ and $X(x, \xi)$, occurring in Eqs. (196), were defined in terms of the associated operators ($O = X, D = d/dt$),

$$ Of(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} O(x, \xi) f(\xi) \, d\xi, \qquad (197) $$

which Eckart also took from the Born–Wiener paper. (See Born and Wiener, 1926b, p. 175, Eq. (4).)$^{93}$
He simultaneously noticed that the kernels were just the kernels in Lanczos' integral equations; hence, he proposed to expand $D(x, \xi)$ and $X(x, \xi)$ as:$^{94}$

$$ D(x, \xi) = \sum_{j,k} D_{jk} \psi_j(x) \psi_k(\xi), \qquad (198\mathrm{a}) $$

and

$$ X(x, \xi) = \sum_{j,k} X_{jk} \psi_j(x) \psi_k(\xi). \qquad (198\mathrm{b}) $$

***

### The Solution of the Equations of Quantum Dynamics: Carl Eckart’s Equivalence Demonstration

Later on Eckart wrote: ‘The recent advances in quantum dynamics made by Heisenberg [1925c], Born and Jordan [1925b], Dirac [1925d, 1926a], and most recently, by Schrödinger [1926c], have led to various mathematical formulations of the various physical hypotheses involved. In the present paper it is proposed to give a unified mathematical treatment, which, though it cannot pretend to be the final form of the theory, leads to methods of solution of the equations of Born and Jordan, and Dirac which are much simpler than those previously developed. Very little attempt to justify the mathematical steps by physical hypothesis will be made. The final achievement will be the inclusion of the results of Schrödinger in a single calculus with those of the other authors mentioned above. This would seem to be the strongest support which either of the two dissimilar theories have thus far received’ (Eckart, 1926b, p. 711).

On 7 June 1926, Carl Eckart completed a second paper entitled ‘Operator Calculus and the Solution of the Equations of Quantum Dynamics’ and submitted it to *Physical Review*, where it was published in the issue of October 1926. In spite of the relatively late date of publication, the interval between Eckart’s composition of the two papers—i.e., the one in *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences* discussed earlier and that in *Physical Review* which will be analysed below—was very short, merely a week, as can be seen from the submission dates: 31 May and 7 June, respectively. As Eckart recalled later: ‘This merely indicates the speed with which things were moving [in those days]. Certainly, the first one in the *Proceedings* was written in extreme haste, in an effort to obtain priority. The one in the *Physical Review* was not delayed, but it was written more carefully, and a number of things were thought out that had been unclear in the first one’ (Eckart, AHQP Interview, p. 14).

What had been unclear in the first paper, in which Eckart had solved the one-dimensional oscillator problem in Schrödinger theory and showed the solution obtained to be identical to that found earlier from matrix mechanics by explicitly calculating the matrix elements of the position and momentum matrices due to the prescription of Lanczos? The essential missing point consisted, Eckart argued, in the task of establishing a general method of calculating matrix elements (i.e., the matrix elements of the Born–Jordan theory) and of relating Schrödinger’s method directly to the other quantum mechanical methods. For this purpose, Eckart developed ‘a formal calculus which includes the Born and Jordan matrix dynamics, and also the remarkable quantum condition of Schrödinger’ (Eckart, 1926b, p. 711). As an appropriate formal calculus to accomplish all that, he

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0317 -->

676 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

suggested the operator calculus, i.e., a slight generalization of methods that were available in the mathematical literature for quite some time. Of course, one may wonder how he arrived at this idea.

Eckart surely obtained the first indication of using operators from Max Born’s lectures at Caltech on quantum mechanics, and from the paper published by Max Born and Norbert Wiener on the operator formulation of quantum mechanics.${}^{96}$ The operator formalism developed in that paper, although it could easily be applied to the harmonic oscillator problem—and it had actually been by Born and Wiener—was difficult to handle in other atomic problems, such as the nonrelativistic hydrogen problem. In each such case a solution had to be *guessed* in terms of the operators $t$ and $D = d/dt$, which seemed to be an easy job only in very simple problems. The question arose, therefore, whether there existed more general operators than those proposed by Born and Wiener. Born and Wiener had referred, in connection with the exact formulation of their methods, to an article by the Italian mathematician Salvatore Pincherle (1853–1936) on functional operators in the *Encyklopädie der mathematischen Wissenschaften* (Pincherle, 1906). Pincherle had given there a review of the (until 1906) accepted mathematical results that included an application of operator methods—to the theory of differential and difference equations, to selected problems of number theory and to linear integral equations. As examples of such operators he had considered, for a given independent variable $x$, the associated differential operator $d/dx$, as well as its inverse, the integral operator $\int dx$. Eckart, in his paper on the operator calculus, would refer in particular to the article by Pincherle at that point, where he talked about the role of the operator $dQ/dX$, with $Q$ denoting an operator function of the (independent) variable $X$, which is also an operator.${}^{97}$ However, in the same context he referred simultaneously to the matrix mechanics paper by Born and Jordan (1925b) and to two papers by Paul Dirac, who had developed his own calculus of quantum mechanical objects, the $q$-numbers (Dirac, 1925d, 1926a).${}^{98}$

However, if one is looking for the first stimulus to Eckart’s interest in the operator formulation, one should take very seriously his later remark that he had derived the initiative from Max Born’s ‘lucid lectures’. These lectures on quantum mechanics—or ‘atomic dynamics’ as Born called them—obviously included the most recent operator formulation which Max Born had obtained in Cambridge, Massachusetts, together with Norbert Wiener. Actually, Born had already outlined the method in Lecture 20 of his M.I.T. course on ‘*Problems of Atomic Dynamics*,’ presenting the main ideas and results for a less specialized public. Born had

---

Journal of Mathematics and Physics* (Born and Wiener, 1926a)—although the latter should have been available in California earlier than the German publication.
${}^{97}$See Eckart, 1926b, p. 717, and footnote 6, p. 715.

677

remarked, in particular, after introducing the operator definition, Eq. (171):

It is then easy to show that operator products, formed by successive application of operators, correspond to matrix products. An explicit representation of operators is not, however, necessary. It is sufficient to consider linear operators in general, that is, such operators for which the simple formula

$$q[x(t) + y(t)] = qx(t) + qy(t) \tag{203}$$

holds. The multiplication by a function of *t*, differentiation and integration with respect to *t*, for example, are all operators. Of special importance is the differential operator $D = d/dt$. (Born, 1926d; reprint, p. 126)

With these remarks Born had addressed the topic that the mathematician Pincherle had earlier called ‘elements of the operator calculus’ (‘*Elemente des Operatorkalküls*’) in his encyclopedia article (Pincherle, 1906, p. 766). After defining operators by the symbols $A, B, \ldots$, acting on functions $\alpha, \beta, \ldots$, and yielding other functions as results, he had spoken about combinations of operators, like sums and multiplication by a number $c$. He had further emphasized that the product of two operators, $AB$, is in general not commutative, i.e.,

$$AB \neq BA, \tag{204}$$

but that one usually assumes that products of operators and their combinations satisfy the associative and distributive laws, namely,

$$A(B\Gamma) = (AB)\Gamma \tag{205}$$

(with $\Gamma$ denoting a product of further factors), and

$$A(\alpha + \beta) = A(\alpha) + A(\beta), \tag{206a}$$

as well as (with $c$ a constant factor)

$$A(c\alpha) = cA(\alpha), \tag{206b}$$

respectively. By these properties linear operators are indeed defined and Pincherle had treated, in the following sections of his article, simple examples of linear operators, such as the operators $D$ (differentiation) and $\Delta$ (finite difference), and their applications in mathematical problems.
Eckart, in developing his operator calculus, took over the definitions given by Pincherle. Thus he displayed in Section I of his article in the *Physical Review*, entitled ‘The Operator Calculus in the Classical Theory’, more or less the definitions and results presented in the encyclopedia article and then applied them to reformulate the problem of classical dynamics. For example, he translated the Hamiltonian equations of a classical mechanical system having *n* degrees of

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0319 -->

678 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

freedom into the operator language as
$$ \frac{dP_j}{dT} = - \frac{\partial H(P, Q)}{\partial Q_j}, $$
and
$$ \frac{dQ_j}{dT} = \frac{\partial H(P, Q)}{\partial P_j}, \qquad\qquad\qquad (207) $$

$j = 1, 2, \dots, n$. That is, he replaced in usual equations simply the position and momentum variables, $q_j$ and $p_j$, by the corresponding operators, $Q_j$ and $P_j$, and similarly the time $t$ by the time operator $T$. Evidently, now the Hamiltonian also became an operator, depending in the same way on the operator variables as did the classical Hamiltonian on the $q_j$ and $p_j$.

Eckart claimed: ‘In translating ordinary equations into operator notation, nothing new is introduced. The translation involves merely a change of mental focus. Instead of concentrating the attention on the numerical quantities, it is directed to the operations of combining them’ (Eckart, 1926b, p. 713). This feature becomes obvious in the way of solving equations. For example, the operator equation for the harmonic oscillator,
$$ \frac{d^2Q}{dT^2} + \omega^2Q = 0 \qquad\qquad\qquad (208) $$

(with $\omega$ a constant proportional to the frequency of the system) could be rewritten with the help of the differentiation formula ($X$ being the position operator)
$$ \frac{dQ}{dX} = \frac{d}{dx}Q - Q\frac{d}{dx}, \qquad\qquad\qquad (209) $$
as
$$ \frac{d^2}{dt^2}Q - 2\frac{d}{dt}Q\frac{d}{dt} + Q\frac{d^2}{dt^2} + \omega^2Q = 0. \qquad\qquad\qquad (208') $$

The solution consisted in finding a function $q = q(t)$ satisfying the equation
$$ \frac{d^2}{dt^2}(qf) - 2\frac{d}{dt}\left(q\frac{df}{dt}\right) + q\frac{d^2f}{dt^2} + \omega^2qf = 0. \qquad\qquad\qquad (208'') $$

Eckart first simplified this equation to
$$ f\left(\frac{d^2q}{dt^2} + \omega^2q\right) = 0, \qquad\qquad\qquad (210) $$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0320 -->

IV.3 Formal Equivalence of Wave Mechanics 679

that had to be valid for any arbitrary function $f = f(t)$. Evidently, Eq. (210) therefore implied the equation

$$\frac{d^2q}{dt^2} + \omega^2q = 0, \quad (210')$$

whose solution was just the result of the usual, non-operator approach in classical dynamics.

A different possibility of treating the problem in operator theory was to introduce explicitly, in Eq. (208'), the differential operator $\theta = d/dt$, now considered as depending on the pair of operators $q$ and $d/dq$, i.e.,

$$\frac{d}{dt} = \theta\left(q, \frac{d}{dq}\right). \quad (211)$$

In doing so, Eckart obtained the equation

$$(\theta^2q - 2\theta q\theta + q\theta^2 + \omega^2q)\phi = 0, \quad (212)$$

which had to be valid for arbitrary functions $\phi$ (of $q$ and $d/dq$). If he inserted for $\theta$ the *Ansatz*

$$\theta = \frac{\partial S}{\partial q} \frac{d}{dq}, \quad (213)$$

he derived the Hamilton–Jacobi equation,

$$\frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{dS}{dq}\right)^2 + \omega^2q = W = \text{const.} \quad (214)$$

for the linear harmonic oscillator, involving the characteristic function $S$ which satisfied the equation

$$\frac{dq}{dt} = \frac{dS}{dq}. \quad (214a)$$

While so far he had only reproduced well-known results of the classical theory, Eckart expected that the operator point of view would also help in formulating the new quantum mechanics. Thus he stated in his paper:

Since the great problem of the quantum theory seems to be to find new methods of computation, new operations of combining numerical quantities, it may be supposed that this change of view-point will be of value in the development of the theory. This value may be purely heuristic, and it may be possible to reduce the

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0321 -->

680

equations finally obtained to ordinary differential equations, or at least, to equations involving only ordinary mathematical operations with which we are already familiar.
(Eckart, 1926b, p. 713)

The other possibility was that a reduction of the operator equations (describing quantum systems) to ordinary differential equations cannot be found. Matrix mechanics on first inspection seemed to represent a scheme of the latter type, since its matrices obeyed relations which were not satisfied by the corresponding quantities in the classical theory. Still, Eckart hoped that he would be able, by suitable transformations, to rewrite the equations of the operator calculus describing quantum dynamical systems in terms of ordinary differential equations. Of course, he had first to devise for that purpose a suitable quantum-theoretical operator scheme, certainly some generalization of the one that he had used in the classical case.

To approach this goal, he considered general linear operators satisfying Born's equation (203), assuming simultaneously the non-commutativity of the operators as a rule. Further, he defined an operator $D_x$ by the equation

$$D_x X - X D_x = [1 \otimes], \tag{215}$$

(where the right-hand side denoted multiplication by unity) and wrote for the quantum-theoretical differentiation

$$\frac{dQ}{dX} = D_x Q - Q D_x. \tag{216}$$

He formally took over Eq. (216) from the matrix calculus of Born and Jordan, or the $q$-number calculus of Dirac, referring explicitly to these developments.$^{99}$ From the latter he especially copied the two equations

$$\frac{d}{dX} (Q + P) = \frac{dQ}{dX} + \frac{dP}{dX}, \tag{217}$$

and

$$\frac{d}{dX} (QP) = \frac{dQ}{dX} P + Q \frac{dP}{dX}. \tag{218}$$

(See Dirac, 1925d, Eqs. (I) and (II) on p. 645.)$^{100}$ He finally generalized Eqs. (215) and (216) by considering operator functions in the theory depending on several independent (operator) variables, $Q_1, \ldots, Q_n$. Thus he formulated the

$^{100}$ Eckart, in his paper, proved Eqs. (217) and (218) from the defining Eq. (215).

IV.3  Formal Equivalence of Wave Mechanics                                                                                                        681

equations

$$D_j Q_i - Q_i D_j = [\delta_{ij} \otimes ],$$                                                                                                        (219)

and

$$\frac{\partial F}{\partial Q_j} = D_j F - F D_j.$$                                                                                                    (220)

With this general operator scheme at hand—especially the following multiplication rule, which he interpreted as being ‘more closely analogous to vector than to arithmetic multiplication’ (Eckart, 1926b, p. 716)—Eckart entered into the formulation of the fundamental equations of quantum mechanics. He proceeded in the spirit of Paul Dirac, who had claimed that ‘the classical equations are to be retained formally without alteration’ and ‘only the operations by which the quantities involved are combined are to be altered’ (Eckart, 1926b, p. 717), and wrote down the ‘commutator’ equations, i.e.,

$$
\left.
\begin{aligned}
P_i Q_j - Q_j P_i &= \left[ \frac{h}{2 \pi i} \delta_{ij} \otimes \right], \\
Q_i Q_j - Q_j Q_i &= 0, \\
P_i P_j - P_j P_i &= 0,
\end{aligned}
\right\} \qquad (221)
$$

and the dynamical equations, i.e.,

$$
\left.
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d P_j}{d T} &= \frac{d}{d t} P_j - P_j \frac{d}{d t} = - \frac{\partial H(P Q)}{\partial Q_j}, \\
\text{and } \frac{d Q_j}{d T} &= \frac{d}{d t} Q_j - Q_j \frac{d}{d t} = \frac{\partial H(P Q)}{\partial P_j},
\end{aligned}
\right\} \qquad (222)
$$

in his operator language.

From there Eckart continued immediately: ‘It is possible to define a numerical quantity related to each operator of the new theory by a relation which has already been used by Born and Wiener:

$$\frac{1}{\psi} P_j \psi = p_j, \qquad [(223\text{a})]$$

$$\frac{1}{\psi} Q_j \psi = q_j, \qquad [(223\text{b})]$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0323 -->

682 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

and in general

$$ \frac{1}{\psi} F \psi = f, \quad [(223c)] $$

where $F$ is any function of $P_j$ and $Q_j$ (Eckart, 1926b, p. 718).$^{101}$

Born and Wiener had observed that the function $\psi$ assumes the numerical value $\exp[2\pi i Wt/h]$, with $W$ denoting the energy of the state under consideration. Eckart expressed this fact in operator language as

$$ \frac{1}{\psi_n} H(P_j Q_j) \psi_n = W_n, \quad (224) $$

where $n$ refers to a given stationary state. He now claimed that Eq. (224) ‘will be seen [to be] the equation published by Schrödinger in another form ... which, in addition to defining $\psi_n$, serves to distinguish a certain discrete sequence of values $W$ from all others’ (Eckart, 1926b, p. 718).

As the next step one had to define the operator $\theta$ substituting the differential operator $d/dt$. By combining Eqs. (219) to (222)—which resulted in the intermediate equations

$$ \frac{d}{dt} P_j - P_j \frac{d}{dt} = \frac{2\pi i}{h} (HP_j - P_j H) \quad (225a) $$

and

$$ \frac{d}{dt} Q_j - Q_j \frac{d}{dt} = \frac{2\pi i}{h} (HQ_j - Q_j H) \quad (225b) $$

—Eckart derived the crucial equation

$$ \theta = \frac{2\pi i}{h} H(PQ). \quad (226) $$

Now he assumed that the position operator $Q_j$ in his theory meant simply ‘multiplication by $q_j$,’ or $[q_j \otimes]$, and asked for the corresponding representation of the canonically conjugate momentum operator $P_j$. Since the latter had to satisfy the first ‘commutator’ relation (221) with $Q_j$, $P_j$ had to be replaced by

$$ P_j = \frac{h}{2\pi i} \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial q_j} \right). \quad (227) $$

---

$^{101}$ Actually, Born and Wiener had used the equation $y(t) = qx(t)$, where the right-hand side denoted the application of an operator $q$ (of the form $\lim_{\tau \to \infty} \int_{-\tau}^{+\tau} q(t, s) ds$) on the function $x(t)$, yielding another function $y(t)$. Of course, Eqs. (223) could be interpreted in this way.

IV.3 Formal Equivalence of Wave Mechanics                                                                                     683

Hence the operator $\theta$ in the same representation was described by

$$\theta = \frac{2\pi i}{h} H\left( \frac{h}{2\pi i} \frac{\partial}{\partial q_j}, q_j \right). \qquad (226')$$

With these representations of the main operators of quantum dynamics, the fundamental equation (224) became

$$\frac{1}{\psi} H\left( \frac{1}{2\pi i} \frac{\partial}{\partial q_j}, q_j \right) \psi = W. \qquad (224')$$

Evidently, that equation assumed the perfect shape of Schrödinger's equation for the nonrelativistic hydrogen equation, i.e.,

$$-\frac{h^2}{8\pi^2\mu} \frac{1}{\psi} \nabla^2 \psi - \left( \frac{e^2}{r} + W \right) = 0, \qquad (228)$$

on substituting the corresponding Hamiltonian operator

$$H(PQ) = \frac{1}{2\mu} [P_x^2 + P_y^2 + P_x^2] - \frac{e^2}{r}. \qquad (229)$$

And, obviously, Eq. (228) possessed solutions having suitable smoothness properties only for discrete values of the energy,

$$W = W_n = -\frac{2\pi^2\mu e^4}{h^2n^2}, \quad n = 1, 2, 3, \dots . \qquad (230\text{a})$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions were, in agreement with Born and Wiener,

$$\psi_n = \exp\left( \frac{2\pi i}{h} W_n t \right). \qquad (230\text{b})$$

The crucial point in Eckart's equivalence demonstration was the following observation: Given the representation, Eq. (226), of the operator $\theta$ and the eigenfunctions $\psi_n$ due to Eq. (230b), then the operator $Q_j$ could no longer be represented as $[q_j \otimes ]$, but rather by a matrix $Q_j(nk)$ which was obtained from the expansion

$$q_j \psi_n(q) = \sum_k Q_j(nk) \psi_k(q). \qquad (231)$$

Evidently, $Q_j$ operates on an arbitrary function $f(q) (= \sum_n F_n \psi_n)$ as

$$Q_j f = \sum_{n,k} F_n Q_j(nk) \psi_k. \qquad (232)$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0325 -->

684 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

Similarly, a matrix representation can be written for the canonically conjugate momentum variable $P_j$ and thus also for all other operators.$^{102}$
Finally, Eckart showed that the eigenfunctions $\psi_n$ satisfy the orthogonality relations
$$ \iiint_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \psi_m \psi_n dx dy dz = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{for } n \neq m, \\ C_n & \text{for } n = m, \end{cases} \quad (233) $$
where $C_n$ was a constant factor. He concluded his presentation by saying: ‘The method of obtaining the matrices which has just been outlined differs very little from Lanczos’ interpretation of the matrix calculus which is thus included in the present calculus’ (Eckart, 1926b, p. 723). This completed his formal equivalence proof.
In the last part of his paper, Eckart returned to the one-dimensional harmonic oscillator, the example from his previous paper (Eckart, 1926b, pp. 724–726). He showed again that the matrix representation obtained from the operator formalism agreed with the one found earlier by Born and Jordan. Eckart would continue to use his operator methods in the following months and derive, for example, a solution of the nonrelativistic hydrogen problem (Eckart, 1926c), to which we shall return in the next section.

**IV.4 Response to Wave Mechanics II. Applications and Extensions**

Several eminent physicists reacted, as we have reported in Section IV.2, very quickly to the proposal of an undulatory theory of atoms, sometimes even before the publication of Schrödinger’s first communication on the subject. However, these, in general very positive, responses from Munich, Berlin or Leyden did not immediately result in active work by others. One noticed and applauded the concepts and results of wave mechanics; one criticized this or that assumption in it; still, neither Sommerfeld, Einstein nor Planck personally sat down to try out a new example not previously considered by Schrödinger, or suggested a further application or extension of the scheme. But all three spread the rumour about undulatory mechanics to their colleagues. Thus the Berlin chemist Fritz Haber, a close friend of Einstein and Planck, mentioned Schrödinger’s new theory in a talk ‘Über die Grenzgebiete der Chemie’ (‘On the Border Areas of Chemistry’), with which he addressed a group of American physicians visiting the medical faculty of the University of Berlin on 16 June 1926.$^{103}$ He especially remarked—after speaking on the atomic model of Bohr and Sommerfeld in the old quantum

685

theory: ‘We do have certain doubts as to whether the intuitive content of this theory may be valid forever, in particular since Schrödinger has most recently shown that the non-visualizable, quantitative relations [of atomic physics] also follow, in complete agreement, from a quite different method. But it is too early to attempt an elementary presentation of the new method’ (Haber, 1926, p. 850, footnote 1).¹⁰⁴

In July 1926, Schrödinger went to Berlin and Munich, providing an introduction to his theory in both places. A couple of months earlier, on 16 May 1926, Erwin Fues, a member of Schrödinger’s Zurich institute, spoke on the theory to the physicists who had assembled at the Stuttgart meeting of the German Physical Society. At the same meeting Gregor Wentzel from Munich also presented in his talk (on the Stark effect and related topics) some results from wave mechanics.

Schrödinger found a further strong advocate of his atomic theory in his countryman Wolfgang Pauli, who, after studying the first communication, had found in April 1926 that the same results followed from wave mechanical and matrix mechanical calculations, respectively. A few months after that, Schrödinger received two letters: one from David Mathias Dennison, then in Copenhagen, the other from Ivar Waller in Göteborg. Both had learned about undulatory mechanics at Copenhagen, where Pauli had completed his equivalence proof. While Dennison inquired whether he might, later in the year, come to Zurich to study under Schrödinger (Dennison to Schrödinger, 15 June 1926), Waller wrote: ‘During this spring I have carried out here in Copenhagen a small calculation derived from your new foundations of quantum theory. Allow me to send you, together with this letter, a set of proofs of my article’ (Waller to Schrödinger, 16 July 1926). A little further in the letter he continued: ‘I have recently endeavoured to treat the $\text{H}_2^+$ molecule according to your methods. Until now I have not succeeded in solving this problem; however, I have not given up hope of doing so.’

The publications on wave mechanics in the *Annalen der Physik* stimulated considerable interest among the quantum physicists in Germany, Central Europe and Scandinavia. For example, in Vienna Ludwig Flamm, a former colleague and friend of Schrödinger, wrote a review of the principles of that theory for the *Physikalische Zeitschrift*, entitled ‘Die Grundlagen der Wellenmechanik’ (‘The Foundations of Wave Mechanics’), probably constituting the first review of the subject (Flamm, 1926a). Erwin Fues, Gregor Wentzel, Ivar Waller, Max Born, Werner Heisenberg and Paul Dirac, all at different universities in Europe, wrote substantial papers in which they applied undulatory mechanics to new problems and extended its scope; we shall discuss these contributions in this section (IV.4). The Belgian Charles Manneback, then in Zurich, Fritz Reiche in Breslau, Walter Gordon in Berlin, and again Gregor Wentzel in Leipzig, the Russian Waldemar

Alexandrow, then in Zurich, and the Dane Øyvind Burrau in Copenhagen, all made further applications of wave mechanics to atomic problems; foreign visitors and students in Germany, such as the American J. Robert Oppenheimer in Göttingen, also contributed their share and we shall discuss their papers in Section IV.5.

In America, the California Institute of Technology became a centre for the early use of wave mechanics. Besides the young Carl Eckart, it was Paul Sophus Epstein in particular, a former Sommerfeld disciple and a professor, who competently dealt with atomic problems in the framework of the undulatory theory. Several months later the physicists on the East Coast joined the bandwagon, when Ralph Kronig and Isidor Rabi worked out the symmetrical top in Schrödinger’s scheme (Kronig and Rabi, 1927). We shall discuss these contributions also later in Section IV.5.

Remarkably little happened in France, the homeland of matter waves. The best-known contribution came from the Belgian physicists Théophile De Donder and Frans Henri van den Dungen from Brussels; in two notes, submitted to the Paris Academy of Sciences, they suggested a relativistic extension of Schrödinger’s wave equation (which Schrödinger also proposed), arriving at similar results as several other colleagues—in Germany (Walter Gordon), Sweden (Oskar Klein), Russia (Vladimir Fock) and Hungary (Janos Kudar)—at that time (De Donder and van den Dungen, 1926; De Donder, 1926); we shall also deal with these papers in Section IV.5. Further, the Paris physicist Léon Brillouin had two notes, entitled ‘*La mécanique ondulatoire de Schrödinger; une méthode générale de résolution par approximations successives*’ (‘The Undulatory Mechanics of Schrödinger; A General Method of Solution by Successive Approximations’) and ‘*Sur un type général de problèmes, permettant la séparation des variables dans la mécanique ondulatoire de Schrödinger*’ (‘On a General Type of Problems, which Allows the Separation of Variables in the Wave Mechanics of Schrödinger’), presented (in July 1926) to the Paris Academy of Sciences. In the first note he proposed to rewrite Schrödinger’s wave equation as an expansion of terms, whose first approximation coincided with the corresponding equation of the old Bohr–Sommerfeld quantum theory of atomic systems (L. Brillouin, 1926a); in the second note he developed a general class of problems which could be solved in wave mechanics by separation of variables (L. Brillouin, 1926b). Louis de Broglie, the inventor of the conception of matter waves, did of course take notice of Schrödinger’s work; in a note, also submitted to the Paris Academy of Sciences, he declared it as having ‘confirmed our ideas on the wave nature of mechanics’ (‘*confirmé nos idées sur la nature ondulatoire de la mécanique*,’ L. de Broglie, 1926a, p. 272). Basically, he did not pick up on the new theory, because his own ideas deviated strongly from Schrödinger’s; in particular, de Broglie stressed the particle aspect as representing the real nature of microscopic objects, rather than the undulatory aspect.105 In general, the quantum physicists in France represented a very small

Incidentally, Gregor Wentzel, Sommerfeld’s student and assistant in Munich, had also expressed a desire to discuss, in greater detail, the wave mechanical methods which he had learned from seeing Schrödinger’s papers prior to publication (through Sommerfeld). In that vein he had written a letter to Schrödinger, who had replied:

Now, as far as your Stuttgart talk is concerned, I might not object *per se* when you include some results from my last two papers which have not yet appeared in print. It is just that the *time* granted to you is really *very* short for a *review* of the whole complex of problems. Your lecture has been scheduled with three others on a morning from 9 to 12. You will not hold it against me if I do not wish to have these topics—which are really difficult and demand much care—covered before a large circle (just in key-words) prior to the appearance of my publications; because only then misunderstandings, which may easily arise and settle from such a short report, can be corrected. (Schrödinger to Wentzel, 11 May 1926)

Schrödinger had further added:

Actually, it was the intention that Fues, who has now submitted his first communication on the band spectra according to wave mechanics to the *Annalen*, should not only talk about this, i.e., his own paper, but also discuss, in a review of approximately one hour, the foundations and results of wave mechanics up to the present. Since, however, he has also been scheduled, contrary to expectation (and really against previous agreement), only for a speaking time of 3/6 of an hour [i.e., 1/2 an hour], this plan must be dropped. (Schrödinger to Wentzel, 11 May 1926)

Thus there did not occur, at the Stuttgart meeting, the first *general* presentation of the new wave mechanical theory of atomic systems; especially, Fues’ and Wentzel’s time was cut even shorter because six (rather than four) physicists gave papers in the morning session of 16 May.¹⁰⁸ However, both Fues and Wentzel did refer to Schrödinger’s unpublished results, backed by explicit permission from Schrödinger—who had written, e.g., to Wentzel, that he might ‘mention your knowledge of my manuscripts, where you need them as the starting point for reporting your own results which go beyond mine’ (Schrödinger to Wentzel, 11 May 1926). Consequently, Fues summarized his talk ‘*Das Eigenschwingungsspektrum zweiatomiger Moleküle in der Undulationsmechanik*’ (‘The Eigenvibration Spectrum of Diatomic Molecules in the Undulatory Mechanics’) as follows: ‘After a short review of the new Schrödinger wave mechanics, it will be shown how the spectra of diatomic molecules can be understood from this point of view. Exactly, one deduces the band formula of [Adolf] Kratzer, with half-integral vibrational and rotational quanta, in agreement with empirical data. The [full] paper will be published in the *Annalen der Physik*’ (

In a similar sense, Wentzel formulated the abstract of his talk ‘Über den Starkeffekt in der neuen Mechanik’ (‘On the Stark Effect in the New Mechanics’) as: ‘A review of the programme and results obtained thus far on Heisenberg’s quantum mechanics, with particular reference to papers by [Paul] Dirac and the speaker on the calculation of the spectral terms via the “action variables” (with particular application to the second-order Stark effect; to appear in *Zeitschrift für Physik*). Finally, a hint on Schrödinger’s and Pauli’s method of computing the Heisenberg matrices from the eigenfunctions of the Schrödinger wave equation; with an application in obtaining the intensities of the Balmer series and the X-ray spectra (to appear in *Naturwissenschaften*)’ (see *Verh. der Deutsch. Phys. Ges.* (3) **7**, p. 26, 1926).

While physicists in Stuttgart could not hear Schrödinger himself deliver a programmatic presentation of wave mechanics, they still had an opportunity to learn first-hand of the earliest results of the undulatory theory that had not been obtained by Schrödinger. Therefore, they enjoyed, in a way, the world premiere of the new theory at a physics meeting.

**Band Spectra in Undulatory Mechanics**

On 27 April 1926, the *Annalen der Physik* received a paper on ‘Das Eigenschwingungsspektrum zweiatomiger Moleküle in der Undulationsmechanik’ (‘The Eigenvalue Spectrum of Diatomic Molecules in Undulatory Mechanics’), the author being Erwin Fues from Zurich. The published paper constituted, as we have already mentioned, the first contribution to wave mechanics that did not come from Schrödinger himself. Still, Schrödinger made a strong contribution, as Fues acknowledged: ‘I thank Professor Schrödinger for some kind advice in carrying out the investigation; and for the opportunity to participate closely in his work, I owe to a generous grant from the *International Education Board*, to which I also want to express my sincere thanks here’ (Fues, 1926a, p. 396).

The study of band spectra had always provided an excellent testing ground for new ideas in atomic theory. With the Bohr–Sommerfeld approach to atomic structure, Karl Schwarzschild (1916c), Torsten Heurlinger (1918, 1919, 1920), Wilhelm Lenz (1919) and Adolf Kratzer (1920a, 1920b, 1922) had developed an understanding of the line patterns in molecular spectra.¹⁰⁹ In July 1925, Werner Heisenberg had treated various properties of band spectra from the point of view of the just-proposed new quantum mechanics.¹¹⁰ In February 1926, then, Schrödinger had laid, in Section 3 of his second communication, the foundation of the theory of band spectra in wave mechanics by discussing the ‘rigid rotator with free axis’ (Section 3.2) and the ‘non-rigid rotator’ (Section 3.3). The latter could be used, as Schrödinger remarked, to calculate the energy states of diatomic

$$E = E_t + \frac{n(n + 1)h^2}{8\pi^2A} \left(1 - \frac{\mathscr{E}}{1 + 3\mathscr{E}}\right) + \frac{2l + 1}{2} \, h\nu_0\sqrt{1 + 3\mathscr{E}}, \qquad (58)$$

with $n$ and $l$ corresponding to the rotational and oscillational quantum numbers in the old quantum theory, respectively, i.e.,

$$n = 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots ; \qquad l = 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots, \qquad (58a)$$

and $\mathscr{E}$ representing the *small* quantity

$$\mathscr{E} = \frac{n(n + 1)h^2}{16\pi^4 \nu_0^2 A^2}. \qquad (58b)$$

($A$ denoted the moment of inertia of the molecule.)

Equation (58) described the situation roughly. But Schrödinger also realized:

> The $\mathscr{E}$-corrections in [Eq. (58)] do *not yet* take account of the deviations of the nuclear vibrations from the pure harmonic type. Thus a comparison with Kratzer’s formula (vide Sommerfeld, *loc. cit.* [i.e., Sommerfeld, 1924d, p. 833 ff.]) and with experience is impossible. I only desired to mention the case provisionally .... The rotation–vibration problem of the diatomic molecule will have to be re-attacked presently, the non-harmonic terms in the energy of the binding *being taken into account*. The method selected skillfully by Kratzer for the classical mechanical treatment, is also suitable for undulatory mechanics. If, however, we are going to push the calculation as far as is necessary for the fineness of band structure, then we must make use of the theory of *perturbation of eigenvalues and eigenfunctions*. (Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 526; English translation, p. 39)

At the time when he made this statement, namely in late February 1926, Schrödinger already possessed the perturbation theory mentioned earlier, although he would publish the details of the scheme only later, in his third communication, together with an application to the Stark effect of hydrogen Balmer lines (Schrödinger, 1926f).

Instead of carrying out the necessary refined calculation of the molecular eigenvalues himself, Schrödinger left the problem as an exercise to Erwin Fues, his assistant in Zurich. The latter indeed succeeded in performing the rather tricky evaluation skillfully, translating Kratzer’s old approach into the undulatory mechanics.

A diatomic molecule may be described as a system of two atoms, having masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ and Cartesian co-ordinates $(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2, z_2)$, respectively. These atoms are bound in the molecule by attractive and repulsive forces, such that an equilibrium state determined by an equilibrium distance $r_0$ is reached. Fues further assumed: ‘Sufficiently small harmonic fluctuations of their [i.e., of the atoms’] distances occur, if rotation is absent, with the eigenvibration frequency

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0332 -->

$\nu_0$, if the potential energy of the binding forces is written as the following expansion

$$E_{\text{pot}} = -D + (2\pi\nu_0)^2 \frac{\mu}{2} (r - r_0)^2 + \dots \tag{(234)}$$

In this equation $\mu$, given by the relation

$$\mu = \frac{m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}, \tag{(234a)}$$

denotes the "resulting mass" and $-D$ the potential energy in the equilibrium state of the rotation-free molecule ($E_{\text{pot}}$ must, of course, be normalized such that it assumes the value 0 for $r = \infty$, in order that $D$ represents the "dissociation work")' (Fues, 1926a, pp. 368–369).

With the above *Ansatz*, which Fues adopted from Kratzer's paper (1920a) or Sommerfeld's book (1924d, p. 834), he now established the wave equation of the problem, namely,

$$\frac{1}{m_1 + m_2} \left( \frac{\partial^2 \Psi}{\partial \xi^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \Psi}{\partial \eta^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \Psi}{\partial \zeta^2} \right) + \frac{1}{\mu} \left( \frac{\partial^2 \Psi}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \Psi}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \Psi}{\partial z^2} \right) + \frac{8\pi^2}{h^2} [E - E_{\text{pot}}(x, y, z)]\Psi = 0. \tag{235}$$

The $\xi$, $\eta$ and $\zeta$ denoted centre-of-mass co-ordinates, defined by the equations

$$\left. \begin{aligned} (m_1 + m_2)\xi &= m_1 x_1 + m_2 x_2, \\ (m_1 + m_2)\eta &= m_1 y_1 + m_2 y_2, \\ (m_1 + m_2)\zeta &= m_1 z_1 + m_2 z_2, \end{aligned} \right\} \tag{235a}$$

and the $x, y, z$ the relative co-ordinates

$$\left. \begin{aligned} x &= x_1 - x_2, \\ y &= y_1 - y_2, \\ z &= z_1 - z_2. \end{aligned} \right\} \tag{235b}$$

Fues continued: 'One recognizes that [the wave function] $\Psi$ splits up into two factors, each of which separately depends only on a triple of co-ordinates, i.e.,

$$\Psi = f(x, y, z) \cdot g(\xi, \eta, \zeta), \tag{(236)}$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0333 -->

692 **Chapter IV Early Response and Applications**

and which satisfy the differential equations

$$\frac{1}{m_1 + m_2} \left( \frac{\partial^2 g}{\partial \xi^2} + \frac{\partial^2 g}{\partial \eta^2} + \frac{\partial^2 g}{\partial \zeta^2} \right) + \frac{8 \pi^2}{h^2} E_t \cdot g = 0 \qquad [(237)]$$

and

$$\frac{1}{\mu} \left( \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z^2} \right) + \frac{8 \pi^2}{h^2} [E - E_t - E_{\text{pot}}(x, y, z)] \cdot f = 0, \qquad [(238)]$$

respectively. To this . . . the "boundary conditions" have to be added, stating that $f$ and $g$ must be finite, unique and continuous in the entire $q$-space [i.e., the space of position co-ordinates $x, y, z$ and $\xi, \eta, \zeta$]' (Fues, 1926a, pp. 369–370).

The separation of Eq. (235) into the two Eqs. (237) and (238) had been forecast already in Schrödinger's previous paper: they were slightly generalized versions of Eqs. (41) and (42) of the second communication. (See Schrödinger, 1926d, pp. 523 and 524, or our Eqs. (50) and (52) in this chapter.) The interpretation of Eq. (237) as describing the translational part of the motion had also been pointed out by Schrödinger (1926d, pp. 523–524). Fues now adopted these results and restricted himself to discussing only Eq. (238). In approaching its solution, he again referred to a step performed earlier by Schrödinger, namely the introduction of spherical co-ordinates, which made it possible to separate the wave function $f$ in a manner similar to the wave function of the nonrelativistic hydrogen problem (see Schrödinger, 1926c, p. 363). Thus he wrote:

$$f = R(r) Y(\theta, \phi), \qquad (239)$$

where $Y(\theta, \phi)$ denoted the so-called surface harmonics of order $n$ having eigenvalues $n(n + 1)$, with $n = 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots$. The remaining second-order equation for the radial function could be reformulated as

$$\frac{d^2 F}{d\rho^2} + \left\{ \frac{8 \pi^2 A}{h^2} [E - E_t - E_{\text{pot}}(\rho)] - \frac{n(n + 1)}{\rho^2} \right\} F = 0, \qquad (240)$$

where $\rho$ is the 'normalized' radial variable

$$\rho = \frac{r}{r_0}, \qquad (240\text{a})$$

and $F$ the function

$$F(\rho) = \rho R(\rho). \qquad (240\text{b})$$

Equation (240) represented the basic equation for the diatomic molecule, whose solution Fues wished to achieve.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0334 -->

IV.4 Response to Wave Mechanics II. Applications and Extensions
693

He continued with the following consideration: ‘For further calculation it now depends on whether one wants to start in first approximation from the concept of a purely harmonic oscillator, or whether one wants to describe the potential of the binding forces—as suggested by Kratzer (1920a)—by a Coulomb attraction of the atoms (considered as being ions) plus a repulsive term proportional to $1/\rho^2$. Without doubt one approaches the already existing potential more closely in the sense of the old [classical] picture, if one assumes with Kratzer:

$$E_{\text{pot}} = E' - (2\pi\nu_0)^2 A \left\{ \frac{1}{\rho} - \frac{1}{2\rho^2} + c_3(\rho - 1)^3 + c_4(\rho - 1)^4 + \cdots \right\} [(241)]'$$

(Fues, 1926a, p. 371). Although both possibilities should eventually lead to the same final result, Fues would show that the latter choice not only made it possible to simplify the expression for the potential energy, but also led more quickly to the term formula.
Especially, he put $E' = 0$ and introduced the expression for the ‘dissociation work’ $D$,

$$D = \frac{(2\pi\nu_0)^2 A}{2}, \qquad (242)$$

and rewrote Eq. (240) as$^{111}$

$$\frac{d^2 F}{d\rho^2} + \left\{ A' + \frac{2}{\kappa^2} \left[ -\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\rho} - \frac{1}{2\rho^2} + c_3(\rho - 1)^3 + c_4(\rho - 1)^4 + \cdots \right] - \frac{n(n+1)}{\rho^2} \right\} F = 0,$$
(243)

with

$$A' = \frac{8\pi^2 A(E - E_t + D)}{h^2}, \qquad (243a)$$

and

$$\frac{1}{\kappa} = \frac{4\pi^2 \nu_0 A}{h}.$$ (243b)

The data, i.e., the observed values for $\nu_0$ and $A$, tell us that $\kappa$ must be considered to be a small dimensionless constant of the order of magnitude $10^{-2}$. Further, one finds for sufficiently small ‘rotational quantum numbers’ $n$ that $(\rho - 1)$, the

***

$^{111}$ Fues denoted the moment of inertia by $J$ (instead of $A$) and our quantity $A'$ by $A$; he later introduced $A'$, which we shall call $A''$.

694 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

maximum amplitude of the atomic oscillations, is proportional to $\sqrt{\kappa}$, hence the $c_3$- and $c_4$-terms may be considered as small perturbations.$^{112}$ Thus the unper-turbed wave equation assumed the shape

$$\frac{d^2F}{d\rho^2} + \left( A'' + \frac{2}{\kappa^2 \rho} - \frac{1 + \mathscr{E}}{\kappa^2 \rho^2} \right) F = 0, \qquad (244)$$

where

$$\mathscr{E} = \kappa^2 n(n + 1), \qquad (244a)$$

and

$$A'' = A' - \frac{1}{\kappa^2}. \qquad (244b)$$

The additional terms would contribute only to higher-order approximations. Fues now solved Eq. (244) by referring to the method which Schrödinger had originally applied to the nonrelativistic hydrogen atom.$^{113}$ Especially, he sug-gested the *Ansatz*

$$F = \rho^{\alpha_1} G, \qquad (245)$$

by which Eq. (244) was turned into a Laplace equation, i.e.,

$$\frac{d^2G}{d\rho^2} + \frac{2\alpha_1}{\rho} \frac{dG}{d\rho} + \left[ A'' + \frac{2}{\kappa^2 \rho} \right] G = 0. \qquad (246)$$

As in the case of hydrogen, any physical solution $F$, or $G$, had to be an integral transcendental function and assume finite values for $\rho \to +\infty$ also. As in Schrödin-ger's first example Fues found that the solution consisted of two parts:

(i) For $A''$ assuming values between 0 and $+\infty$, or $E > E_t$, a continuous spectrum resulted, representing physically a dissociated molecule, whose energy ceased to be quantized.
(ii) For negative $A''$, only discrete values were admissible, namely those satisfying the equation

$$-A'' = \frac{1}{\kappa^2} [\sqrt{1 + \kappa^2(n + \frac{1}{2})^2} + \kappa(l + \frac{1}{2})]^{-2}, \qquad (247)$$

---
$^{112}$ This estimate is certainly correct for the first ten band lines, as Fues argued.
$^{113}$ Fues even referred to the same mathematical textbook, namely, L. Schlesinger's *Einführung in die Theorie der gewöhnlichen Differentialgleichungen*. (See Fues, 1926a, p. 375, footnote 1.)

IV.4 Response to Wave Mechanics II. Applications and Extensions 695

with $l$ assuming integral values

$$l = 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots \tag{247a}$$

Evidently, from Eq. (247) the following discrete energy eigenvalues arose for the first approximation of the molecular terms:

$$E_{n,l} = E_t - D + h\nu_0(l + \frac{1}{2}) + \frac{h^2}{8\pi^2 A}(n + \frac{1}{2})^2 \dots \tag{248}$$

Fues concluded: ‘Hence one obtains the first terms of the known band formula. ($l + \frac{1}{2}$) plays the role of the oscillational quantum number ... . As a result of the new theory one first observes the occurrence of a continuous spectrum, and second, the half-integralness of both the “oscillational” and the “rotational quantum numbers” in the frequencies of the discrete spectra’ (Fues, 1926a, p. 379).$^{114}$

For the purpose of evaluating the perturbed energy terms of the molecule, Fues had to generalize the perturbation scheme given by Schrödinger in Section I of his third communication.$^{115}$ The self-adjoint wave equation for a perturbed atomic system may be written in the form

$$L[y] + \lambda M(x)y + \lambda^2 N(x)y + \dots + D(x)E \cdot y = 0, \tag{249}$$

with $L[y]$ representing a second-order differential expression of the wave function $y$, $\lambda$ a small parameter, and $M, N, \dots$ and $D$ functions of the position variables $x$.$^{116}$ Now if the functions $M, N, \dots$ also depended on the eigenvalue $E$ of the differential equation, namely,

$$M = M(E, x) = M(E_i, x) + \lambda \frac{\partial M}{\partial E_i} E'_i + \lambda^2 \frac{\partial^2 M}{\partial E_i} E''_i + \dots, \tag{250}$$

where the values $E_i, E'_i, \dots$ are derived from the perturbation expansion of the $i$th (discrete) energy eigenvalue $E^*_i$,

$$E^*_i = E_i + \lambda E'_i + \lambda^2 E''_i + \dots, \tag{251}$$

then the set of differential equations that had to be solved for the perturbed

---
$^{114}$ For the agreement of Eq. (248) with the data, Fues referred to a recent letter from Adolf Kratzer, the leading expert on band spectra, and to the recent observations of Robert S. Mulliken on the isotope effect in boron oxide spectra (Mulliken, 1925b).

$^{115}$ See the reference in Fues, 1926a, p. 379, to Schrödinger, 1926f, Part 1 (pp. 440–457).

$^{116}$ The function $D(x)$ helps to establish the self-adjointness of the left-hand side of Eq. (249).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0337 -->

696 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

system became

$$
\left. \begin{aligned}
L[u_i] + DE_i u_i &= 0, \\
L[v_i] + DE_i v_i &= - [M(E_i, x) + DE'_i] u_i, \\
L[w_i] + DE_i w_i &= - \left[ N(E_i, x) + \frac{\partial M}{\partial E_i} E'_i + DE''_i \right] u_i \\
&\quad - [M(E_i, x) + DE'_i] v_i.
\end{aligned} \right\} \tag{252}
$$

Clearly, the $u_i$, $v_i$ and $w_i$ are the expansion terms of the $ith$ eigenfunction $u_i^*$,
$$ u_i^*(x) = u_i(x) + \lambda v_i(x) + \lambda^2 w_i(x) + \cdots; \tag{253} $$
and the essential difference with Schrödinger's perturbation scheme is that Eqs. (252) included the dependence of $M$ on the eigenvalue. The first-order (in $\lambda$) correction yielded the energy contribution
$$ E'_i = - \int M u_i^2 \, dx, \tag{254} $$
and the eigenfunction correction
$$ v_i = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \gamma_{ik} u_k, \tag{255} $$
with
$$ \gamma_{ik} = \frac{c_{ik}}{E_i - E_k}, \quad c_{ik} = \begin{cases} - \int M u_i u_k \, dx & \text{for } i \neq k, \\ 0 & \text{for } i = k. \end{cases} \tag{255a} $$

This result agreed with Schrödinger's equations (see Schrödinger, 1926f, Eq. (7'') on p. 443, and Eqs. (8) and (13) on p. 444). The term contribution in $\lambda^2$ turned out to be
$$ E''_i = - \int N u_i^2 \, dx + \sum c_{ik} \gamma_{ik} - E'_i \int \frac{\partial M}{\partial E_i} u_i^2 \, dx. \tag{256} $$

Evidently, the last term had not been considered in Schrödinger's original scheme. In the

perturbation scheme by including terms from the continuous spectrum, such as integrals over eigenfunctions of the continuous spectrum; second, to avoid the complication altogether by singling out the discrete spectrum through a suitable transformation. He displayed in detail the latter solution, and therefore introduced the transformation

$$\sigma = 2\sqrt{-A''}\rho,\qquad (257)$$

by which Eq. (246) changed into the equation

$$\frac{d^{2}G}{d\sigma^{2}}+\frac{2\alpha_{1}}{\sigma}\frac{dG}{d\sigma}+\left[-\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{\kappa^{2}\sqrt{-A''}\sigma}\right]G=0.\qquad (258)$$

This equation possesses finite solutions on the entire positive real $\sigma$-axis only for the discrete values

$$B_{l}=\frac{1}{\kappa^{2}\sqrt{-A_{l}''}}=\frac{1}{\kappa}\left[\sqrt{1+\mathscr{E}+\frac{\kappa^{2}}{4}}+\delta\right],\qquad (259)$$

with

$$\delta=\kappa\left(l+\frac{1}{2}\right).\qquad (259\text{a})$$

Similarly, Fues obtained the eigenfunctions solving Eq. (258), which are—as in the case of the hydrogen atom—essentially the derived Laguerre polynomials. Finally, he reformulated the perturbation terms in Eq. (243) as functions of $\sigma$ and $B_{l}$. Ultimately, he then arrived at the following correction of the eigenvalue $B_{l}$,

$$\Delta B_{l}=\frac{1}{\kappa}\left[-3c_{3}\left(\mathscr{E}+\frac{\kappa^{2}}{4}\right)\delta-\left(\frac{15}{2}c_{3}+\frac{15}{4}c_{3}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}c_{4}\right)\delta^{2}-\left(\frac{7}{8}c_{3}+\frac{7}{16}c_{3}^{2}+\frac{3}{8}c_{4}\right)\kappa^{2}\right].\qquad (260)$$

Now the term formula of the perturbed system, up to the order $\lambda^{2}$, was readily obtained by considering the relation between $B_{l}$ and $A_{l}''$, and therefore—via Eqs. (244b) and (243a)—also between $B_{l}$ and the energy $E$. Fues found:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E &= E_{t}-D-\frac{(2\pi\nu_{0})^{2}}{2} A\left(\frac{7}{4}c_{3}+\frac{7}{8}c_{3}^{2}+\frac{3}{4}c_{4}\right) \\
&\quad + h\nu_{0}\left(l+\frac{1}{2}\right)\left[1-\frac{3}{2}\kappa^{2}(1+2c_{3})\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}\right] \\
&\quad + \frac{h^{2}}{8\pi^{2}A}\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}\left[1-\kappa^{2}\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}\right] \\
&\quad - \frac{h^{2}}{8\pi^{2}A}\left(l+\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}\left[3+15c_{3}+\frac{15}{2}c_{3}^{2}+3c_{4}\right]. \qquad (261)
\end{aligned}
$$

## Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

He happily concluded his lengthy calculation by exclaiming: ‘This is exactly A. Kratzer’s old equation for the band spectra of diatomic molecules in all details, except that his integral quantum numbers are replaced by half-integral ones. It [i.e., Eq. (261)] has the same range of validity as the old one, namely, for not too large “quantum numbers” (or as one would say, perhaps more correctly from the present point of view, “vibration numbers”), and enjoys similarly in that range a multiple confirmation by experience’ (Fues, 1926a, p. 388).

In the last section of his paper, Fues showed that the undulatory evaluation of the energy terms of diatomic molecules yielded the same result, independent of the manner of approximation. In particular, if he started from the harmonic oscillator equation describing the unperturbed system, and then considered the necessary perturbation corrections, formula (261) again followed. An advantage of the procedure given here was that it allowed, at least in principle, treatment of the continuous energy spectrum of the molecule, which had no place in the harmonic oscillator approximation.

Fues’ work on the diatomic molecule clearly showed that he was able to master fully the methods of undulatory mechanics at this early stage, such that he could apply them to a very complicated case. His solution compared favourably with a result which Lucy Mensing in Göttingen had calculated a month earlier on the basis of matrix mechanics (Mensing, 1926a). She had arrived at the term formula

$$W_{l,n} = U_0 + \frac{h^2n(n + 1)}{8\pi^2A} + h(l + \frac{1}{2})[\nu_0 + \beta n(n + 1)] + \alpha h^2[l(l + 1) + \frac{11}{30}] + \dots$$
<br>
(262)

for the diatomic molecule, where $U_0$, $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are suitable constants. Fues, in an addendum to the proofs of his paper, took note of Mensing’s work, but criticized it at the same time: ‘She [Mensing] ... does not take into account, however, the influence of the perturbation term of second order, which has the same order of magnitude as that of first order. Also, she does not make it clear that, in proceeding to higher approximations, the change from $n(n + \frac{1}{2})$ to $(n + \frac{1}{2})^2$ is established exactly’ (Fues, 1926a, p. 391, footnote 1).$^{117}$

### Intensity Calculations of Schrödinger, Pauli, Wentzel and Fues

The first intensity calculation for atomic lines in the new quantum mechanics was performed by Werner Heisenberg in his pioneering paper of July 1925: he succeeded in obtaining the transition amplitudes in the cases of the anharmonic oscillator and the (rigid) rotator—the latter satisfying the semi-empirical intensity rules for multiplet spectra and anomalous Zeeman effects (Heisenberg, 1925c,

$^{117}$ In his undulatory treatment, Fues had noticed that in a perturbation calculation, starting with the harmonic oscillator as the unperturbed system, one had to evaluate a higher-order approximation than in the case where one uses the Kratzer *Ansatz*, if one wants to achieve the same degree of accuracy.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0340 -->

IV.4 Response to Wave Mechanics II. Applications and Extensions 699

pp. 892–893). Max Born and Pascual Jordan had then proved Heisenberg’s fundamental assumption ‘that the squares of the absolute values of the elements in a matrix representing the electrical moment of an atom provide a measure of the transition probabilities’ (Born and Jordan, 1925b, p. 860).<sup>118</sup> Again within the matrix scheme, Lucy Mensing in her paper ‘*Die Rotations-Schwingungsbanden nach der Quantenmechanik*’ (‘The Rotation-Oscillation Bands on the Quantum Mechanics’), which she submitted in March 1926 to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, found the expressions for the intensities of lines contained in the band spectra of diatomic molecules (Mensing, 1926a).<sup>119</sup> In doing so, she followed Heisenberg’s original prescription, namely calculating the matrix elements of the Cartesian co-ordinates $x, y$ and $z$; these matrix elements should describe, up to a multiplicative factor, the transition amplitudes from states denoted by the triple numbers $(l, n, m)$ to states $(l', n', m')$—with $l$ connected to the oscillation and $n$ and $m$ to the rotation ($m$ representing the $z$-component of $n$).<sup>120</sup>

Such successes in Göttingen quantum mechanics in computing the intensities of spectral lines had led Schrödinger (in his second communication) to state: ‘The strength of Heisenberg’s programme lies in the fact that it promises to give the *line intensities*, a question that we have not approached as yet. The strength of the present attempt [i.e., of wave mechanics] lies in the guiding physical point of view . . . . For me, personally, there is a special charm in the conception . . . of the emitted frequencies as “beats” which I believe will lead to an intuitive understanding of the intensity formulae’ (Schrödinger, 1926d, pp. 513–514; English translation, p. 30).

On the other hand, the ‘guiding physical point of view,’ namely the ‘intuitive’ picture of the process of emitting spectral lines in the atom, did cause Schrödinger some problems. While the clarification was underway, Schrödinger completed his note showing the relation of wave mechanical and matrix mechanical schemes (Schrödinger, 1926e).<sup>121</sup> In the last section of that paper, subtitled ‘*Ausblick auf ein klassisches Verständnis der Intensität und Polarisation der emittierten Strahlung*’ (‘Prospect of a Classical Understanding of the Intensity and Polarization of the Emitted Radiation’), he approached the intensity question from what he called ‘the cardinal question of all atomic dynamics . . . , that of the *coupling* between the dynamic process in the atom and the electromagnetic field’ (Schrödinger, 1926e, p. 753; English translation, p. 59). He then concluded, in particular, that the component of the electric dipole moment in the direction of the (Cartesian)

<sup>118</sup> The proof of Born and Jordan can be found in their paper (Born and Jordan, 1925b, pp. 887–888).

<sup>119</sup> We have already referred to Mensing’s paper.

<sup>120</sup> A few months later, by the end of July 1926, Lucy Mensing again submitted another paper on the line-intensities (based on the matrix scheme)—dealing especially with ‘*Die Intensitäten der Zeemankomponenten bei partiellen Paschen-Back-Effekt*’ (‘The Intensities of the Zeeman Components for Partial Paschen–Back Effect’)—to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Mensing, 1926b).

IV.4 Response to Wave Mechanics II. Applications and Extensions 701

The multiplication of the square of the $q$-quotients by the ratio of the fourth power of the emission frequencies *was adopted from Born and Jordan.* (See Born and Jordan, 1925b, p. 888, Eq. (109).) In the example which Schrödinger was going to treat, namely the calculation of the relative intensities of the Stark components of given hydrogen lines, the frequency-factor did not play a great role, because only intensities of lines were compared which possessed practically the same frequency. Schrödinger therefore just evaluated the right-hand side of Eq. (264), inserting for the position co-ordinate the Cartesian components $z$ (the component parallel to the electric field), $x$ and $y$ (the components perpendicular to the electric field), and for the wave functions the eigenfunctions

$$\psi_{nk_1k_2} = \lambda_1^{n/2} \lambda_2^{n/2} \exp\left(-\frac{\lambda_1 + \lambda_2}{2la_0}\right) L_{n+k_1}^n \left(\frac{\lambda_1}{la_0}\right)$$

$$L_{n+k_2}^n \left(\frac{\lambda_2}{la_0}\right) \begin{cases} \sin(n\phi), \\ \cos(n\phi), \end{cases} \qquad (265)$$

which are associated with the energy eigenvalues, Eq. (165) of Chapter III.$^{122}$ After going through lengthy calculations by integrating Laguerre polynomials—Schrödinger only sketched them in the published paper—he presented the results on the intensities of the Stark components for the four hydrogen lines H$_\alpha$, H$_\beta$, H$_\gamma$ and H$_\delta$ in four tables, each of which contained both the computed values and the experimental data for the components polarized parallel and transverse to the applied electric field. Schrödinger further demonstrated the comparison between theory and experiment in eight figures, on which he commented as follows:

> A consideration of the diagrams shows that the agreement is tolerably good for almost all the strong components, and taken all over it is somewhat better than for the values deduced from correspondence considerations [i.e., Kramers, 1919].... Passing now to the weaker components, we notice first that the contradiction which exists for some weak observed components of H$_\beta$ to the selection and polarisation rules, of course, still remains in the new theory, since the latter gives the rules in conformity with the older theory. (Schrödinger, 1926f, pp. 470–471, 474; English translation, pp. 88, 90)$^{123}$

The discrepancy existing in the case of the weak lines did not seem, in Schrödinger's opinion, to be too serious: to a lesser extent it could be ascribed

$^{122}$ In the calculation of the intensities, the variables $x$, $y$ and $z$ have, of course, to be expressed in terms of Stark effect variables $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_2$ and $\phi$, through Eqs. (77).
$^{123}$ Schrödinger's conclusion was confirmed by the experimentalists John Stuart Foster and M. Laura Chalk of McGill University in Montreal, who compared their recent data on the $p$- and $s$-components of H$_\beta$ with Schrödinger's theoretical results: they found good agreement for the stronger line components, while the weaker components appeared to be somewhat stronger than predicted (Foster and Chalk, 1926).

702 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

to errors in experiment, and to a large extent to the fact that in the theoretical calculation the full perturbed hydrogen functions had not been used. One would suspect that such a procedure particularly affected the weak components, because, as Schrödinger argued:

> The reason for the low line intensity is to be found in a high degree of *symmetry* in the motion of the electricity [i.e., of the electrons in the atom], through which only a small, or even no, dipole moment arises ... Therefore it is to be expected that the *vanishing* of a line component in the presence of perturbations of any kind is a relatively *unstable* condition, since the symmetry is probably destroyed by the perturbation. (Schrödinger, 1926f, p. 475; English translation, p. 91)

Schrödinger also performed another check, this time including especially the fourth power of the frequency in the intensities: he compared the sum of intensities of all Stark components for a given hydrogen line to the observed values, reaching sufficient agreement with the data derived from dispersion measurements.$^{124}$ Finally, in an ‘Addition at the Correction of Proofs’ of the third communication (which contained all results on the Stark effect), he wrote: ‘Hr. W. Pauli, jun., informs me that he has arrived at the following closed formulae for the total intensity of the lines in the Lyman and Balmer series .... For the Lyman series these are

$$\nu_{l,1} = R \left( \frac{1}{1^2} - \frac{1}{l^2} \right); \quad J_{l,1} = \frac{2^7(l - 1)^{2l-1}}{l(l + 1)^{2l+1}}; \quad [(266)]$$

and for the Balmer series

$$\nu_{l,2} = R \left( \frac{1}{2^2} - \frac{1}{l^2} \right); \quad J_{l,2} = \frac{4^3(l - 2)^{2l-3}}{l(l + 2)^{2l+3}} (3l^2 - 4) \cdot (5l^2 - 4). \quad [(267)]$$

The total emission intensities (square of amplitudes into the fourth power of the frequency) are proportional to these expressions, within the series in question. The numbers obtained from the formula for the Balmer series are in complete agreement with those given [by Schrödinger] on pp. 91, 92’ (Schrödinger, 1926f, pp. 489–490; English translation, p. 101).

Wolfgang Pauli had tried, after the calculation of the nonrelativistic hydrogen states, to obtain in matrix mechanics formulae for the intensities of the hydrogen lines also.$^{125}$ In spite of initially being very optimistic—this was after he had found the extension of matrices to include a treatment of action and angle
