variables—he did not really make sufficient progress until several months later, i.e., after discovering wave mechanics. Then he wrote, e.g., in a letter to Gregor Wentzel:

> The application to the hydrogen atom, for which Schrödinger already calculated the eigenfunctions, is very simple, in principle, though not always so in technical procedure. In particular, one obtains for the intensities of the *series lines* expressions that are *rational* functions of the quantum numbers, since the associated eigenfunctions are of the form of the exponential function times a polynomial. At first there result, however, intricate-looking (though *finite*) double sums, which I have not yet succeeded in simplifying in the general case. I am, however, convinced that essential simplifications are possible, perhaps even closed expressions might follow. (Pauli to Wentzel, 8 May, 1926)

After that he suggested such a closed expression for the oscillator strength of the Lyman series, which came close to the one reported later by Schrödinger, Eq. (266).^126

A few weeks later, Pauli informed Alfred Landé of his further progress: ‘Recently I have derived, based on the connection between Schrödinger[’s theory] and [the] Göttingen [theory], formulae for the absolute intensity of the Balmer lines. Ladenburg is supposed to test them by dispersion measurements. Since, however, Schrödinger is calculating similar things himself, I do not yet know where, how and when I shall publish the results’ (Pauli to Landé, 2 June 1926). Finally, he again wrote to Wentzel: ‘Schrödinger will publish my formulae on the H-intensities, such as I wrote to you some time ago, in his third communication—according to my “letter-publication method” of long standing’ (Pauli to Wentzel, 5 July 1926).^127

In the months of spring and early summer 1926, Pauli also discussed in his correspondence with Wentzel other problems of atomic theory.^128 For example, he mentioned in the letter of 8 May:

> Just now I realize that I have not written at all about the Stark effect of second order. Your remark on the sum rule rests, I believe, on a misunderstanding. Such a rule can be expected to hold only for “weak” fields (i.e., the Stark effect of fine structure), in those terms which contain the square of the velocity of light in the denominator. For the effect calculated by you *no* sum rule is valid. . . . The number $\frac{165}{2}$ [which evidently Wentzel had obtained and written about to Pauli] hardly disturbs me. However, I would like to see your complete method of calculation once in its final form; so far all of the details have not become clear to me. Still it is very important, you must certainly soon publish it. (Pauli to Wentzel, 8 May 1926)

^126 It appears that the expression in the published letter (Pauli, *Wissenschaftlicher Briefwechsel* I, p. 323) has not been transcribed correctly.

^127 In previous years, Pauli had occasionally encouraged colleagues to use results, which he wrote them in letters, in their publications. (See, e.g., Pauli to Landé, 26 July 1923.)

^128 Pauli not only knew Wentzel from the days at Sommerfeld’s Institute where they had become friends; Wentzel also spent the winter semester of 1925/1926 in Hamburg with Pauli.

704 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

To understand the meaning of these sentences correctly, we must mention that Wentzel at that time had become very interested in wave mechanics. We know that a little earlier he had completed a paper providing a method of calculating, within the Göttingen quantum mechanics, multiply periodic systems; and he had applied the method in evaluating the terms of the relativistic hydrogen atom (Wentzel, 1926a).$^{129}$ In his Stuttgart talk on 16 May 1926 he presented the content of this paper, together with an application to the second-order Stark effect.$^{130}$ He reported the new results in letters, written in early May 1926, to both Schrödinger and Pauli. He eventually worked out an improved procedure for calculating the second-order Stark effect within the wave mechanical theory. We shall discuss the paper containing that procedure, ‘Eine Verallgemeinerung der Quantenbedingungen für die Zwecke der Wellenmechanik’ (‘A Generalization of the Quantum Conditions for the Purposes of Wave Mechanics,’ Wentzel, 1926d), elsewhere, because it plays an interesting role in the later development of the unification of matrix and wave mechanics. Here we restrict ourselves to suggesting that first Pauli, in his letter of 8 May, may have referred to an intermediate stage of Wentzel’s calculation procedure, i.e., half-way between his old matrix method and the new wave mechanical approximation method described in the later paper; and second to noting that Wentzel also calculated the second-order Stark effect with the new procedure (see Wentzel, 1926d, §6).$^{131}$

During those weeks, Wentzel showed enthusiasm in exploring wave mechanics in order to solve all kinds of problems of atomic theory. For example, he worked on the intensities of the hydrogen spectrum—the discrete as well as the continuous part. We learn of the first from a letter by Schrödinger;$^{132}$ with respect to the second problem, Pauli wrote: ‘For the *continuous* absorption beyond the series limit and the continuous “hyperbola spectrum”, the intensities will hardly be described by rational functions—that would be asking too much. Certainly, it will be difficult to compute this mathematically in detail; I do not intend at present to sink my teeth into it’ (Pauli to Wentzel, 8 May 1926). Evidently, Wentzel did not mind trying to sink his teeth into it without, however, getting through the problem. His long letter, in which he reported to Pauli in the beginning of July, seems to have been lost. But we know Pauli’s reply, where Pauli mentioned: ‘The normalization of the eigenfunctions of the continuous spectrum has already been worked out by Fues, and he has also made extended calculations

IV.4 Response to Wave Mechanics II. Applications and Extensions 705

on the subject’ (Pauli to Wentzel, 5 July 1926). Wentzel did not pursue the problem any further, but turned to a different intensity problem and published the results in a letter to *Naturwissenschaften*, ‘Über die Intensitäten in den Röntgenspektren’ (‘On the Intensities in the X-Ray Spectra’), dated 20 May 1926 (Wentzel, 1926b).

Wentzel got the idea of calculating the intensities of X-ray spectra from Schrödinger’s previous work on the intensities of the Stark effect components. Wentzel started his note by saying: ‘Schrödinger has shown recently [see Schrödinger, 1926e—the paper had just been published] that one can construct the matrices of Heisenberg’s quantum mechanics from the eigenfunctions of his mechanical wave equation by simple quadratures. Therefore, one is for the first time in possession of a generally applicable method of calculating the intensities of spectral lines on the prescriptions of quantum mechanics’ (Wentzel, 1926b, p. 621). Since Schrödinger had already solved the problem of the Stark effect intensities, in which—as we know—Wentzel was also interested, he used the method in a slightly modified problem, namely: ‘Instead like Schrödinger [in the case of the Stark effect (Schrödinger, 1926f)], choosing a homogeneous, external [electric] field, I have selected an *internal central field* as perturbation, and carried out the analogous calculation’ (Wentzel, 1926b, p. 621). Thus he not only reproduced Schrödinger’s intensity ratios for the hydrogen Balmer lines in the case of no perturbation; in the case of finite perturbation through a central field, he obtained ‘another splitting of the lines than that by Schrödinger, namely the one corresponding to the series structure of the alkaline spectra and the X-ray spectra, respectively’ (Wentzel, 1926b, pp. 621–622). Wentzel hoped that the evaluation might provide a success similar to that of Schrödinger for the Stark effect of hydrogen, expecting particularly reliable results for the spectrum of the lithium atom and the *K*- and *L*-lines of the X-ray spectra.

Unfortunately, in the case of the lithium spectrum (having an especially close hydrogen-like structure) no intensity data were available on *p*-, *d*- and *f*-terms, while in the X-ray spectra the existence of radiationless jumps could possibly spoil the comparison with the theoretical calculations. Still, Wentzel did refer to observations on the *L*-spectra of tungsten that had been published by Axel Jönsson from Uppsala in a recent issue of *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Jönsson, 1926). He concluded in general a satisfactory agreement, if he compared the sum of the intensities of the two lines (for a Sommerfeld doublet) and the three lines (for so-called ‘composed doublets’), respectively.

At the end of his note, Wentzel mentioned briefly that Helmut Hönl’s intensity formulae for anomalous multiplets plus the associated selection rules (Hönl, 1925, 1926) would also follow from the properties of Schrödinger’s eigenfunctions—essentially integral relations between surface harmonics. Further, he argued that the intensity rules for rotation–oscillation band spectra, such as had been obtained earlier by Ralph Fowler on correspondence principle arguments (Fowler, 1925a), could be derived from wave mechanics as well, because the eigenfunctions of the rigid rotator with free axis were related to the spherical

706  
Chapter IV Early Response and Applications  

harmonics (see Schrödinger, 1926d, Section 3.3). However, Erwin Fues would deal in greater detail with this problem in his second paper on the band spectra in wave mechanics, ‘Zur Intensität der Bandenlinien und des Affinitätsspektrums zweiatomiger Moleküle’ (‘On the Intensity of the Band Lines and of the Continuous Spectrum of Diatomic Molecules’), which was received by *Annalen der Physik* on 9 July 1926 and published in a September issue (Fues, 1926b).  
As usual, Fues approached the problem with great care. He departed from a relation proposed by Schrödinger in his fourth communication on ‘*Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem*’ (Schrödinger, 1926h): namely, that the spatial density of electricity in an atom was given by the product of the wave function $\psi$ with its complex conjugate $\bar{\psi}$. Now $\psi$ contained *all* eigenvibrations of the system under investigation and therefore had to be written as  

$$
\psi = \sum_l a_l u_l \exp\left[2\pi i \left(\frac{E_l}{h}t + \delta_l\right)\right], \tag{268}
$$  

with $u_l$ denoting the (time-independent) eigenfunction, $E_l$ the energy, $\delta_l$ a phase connected with the $l$th eigenvalue, and $a_l$ an amplitude factor—which depended, e.g., on excitation conditions, temperature and radiation damping. The $(jl)$-component of the electric moment in the $q$-direction had the form  

$$
M_q^{jl} = a_j a_l q^{jl}, \tag{269}
$$  

and the intensity of the total radiation with frequency $\nu_{jl}$ in the direction of $q$ became  

$$
J_{\nu_{jl}} \sim \nu_{jl}^4 a_j^2 a_l^2 (q^{jl})^2. \tag{270}
$$  

Thus the problem of calculating the intensity of the transition line $\nu_{jl}$ consisted, up to a factor, of finding the matrix elements $(q^{jl})^2$, where $q$ represented the various position variables of the system.¹³³  
In the case of the $x$-, $y$- and $z$-vibrations of band spectra, the ‘relative’ intensities—especially up to the frequency factor—are  

$$
\left. \begin{array}{c} X \\ Y \\ Z \end{array} \right|_{ln, l'n'} = \sum_{m=0}^n \sum_{m'=0}^{n'} \left\{ \int \left| \begin{array}{c} x \\ y \\ z \end{array} \right| u_{lnm} u_{l'n'm'} \, d\tau \right\}^2 . \tag{271}
$$  

Of course, the $u_{lnm}$ were the eigenfunctions which he had calculated previously,  

¹³³ Fues indicated that the derivation of Eqs. (269) and (270) provided, in the case of many-body systems, certain conceptual problems; he referred to Schrödinger’s paper for a detailed discussion of those (Schrödinger, 1926h, §7).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0348 -->

IV.4  Response to Wave Mechanics II. Applications and Extensions 707

and the $\tau$-integration extended over the entire three-dimensional space.$^{134}$ In the case of the continuous spectrum he now derived the eigenfunctions

$$u_{nm}(E) = a_r \rho^{(k-1)/2} G_n(E, \rho) a_\theta P_{nm}(\cos \theta) \cdot a_\phi \begin{cases} \sin(m\phi), \\ \cos(m\phi), \end{cases} \quad (272)$$

where the radial eigenfunction $G_n(E, \rho)$—with $E$ an eigenvalue in the continuum (i.e., for the two atoms of the molecule being separated)—can be represented by exponential functions. (See Fues, 1926b, p. 289, Eq. (26), where Fues used a slightly different energy parameter.)

The evaluation of Eqs. (271) for the discrete molecular spectrum provided the known selection rules: thus, for the $x$- and $y$-components only transitions with $m - m' = \pm 1$, and for the $z$-component only transitions with $m = m'$, have finite intensities. All the non-zero components possess the same intensity, namely,

$$X \Big|_{ln, l'n'} = r_0^2 \left(\frac{\kappa}{2}\right)^{\Delta l} \frac{l!}{l'!} \frac{n}{3}, \quad \text{with} \quad \kappa = \frac{h}{4\pi^2 \nu_0 A^2}. \quad (273)$$

Fues concluded: ‘In this equation not only is there contained the intensity formula by R. H. Fowler [1925a] and by H. Hönł and F. London [Hönł and London, 1925] for the intensities of the lines of a partial band (without the zero branch), but also a dependence on the oscillator quantum number $[l]$. It states that the combination $\Delta l = 0$ (pure rotation band) has a strongly preferred intensity, and that the intensity factor decreases strongly for growing $\Delta l$ (rotation-oscillation band), because $\kappa/2$ is a small quantity of the order of magnitude of $10^{-2}$’ (Fues, 1926b, p. 294).$^{135}$

Fues noted at the beginning of Section 3 of his paper: ‘Different people have pointed out the increased importance that has to be attributed to the continuous spectra in the new mechanics, whether it is formulated as undulatory or as a matrix scheme’ (Fues, 1926b, p. 295). He referred especially to the endeavours of Born, Heisenberg and Jordan to describe these spectra mathematically with the help of the matrix method, and added: ‘Professor H. Weyl kindly supplied me with papers of his own, from which everything that is necessary for [dealing with continuous spectra in] wave mechanics can be determined’ (Fues, 1926b, p. 295).

$^{134}$ The $u_{lnm}$ for the discrete spectrum are
$$a_r \rho^{(k-1)/2} G_{ln}(\rho) a_\theta P_{nm}(\cos \theta) \cdot a_\phi \begin{cases} \sin(m\phi), \\ \cos(m\phi), \end{cases}$$
where $a_r$, $a_\theta$ and $a_\phi$ denote constants for the separated eigenfunctions: i.e., for $G_{ln}(\rho)$, the eigenfunction of the radial wave equation, and for $P_{nm}(\theta)$ and $\sin(m\phi)$ or $\cos(m\phi)$, the eigenfunctions for the spherical angle variables ($k = (2/\kappa)\sqrt{1 + \kappa^2(n + \frac{1}{2})^2}$). (See Fues, 1926b, p. 287, Eq. (22).)

$^{135}$ Of course, the intensities had still to be multiplied by the fourth power of the frequency; further, the electronic terms, which had not been implied in Fues' calculation, might influence the intensities of the band spectra.

708	Chapter IV	Early Response and Applications

Fues now worked hard through the sixteen-year-old papers of Hermann Weyl dealing with ordinary differential equations and with singularities and their eigenfunctions (Weyl, 1910a, b). In Section 5 of his paper he finally formulated the conclusions for wave mechanics.

As the starting point of the consideration, he took the expansion of an arbitrary function $f(x)$ in a Fourier sum *and* a Fourier integral, i.e.,

$$f(x) = \sum_{l=0}^{\infty} c_l U_l(x) + \int_0^{\infty} \gamma(E) U(E, x) dE, \tag{274}$$

where

$$c_l = \int D(x) f(x) U_l(x) dx, \tag{274a}$$

are the coefficients of the (discrete) Fourier spectrum,$^{136}$ and $\gamma(E)$ are the corresponding coefficients of the continuous spectrum. The integral on the right-hand side of Eq. (274) may be interpreted as a limit of a sum, namely,

$$\int_0^{\infty} \gamma(E) U(E, x) dE = \lim_{\Delta_n E \to 0} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \gamma(\mathcal{E}_n) \Delta_n F(x), \tag{275}$$

where the $\Delta_n F(x)$, or the so-called ‘eigendifferentials’, play the same role in the continuous (energy) region as the eigenfunctions $U_l(x)$ do in the discrete region. The order of magnitude of $\Delta_n F(x)$ is evidently the same as that of $\Delta_n E$; they can be written likewise as

$$\Delta_n F(x) = \int_{\Delta_n E} U(\mathcal{E}, x) d\mathcal{E} = \int_{\Delta_n E} \psi(\mathcal{E}) u(\mathcal{E}, x) d\mathcal{E}. \tag{275a}$$

Further, the $\Delta_n F(x)$ are orthogonal to each other and to the $U_l(x)$, i.e.,

$$\int D(x) U_l(x) \Delta_n F(x) dx = 0, \tag{276a}$$

and

$$\frac{1}{\Delta_n E} \int D_n(x) \Delta_n F(x) \Delta_m F(x) dx = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{for } n \neq m, \\ 1 & \text{for } n = m. \end{cases} \tag{276b}$$

$^{136}$The $U_l$ are orthogonal functions satisfying the equations $\int DU_kU_l dx = 0$, for $k \neq l$, and $\int DU_l^2 dx = 1$, with a suitable density function $D = D(x)$.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0350 -->

IV.4 Response to Wave Mechanics II. Applications and Extensions 709

Finally, the coefficient $\gamma(\mathscr{E}_n)$ in Eq. (275) is defined similar to $c_l$, Eq. (274), through the equation
$$\gamma(\mathscr{E}_n) = \frac{1}{\Delta_n E} \int D(x)f(x)\Delta_n F(x) dx, \quad (277)$$
hence for the coefficients $\gamma(E)$ in Eq. (274) there follows the expression:
$$\gamma(E) = \lim_{\Delta E \to 0} \frac{1}{\Delta E} \int \left\{ D(x)f(x) \left[ \int_E^{E+\Delta E} \psi(\mathscr{E})u(\mathscr{E}, x) d\mathscr{E} \right] \right\} dx. \quad (274b)$$

With such slightly technical notions and definitions, Fues split the differential equation for a wave mechanical problem into two parts, namely symbolically,
$$L[u_l] + DE_l u_l = 0, \quad (278a)$$
and
$$L[u(E)] + DEu(E) = 0. \quad (278b)$$

These equations had to be solved explicitly for the molecular case; the solutions, evidently, were the discrete eigenfunctions $u_l$, on the one hand, and the continuous eigenfunctions, Eq. (272), on the other hand. Fues now inserted both in the expression for the general wave function of diatomic molecules, writing in particular,
$$\psi = \sum_{l=1}^\infty a_l u_l \exp\left[ 2\pi i \left( \frac{E_l}{h} t + \delta_l \right) \right] + \int_0^\infty \alpha(E) u(E) \exp\left\{ 2\pi i \left[ \frac{E}{h} t + \delta(E) \right] \right\} dE. \quad (279)$$

Clearly, $\alpha(E)$ represents a normalization factor of the continuous eigenfunction $u(E)$, in analogy to $a_l$ in the discrete case.

With Eq. (279) in hand, the electric moment for the transitions between different states of the discrete spectrum ($E_l, E_j$) and of the continuous spectrum ($E, \mathscr{E}$) in the $q$-direction becomes a complicated expression, i.e.,$^{137}$
$$\begin{aligned} M_q &\sim \text{time-independent terms} \\ &\quad + \sum_l \sum_j a_l a_j \exp[2\pi i (\nu_{lj} t + \delta_{lj})] (q^{lj}) \\ &\quad + \sum_l \int_0^\infty a_l \alpha(E) \exp[2\pi i (\nu_{El} t + \delta_{El})] (q^{El}) dE \\ &\quad + \int_0^\infty \int_0^\infty \alpha(E) \alpha(\mathscr{E}) \exp[2\pi i (\nu_{E\mathscr{E}} t + \delta_{E\mathscr{E}})] (q^{E\mathscr{E}}) dE d\mathscr{E}, \quad (280) \end{aligned}$$

$^{137}$ The frequencies are defined as $\nu_j = (E_l - E_j)/h$, etc.

**European–American Competition on the Stark Effect and the Hydrogen Spectrum**

On 16 July 1926, Ivar Waller from Göteborg sent, in a letter to Erwin Schrödinger, a copy of the proofs of a paper based on wave mechanics. He had performed the work while staying in Copenhagen and submitted it from there on 18 June; the paper, ‘*Der Starkeffekt zweiter Ordnung bei Wasserstoff und die Rydbergkorrektion der Spektra von He and Li$^+$*’ (‘The Stark Effect of Second Order in Hydrogen

IV.4  Response to Wave Mechanics II. Applications and Extensions  711

and the Rydberg Correction of the He and Li$^+$ Spectra’), would be published in an issue of *Zeitschrift für Physik* of August 1926 (Waller, 1926).

Waller, who was born in Flen, Sweden, on 11 June 1898, had graduated in 1916 from the University of Uppsala. He obtained his doctor’s degree in 1925, upon which he joined the Uppsala faculty (becoming professor of theoretical physics in 1934). Already before that he had contributed to atomic theory, notably the theory of X-ray interference.$^{140}$ In the spring of 1926 he spent some time in Copenhagen, where the news of Schrödinger’s undulatory theory had been spread, especially by Wolfgang Pauli. Werner Heisenberg was also at Bohr’s Institute from late April 1926 as lecturer for theoretical physics, succeeding Hendrik Kramers in this position. In the lively Copenhagen atmosphere all the problems of atomic theory were eagerly discussed, especially those to which the various methods could be applied that had been developed so far in quantum mechanics—the Göttingen quantum mechanics and Schrödinger’s wave mechanics being considered since Pauli’s equivalence proof as describing the same atomic theory. For example, Heisenberg discovered at that time how to use the wave function method in order to evaluate certain matrix elements which he needed to calculate the helium energy states. Waller, in working on Stark effect, profited from the advice of Niels Bohr and his experienced associates.$^{141}$

The first quantum mechanical calculation of the Stark effect had been performed by Wolfgang Pauli in the autumn of 1925 on the basis of the matrix theory, and been included in Section 5 of his paper on the hydrogen spectrum (Pauli, 1926a). Pauli only took into account the effect proportional to the strength of the electric field, obtaining the so-called Stark effect of *first order* in complete agreement with the old result of Paul S. Epstein on the basis of the Bohr-Sommerfeld theory (Epstein, 1916a, c). When Waller began to work on the problem, he knew—from a remark at the end of Schrödinger’s second communication—that Schrödinger had meanwhile arrived at the same conclusion in wave mechanics.$^{142}$ Waller therefore immediately turned to the more complicated problem of the *second-order* Stark effect within the wave theory, asking in particular whether the terms proportional to the square of the electric field strength also came out the same as in the old quantum theory.

Without knowing Schrödinger’s procedure in the third communication, Waller wrote down the wave equation for the hydrogen atom in an external electric field. Then he introduced parabolic variables $u, v$ and $\phi$, and separated the three-dimensional problem into three one-dimensional problems; i.e., he derived three

$^{140}$ See his paper on the influence of heat motion on the X-ray interference (Waller, 1923).
$^{141}$ At the end of his paper, Waller expressed his thanks to Bohr, Kramers and Heisenberg ‘for their valuable interest in this work’ (‘*für ihr wertvolles Interesse an dieser Arbeit*, Waller, 1926, p. 646).
$^{142}$ Waller referred to Schrödinger’s remark, ‘that (of course, the not completely published) perturbation theory of his [i.e. Schrödinger’s] form of quantum mechanics yields, in that approximation, Epstein’s formula’ (Waller, 1926, p. 635). Schrödinger made this remark on the last page of his paper: Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 527. He submitted his third communication, containing an explicit discussion of the perturbation theory and its application to the first-order Stark effect, early in May 1926; this paper (Schrödinger, 1926f) became available in print only after the middle of July 1926.

ordinary differential equations for each variable *u*, *v* and *ϕ*, separately. These three equations agreed perfectly with those found earlier by Schrödinger. For example, the equation for the wave function *U*(*u*) was

$$
u \frac{d^2 U}{du^2} + \frac{dU}{du} - \frac{k^2}{4u} U + \left( \frac{m_e}{2K^2} E u - \frac{m_e e}{4K^2} F u^2 + \alpha \right) U = 0. \tag{283}
$$

It coincided fully with the second Eq. (38) of the third communication (Schrödinger, 1926f, p. 459), if one took note of Schrödinger’s slightly different notation (besides *K* = *h*/2π, *m*<sub>e</sub> and *e* being mass and charge of the electron and *k* the integral number occurring in the *ϕ*-equation: *d*²*W*(*ϕ*)/*dϕ*² = −*k*²*ϕ*).¹⁴³
Instead of evaluating Eq. (283) directly—as Schrödinger had done in his paper (see our discussion in Section 2)—Waller introduced a further variable transformation with the relation

$$
\xi = \frac{\sqrt{-2 m_e E_0}}{K} u \tag{284}
$$

(*E*₀ being the energy of the free hydrogen atom) and replaced the wave function *U*(*u*) by *X*(*ξ*) via the *Ansatz*

$$
U(u) = \xi^{k/2} \exp\left(-\frac{\xi}{2}\right) X(\xi). \tag{285}
$$

Then Eq. (283) assumed for *zero electric field* (denoted by suffix ‘zero’) the form

$$
\xi \frac{d^2 X_0}{d\xi^2} + (-\xi + k + 1) \frac{dX_0}{d\xi} + \left( a_0 - \frac{k + 1}{2} \right) X_0 = 0, \tag{286}
$$

and Waller obtained a solution in terms of the *finite* power series

$$
X_0(\xi) = \sum_{r=0}^{h} A_r \xi^r, \tag{287}
$$

with

$$
A_r = (-1)^{h-r} \frac{(h + k)! h!}{(k + r)! r! (h - r)!} \tag{287a}
$$

(We have corrected, in Waller’s equation, the field-dependent term which the author erroneously gave as −(*m*<sub>e</sub>*e*/*4K*²)*eFu*² instead of −(*m*<sub>e</sub>*e*/*4K*²)*Fu*² in his Eq. and $h$ a positive integer determined by the equation

$$h = a_0 - \frac{k+1}{2} = \frac{K}{\sqrt{-2m_e E_e}} \alpha_0 - \frac{k+1}{2}, \qquad (287b)$$

(where $\alpha_0$ replaces $\alpha$ in Eq. (283) when $F=0$). Similarly, Waller transformed and solved the equation for the parabolic variable $v.$^{144}
In order to treat the wave equations *including the electric field $F$*, Waller proposed to write the wave functions in a power series as

$$U = U_0 + U_1 F + U_2 F^2 + \cdots, \qquad (288a)$$

and

$$V = V_0 + V_1 F + V_2 F^2 + \cdots. \qquad (288b)$$

He similarly expressed the parameters of the wave equations, namely the energy parameter ($E = E_0 + E_1 F + E_2 F^2 + \cdots$) and other ‘constants’ (such as $\alpha = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 F + \alpha_2 F^2 + \cdots$). He then introduced the transformation provided by Eqs. (284) and (285) and found solutions for the functions $X_1$ and $X_2$ again in power series of $\xi$, namely, $X = X_0 + X_1 F + X_2 F^2 + \cdots$, with

$$X_1 = \sum_{r=0}^{h+2} B_r \xi^r \quad \text{and} \quad X_2 = \sum_{r=0}^{h+4} C_r \xi^r. \qquad (289)$$

The resulting algebraic equations relating the $A_r$, $B_r$ and $C_r$ yielded the sought-after energy corrections, viz.,

$$E_1 = - \frac{3h^2}{8\pi^2 m_e e Z} nn_e \qquad (290a)$$

and

$$E_2 = - \frac{h^6}{16(2\pi)^6 m_e^3 e^6 Z^4} n^4(17n^2 - 3n_e^2 - 9k^2 + 19), \qquad (290b)$$

---
$^{144}$The equation for $v$ had a shape closely resembling Eq. (283), except that the field-dependent term was $+(m_e e/4K^2)Fv^2$ and the parameter $\beta$ replaced $\alpha$. The sum of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ assumed the value $Zm_e e^2/K^2$, with $Ze$ the charge of the nucleus. On transforming the wave equation for $v$, Waller arrived at an equation whose solution, in terms of a power series, involved another positive integer, $j$, given by the equation $j = b_0 - (k+1)/2$. On adding this equation to Eq. (287b), he obtained the Rydberg–Bohr formula for hydrogen and hydrogen-like spectra,

$$E_0 = \frac{m_e e^4 Z^2}{2n^2 K^2} = - \frac{RhZ^2}{n^2},$$

with $n = h + j + k + l$ integer $(\ge 1)$.

with

$$-n + k + 1 \le n_e \le n - k - 1. \qquad (290c)$$

On the second-order term $E_2$, Waller remarked: 'This expression deviates formally from the one given by Epstein only by the fact that the term +19 [in parentheses] has been added. One should, however, note that in the new quantum mechanics the value $k = 0$ is also admitted. Therefore, one obtains for small quantum numbers energy values that are totally different from Epstein's—for $n = 1$, e.g., the $4\frac{1}{2}$-fold value' (Waller, 1926, pp. 640–641).

Waller was not the only one to arrive at Eqs. (290) for the Stark effect. On the same day as he signed his paper, 18 June 1926, the *Zeitschrift für Physik* received Gregor Wentzel's paper, *'Eine Verallgemeinerung der Quantenbedingungen für die Zwecke der Wellenmechanik'* ('A Generalization of the Quantum Conditions for the Purposes of Wave Mechanics')—referred to earlier—in which the author proposed an approximative solution method for Schrödinger equations (Wentzel, 1926d). On applying it to the hydrogen atom in a constant external electric field of strength $F$, Wentzel had found the energy formula

$$E_{n_1n_2n_3} = -\frac{2\pi^2 m_e e^4}{h^2 n^2} - \frac{3h^2 F}{8\pi^2 m_e e} n(n_1 - n_2)$$
$$- \frac{h^6 F^2}{2^{10} \pi^6 m_e^3 e^6} n^4[17n^2 - 3(n_1 - n_2)^2 - 9(n_3 - 1)^2 + 19]. \qquad (291)$$

When one puts $Z = 1$ in Waller's formulae (290), and in addition $n_e = n_1 - n_2$ and $k = n_3 - 1$, then the identity of the two results is evident. Both Wentzel and Waller compared their formula to the available data on the second-order Stark effect, especially those presented by Toshio Takamine and N. Kokubu (1919), M. Kiuti (1925) and John Stuart Foster (1926). Wentzel concluded: 'The most accurate measurements have been performed with the middle component of $\text{H}_\gamma$. Takamine and Kiuti agree in the fact that the red-shift is larger than expected on the basis of Epstein's formula; the deviation is, if judged on the graphical presentations of Kuiti, about 20 percent. This is exactly what one would expect from formula [(291)]. . . . Foster's measurements concern $\text{H}_\delta$ and $\text{H}_\epsilon$, but they are less accurate: for $\text{H}_\delta$, he finds a deviation of roughly +30 percent, for $\text{H}_\epsilon$ (i.e., the middle component), however, no noticeable deviation from Epstein; Eq. [(291)] yields a deviation of +5 to 10 percent' (Wentzel, 1926d, pp. 527–528).

The differences between the second-order terms in the 'classical' formula of Epstein, namely,

$$E_2^{(\text{cl})} = -\frac{h^6 F^2 n^4}{16(2\pi)^6 m_e^3 e^6} [17n^2 - 3(n_1 - n_2)^2 - 9n_3^2], \qquad (292)$$

and the corresponding term in Eq. (291) should be particularly large for small quantum numbers; for the ground state especially with $n_1 = n_2 = 0$, and $n_3 = n = 1$ the ratio of the quantum mechanical $E_2$ to $E_2^{(\text{cl})}$ becomes 4.5:1. Wentzel now argued that the values of the quantum mechanical second-order Stark effect might help to explain the spectra of the excited helium atom, because the former can be physically related to the polarization of the He$^+$-core. The correction constant $\delta$ in the helium terms $R/(n - \delta)^2$, as calculated on this idea, assumed the values 0.028, 0.0022 and 0.0004 for the $p$-, $d$- and $f$- series, respectively; these values turned out to be the average of the values derived from the corresponding data for ortho- and para-helium states.

Waller, independently of Wentzel, arrived at exactly the same conclusions when comparing his new quantum mechanical result with the available data of Takamine and Foster.$^{145}$ Like Wentzel, he also tried to extend the result of the second-order Stark effect for the purpose of explaining the spectra of two-electron atoms (or ions). Unlike Wentzel, who had just given some estimates, Waller went into the details of the quantum mechanical calculation of the polarization effect caused by the inner core. Especially, he assumed that the outer electron of the two-electron atom moves in a potential (of the core formed by the atomic nucleus with charge Ze and the inner electron), namely,

$$
U(r) = -\frac{(Z-1)e^2}{r} - \frac{\alpha e^2}{2r^4} \tag{293}
$$

The constant $\alpha$ was obtained when he considered the energy change created by the electric field $F$ on the inner electron to be given by $-\frac{1}{2}\alpha F^2$. In a footnote, Waller stated: ‘I owe to Dr. Heisenberg the hint to this relation and, therefore, the stimulation to apply the results of §1 [i.e., the section containing the Stark effect calculations] to He and Li$^+$’ (Waller, 1926, p. 642, footnote 1).$^{146}$ He computed, from his Stark effect formula (290b), the numerical value of $\alpha$, i.e.,

$$
\alpha = \frac{66.4}{Z^4} \cdot 10^{-26} \tag{294}
$$

In order to evaluate the perturbation term $\alpha e^2/2r^4$, Waller needed an expression for the average of $r^{-4}$ over the unperturbed Kepler orbit in a hydrogen-like atom, as was represented by the cores of He or Li$^+$ (i.e., He$^+$ and Li$^{++}$). This expression

---

$^{146}$ Indeed Heisenberg had, for a long time, been interested in the problem of the helium spectrum, and also in the connection between the second-order Stark effect and the non-hydrogen-like spectra. In early 1924, he had discussed the situation in some detail in a joint paper with Max Born, where one can find the considerations used by Waller (see Born and Heisenberg, 1924b, especially p. 391).

where $\psi_{nkm}$ were the unperturbed hydrogen eigenfunctions and the integration extended over the entire three-dimensional space. After a lengthy, but straightforward evaluation, Waller arrived at the following result:

From Eq. (296) he derived the Rydberg correction$^{147}$

For a critical test of the result, Eq. (297), against the spectroscopic data on He and Li$^+$—the latter being provided by Sven Werner in Copenhagen (Werner, 1925, 1926)—one had to take into account 'that the difference between para- and ortho-helium terms must be attributed, according to Heisenberg, to a special resonance interaction between the outer and the inner electron, such that no sharp distinction can be made between the type of binding of the two electrons' (Waller, 1926, p. 646). As a consequence of this situation, so Waller argued, one had to use the average values of the ortho- and para-helium states (or the corresponding average of the Li$^+$-states) for a comparison with the theoretical result, and then this comparison yielded 'a satisfactory agreement' ('*befriedigende Übereinstimmung*,' Waller, 1926, p. 646). The same procedure and conclusion had also been found by Gregor Wentzel.
Both Waller and Wentzel profited in their contributions from the fortunate situation in that they learned of the recent work on atomic theory, in particular

$$\left(\frac{1}{r^4}\right) = \frac{3}{2} \left[\frac{2Rh(Z - 1)}{e^2}\right]^4 \frac{1 - k^2/3n^2}{n^3k^5},$$

One recognizes that both results exhibit the same structure, except that in quantum mechanics the numbers $k$ and $k^2$ of the old theory have to be replaced by $k - \frac{1}{2}, \dots, k + \frac{3}{2}$ and $k(k + \frac{1}{2})$, respectively. In order to fit the data better, Born and Heisenberg had previously simulated the quantum mechanical corrections by assuming half-integral values for the quantum number $k$.

IV.4 Response to Wave Mechanics II. Applications and Extensions 717

the papers of Heisenberg and Schrödinger, very early, often prior to publication. The physicists in America at that time did not share this advantage. Thus Carl Eckart in Pasadena only learned of—as we have stated earlier (in Section 3)—Schrödinger's *Annalen der Physik* communications on wave mechanics after considerable delay (about a couple of months), which took away priority from his own work on the equivalence proof. He declared in a later interview: 'It influenced me to come back east, because I felt that if this delay in the mails could have that much effect once, it might have again. It was obviously before the days of aircraft and one had to add to the trans-Atlantic steamship time the transcontinental train time and all the delays in transferring' (Eckart, AHQP Interview, p. 15). As a consequence of this delay, Eckart and Paul Sophus Epstein may also have lost out in being first to produce new results on the Stark effect and the hydrogen spectrum (intensity of the Balmer lines). Before turning to their work, let us quickly refer to the European discussion of the relativistic hydrogen atom.

In Pauli's scientific correspondence of the spring of 1926 there are some comments concerning the calculation of fine structure in wave mechanics. Pauli, in his paper on the hydrogen spectrum, submitted in January to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, had pointed out the difficulties of solving the relativistic problem within the matrix scheme. A little later he, Heisenberg and Wentzel had developed the action-angle theory, and Wentzel had succeeded in repeating the Sommerfeld fine-structure calculation, obtaining formally the same formula as Sommerfeld had in 1915 (Wentzel, 1926a). The equivalence with the old result, however, was complete only if one inserted for the angular-momentum intergral, $I_{\phi}$, integral values. Wentzel had then mentioned in a footnote: 'According to an oral communication, Pauli has . . . found that the angular momenta $I_{\phi}$ must be taken to assume half-integral values, which contradicts, as is well known, the original interpretation of the H-fine structure by Sommerfeld.' He added at the same time: 'The agreement with experience is re-established, however, by the fact that one ascribes to the electron, according to Goudsmit, a magnetic moment' (Wentzel, 1926a, p. 94, footnote 1). For the agreement of the quantum mechanical calculation including relativistic effects *and* the spin hypothesis, Wentzel had cited a paper by Heisenberg and Jordan; these authors had calculated both effects for one-electron atoms and had, by simple addition of the corresponding matrix elements, recuperated Sommerfeld's full fine structure formula (Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926, §5).

Heisenberg's and Jordan's evaluation, although having led to a clear result, involved assumptions that could still be doubted at that time. One question concerned the electron spin hypothesis. Certainly, in the spring of 1926 most quantum physicists—including Pauli and Wentzel—had accepted the concept *per se*; still, some feared that it would involve unacceptable consequences. In particular, Wentzel discovered a difficulty when he tried to extend the result of Heisenberg and Jordan to the X-ray spectra—in a paper entitled 'Eine Schwierigkeit für die Theorie des Kreiselektrons' ('A Difficulty in the Theory of the Spinning Electron'), which was received on 22 May 1926 by *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Wentzel,

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0359 -->

718  
Chapter IV  Early Response and Applications  

1926c). On calculating the so-called screening constant for relativistic doublets, he found theoretical values that were considerably—i.e., 50 to 100 percent—higher than those derived from spectroscopic data. Does the reason for this failure of agreement lie in the incorrect *Ansatz* for the atomic potentials, ‘or is the model of the spinning electron not yet sufficient in order to reproduce all details of the spectroscopic experience?’, he finally asked (Wentzel, 1926c, p. 914).  
Wentzel’s critical argument was debated in England soon after his paper appeared in print. Thus a Dr. L. C. Jackson wrote a letter to *Nature*, pointing out the extra force term,  

$$\Phi = \frac{1}{c} \mu[\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{E}],$$  
(298)  

arising for an electron with an intrinsic magnetic moment $\mu$ moving with velocity $\mathbf{v}$ in an electric field $\mathbf{E}$—as derived by Wentzel as a consequence of the spin hypothesis—would contradict Walther Kaufmann’s famous experiment on the deflection of electrons in electric and magnetic fields (Jackson, 1926). Llewellyn H. Thomas, in reply to this letter (which appeared in the issue of 21 August 1926), pointed out several errors in Jackson’s arguments and suggested rather: ‘For an electron describing a periodic orbit in an atom energy $\mu[\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{E}]/2c$ would, I think, lead to the correct first-order perturbation, but the equations of motion are not of [the classical] Hamiltonian form’ (Thomas, 1926b, p. 374). By the time Thomas’ letter appeared in *Nature*—in the issue of 11 September 1926—the question as to whether spin had to be included or not had also been approached in wave mechanics. Independently, Pauli in Germany and Eckart in California arrived at the same result, namely that *the electron spin was necessary* to explain the properties of the hydrogen spectrum.  
Since there exists no published paper by Pauli on the topic, the information must come from his correspondence. Thus he stated in a letter to Wentzel, dated 11 June 1926: ‘The exact formula of Sommerfeld with half-integral $k$ for the relativistic Kepler motion can also be deduced directly from the Schrödinger equation based on his [Schrödinger’s] methods’ (Pauli to Wentzel, 11 June 1926). On 5 July he touched on the same point, when writing again to Wentzel (evidently replying to a letter of Wentzel that has not been preserved): ‘In particular I want to write to you today, because in the meantime I have had the gravest doubts about accepting your result on the higher relativistic corrections, i.e., the validity of Sommerfeld’s formula with half-integral $k$ and neglecting the electron’s moment’ (Pauli to Wentzel, 5 July 1926). Pauli then criticized (in his letter), that the relativistic differential equation proposed by Wentzel (in the lost letter),  

$$\Delta \psi - \frac{1}{K^2 c^2} (E - E_{\text{pot}})^2 \psi + \frac{m_e^2 c^2}{K^2} \psi = 0$$  
(299)  

($K = h/2\pi i$, $E$ total energy including $m_e c^2$), was not self-adjoint and its eigenfunctions failed to be orthogonal. Instead, he proposed to start the procedure

IV.4 Response to Wave Mechanics II. Applications and Extensions 719

from the relativistic energy equation, i.e.,

$$\sqrt{(m_{\mathrm{e}}c^{2})^{2}+c^{2}(p_{x}^{2}+p_{y}^{2}+p_{z}^{2})}-\frac{Ze^{2}}{r}=E \quad (300)$$

for the electron with momentum ($p_x$, $p_y$, $p_z$) in the Coulomb field of an atomic nucleus of charge $Ze$, and derive from it a wave equation which had a different structure from the usual ones (considered so far by Schrödinger). He argued: 'If one translated ... [Eq. (300)] into a statement on the eigenfunctions, then one must construct a differential operator which corresponds to the square root. One will be able to achieve this only by expanding the root in a power series and by calculating the relativity corrections of different order successively in perturbation theory' (Pauli to Wentzel, 5 July 1926). Pauli did not go on to develop this interesting and remarkable idea, which would underlie a later fundamental extension of the wave equation for the electron automatically including the spin property.$^{148}$ But his conclusion was the correct one, namely: 'The whole problem can certainly be treated reasonably *by* taking into account the electron's moment' (Pauli to Wentzel, 5 July 1926).

Doubts about the completeness of the description of the hydrogen atom in wave mechanics, without involving the electron spin hypothesis, were also put forward by Carl Eckart, who had no information about these discussions that had occurred thousands of miles away in Central Europe (see Eckart, 1926c). In July 1926, he also knew that the problem of computing line-intensities in the undulatory theory had meanwhile been solved for several atomic systems, such as the band spectra of diatomic molecules, the hydrogen spectrum and its Stark effect. Having just produced a method for calculating Heisenberg's matrix elements with the help of Schrödinger's eigenfunctions, Eckart now attacked the problem of computing intensities of the Balmer lines by evaluating the elements of the matrices $\mathbf{x} + i\mathbf{y}$ and $\mathbf{z}$ (with $\mathbf{x}$, $\mathbf{y}$ and $\mathbf{z}$ denoting the Cartesian position co-ordinates in quantum mechanics). More accurately, he considered the expressions$^{149}$

$$R(mnl, \mu\nu\lambda) = \iiint r^{2}(x+iy)\psi(mnl)\psi(\mu\nu\lambda) d\tau, \quad (301\mathrm{a})$$

$$S(mnl, \mu\nu\lambda) = \iiint r^{2}(x-iy)\psi(mnl)\psi(\mu\nu\lambda) d\tau, \quad (301\mathrm{b})$$

and

$$Z(mnl, \mu\nu\lambda) = \iiint r^{2} z\psi(mnl)\psi(\mu\nu\lambda) d\tau, \quad (301\mathrm{c})$$

---
$^{148}$ This essential step to a consistent relativistic equation would be taken by Paul Dirac in late 1927 and lead to his spinor equation (Dirac, 1928a).

$^{149}$ The multiplicative factor $r^2$ arises from the normalization of the wave functions.

After some skillful calculations he obtained expressions for all the desired matrix elements, and thus derived the intensity for a transition from the state of the hydrogen atom described by $\kappa\lambda$ to the state described by $kl$, i.e.,$^{150}$

$$I(kl; \kappa\lambda) = \sum_m \left(\frac{1}{2}R^2 + \frac{1}{2}S^2 + Z^2\right). \tag{303}$$

On inserting the numbers for the transition providing the line H$_\alpha$ (i.e., $\lambda = 3$, $l = 2$), Eckart found for its three components the intensity ratios

$$I(\frac{1}{2} 3; \frac{3}{2} 2) : I(\frac{3}{2} 3; \frac{1}{2} 2) : I(\frac{5}{2} 3; \frac{3}{2} 2) = 0.879 : 9.42 : 45.2. \tag{304}$$

In his paper Eckart emphasized: 'These values are not in accordance with observation. According to the experiments of W[alter] V. Houston, the actual ratio of the intensities of the two brighter components is more nearly 8:10 than 2:10' (Eckart, 1926c, p. 934). A similarly unsatisfactory result followed from his calculations on the brightness ratio of the H$_\beta$-components. He excused the failure, referring to the result on the relativistic treatment reported earlier by Schrödinger: 'The model is certainly incomplete, as is shown by the energy levels of the fine-structure predicted by this theory. The rotation [spin] of the electron, which is expected to remove this discrepancy, is also expected to predict a fourth component whose intensity is included in that of the fainter of the two components observed' (Eckart, 1926c, p. 935).$^{151}$

Whereas Eckart's results on the hydrogen line-intensities appeared not to bear too much resemblance with observations, another wave mechanical calculation made in Pasadena, that of Paul Sophus Epstein on the Stark effect, certainly did. Epstein, from the early 1920s a professor of theoretical physics at Caltech, had (back in 1916, then in Munich) been responsible for the first successful interpretation of the Stark effect on the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory. Now, in the early summer of 1926, he was drawn—partly by his younger associate Carl Eckart—into the undulatory theory of atoms which, he soon realized, 'opens new avenues of thought and seems to afford our first glimpse of the true nature of the quanta' (Epstein, 1926b, p. 695). This positive attitude towards wave mechanics might have been triggered by the fact that Epstein had already acquainted himself early in his professional life—i.e., while working on his doctoral thesis—with the

IV.4 Response to Wave Mechanics II. Applications and Extensions

mathematical tool of spherical harmonics which played an important role in the new theory. This acquaintance enabled him in July 1926 to reproduce quickly the first- and second-order Stark effects in wave mechanics. Epstein presented the results in a letter to *Nature*, dated 24 July (Epstein, 1926a), and in an extended paper, dated 29 July and submitted to *Physical Review* (Epstein, 1926b). With respect to both the submission and the publication dates—the letter to *Nature* appeared in print in the issue of 25 September, the paper in the *Physical Review* in the October 1926 issue—his contributions could not achieve priority over the European results; but it must be clearly emphasized that Epstein’s work on the second-order Stark effect was *independent* of the European work in that field and of *equal quality*.

As far as procedure is concerned, Epstein’s calculation of the Stark effect followed the same lines as Schrödinger and Waller had already taken in Europe. He introduced parabolic co-ordinates—after all, he (Epstein) had used that device in his 1916 calculation and people had followed it ever since—and derived three wave equations in each of the variables separately, the same as Schrödinger and Waller had obtained.¹⁵² The path of solution went more or less along the same lines, one which we have outlined above in our report on Waller’s paper.¹⁵³ Like Waller, Epstein did not have available Schrödinger’s third communication containing the perturbation theory in wave mechanics, but, like his European colleague, he experienced no problem in developing his own perturbation scheme based on the expansion of the wave functions and the parameters of the wave equations in terms of a series with increasing powers of the electric field strength. In this way he found the differential equations for the first approximation by selecting the terms independent of the field strength; the equations for the second approximation he found by taking the terms proportional to the field strength; and those for the third approximation he found by collecting the terms quadratic in the electric field strength.

Epstein solved the differential equations for the Stark effect, obtaining eigenfunctions that could be expressed through hypergeometric functions.¹⁵⁴ After a lengthy, but direct, evaluation he arrived at results for the energy terms which agreed in first order with the electric field strength with Waller’s formula, Eq. (290a), if one replaces Waller’s integral number $n_e$ by Epstein’s $(m - n)$. His

¹⁵³ It may seem remarkable that Epstein also applied a transformation very similar to Waller’s Eq. (285) in order to arrive at modified differential equations for his wave functions. (See Epstein, 1926b, p. 697, Eq. (9).)

Epstein also made use of the known relations (and differential relations) between hypergeometric functions.

Epstein further calculated the intensities of the Stark lines with the help of the Schrödinger–Eckart formulae for the matrix elements. He presented, in Section 8 of his paper (Epstein, 1926b), explicit expressions, for example, for the position variable \( q_z \) (in the direction of the electric field)  

$$
\begin{aligned}
q_z(m, n, s; m', n', s) &= \frac{k^2}{4\mu Z e^2} \sqrt{\frac{(s + m - 1)! (s + n - 1)! \, m! \, n!}{(s + m' - 1)! (s + n' - 1)! \, m'! \, n'!}} \\
&\quad \times \frac{(1 - u^2)^{s+1} u^{l - l' - 2}}{(m - m')! (n - n')!} \left\{ \left[ (1 + u^2)(m - n) - (1 - u^2)(m' - n') \right] \cdot \Phi(m, m') \Phi(n, n') \right. \\
&\quad \left. - 2 \left[ (m - m') \Phi(m - 1, m') \Phi(n, n') - (n - n') \Phi(m, m') \Phi(n - 1, n') \right] \right\}, \tag{307}
\end{aligned}
$$  

with \( \Phi \) denoting hypergeometric functions, e.g.,  

$$
\Phi(m, m') = F(s + m, -m', m - m' + 1, u^2), \tag{308}
$$  

depending on the variable \( u = (l - l')/(l + l') \) (\( l = m + n + s \), ‘principal’ quantum number according to Epstein).¹⁵⁵ On comparing the theoretical intensities with the data for the hydrogen lines \( \text{H}_\alpha \) to \( \text{H}_\delta \), Epstein concluded: ‘We see that the agreement is fair, and decidedly better than that obtained from Bohr’s correspondence principle in Kramers’ work [Kramers, 1919]’ (Epstein, 1926b, p. 710).

IV.4 Response to Wave Mechanics II. Applications and Extensions 723

Epstein’s intensity results did not fully coincide with those computed by Schrödinger. A particular difference was mentioned by Francis G. Slack (1897–1985), an American visitor at Sommerfeld’s institute, who wrote to Erwin Schrödinger on 14 January 1927: ‘In calculating the intensities of the components of $H_\alpha$ and $H_\beta$ in the Stark effect from your expression (*Annalen der Physik* 80 [Schrödinger, 1926f], p. 464, Eq. (65)) I have obtained somewhat different values than given by yourself. I have not used your equation 120 (p. 488) but have written out the expressions for the Laguerreschen Polynoms and integrated each part. My values are in close agreement with those given by P. S. Epstein in the *Physical Review* of last October. They show good agreement with the experimental results for the parallel $H_\alpha$ component $\Delta = 3$ and the $H_\beta$ component $\Delta = 8$ for which you have given too large values.’ A little later, Slack published these conclusions in a paper which he had submitted to *Annalen der Physik* on 24 December 1926 (Slack, 1927). Thus Epstein’s calculation of the Stark effect intensities was not only independent of Schrödinger’s, but even yielded at times the more reliable result.$^{156}$

During the later months of 1926, another topic arose in wave mechanics on which European and American physicists worked independently: the rotator and the symmetrical top. We shall report about this competition in Section IV.5.

**Collision Processes in Wave Mechanics**

In his *Recollections* Max Born recalled the story of the impact of Schrödinger’s wave mechanics, that is, the appearance in print of the first communication (Schrödinger, 1926c) in the middle of March 1926, about a month after the three-man paper (Born, Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926) and shortly after Paul Dirac’s second paper on quantum mechanics (Dirac, 1926a, published at the beginning of March 1926). He wrote:

> A short time after the appearance of our three-man paper and the corresponding papers by Dirac, we were taken by surprise by Schrödinger’s papers on wave mechanics which appeared in 1926 in *Annalen der Physik*. This was a new approach to quantum mechanics which, at first glance, had no connection with our own work. It was of fascinating power and elegance, and as it used mathematical methods well known to every physicist (while our matrix method was not familiar to many of them), it quickly became the standard theory. The connection with matrix mechanics was soon demonstrated by Schrödinger himself and could also be gathered from Dirac’s paper. (Born, 1978, pp. 229–230)

***

$^{156}$See also Epstein’s note on the second-order Stark effect in *Science* of 24 December, where he compared his results to the new data of M. Kiuti (Epstein, 1926e).

Far from being discouraged by the priority of his European colleagues, Epstein continued to work on wave mechanics: thus he evaluated again the intensities of the hydrogen lines, arriving at the same results as Eckart (Epstein, 1926c); he calculated the normal Zeeman effect (Epstein, 1926d); and he would present at the Los Angeles meeting of the American Physical Society on 5 March 1927 results from treating a magnetic dipole in Schrödinger’s theory (Epstein, 1927).

Chapter IV  Early Response and Applications

At that time Born had just returned from his tour of the United States, where he had lectured extensively at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (Cambridge), the University of Wisconsin (Madison), the California Institute of Technology (Pasadena), and at Washington, D.C., propagating everywhere the scheme of quantum mechanics.¹⁵⁷ Upon recovering from the strains of travelling, he sat down and worked on his M.I.T. lectures (‘*Problems of Atomic Dynamics*’, Born, 1926d) to prepare a German edition (Born, 1926e).¹⁵⁸ The preface to the German edition—which is dated Göttingen, 21 April 1926—begins with the sentences:

> In the short time between the end of my Cambridge lectures and the printing of this German edition the new quantum mechanics has developed in such a way that it did not seem appropriate to me to neglect the new results. The present little book therefore differs considerably from the English [American] edition, not only as far as contents are concerned but also in the manner of representation; while there [i.e., in the American edition] the new methods have been displayed with the well-founded hope that they might contribute to the solution of atomic structure, here [in the German edition] the solutions of many problems could be expounded. This large progress is based as much on the new quantum mechanics as on the model of the electron with intrinsic rotation, due to Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, by means of which the interpretation of the electron orbits with each having four quantum numbers—founded by Pauli and Heisenberg—has been made accessible to quantitative calculations. (Born, 1926e, pp. IV–V)¹⁵⁹

He finally regretted:

> Unfortunately, the fine methods of Dirac could only [just] be mentioned; the fundamental connections which have recently been established by Schrödinger between quantum mechanics, on the one hand, and the de Broglie waves and the Bose–Einstein statistics, on the other, had to be left out completely. (Born, 1926e, p. V)

**Schrödinger’s theory, especially the demonstration of the relation of quantum mechanics to the de Broglie waves and the statistical methods of Bose and Einstein**

IV.4 Response to Wave Mechanics II. Applications and Extensions 725

did interest Born, for he had been concerned with these topics in the previous year.$^{160}$ And yet, it took him some time before he entered into a deeper study, as he had to prepare for his official tasks for the summer semester (starting in May). However, on 25 June 1926, the *Zeitschrift für Physik* received a ‘preliminary communication’ (‘*vorläufige Mitteilung*’) that was entitled ‘*Zur Quantenmechanik der Stoßvorgänge*’ (‘On the Quantum Mechanics of Collision Processes,’ Born, 1926a). Born had first submitted it to *Naturwissenschaften*, a journal for the rapid publication of short notes; but it was not accepted there ‘because of lack of space’ (Born, 1926a, p. 863, footnote 1).$^{161}$

In the introduction to his note, Born explained the main goal of his communication: namely, to answer ‘the question about the very nature of [quantum-theoretical] “transitions”’ (‘*die Frage nach dem Wesen der “Übergänge” selbst*’, Born, 1926a, p. 863). He especially argued that (the Göttingen) quantum mechanics constituted a logically complete theory which ought to describe the problem of atomic transitions properly. However, until now Born had not found a way of attacking the transition problem itself; hence, he searched for a slightly different but related problem. In this context he was reminded that: ‘Bohr has already directed attention to the fact that all the principal difficulties of the quantum concepts, which we meet when considering the emission and absorption of light by atoms, also occur in the short-range interaction of atoms, i.e., in collisions’ (Born, 1926a, p. 863).$^{162}$ Clearly, in this particular problem the radiation field would not enter directly and only material particles were involved, to which quantum mechanics had to apply anyway. ‘Therefore,’ he continued, ‘I have attacked the problem to study more closely the interaction of a free particle (of an *α*-ray or electron) and an arbitrary atom, and to see whether a description of the collision process can be achieved within the framework of the present theory’ (Born, 1926a, p. 863).

Born also knew that in the collision problem continuous spectra of the particles involved in the interaction played a crucial role, hence the matrix formalism would not provide an easy access. Far more suitable appeared to be the operator methods, which he had developed at M.I.T. with the mathematician Norbert Wiener (Born and Wiener, 1926a). Since Schrödinger’s theory could be considered an extension of the Born–Wiener operator approach, and Born knew about the equivalence of matrix and wave mechanics (from Pauli’s letter to Jordan in Göttingen, dated 12 April 1926), he immediately turned to it, observing that it ‘alone proved to be [really] suitable in this case’ (‘*sich hierbei allein als geeignet erwiesen*’, Born, 1926a, p. 864).

$^{160}$ See his exchange with Albert Einstein in 1925 and Walter Elsasser’s explanation of the Ramsauer effect in Göttingen at that time. (We have discussed these items in Volume 1, Chapter V.)

$^{161}$ The unsuccessful procedure with *Naturwissenschaften* may have delayed the submission of the paper by at least a couple of weeks; we conclude that Born had the note ready in late May or early June 1926.

$^{162}$ See Bohr’s considerations in his paper, Bohr, 1925a, which we have discussed repeatedly, e.g., in some detail in Volume 4, Section IV.1.

726
Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

The difficulty in dealing with the interaction of two atoms or atomic systems in quantum mechanics lay—as Born and his associates had discovered earlier (see especially the three-man paper: Born, Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926)—in the intricate coupling of all states of the two systems. On the other hand, the asymptotic behaviour of the two atomic systems—i.e., at large distances from the point of collision—had to be simple, namely a uniform motion in a straight line. While such a straight-line motion could not be described by matrix methods, it could be done rather easily in Schrödinger’s theory.$^{163}$ In the latter, there corresponded to an (undisturbed) atom in the $n$th quantum state (with energy $W_n^0$) a vibration of frequency $(1/h) W_n^0$, and an electron with uniform, straight-line motion was represented by a plane wave; the interaction between the two wave phenomena should then determine the behaviour of the electron when colliding with the atom. The whole problem had thus to be considered as a special ‘diffraction problem’, or stated more accurately: ‘One has to solve the Schrödinger equation for the combined atom–electron system, with the boundary condition that the solution in a given direction of the electron space should pass over asymptotically into a plane wave propagating exactly in this direction (of the incoming electron)’; and also, ‘of the solution thus characterized, what interests us now is mainly the behaviour of the “scattered” wave at infinity’ (Born, 1926a, p. 864).$^{164}$ After these general remarks, Born sketched the solution of the collision problem in his preliminary communication.

The eigenfunction of the unperturbed state of the system, consisting of an electron which comes from $z = +\infty$ along the $z$-axis and possesses mass $\mu$ and kinetic energy $\tau$—such that the de Broglie wavelength is given by the equation

$$ \lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2\mu\tau}} \tag{309} $$

—and an atom which is undisturbed at a great distance from the electron and possesses the eigenfunctions $\psi_n^0(q_k)$, with $q_k$ the position variables of the atom, can be written as

$$ \psi_{n\tau}^0(q_k, z) = \psi_n^0(q_k) \sin \left( \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} z \right). \tag{310} $$

That is, it is represented simply by the product of the wave functions of the undisturbed parts. Further, if $V(x, y, z; q_k)$ denotes the potential energy of the

$^{163}$ Before the advent of wave mechanics, Born and Wiener had already described the uniform motion of a particle in a straight-line in their operator formalism (Born and Wiener, 1926a, b, last part). However, the interaction of the charged particle with an atom seemed difficult to approach by the same method, while Schrödinger’s wave theory of atomic systems offered an immediate access, as Born showed.

$^{164}$ At an infinite distance from the atom after the collision, the electron could be described again by a plane wave.

(i) one is able to demonstrate, by using perturbation theory, the existence of a solution of the Schrödinger equation of the perturbed system, which for $z = +\infty$ passes over into $\psi_{n\tau}^0(q_k, z)$, Eq. (310);
(ii) the scattered wave, on the other hand, assumes at asymptotic distances from the atom—which is thought to be very heavy and at rest practically at the point $z = 0$—the form

$$
\psi_{n\tau}^{(1)}(x, y, z; q_k)

= \sum_m \iint_{\alpha x + \beta y + \gamma z > 0} \Phi_{nm}^{(\tau)}(\alpha, \beta, \gamma) \sin \left[ \frac{2\pi}{\lambda_{nm}^{(\tau)}} (\alpha x + \beta y + \gamma z + \delta) \right]
$$
$$
\qquad \cdot \psi_m^0(q_k) d\omega.
$$
(311)

Here $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ denote the direction cosines and $\lambda_{nm}$ the de Broglie wavelength obtained on inserting the energy,

$$

Born concluded: ‘The perturbation at infinity may be interpreted as the superposition of solutions of the non-perturbed process’ (Born, 1926a, p. 865). Further, the coefficients $\Phi_{nm}^{(\tau)}(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)$ should represent, from the corpuscular view, as giving ‘the probability for the situation that the electron coming from the $z$-direction will be scattered in the direction determined by $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ (and with the phase shift $\delta$), such that its energy $\tau$ is increased by a quantum $h\nu_{mn}^0$, at the expense of the atomic energy’ (Born, 1926a, pp. 865–866). However, instead of presenting the detailed calculation of the $\Phi_{nm}^{(\tau)}(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)$ on the basis of a perturbation theory, Born in his short note rather discussed the introduction of a probability in the quantum mechanical collision problem; he argued, in particular, that *it was necessary to give up the deterministic description of the scattering process*. We shall not enter into a discussion of this here, as it provides the starting point of a great debate that will be reported in the next volume. Instead, we shall go on to discuss the details of the quantitative calculation, as presented by Born in a subsequent longer paper, ‘*Quantenmechanik der Stoßvorgänge*’ (‘Quantum Mechanics of Collision Processes’). This paper was received four weeks later, on 21 July 1926, again by *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Born, 1926b).<sup>165</sup>
The fact that Schrödinger’s wave mechanics allowed one to describe collision problems had induced Born to state in his first note: ‘I wish to consider it, just because of this reason, to be the deepest formulation of the quantum laws’ (‘*Ich möchte gerade aus diesem Grunde sie als die tiefste Fassung der Quantensetze*

<sup>165</sup>Born announced the longer paper in his short note (see Born, 1926a, p. 867).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0369 -->

728 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

*ansehen'* Born, 1926a, p. 864). Happily he went on to work out, in early summer of 1926, the wave mechanical approach to general aperiodic atomic systems, i.e., situations in which the matrix mechanical description did not seem to be possible. These situations included especially the collision processes which—so Born argued—'have not only provided the most convincing evidence for the fundamental postulates of quantum theory, but also seem to be suited to yielding a clarification of the physical significance of the formal laws of the so-called "quantum mechanics"' (Born, 1926b, p. 803). The matrix formulation excluded the representation of atomic processes in space and time; in Schrödinger's theory, on the other hand, the atomic processes were actually described by wave motions which, of course, possess reality in space and time. Still Born concluded: 'Neither of these two interpretations seems satisfactory to me' ('*Keine dieser beiden Auffassungen scheint mir befriedigend*,' Born, 1926b, p. 803). He suggested a third interpretation emerging from a remark by Einstein, namely that the wave field associated with radiation guides the corpuscular light-quantum like a 'ghost field' ('*Gespensterfeld*'), i.e., it possesses no energy and momentum and determines the probability of a light-quantum (which is the carrier of energy and momentum) proceeding along a definite path. If Schrödinger's wave described the 'ghost field' of mass particles, one had to conclude: 'The guiding field, represented by a scalar function ψ of the co-ordinates of all particles involved and of time, propagates according to Schrödinger's differential equation. Momentum and energy, however, are transferred in such a manner as if corpuscles (electrons) do actually rush around. The orbits of these corpuscles are determined only insofar as they are restricted by energy and momentum conservation; apart from this, only a probability for taking a definite path is determined by the value distribution of the ψ-function' (Born, 1926b, p. 804). As indicated above, we shall not give an analysis of these statements here, which involved a probability interpretation of the conventional orbit (a trajectory in space and time) of a particle; rather, we shall display how Born applied his ideas in order to extend the applications of quantum and wave mechanics.

In the case of periodic atomic systems Born found the existence of several stationary states to be a consequence of his probabilistic arguments on the basis of the following reasoning:

(i) An arbitrary wave function ψ(q), solving the Schrödinger equation of the system, may be written as the sum of eigenfunctions ψₙ(q),

$$ \psi(q) = \sum c_n \psi_n(q), $$

where the cₙ denote complex coefficients whose absolute square sum, Σₙ |cₙ|², should be interpreted to mean the number of atoms.

(ii) From the Schrödinger equation for a particle of mass μ moving in a potential U one derives the relation

$$ W = \iiint \left\{ \frac{h^2}{8\pi^2\mu} |\text{grad } \psi|^2 + U|\psi|^2 \right\} dx\,dy\,dz \tag{313} $$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0370 -->

IV.4 Response to Wave Mechanics II. Applications and Extensions 729

for its energy $W$.$^{166}$ On inserting expression (312), the energy of the periodic system becomes

$$W = \sum_{n} |c_n|^2 W_n; \quad (314)$$

hence the right-hand side describes the average energy of the atomic system.

Going over to a completely aperiodic situation, the case of a free particle of mass $\mu$ moving with uniform velocity along the $x$-axis, Born wrote the general wave function

$$\psi(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} c(k) \exp(ikx) \, dk. \quad (315)$$

The $|c(k)|^2$ denotes the probability of the particle having a wave number in the interval $(k, k + dk)$, with $k$ being related to the energy $W$ as

$$k^2 = \frac{8\pi^2 \mu}{h^2} W, \quad (316a)$$

and to the momentum $p$ as

$$\frac{h}{2\pi} k = \frac{h}{\lambda} = p; \quad (316b)$$

hence $|c(k)|^2$ also determines the probability of the particle having momentum $p$. Further, the equation

$$\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} |\psi(x)|^2 \, dx = |\bar{c}|^2 \frac{\Delta p}{h} \quad (317)$$

can be derived where $\bar{c}$ is the average coefficient in the momentum interval $\Delta p$. This equation states that a cell in (the two-dimensional) phase space of the particle, which possesses unit length $\Delta x = 1$ and momentum extension $\Delta p = h$, will have the weight unity, in agreement with the old results of Otto Sackur and Hugo Tetrode.$^{167}$

$^{166}$ To prove Eq. (313), one writes the Schrödinger equation and inserts the eigenfunction $\psi_n$; then one multiplies the equation with $\psi_m^*$—the complex conjugate of the eigenfunction $\psi_m$—and integrates over the three-dimensional configuration space; finally, one applies Green's theorem yielding the result

$$\delta_{nm} W_n = \iiint \left\{ \frac{h^2}{8\pi^2 \mu} (\text{grad } \psi_n \cdot \text{grad } \psi_m^*) + U \psi_n \psi_m^* \right\} dx \, dy \, dz,$$

which agrees with Eq. (313).

$^{167}$ We have mentioned these results, obtained in 1911 and 1912, in Volume 1, Section I.7.

730
Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

Finally, passing on to the collision processes, one also had to include, in principle, the description of accelerated particles. However, as Born had indicated in his previous note, the treatment was considerably simplified by assuming the particles to be in a free state (i.e., in uniform motion) at asymptotic times before and after the collision (i.e., at lengthy times compared to the collision time). The problem therefore was reduced to answering the question: ‘If $|c(k)|^2$ is the known distribution function for the asymptotic motion before collision, can one compute from it the [asymptotic] distribution function after the collision?’ (Born, 1926b, p. 808).

Born first solved the problem in the one-dimensional case by considering the continuous eigenvalue spectrum of the Schrödinger equation

$$\frac{d^2\psi}{dx^2} + k^2\psi = V\psi, \qquad (318)$$

with $k$ given by Eq. (316a) and $V(x)$ being related to the potential energy $U(x)$ through the equation

$$V(x) = \frac{8\pi^2\mu}{h^2} U(x). \qquad (318a)$$

Evidently, Eq. (318) describes the behaviour of a particle having mass $\mu$ and energy $W$ moving in a potential $U(x)$ along the $x$-axis. Born then studied the asymptotic solutions, assuming that $U(x)$ decreased at large $x$ faster than $x^{-2}$. On applying an iterative procedure involving the successive approximation equations

$$\frac{d^2u_n}{dx^2} + k^2u_n = Vu_{n-1}, \qquad (319)$$

he could express the general solution of Eq. (318) as an infinite sum

$$\psi(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} u_n(x), \qquad (320)$$

with

$$u_0(x) = \exp(ikx) \qquad (320a)$$

and

$$u_n(x) = \frac{1}{k} \int_x^{\infty} u_{n-1}(\xi) V(\xi) \sin[k(\xi - x)] d\xi. \qquad (320b)$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0372 -->

IV.4 Response to Wave Mechanics II. Applications and Extensions 731

Since all $u_1, u_2, \dots$ disappear for $x \rightarrow +\infty$, the function $\psi$, Eq. (320), reduces to $u_0(x)$ for positive, asymptotic $x$. However, for $x \rightarrow \infty$ a second solution, $\exp(-ikx)$, can also be shown to exist; hence, the most general asymptotic solution for large, positive $x$ has to be written as

$$\psi^+(x) = a \exp(ikx) + b \exp(-ikx). \qquad (321)$$

Similarly, for asymptotic, negative $x$ (i.e., $x \rightarrow -\infty$), the most general solution becomes

$$\psi^-(x) = A \exp(ikx) + B \exp(-ikx), \qquad (322)$$

and the (complex) amplitudes $A$ and $B$ can be expressed as functions of the (complex) amplitudes $a$ and $b$ in Eq. (321).

For the description of the physical situation of particle collision one usually considers in- and outgoing waves; that is, the expressions $\psi^+(x)$ and $\psi^-(x)$ are decomposed and multiplied with suitable time-dependent factors, namely,

$$\psi^+(x, t) = c_e \exp[ik(x + vt + \phi_e)] + c_a \exp[-ik(x - vt + \phi_a)] \qquad (321')$$

and

$$\psi^-(x, t) = C_a \exp[ik(x + vt + \Phi_a)] + C_e \exp[-ik(x - vt + \Phi_e)]. \qquad (322')$$

If only one wave is incoming at $x = +\infty$, which corresponds to the physical situation of a particle arriving from $+\infty$, these equations simplify to ($C_e = 0$, $\phi_e = 0$):$^{168}$

$$\psi^+(x, t) = c_e \exp[ik(x + vt)] + c_a \exp[-ik(x - vt + \phi_a)] \qquad (321'')$$

and

$$\psi^-(x, t) = C_a \exp[ik(x + vt + \Phi_a)]. \qquad (322'')$$

From energy conservation Born further derived the equation

$$\overline{\frac{\partial\psi^-}{\partial x} \frac{\partial\psi^-}{\partial t}} = \overline{\frac{\partial\psi^+}{\partial x} \frac{\partial\psi^+}{\partial t}}, \qquad (323)$$

which states that in the time average (indicated by the bar) the ingoing energy

---

equals the outgoing energy.¹⁶⁹ By inserting the averaged functions $\overline{\psi^+(x, t)}$ and $\overline{\psi^-(x, t)}$, he thus found the equation

$$c_e^2 = c_a^2 + C_a^2. \tag{324}$$

This states that each incoming elementary wave of given intensity splits into two scattered waves going to the right and to the left, respectively, or, in the language of corpuscular theory: ‘If a particle of a given energy hits an atom, then it will either be reflected or proceed undisturbed; the sum of the probabilities for both of these events is equal to unity’ (Born, 1926b, p. 813).

In the following sections of his paper (§5 and §6), Born generalized the above calculation from one to three degrees of freedom. While the calculations now became much more complicated, they still followed the same lines as before. Again an iterative solution of the three-dimensional form of Eq. $$\psi(x, y, z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} u_n(x, y, z), \tag{325}$$

with $u_0(x, y, z)$ denoting the expression

$$u_0(\mathbf{r}) = \int c(\mathbf{s}) \exp[ik(\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{s})] d\omega, \tag{325a}$$

(**s** a unit vector, $\int d\omega$ the integration over the spatial angle), and (cf. Eq. (320b))

For the asymptotic solutions Born obtained, after lengthy calculations (cf. Eq. (321)),

$$u^\infty = u_0^\infty + \sum_{n=1}^\infty u_n^\infty = \frac{2\pi}{k} \left\{ |c(\mathbf{s})|\exp[ik(r + \delta)] + k\pi \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_{n-1}^\infty(-ks) \exp(-ikr) \right\}, \tag{326}$$
