$$= \frac{1}{4\pi^2ik} \int_0^{\infty} \left[ V u_{n-1}(\rho s) \exp(-ik\rho) - V_{n-1}(-\rho s) \exp(+ik\rho) \right] \rho \, d\rho. \tag{326a}$$

He thus concluded: 'The probability that an electron will be deflected into an element $d\omega$ of a spatial angle having the average direction $\mathbf{s}$ is therefore

$$\Phi \, d\omega = \pi^2 k^2 \left| \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_{n-1}^\infty(-k\mathbf{s}) \right|^2 d\omega' \tag{327}$$

(Born, 1926b, p. 819).

Equations (326) and (327) applied only to the special case of the elastic scattering of an electron by an atom. In the case that the atom absorbs or loses energy in the collision, a perturbation scheme involving a coupling term, between the electron and the atomic radiation field, had to be developed. In first approximation the following Schrödinger equation,

$$\Delta u_{nm}^{(1)} + k_{nm}^2 u_{nm}^{(1)} = V_{nm} \psi_k^{el}, \tag{328}$$

with

$$k_{nm}^2 = \frac{8\pi^2\mu}{h^2} (h\nu_{nm} + W^{el}) \tag{328a}$$

and

$$V_{nm} = \frac{8\pi^2\mu}{h^2} U_{nm} \tag{328b}$$

had to be solved. Here $\psi_k^{el}$ denotes the wave function of the free electron and $W^{el}$ its energy. The $U_{nm}$ represent the coefficients of the matrix associated with the potential energy; they are connected with transitions from the state $n$ to the state $m$ of the atom.$^{170}$ Equation (328) possesses the same final structure as the one describing the case of elastic scattering; hence, a similar evaluation leads to the expression

$$\Phi_{nm} = \pi^2 k_{nm}^2 |f_0^\infty(-k_{nm}\mathbf{s})|^2, \tag{329}$$

$^{170}$The matrix $U_{nm}$ can be obtained from the expression for $U\psi_{nk}^0$, with $\psi_{nk}^0$ the zeroth-order (perturbation free) wave function of the total system, namely, $U\psi_{nk}^0 = \psi_k^{el} \sum_m U_{nm} \psi_m^a$. ($\psi_m^a$ denotes the $m$th eigenfunction of the free atom.)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0375 -->

734
Chapter IV
Early Response and Applications

which provides in first-order approximation the probability for inelastic electron scattering in the direction given by the unit vector **s**.
Born finally demonstrated that these results correctly described at least the qualitative behaviour of atoms undergoing collisions with electrons: there existed elastic reflections for electron energies $W^{\text{el}} < h \nu_{10}^a$, where $\nu_{10}^a$ was the ground frequency of the atom; for larger electron (and atom) energies the phenomena of inelastic scattering, including so-called collisions of the second kind (in which the electron absorbs energy from an excited atom) occur. Born also tried to derive an expression for the 'yield function' ('*Ausbeutefunktion*') $\Phi_{nm}$, by assuming the potential of the atom to be given by a dipole term, i.e.,

$$U(x, y, z) = \frac{e}{r^3} (\mathbf{P} \cdot \mathbf{r}), \tag{330}$$

with $\mathbf{P}$ describing the electric moment of the atom. He obtained the result:

$$\Phi_{nm} = \frac{16 \pi^2 \mu^2 e^2}{h^4} |(\mathbf{P}_{nm} \cdot \mathbf{s})|^2 A^2, \tag{331}$$

where $\mathbf{P}_{nm}$ were the matrix elements of the atomic moment (in first-order approximation) and $A$ denoted the integral-cosine

$$A = \int_{r_0}^{\infty} \cos[\rho(k \cos \theta) - k_{nm}] \frac{d\rho}{\rho} \tag{331a}$$

($r_0$ large enough to exclude central collisions, $\theta$ the scattering angle).
In Eq. (331) if one averages over all directions, $|(\mathbf{P}_{nm} \cdot \mathbf{s})|^2$ will be replaced by $\frac{1}{3}|P_{nm}|^2$, hence $\Phi_{nm}$ becomes proportional to $|P_{nm}|^2$. Since the diagonal elements $P_{nm}$ are zero, one must go for elastic collisions usually to higher-order approximations, especially for atoms that are in the ground state or in the *s*-states. Born argued: 'Therefore we can understand that the normal cross section of atoms ([i.e., in the state] $n = 0$) is very much smaller for slow electrons (namely, of the order of magnitude of the "gas-kinetic" cross section) than for fast electrons which can excite [atoms]. The dependence of the yield on the direction is determined by the function $A^2$, Eq. (331a). Evidently, it corresponds to a *diffraction phenomenon*' (Born, 1926b, p. 825). That diffraction phenomenon, he added further, had first been discussed by Walter Elsasser in Göttingen as a consequence of assuming de Broglie waves (Elsasser, 1925). Recent experimental observations on the scattering of electrons by helium atoms seemed to confirm Elsasser's (and Born's) arguments (Dymond, 1926).$^{171}$

---
$^{171}$On completing the tedious calculations on the collision problem, which he did all by himself, Born gave the paper to J. Robert Oppenheimer—who was then working with him in Göttingen—to check it. Oppenheimer read it and remarked to Born: 'It is perfectly alright. Have you done this alone?' Born always used to make mistakes in the calculations that he performed, 'and Oppenheimer was very surprised that it was alright, but he was the only one who was frank enough to say so' (Born, Conversations with Mehra, March 1955, p. 59; cf. AHQP Interview with Born, 17 October 1962, p. 25). The approximation involved in the collision problem calculation later on came to be called the 'Born Approximation'.

**IV.4 Response to Wave Mechanics II. Applications and Extensions**  
**735**

Thus Born’s wave mechanical collision theory seemed to be well in accord with the observed phenomena. The success also encouraged Born to derive conclusions, from his statistical interpretation of matter waves, on the nature of radiation phenomena. Instead of going into this complex problem, we briefly mention here a calculation by Enrico Fermi from Florence, which he presented in a note entitled ‘*Zur Wellenmechanik des Stoßvorganges*’ (‘On the Wave Mechanics of the Collision Process’) and submitted to *Zeitschrift für Physik* in October 1926 (Fermi, 1926c). Fermi, a former visitor to Born’s Institute in Göttingen (in the winter of 1923/1924), applied the recently published theory by Born to a mass point (mass *m*), moving in two dimensions (*x*, *y*) and colliding with a rotator of inertia *J* whose axis is fixed in space. On introducing suitable co-ordinates (i.e., *ξ* = √(*mx*), *η* = √(*my*), *ζ* = √(*Jϕ*)), he obtained the Schrödinger equation

$$
\frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial \xi^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial \eta^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial \zeta^2} + \frac{8\pi^2}{h}(E - V)\psi = 0, \tag{332}
$$

where the potential *V* assumes non-zero values only in the vicinity of the *ζ*-axis, being periodic with a period 2π√*J*.

Fermi now drew an optical analogy, interpreting Eq. (332) as a wave equation in a homogeneous medium wherever *V* was zero; however, close to the *ζ*-axis the index of refraction exhibited a periodic anomaly, such that the axis represented a linear lattice with period 2π√*J*. ‘Each order of diffraction corresponds . . . to a different type of collision,’ he concluded (Fermi, 1926c, p. 400); that is, either to an elastic collision, or an inelastic collision, or a collision of the second kind. The scattering angle *θ_n* between the scattered matter waves and the *ζ*-axis determines the type of collision: if it is the same as the angle of the incident wave, the collision is elastic, in the other cases it is inelastic, or a collision of the second kind depending on the quantum transitions of the rotator.¹⁷² Thus Fermi’s example provided a detailed, quantitative illustration of the situation outlined qualitatively by Born. Moreover, he fully substantiated Born’s assertion ‘that quantum mechanics . . . also allows one to formulate and so solve the problem of transition processes’ (‘*daß die Quantenmechanik . . . auch das Problem der Übergangsvorgänge zu formulieren und lösen erlaubt*’), and that ‘Schrödinger’s scheme seems in this situation to be by far the most suitable, adequate description’ (‘*die Schrödingersche Fassung dabei der Sachlage am leichtesten gerecht zu werden scheint*,’ Born, 1926b, p. 826).

### Cracking the Helium Problem

Max Born received the news on wave mechanics after some delay, that is, after he had returned from the United States and after the publication of Schrödinger’s

For example, the energy of the rotator, *E*₂* (= (*h*²/8π²*J*)(*n* + *k*)²), was given by ½(*h*²/*λ*²) cos² *θ_n* (with *λ* or *h*/√(2*E*) the de Broglie wavelength of the system).

736 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

first communication. A similar situation occurred in the case of Heisenberg, although for different reasons. He had left Göttingen at the end of the winter semester (in late February 1926) for an extended vacation; from there he first went to Munich (at the beginning of April) and had written to Pascual Jordan announcing that he would be back in Göttingen on 20 April and then go on to Copenhagen on 24 or 25 April, where he was supposed to take up his position as lecturer in theoretical physics.<sup>173</sup> On his way to Copenhagen, however, he had to make two stops: first, he went to Leipzig to discuss the offer of an extraordinary professorship at the university (25 to 26 April); then he presented (on 28 April) a talk on quantum mechanics at the Berlin *Kolloquium*. In Munich—at Sommerfeld’s Institute—as in Göttingen and Berlin, he certainly heard more about Schrödinger’s wave mechanics, but his many obligations did not leave him much time to take a deeper look at the new theory.<sup>174</sup> Upon arriving in Copenhagen, he immediately assumed his duties as the successor to Hendrik Kramers, and simultaneously attacked a new task: the problem of calculating the helium spectrum in quantum mechanics.

The helium problem was an old acquaintance of Heisenberg’s, and he had tried to develop a satisfactory description of it from 1922.<sup>175</sup> In this description, based of course on the old (Bohr-Sommerfeld) quantum theory of atomic structure, half-integral quantum numbers had played a crucial and controversial role. In the spring of 1926 such quantum numbers could be shown to arise at two different places in atomic theory: first, in the quantum mechanical formalism of angular momentum; and second, in the hypothesis of electron spin. The latter concept, especially, offered great hopes of providing a final, satisfactory solution of the helium problem. Thus, when in February 1926 Samuel Goudsmit, co-discoverer of the electron spin, visited Copenhagen, he and Niels Bohr studied the helium problem in some detail. As Goudsmit recalled later:

> By looking at the helium spectrum Bohr understood right away that if you turned over one of the two spins [of the electrons in the helium atom] the energy suddenly would be entirely different.... I invented all kinds of magnetic interactions [to explain the large differences between corresponding singlet and triplet terms of helium], and I have a letter from Bohr in which he tells me that I am all wet....

<sup>173</sup> Heisenberg’s letter to Jordan is dated 4 April 1926; Heisenberg was collaborating with Jordan in early 1926 on the quantum mechanical treatment of the anomalous Zeeman effects (Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926).

<sup>174</sup> At Sommerfeld’s Institute, Schrödinger’s undulatory theory was known from early February 1926; while in Göttingen Jordan received Pauli’s letter (dated 12 April 1926) containing the demonstration of the equivalence of wave and matrix mechanics soon after the publication of Schrödinger’s first paper in *Annalen der Physik* (1926c). However, in Göttingen Heisenberg also had to discuss with Jordan the problem of electron spin, especially L. H. Thomas’ solution of the problem of factor 2, which played a role in their joint paper on the anomalous Zeeman effect (Thomas, 1926a). During the hectic days in Leipzig and Berlin, Heisenberg probably was not able to touch on specific issues of the undulatory theory; in Berlin, for example, the extended conversation with Albert Einstein on the epistemological problem of quantum mechanics left the deepest impression on him.

<sup>175</sup> See our discussion in Volume 2, Section II.3.

IV.4 Response to Wave Mechanics II. Applications and Extensions 737

Then he called [upon] Heisenberg who indeed found the solution—the antisymmetric wave functions and so on. (Goudsmit, AHQP Interview, 7 December 1963, p. 25)

Although some of the details of Goudsmit’s recollections are fuzzy he was right in two important respects: first, that he, Goudsmit, did not succeed in constructing, on the basis of Bohr’s intuitive data, a theory of the helium atom that would account for the large singlet-triplet separation observed in the helium (and like) spectra; second, that Heisenberg finally solved the problem in Copenhagen. Indeed, a few days after his arrival (in late April 1926), Heisenberg wrote a postcard to Pauli in Hamburg stating that ‘we have found a rather decisive argument that your exclusion of equivalent orbits [of two electrons in an atom] is connected with the singlet-triplet separation,’ because: ‘Consider the energy written as a function of the transition probabilities. Then a large difference results, if one—at the energy of H-atoms—has transition to 1S, or if, according to your ban [exclusion principle], one puts them equal to zero. That is, para- and ortho-[helium] do have different energies, independently of the interaction between magnets [i.e., the magnetic moments associated with the spinning electrons]’ (Heisenberg to Pauli, 5 May 1926). The new Copenhagen view seemed to be exactly along the lines on which Pauli expected to solve the helium problem, namely by a connection of his exclusion principle with the singlet-triplet separation.$^{176}$ The idea now had to be carried out in a detailed quantum mechanical model, and this was what Heisenberg embarked on during the following three weeks. Then he rather happily reported to Göttingen: ‘Since coming here I have worked very seriously on the helium spectrum, and I believe that now all the essential things are right; however, I have not yet completed the quantitative calculation’ (Heisenberg to Born, 26 May 1926).

In his letter to Born, Heisenberg presented the main physical ideas of his solution to the helium problem, which was based on the assumption that the difference between corresponding ortho- and para-helium states arose from the Coulomb repulsion of the electrons.$^{177}$ If, in particular, two electrons move around a (heavy) nucleus and the mutual influence of the electron spins was neglected, the (matrix) Hamiltonian of the system, $H^0$, consisted of the terms, $H^a$ and $H^b$, each referring to one electron moving under the influence of the Coulomb field of an effective nucleus (having a charge between $e$ and $2e$, due to the shielding of the other electron). Since the energy states of $H^a$ and $H^b$ were exactly identical,

$^{176}$See, e.g., Pauli’s letter to Gregor Wentzel, dated 8 May 1926, especially the statement: ‘In the case of the spectra of the alkaline-earth type, there are still unexplained difficulties: one does not see how the separation between the singlet and triplet separation, arises; moreover, one does not yet have an interpretation of my “housing office for equivalent orbits” (“*Wohnungsamt für äquivalente Bahnen*” [i.e., the exclusion principle]). (Both problems are perhaps connected.)’

$^{177}$We have displayed the essential features of Heisenberg’s solution in detail in Volume 3, Section V.6, because they were developed completely with the matrix mechanical scheme. Here we just recapitulate the necessary results before proceeding to the application of wave mechanical methods for evaluating the matrix elements.

738
Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

the Hamiltonian $H^0$ exhibited a particular degeneracy: the exchange of the two electrons in two different states, say $W_n$ and $W_m$, would not alter the energy values of $H^0$. Only the Coulomb repulsion of the electrons removed the degeneracy; it could be treated in a matrix perturbation theory, yielding the first-order corrections

$$W_{nm}^{1\bullet} = H^1(nm, nm) + H^1(nm, mn), \quad (333a)$$

and

$$W_{nm}^{1\times} = H^1(nm, nm) - H^1(nm, mn). \quad (333b)$$

Heisenberg commented on these results with the words: 'For all following considerations the decisive result now is: The term-system can be divided into two separate parts ($\bullet$ and $\times$), such that transitions occur only within the $\bullet$ system or within the $\times$ system, but never from the $\bullet$ system to the $\times$ system' (Heisenberg to Born, 26 May 1926; see Figures 2 and 3 in Volume 3, pp. 294 and 295, respectively).

Evidently, this model could be applied to describe the situation of the helium atom in the following sense. In first approximation the electrons have no magnets, i.e., one can drop the interaction between the magnetic moments of the spinning electrons. The spectrum then consists of two term systems, denoted by dot ($\bullet$) and cross ($\times$), respectively, whose separation is of the order of the Rydberg correction in the term formula; that is, it must be created by the Coulomb energy between the electrons. Further, no combinations occur between the two systems, and the lowest term in one system—which may be associated with the states of ortho-helium—is also missing. If one added the electron spin to the model, the structure became much richer: now two term systems, which should again be denoted by dot ($\bullet$) and cross ($\times$), resulted, each of which consisted of a subsystem of singlet- and subsystem of triplet-states (see Figure 4, p. 297 in Volume 3). Obviously, nature did not make use of all these possibilities, hence Heisenberg wrote to Born: 'The system $\bullet$ [including singlet and triplet terms] represents the helium spectrum and [the system] $\times$ does not exist at all'; and this exclusion of the cross-states 'agrees with the Bose statistics, which reduces the statistical weights by a factor of two and automatically yields Pauli's ban [i.e., the exclusion of two equivalent electron orbits in the helium atom]' (Heisenberg to Born, 26 May 1926).

Heisenberg assembled the details, which he had worked out, in a paper entitled 'Mehrkörperproblem und Resonanz in der Quantenmechanik' ('Many-Body Problem and Resonance in Quantum Mechanics'), and submitted it two weeks later to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Heisenberg, 1926b). One of the major points proved in this paper was the fact that no transitions occurred between ($\bullet$) and cross ($\times$) terms. The reason was that the radiation amplitudes $f_{n_1m_1, n_2m_2}$ of the unperturbed two-electron system were symmetric with respect to the exchange of the two electrons—i.e., $f_{n_1m_1, n_2m_2} = f_{m_1n_1, m_2n_2}$—and the perturbed amplitudes obtained

IV.4 Response to Wave Mechanics II. Applications and Extensions 739

through a canonical transformation could be found to be

$$f'_{n_1 m, n_2 m} = f_{n_1 m, n_2 m} + f_{n_1 m, mn_2} \qquad (334a)$$

for the transition between the dot-terms $(n_1 m) \rightarrow (n_2 m)$ with $n_1, n_2 < m$, and

$$f'_{n_1 m, mn_2} = f_{n_1 m, n_2 m} - f_{mn_1, mn_2} \qquad (334b)$$

for the transitions between the dot- and cross-terms $(n_1 m) \rightarrow (mn_2)$ with $n_1, n_2 < m.$[^178] Evidently, the right-hand side of Eq. (334b) is zero and that of Eq. (334a) is finite. Finally, the singlet–triplet separation assumed the value

$$\Delta_{nm} = 2H^1(nm, mn), \qquad (335)$$

where the perturbation matrix element $H^1(nm, mn)$ could be physically interpreted as the difference of the perturbation energies created by the Coulomb repulsion between the electrons. The very same quantity should be responsible for the so-called Rydberg correction in the empirical term formula for the helium atom.

The above consideration could be extended to the case of the two-electron atom containing real electrons with spin and associated magnetic moment. Again Heisenberg found that only transitions between dot- or cross-terms were possible (i.e., possessed a finite amplitude). However, as we have mentioned earlier, in this case each term system consisted of a singlet- and a triplet-system; the separation between similar terms of the singlet and the triplet, respectively, assumed—up to a small correction emerging from the magnet–magnet interaction—the value given by Eq. (335). Only one of the two super-term systems, namely the one with triplet-terms for ortho-helium and with singlet-terms for para-helium, existed in nature. Heisenberg concluded:

> This fact seems to me—provided we assume that our results derived for two systems [electrons] can be generalized to the case of arbitrarily many systems [electrons]—to constitute the real connection between the emphasized quantum mechanical uncertainty, on the one hand, and the rule of Pauli and the Einstein–Bose counting method, on the other hand. (Heisenberg, 1926b, p. 422)[^179]

He further claimed that the reduction of the statistical weights in the Bose method *and* the validity of Pauli's ban (or exclusion principle) can be achieved simultaneously by this selection of the proper term system in the quantum mechanical theory of the helium atom.

At the time of writing his fundamental paper on the quantum mechanics of many-electron systems, Heisenberg also studied (in some detail) Schrödinger's

740 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

first publications on wave mechanics.$^{180}$ Indeed, he outlined at the end of Section 2 of his paper (dealing with the transition amplitudes between the term-systems without electron spin) how to formulate the two-electron system in the language of undulatory theory. In particular, he wrote the formula for the $(n_1 n_2)$-matrix element of the co-ordinate $q_k^a$ of a system having $f$ degrees of freedom as

$$q_k^a(n_1, n_2) = \int \cdots \int q_k^a \phi_{n_1}^a \overline{\phi_{n_2}^a} \, dq_1^a \dots dq_f^a, \quad (336)$$

where $\phi_n^a$ denoted the eigenfunctions and $\overline{\phi_{n_2}^a}$ their complex conjugates. Now the eigenfunction of the unperturbed two-electron system was a product of the two individual eigenfunctions, $\phi_n^a \phi_m^b$, while the eigenfunctions of the perturbed dot-system could be expressed as

$$\psi^{\bullet} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (\phi_n^a \phi_m^b + \phi_m^a \phi_n^b), \quad (337\text{a})$$

and those of the perturbed cross-system as

$$\psi^{\times} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (\phi_n^a \phi_m^b - \phi_m^a \phi_n^b). \quad (337\text{b})$$

The result, that terms of different systems would not combine, followed directly from the observation that the integral containing a symmetric operator $f$ (describing the unperturbed transition amplitude) vanishes identically, i.e.,

$$\int \cdots \int \frac{f}{2} (\phi_n^a \phi_m^b + \phi_m^a \phi_n^b) (\overline{\phi_n^a \phi_m^b} - \overline{\phi_m^a \phi_n^b}) \, dq_1^a \dots dq_f^b = 0. \quad (338)$$

Evidently, a similar conclusion could be derived in cases of systems containing more than two identical particles (e.g., electrons).

Thus the wave mechanical formulation offered a comfortable access to many-electron systems in quantum mechanics. The typical resonance behaviour that Heisenberg had observed in matrix mechanics further seemed to correspond (in the language of de Broglie waves) to phase relations between particles created by specific interference effects. Still, a general wave-like interpretation of atomic phenomena did not satisfy Heisenberg. He wrote to Pauli: 'The more I ponder about the physical part of Schrödinger's theory, the more horrible I find it' ('*Je mehr ich über den physikalischen Teil der Schrödingerschen Theorie nachdenke, desto abscheulicher finde ich ihn,*' Heisenberg to Pauli, 8 June 1926). He criticized such concepts as electrons, with charges distributed over the whole space and

742 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

(The bar indicates averaging over the full orbit.) The perturbation energy (i.e., the mutual Coulomb repulsion of the two electrons and their influence on the potential of the nucleus) is given by the expression

$$H^1 = \frac{e^2}{r_{12}} - f(r_1) - f(r_2), \qquad (341)$$

with $r_{12}$ denoting the distance of the two electrons, and $r_1$ and $r_2$ the distances of electrons a and b from the nucleus, respectively.

The main task of the helium calculation now consisted of evaluating the matrix elements of the interaction Hamiltonian (341) entering Eqs. (333), namely $H^1(vw, vw)$ and $H^1(vw, wv)$, where $v$ denoted the state of the electron a—characterized in our case by the quantum numbers $n = 1$, $k = m = 0$—and $w$ the state of the electron b—characterized by the quantum numbers $n > 1$, $k = j$, $m$. According to the results of the earlier investigation (Heisenberg, 1926b), each (degenerate) term of the unperturbed system ($H^0 = H^a + H^b$) splits into two terms, except when both electrons are in equivalent orbits; hence an ortho- and a para-term system arise, the latter containing the states with equivalent orbits.

Thus far Heisenberg had just specified the old matrix considerations of the previous paper, in which he stopped exactly at this point. Now he wanted to go further with the actual evaluation, noticing right away that ‘the calculation of the quantities [$H^1(vw, vw)$ and $H^1(vw, wv)$] is performed in the simplest way on the Schrödinger method of eigenfunctions’ (Heisenberg, 1926c, p. 503). Evidently, the unperturbed eigenfunctions were the hydrogen-like functions $\psi_Z(r, \theta, \phi)$ and $\psi_{Z-1}(r, \theta, \phi)$, which now entered into the expressions for the perturbation matrix elements in the Schrödinger method, i.e.,

$$H^1(vw, vw) = \int \cdots \int H^1 \psi_{v,Z}(r_1, \theta_1, \phi_1) \psi_{w,Z-1}(r_2, \theta_2, \phi_2)$$
$$\qquad \cdot \bar{\psi}_{v,Z}(r_1, \theta_1, \phi_1) \bar{\psi}_{w,Z-1}(r_2, \theta_2, \phi_2) d\Omega_1 d\Omega_2 \qquad (342\text{a})$$

and

$$H^1(vw, wv) = \int \cdots \int H^1 \psi_{v,Z}(r_1, \theta_1, \phi_1) \psi_{w,Z-1}(r_2, \theta_2, \phi_2)$$
$$\qquad \cdot \bar{\psi}_{w,Z-1}(r_1, \theta_1, \phi_1) \bar{\psi}_{v,Z}(r_2, \theta_2, \phi_2) d\Omega_1 d\Omega_2, \qquad (342\text{b})$$

with $\int d\Omega_1 d\Omega_2$ indicating the integration over the configuration space of the two electrons. ‘Of these two expressions,’ Heisenberg stated, ‘the second . . . denotes half the term separation between the O (ortho)- and P (para)-system in the "perturbed" system [atom]. The first value . . . denotes the distance of the centre between the ortho- and para-term from the term value of the unperturbed system [atom]’ (Heisenberg, 1926c, p. 504).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0384 -->

**IV.4 Response to Wave Mechanics II. Applications and Extensions** &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; **743**

When he replaced the first perturbation term $H^{1}(vw, vw)$ with a slightly modified one, $H^{1'}(vw, vw)$, denoting the distance of the term centre from the energy term $\{-RhZ^{2}/1^{2} - Rh(Z - 1)^{2}/n^{2}\}$ rather than from the energy term defined originally, Heisenberg obtained an expression that did not depend on $r_{0}$. He suspected that the evaluation of the integrals would yield in this case a small value (because of the symmetry of the 1S-orbit) and that the second-order perturbation might give a larger contribution. The detailed calculation led to the expression

$$H^{1'}(vw, vw) = -\frac{Ze^{2}}{a} \int_{0}^{\infty} r_{2}^{2} \frac{\exp(-\xi_{2})(2 + \xi_{2})}{\xi_{2}} X_{n,k;Z-1}^{2}(r_{2}) \, dr_{2}, \qquad (343)$$

with

$$\xi_{2} = \frac{2Z}{a} r_{2} \qquad (343\text{a})$$

and $X_{n,k;Z-1}(r_{2})$ the hydrogen-like eigenfunction of the (second) electron (which is in the excited state); $a = h^{2}/4\pi^{2}m_{e}e^{2}$, is the Bohr-radius of the hydrogen atom. Heisenberg then introduced the following approximation: ‘It suffices … to calculate, for a given value of $k$, the average value for the two smallest values of $n$ (namely, $k + 1$ and $k + 2$) and to extrapolate the other average values according to the Rydberg–Ritz formula’ (Heisenberg, 1926c, p. 505). The numerical evaluation then led indeed to a very small contribution for the Rydberg correction $\delta_{1}$ in the formula for the energy terms of the two-electron atom.

Subsequently Heisenberg also sketched a very crude estimate of what the second-order perturbation term would be. Arguing, in particular, that for large $k$-values the latter physically arose from the ‘polarization’ in the interior of the atom, he found a contribution to Rydberg’s correction $\delta_{1}$ which, if added to the first-order contribution above, did fit the experimental values reasonably well.

On the other hand, the first-order perturbation treatment of the ortho–para term separation should already provide fairly reliable results for comparison with experiment. By inserting hydrogen-like wave functions into the expression for $H^{1}(vw, wv)$, Eq. (342b), and evaluating the integral for $n = k + 1$ and $n = k + 2$, Heisenberg arrived at rational expressions whose numerical values represented qualitatively the behaviour of the data. The lack of quantitative agreement can be ascribed to the crude approximations made in the actual computation; these approximations are better in the case of Li$^{+}$ than in the case of He.$^{183}$

In Part II of his paper, Heisenberg discussed qualitatively the inclusion of the electron spin. Since the interaction energy of the two magnets had to be considered in general as being small compared with the perturbation energies $H^{1}(vw, vw)$

and $H^1(vw, wv)$ discussed above, the term-splitting remained roughly the same. However, two sets of term-spectra now arose—as had been discussed in detail in the previous paper (Heisenberg, 1926b)—from which the one having singlet P (para)-states and triplet O (ortho)-states was chosen to describe the real situation in nature. While this theory described perfectly the alkaline-earth spectra, those of He and Li$^+$ seemed to be qualitatively different, as the observed O-states were doublets. Heisenberg blamed this on the 'relatively large interaction of the electron magnets' (Heisenberg, 1926c, p. 514). When treating the magnetic interaction terms in detail—including the relativistic corrections of Llewellyn Hilleth Thomas (1926a)—in wave mechanics, and evaluating the resulting integrals by making several simplifying assumptions, Heisenberg obtained a general formula for the fine structure of two-electron spectra (i.e., Eq. (30) in Heisenberg, 1926c, p. 516). In the special case of $2p$-terms, where reliable data existed at that time, the formula

$$\Delta H_{2p} = \left( \frac{h}{2\pi} \right)^2 \frac{e^2}{2m_e^2c^2} \left( \overline{\frac{1}{r^3}} \right)_{2p} \left\{ (Z - 3) \left( \frac{1}{2}, -\frac{1}{2}, -1 \right) + \left( \frac{3}{8}, -\frac{3}{8}, \frac{3}{2} \right) - \frac{1}{4} \right\} \quad (344)$$

followed for the triplet separation ($k = 1, j = 2, 1, 0$).

The pattern for the transition lines $2p \rightarrow 2s$, derived from Eq. (344), showed in the case of He two strong lines of narrow distance and a third faint line, and in the case of Li$^+$ three fairly separated lines, of which the third was much weaker. Qualitatively, this picture, especially the quasi-doublet structure of the ortho-helium lines, agreed with the then available data. For a quantitative comparison of formula (344) with experiment the average radius-function, $(1/r^3)$, had to be calculated. Since Heisenberg considered an accurate evaluation to be 'quite complicated' ('*recht kompliziert*,' Heisenberg, 1926c, p. 517), he therefore proposed to take the corresponding values for hydrogen-like atoms, namely,

$$\left( \overline{\frac{1}{r^3}} \right)_{2p} = Rh \cdot \alpha^2 \cdot \frac{Z^2}{24} \qquad (345)$$

where $\alpha$ denotes Sommerfeld's fine structure constant. The separation thus obtained for the outer (most distant) components, i.e.,

He: $Rh \alpha^2 \frac{(Z - 1)^3}{24} \frac{21}{8} = 0.62 \text{ cm}^{-1}$, (346a)

Li$^+$: $Rh \alpha^2 \frac{(Z - 1)^3}{24} \frac{15}{8} = 3.65 \text{ cm}^{-1}$, (346b)

had to be compared to the empirical components, i.e., $1.07 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ and $4.4 \text{ cm}^{-1}$, respectively. The discrepancy between theory and experiment could be ascribed partly to the use of Eq. (345), and partly to the approximations leading to Eq. (344).

IV.4 Response to Wave Mechanics II. Applications and Extensions 745

Heisenberg concluded: ‘By the calculations carried out here [in this paper] we wanted to show that quantum mechanics allows, even for atoms with two electrons, a qualitative description of the spectrum including finer details, and that the theory permits one to determine approximately the terms as a function of the quantum numbers.’ He pointed out at the same time the shortcomings of his approach, namely: (i) the lack of foundation in selecting the dot-system (•), and (ii) the lack of accuracy in the calculations. Concerning the latter he added: ‘One should demand that the theoretical term-values are computed so exactly that the agreement of these term-values with the experimental values can be tested up to the last decimal’ (Heisenberg, 1926c, p. 518). In agreement with these statements Heisenberg wrote to Pauli: ‘I have now submitted my paper on the helium spectrum, with dubious feelings, and [I am] not quite satisfied. All the calculations are too inaccurate and incomplete; the nicest thing is still the fine structure which comes out alright. In any case there remains, as far as quantitative agreement [with experiment] is concerned, much still to be done’ (Heisenberg to Pauli, 28 July 1926).¹⁸⁴

Heisenberg’s dissatisfaction notwithstanding, his helium calculation constituted a major triumph in quantum mechanics. It remained one of the standard approaches to two-electron problems which would be discussed in all later reviews of the topic; Heisenberg’s successors would improve the approximation methods—so as to allow the treatment of the helium ground-state or the excited *S*-states—but the basic ideas did not have to be altered.¹⁸⁵ In this respect, Heisenberg’s helium calculation became a classic in atomic theory, and several decades later he recalled: ‘I used Schrödinger’s formalism for help with the mathematics. It was clear to me that in order to calculate the shift of levels in the helium atom, matrix elements were needed, and they could be calculated quite well from Schrödinger’s scheme. Such a calculation in matrix mechanics would have been difficult’ (Heisenberg, Conversations, April 1960 and June 1968, pp. 359–360). Thus the helium calculation—in spite of the fact that wave mechanical methods entered into it only as a tool for evaluating complicated

¹⁸⁴ As Heisenberg later recalled: ‘The helium paper gave the spectrum of helium more or less correctly, but not the normal state. I could not do the normal state with that method, but the perturbation calculations allowed me to calculate the excited states.’ (Heisenberg, Conversations, April 1960 and June 1968, p. 360; cf. AHQP Interview with Heisenberg, 22 February 1963, p. 27.)
The first calculation of the ground state (1*S*) of the helium atom was undertaken by Sommerfeld’s student Albrecht Unsöld in Munich. He obtained from first-order perturbation theory a value of 20.3 volts for the ionization potential and estimated that higher approximation would increase this value (Unsöld, 1927, especially pp. 368–369). Unsöld also found in the same paper the higher *S*-terms. Georg W. Kellner, a student of Max von Laue in Berlin, improved the evaluation considerably by using the variation method of Walther Ritz in his thesis: he thus found, after four approximation steps, a value of 23.75 volts for the ionization potential which came much closer to the experimental result of 24.46 volts (Kellner, 1927). Independently, the Norwegian physicist Egil A. Hylleraas, then in Göttingen, also treated the same problem according to the variation method of Ritz: he arrived first at a theoretical value of 24.35 volts (Hylleraas, 1928), which he further improved in later papers (e.g., Hylleraas, 1929).

## The Advent of Fermi Statistics

In Heisenberg’s treatment of many-body systems, and especially of the helium
atom, the problem of statistics entered his work probably for the first time.¹⁸⁶
Heisenberg arrived at two conclusions: first, in atomic systems consisting of
several identical particles, two classes of states are possible in principle,
which can be distinguished by different symmetry properties either of the radiation
intensity for transitions or of the wave functions for stationary states (see Heisen-
berg, 1926b) with respect to permutations of two particles; second, nature selects
only one of these classes, which corresponds to the statistical description proposed
earlier by Satyendra Nath Bose and Albert Einstein. Heisenberg later recalled
‘that this symmetry would provide a clue to Pauli’s exclusion principle and one
could say that “if two things are always connected symmetrically, then there can
only be one electron in each state”’ (Heisenberg, Conversations, April 1960 and
June 1968, p. 385; cf. AHQP Interview with Heisenberg, 27 February 1963, p.
12). He further recalled: ‘For a long time I continued to mix up Bose–Einstein
and Fermi–Dirac statistics. I did not know Fermi–Dirac statistics at that time [at
the time of writing the papers on helium (Heisenberg, 1926b, c)]; I knew only
the Pauli exclusion principle. I was always confused between Bose–Einstein
statistics and the Pauli exclusion principle which produce different ways of
counting states. When I wrote the equations for two identical electrons, there
were two solutions, one symmetrical and the other anti-symmetrical. First I
thought that I had to take the anti-symmetrical solution to obtain the Bose
statistics, and that [i.e., Bose–Einstein statistics] must be the one which gives the
Pauli principle. Later I saw that it was the other way round. One must take the
symmetrical solution to get Bose statistics, and the anti-symmetrical solution to
get Pauli’s exclusion principle’ (Heisenberg, Conversations, April 1960 and June
1968, pp. 385–386; cf. AHQP Interview with Heisenberg, 27 February 1963, p.
12).¹⁸⁷
Actually, neither in the first paper on the many-body systems (Heisenberg,
1926b) nor in that dealing with the application to the helium atom (Heisenberg,

of Wave Functions and Quantum Statistics’ following the description of Fermi’s work). Pauli, who,

or Dirac, also did not at all recognize the connection established by Fermi and Dirac between the

1926c) did Heisenberg make any statement of the above type; this occurred for the first time in a later work, namely in the paper entitled ‘*Mehrkörperprobleme und Resonanz in der Quantenmechanik. II*’ (‘Many-Body Problems and Resonance in Quantum Mechanics II’) and submitted in December 1926 (Heisenberg, 1927a). In that paper he then referred in particular to the clarification of the problem recently achieved by Paul Dirac (1926f) and to the ‘*Fermische Theorie der Gasentartung*’ (‘Fermi’s Theory of Gas Degeneracy,’ Heisenberg, 1927a, p. 239), citing a note already presented by Fermi in February 1926 to the Rome Academy (Fermi, 1926a). Hence, although Heisenberg claimed that Fermi’s statistical method was not known to him in the summer of 1926, it already existed in print; indeed, it was even available in a German paper published in a May issue of *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Fermi, 1926b) at about the time when Heisenberg became involved in the helium problem. We have to conclude that he overlooked the paper at that time, in spite of the fact that he was familiar with its author.

In the years before 1926, the name of Enrico Fermi had occasionally been attached to contributions on atomic and quantum theory. The young Italian had even stayed abroad for some time, notably in Göttingen (with Max Born) and Leyden (with Paul Ehrenfest) in 1923 and 1924. Still, his new work on the theory of an ideal gas did not make an immediate impression even on people who knew him personally. The reasons for this delayed reception may be sought in his background and the particular type of early scientific work that he did.

Fermi was born on 29 September 1901 in Rome, where he also grew up and attended primary and secondary schools.¹⁸⁸ From the autumn of 1918 he studied at the University of Pisa as a fellow of the *Scuola Normale Superiore*, receiving his doctorate in July 1922. On returning to his hometown he worked as a private tutor (1922–1923) in mathematics and physics, but he was associated with the University of Rome. In the winter of 1923 Fermi was awarded a scholarship by the Italian Government to study abroad and he chose to go to Max Born in Göttingen; in the autumn of 1924 he went to Paul Ehrenfest in Leyden on a Rockefeller fellowship. The period in Göttingen proved to be a difficult one for the young Italian, despite the fact that he spoke German fluently. ‘In Germany his old shyness returned and hampered his social relations,’ reported his widow thirty years later, ‘he could never shed the feeling that he was a foreigner and did not belong in the group of men around Professor Born’ (L. Fermi, 1954, p. 31). Heisenberg, then a member of Born’s inner circle, essentially confirmed this point; he recalled that he saw Fermi only rarely, and: ‘I had some discussions with him. [In Göttingen] he was always a bit shy and kept himself to himself; I found it difficult to get into contact with him. He probably had personal problems; it was not a good time for him. I liked him as a rather different type of physicist’ (Heisenberg, Conversations, April 1960, p. 165; cf. AHQP Interview with Heisenberg, 15 February 1963, pp. 12–13). The type of physics treated in the winter of

He felt, “that is not physics”’, recalled Heisenberg (Heisenberg, *Conversations*, April 1960, pp. 153–154; cf. AHQP Interview, 15 February 1963).<sup>189</sup> Finally, the whole status of atomic theory at that time, when the old Bohr–Sommerfeld theory had been shown to break down in characteristic examples and the experts in Copenhagen and Göttingen were groping for a new mathematical and philosophical foundation, contradicted Fermi’s ‘preferences . . . for concrete problems’ which ‘gave him the immediate sensation of the importance, and a check of the correctness of his work’ (Segrè, 1962, p. XXVI). Compared with Göttingen, Fermi’s visit to Leyden turned out to be more fruitful: Ehrenfest, in particular, provided him with much needed encouragement.<sup>190</sup> Back in Italy, Fermi became a lecturer in 1925 and moved to the University of Florence to teach mathematics and physics. After an unsuccessful competition in February 1926 for a chair of mathematical physics at the University of Cagliari (Sardegna), he was offered (in November of the same year) the newly created professorship for theoretical physics at the University of Rome.<sup>191</sup>

From his early studies at Pisa, Enrico Fermi had become acquainted with topics of modern physics—not all from his teachers, but through his own personal initiative. He read widely, e.g., Walther Nernst’s *Theoretische Chemie*, Owen Willans Richardson’s *The Electron Theory of Matter* (1914), Ernest Rutherford’s *Radioactive Substances and Their Radiations*, and especially Hermann Weyl’s *Raum-Zeit-Materie* and Max Planck’s *Vorlesungen über Wärmestrahlung*. ‘Fermi was already very much acquainted with modern physics, especially relativity,’ his Pisa classmate Enrico Persico remarked more than forty years later, adding: ‘I learned of the existence of relativity through Fermi’ (Persico in AHQP Interview with Persico and Rasetti, 8 April 1963, p. 1). Franco Rasetti, another former colleague of Fermi’s continued: ‘Fermi was the first person ever to mention to me Planck’s constant and the whole [quantum] theory . . .

arguments one had tried to explain the behaviour of electrons in metals, especially
their negligible contribution to the specific heats (see, e.g., Sommerfeld, 1914b).$^{193}$
More than a decade later, Albert Einstein applied Bose's statistical method to
establish the first fundamental quantum theory of ideal gases, suggesting in
particular a relation to the theory of metal electrons (Einstein, 1924c; 1925a, b).
Further, he connected Bose's statistics with an apparently quite different novel
idea, the matter waves of Louis de Broglie (Einstein, 1925a).$^{194}$

Fermi's early contributions to the theory of ideal gases preceded the last-
mentioned developments. In the first paper on the Stern-Tetrode theory of the
(absolute) chemical constant—it was presented on 2 December 1923 to the
*Accademia Lincei* in Rome—Fermi analysed the derivation of the formula

$$
S = Nk \left\{ \frac{5}{2} \ln T - \ln p + \ln \left[ \frac{(2 \pi m)^{3/2}}{h^3} k^{5/2} \right] \right\}, \tag{347}
$$

describing the entropy $S$ of a monatomic gas of $N$ atoms (having mass $m$) at
temperature $T$ and pressure $p$ (with $k$ and $h$ denoting Boltzmann's and Planck's
constant, respectively). Stern had derived it (in 1919) from a comparison of the
kinetic theory of gases and solids, assuming the existence of a finite zero-point
energy (of magnitude $h\nu/2$ connected to each vibrational degree of freedom of
the solid; see Stern, 1919). In Stern's treatment the expression for the saturated
vapour pressure also became modified as

$$
p = \frac{(2 \pi m)^{3/2} \bar{\nu}^3}{(kT)^{3/2}} \exp \left( - \frac{w + \frac{3}{2} h \bar{\nu}}{kT} \right) \tag{348}
$$

(with $\bar{\nu}$ the geometrical average frequency of the solid, and $w$ the energy required
to vaporize an atom, i.e., to liberate it from the solid).$^{195}$ Fermi now argued that
the same equation could be obtained without the explicit assumption of a
zero-point energy, 'by a slight modification of the kinetic calculation' (*perciò
modificare leggermente la deduzione cinetica*, Fermi, 1923c, p. 396).$^{196}$

The topic of the second paper, which Fermi submitted to *Nuovo Cimento* in

IV.4 Response to Wave Mechanics II. Applications and Extensions 751

for the cases of systems having several identical particles (Fermi, 1924a). Starting from the simplest example, the two-electron helium atom, he argued that the path of integration extends from a given electron configuration to the next configuration that cannot be distinguished from the former: in particular, two situations, in which only identical particles have changed places, are indistinguishable. Translating this prescription to the case of an ideal gas consisting of *n* (identical) atoms, Fermi showed that the usual quantization procedure (involving the quantization of the translational motion of the gas atoms and the introduction of quantum cells) yielded the correct entropy expression (by Stern and Tetrode) *only* if one considered subsystems (space cells or volume elements), each containing not more than *one* atom. In all other treatments additional entropy terms arose that had the order of magnitude of the mixing entropy.¹⁹⁷

The advent (in 1924) of Bose’s statistics, and especially its application by Einstein to the ideal gas theory (1924–1925), changed the situation in a qualitative way. That method made it possible to obtain an expression for the entropy of the gas which, unlike that of the classical kinetic theory, immediately satisfied Nernst’s heat theorem. Further, Bose and Einstein treated the particles (i.e., light-quanta and atoms of an ideal gas) as indistinguishable objects. These results certainly interested Fermi very much when they became available in print. But he must have paid even greater attention to a result expounded by Wolfgang Pauli in early 1925: the exclusion principle for electrons, i.e., the ban on two electrons occupying identical states in an atom (Pauli, 1925b). This principle allowed Fermi to justify his own quantum-theoretical treatment of the ideal gas of the previous year. Still, it took him a while to digest the two major advances in the field of quantum statistics, probably caused partly by the fact that he was engaged in moving to Florence and starting experimental spectroscopic research there. Then he assembled the various pieces of his own and others’ work and proposed a new gas theory, first in an Italian publication, the note *‘Sulla quantizzazione del gas perfetto monoatomico’* (‘On the Quantization of the Ideal Monatomic Gas’) which was presented by Antonio Garbasso to the *Reale Accademia Lincei* in Rome on 7 February 1926 (Fermi, 1926a), and soon afterwards in an extended German translation, *‘Zur Quantelung des idealen einatomigen Gases’*, which was received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* on 24 March 1926 (Fermi, 1926b).

Fermi’s goal was the same as that which he had already tried to achieve more than two years earlier, namely to derive a theory describing the ideal gas which, in the limit of absolute zero temperature ($T = 0$), satisfies Nernst’s heat theorem. In particular, Fermi wanted ‘to present a method for the quantization of an ideal gas, which in our opinion is as independent as possible from arbitrary assumptions concerning the statistical behaviour of gas molecules’ (‘*eine Methode für die Quantelung des idealen Gases darzustellen, welche nach unserem Erachten möglichst*¹⁹⁷

¹⁹⁷The problem treated by Fermi in the above paper (Fermi, 1924a) was discussed by several physicists in those years, including Paul Ehrenfest, Max Planck and Erwin Schrödinger (see Volume 1, Section V.5, and this volume, Section II.5). Fermi essentially supported Planck’s point of view on the statistical treatment of identical particles, which was opposed by Ehrenfest and Schrödinger.

*unabhängig von willkürlichen Annahmen über das statistische Verhalten der Gas-
moleküle ist,’* Fermi, 1926b, p. 902).<sup>198</sup>

Fermi referred in his paper to the recent work on the quantum theory of ideal gases by Albert Einstein (1924c; 1925a, b) and Max Planck (1925a).<sup>199</sup> These theories exhibited deviations from the ideal gas theory at very low temperatures and high pressures, as Fermi’s own would do; however, the magnitude, and partly the sign of these deviations, would be different. Unfortunately, the experiments, under the conditions mentioned, did not yet make it possible to decide in favour of any one of the proposed theories. Nevertheless, Fermi felt confident enough to present his own ideas.

In the quantum theory with which Fermi was so far familiar, there existed several methods of quantizing an ideal gas.<sup>200</sup> For example, one could enclose the gas in a vessel with parallel walls which reflect the molecules elastically, such that their motion becomes periodic; another method would be to have the molecules exposed to an external field of such a type as to establish similar periodic boundary conditions. However, whatever procedure one selects, it still does not suffice to determine the quantization completely, since the latter still depends crucially on the size of the vessel—hence for large, macroscopic distances between the walls the discontinuity of the quantum states practically vanishes. Recalling his earlier result (see Fermi, 1924a), Fermi now concluded that ‘one obtains a degeneracy [of the gas] of the expected order of magnitude, if one chooses the vessel to be so small as to contain, on average, only one molecule’ (Fermi, 1926b, p. 903). This extra hypothesis, which had earlier provided the Stern–Tetrode value for the entropy of an ideal gas, he called ‘a supplementary rule to be added to the Sommerfeld quantum conditions’ (‘*eine Zusatzregel zu den Sommerfeldschen Quantenbedingungen*,’ Fermi, 1926b, p. 904). The supplementary rule seemed, as Fermi noticed, to be supported by Wolfgang Pauli’s rule for the occupation of the electron orbits in atoms. Hence he concluded: ‘We shall demonstrate ... that the application of the Pauli rule allows us to present a complete, consistent theory of the degeneracy of ideal gases’ (‘*Wir werden zeigen, ... daß die Anwendung der Paulischen Regel uns erlaubt, eine vollständig konsequente Theorie der Entartung idealer Gase darzustellen*,’ Fermi, 1926b, p. 904).

Evidently, Fermi believed that Pauli’s rule determined not only the statistical behaviour of electrons but of gas molecules as well. In the case of a quantum gas, then, the rule stated that only one atom existed in the entire volume having a given set of quantum numbers, which comprised in general the internal quantum numbers as well as the translational numbers; of course, for an ideal or perfect monatomic gas in the ground state only the translational quantum numbers had to be considered.

IV.4 Response to Wave Mechanics II. Applications and Extensions  
753  

As the appropriate model for demonstrating the consequences of this extended exclusion principle, Fermi chose a system of *N* gas molecules (atoms) of mass *m*, each of which was attracted to a fixed point, the origin, by an elastic central force whose potential was given by the expression  

$$
U = 2\pi^2\nu^2mr^2, \tag{349}
$$

with *ν* the eigenfrequency of the oscillating molecules.$^{201}$ The molecules of a monatomic gas in the ground state are described by the three quantum numbers, *s*₁, *s*₂ and *s*₃, of the translational motion, and the energy of each molecule becomes  

$$
w = h\nu(s_1 + s_2 + s_3) = sh\nu, \tag{350}
$$

i.e., an integral multiple of the energy-quantum *hν*. On the other hand, a given total energy, say *shν*, can be obtained by quite a few different distributions of the individual quantum numbers (*s*₁ = 0, 1, 2, …, *s*₂ = 0, 1, 2, …, and *s*₃ = 0, 1, 2, …), namely altogether in  

$$
Q_s = \frac{(s+1)(s+2)}{2} \tag{351}
$$

possible ways. Then Fermi’s ‘Pauli rule’ states: for any given *s* only *Q_s* molecules can occur in the gas model. This means, in particular, that in the case of absolute zero temperature—for which the energy must be a minimum—the lowest energy states are fully occupied: i.e., one molecule possesses energy zero, three molecules possess the energy *hν*, six the energy 2*hν*, etc. Hence, Fermi concluded that one obtains for the gas ‘a kind of shell-like constitution, which exhibits a certain analogy to the shell-like organization of the electrons in a many-electron atom’ (‘*eine Art schalenförmigen Aufbau, der eine gewisse Analogie zur schalenartigen Anordnung der Elektronen in einem Atom mit mehreren Elektronen aufweist*,’ Fermi, 1926b, p. 906).$^{202}$  

If the temperature rises above zero, the distribution of a given total energy *E* (= *lhν*, with *l* an integer) of a monatomic ideal gas of *N* molecules (in the ground state) can be found by copying a procedure by Einstein from his papers on gas theory. Clearly, the relations  

$$
\sum N_s = N, \tag{352}
$$

and  

$$
\sum s N_s = E, \tag{353}
$$

---
$^{201}$ In this model the motion is obviously periodic—with a single period. The density of the gas is not uniform (as is usually assumed) with most of the molecules assembled close to the origin (*r* = 0).  
$^{202}$ Fermi was quite impressed by Pauli’s success in arranging the electrons in shells and the fruitfulness of this arrangement in subsequent analyses of the structure of many-electron atoms—he referred especially to Friedrich Hund’s paper on complex atoms (Hund, 1925c).

754 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

with the subsidiary condition

$$N_s \leq Q_s \qquad (354)$$

had to be satisfied (with $N_s$ denoting the number of molecules having energy $sh\nu$). Fermi further demanded: ‘Two distributions should then be considered to be alike, if the places occupied by the molecules are identical’ (‘*Zwei Anordnungen sollen dabei als gleich angesehen werden, wenn die von den Molekülen besetzten Plätze dieselben sind*,’ Fermi, 1926b, p. 906).$^{203}$ Since the number of possible distributions of $N_s$ atoms among $Q_s$ places is $\binom{Q_s}{N_s}$, the total number of distributions, $P$, is simply given by the product $\binom{Q_0}{N_0}\binom{Q_1}{N_1}\binom{Q_2}{N_2}\ldots$. This product is then determined—by using Stirling’s approximation formula which is valid for the large numbers involved—by the equation

$$\ln P = \sum_s \ln \binom{Q_s}{N_s} = -\sum_s \left( N_s \ln \frac{N_s}{Q_s - N_s} + Q_s \ln \frac{Q_s - N_s}{Q_s} \right). \qquad (355)$$

The maximum $P$ satisfying the subsidiary conditions (352) and (353) is then determined for

$$\frac{N_s}{Q_s - N_s} = \alpha \exp(-\beta s), \qquad (356)$$

with $\alpha$ and $\beta$ denoting constants independent of the individual distributions associated with the integer $s$ (and the energy $sh\nu$). By inserting Eq. (356) into Eqs. (352) and (353) one arrives at expressions for the total number of molecules and the energy as functions of $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

In order to determine the physical significance of the constants $\alpha$ and $\beta$ one should think of using the well-known formulae of statistics and thermodynamics (i.e., the Planck–Boltzmann relation $S = k \ln P$ for the entropy and the relation $T = dE/dS$). Fermi, however, wished to avoid using them, as they might not really hold in the quantum theory. Instead he turned to a different calculation which employed a correspondence argument: namely, in the limit of $r$, the distance from the origin, tending to infinity the density of the gas becomes negligible, hence the classical statistical behaviour (average energy of each molecule equal to $\frac{3}{2}kT$; Maxwellian distribution) must be valid. To apply this limiting consideration, he calculated the density of the $s$-molecules (i.e., of molecules with energy $sh\nu$) as a function of the distance $r$ from the origin, obtaining for $r \to \infty$ the

---
$^{203}$ Fermi also realized the fact that if he considered two permutations of the type mentioned (i.e., a situation with the same set of distribution numbers $N_s$, in which two molecules were exchanged) as different distributions, the total number of distributions would be multiplied by a factor $N!$ ; however, this factor would not influence the later result.

**Maxwellian distribution**

$$n(L) dL = \text{const.} \sqrt{L} dL \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{L}{kT}\right), \tag{357}$$

with $L$ the kinetic energy of a molecule, provided the constant $\beta$ assumed the value

$$\beta = \frac{h\nu}{kT}. \tag{358}$$

For very large but finite $r$, the distribution was given by the equation

$$n(L) dL = \frac{(2\pi)(2m)^{3/2}}{h^3} \sqrt{L} dL \cdot \frac{A \exp(-L/kT)}{1 + A \exp(-L/kT)}, \tag{359}$$

where $A$ denotes the quantity

$$A = \alpha \exp\left(-\frac{2\pi^2 \nu^2 m r^2}{kT}\right). \tag{359a}$$

Hence the constant $\alpha$ can be related to the density $n$ ($=\int_0^\infty n(L) dL$) of the molecules at a distance $r$, and therefore ultimately to the number of molecules in the gas model.$^{204}$

The equation of state now followed in a straightforward manner as

$$p = \frac{h^2 n^{5/3}}{2\pi m} P\left(\frac{2\pi mkT}{h^2 n^{2/3}}\right), \tag{360}$$

where the function $P(\Theta)$—with $\Theta = 2\pi mkT/h^2n^{2/3}$—is given by

$$P(\Theta) = \begin{cases} \Theta \left[ 1 + \frac{1}{2^{5/2}\Theta^{3/2}} + \cdots \right] & \text{for very large } \Theta, & (360a) \\ \frac{3^{2/3} \pi^{1/3}}{5 \cdot 2^{1/3}} \left[ 1 + \frac{5 \cdot 2^{2/3} \pi^{4/3}}{3^{7/3}} \Theta^2 + \cdots \right] & \text{for very small } \Theta. & (360b) \end{cases}$$

Thus for weak degeneracy, i.e., for large $T$ and small $n$ (i.e., large $\Theta$), the equation for the pressure $p$ assumes the form

$$p = nkT \left[ 1 + \frac{1}{16} \frac{h^3 n}{(\pi m kT)^{3/2}} + \cdots \right]. \tag{361}$$

$^{204}$Fermi gave a detailed expression for the density of the $s$-molecules (i.e., the molecules having energy $sh\nu$), which he showed would go over into the right-hand side of Eq. (359) for suitably large $s (= L/h\nu + (2\pi^2 \nu m/h)r^2)$.

That is, the gas pressure in Fermi’s theory of ideal monatomic gases turns out to be larger than that given by the classical equation; e.g., for helium at $T = 5^{\circ}$ absolute and $p = 10$ atmospheres, the difference amounts to 15 percent.$^{205}$ For very low temperatures and high densities a large degeneracy resulted, and in the case of zero temperature a finite zero-point pressure

$$p_0 = \frac{1}{20} \left( \frac{6}{\pi} \right)^{2/3} \frac{h^2 n^{5/3}}{m} \tag{362a}$$

and a zero-point energy (per molecule)

$$\bar{L}_0 = \frac{3}{40} \left( \frac{6}{\pi} \right)^{2/3} \frac{h^2 n^{2/3}}{m}, \tag{362b}$$

was obtained.$^{206}$ Finally, the specific heat at low temperatures

$$c_v = \frac{d\bar{L}}{dT} = \frac{2^{4/3} \pi^{8/3}}{3^{2/3}} \frac{mk^2T}{h^2 n^{2/3}}, \tag{363}$$

indeed vanishes at absolute zero, in agreement with Nernst’s heat theorem. Since, for high temperatures, there also followed Stern’s and Tetrode’s entropy expression, Eq. (347), Fermi had completely fulfilled the programme he had set up for himself.

It took some time before a reaction to Fermi’s paper came, but it did not come directly. George Uhlenbeck, who knew Fermi at that time, recalled: ‘It [Fermi’s theory] looked strange to us ... he [Fermi] did it so strangely at that time because as a vessel he took a harmonic oscillator’ (Uhlenbeck, AHQP Interview, 9 December 1963, p. 15). Only later did Uhlenbeck learn (from the papers of Heisenberg and, in particular, that of Dirac) of the connection between the statistics and the symmetry properties of the wave functions, and then he went back to Fermi’s original paper. Even Pauli, whose exclusion principle had provided the basis of the new statistics, did not immediately take positive notice of the result. As late as 19 October 1926 he confessed in a letter to Heisenberg: ‘I now think considerably more favourably of the Fermi-Dirac statistics, and at present it appears to me that several arguments support it. Between a crystal lattice and radiation there already exists a difference, namely that of zero-point energy $h\nu/2$.$^{207}$ It is certainly reasonable to assume that in the case of an ideal gas there also exists a zero-point energy. ### Symmetry Properties of Wave Functions and Quantum Statistics

During the first half of 1926, when Schrödinger's papers on wave mechanics were submitted and published, Paul Adrien Maurice Dirac was concerned with working out his own scheme of quantum mechanics.²⁰⁸ The mathematical objects which he employed, the *q*-numbers, exhibited a close relation to the matrices used by the Göttingen physicists; however, their range of application seemed to be greater, since they could be easily applied to describe all kinds of multiply periodic atomic systems (Dirac, 1926c), and even to aperiodic relativistic atomic processes such as the Compton effect (Dirac, 1926f). Being completely absorbed in these investigations, which he also used to obtain his doctoral degree in May 1926, Dirac—the independent and lonely physicist—did not pay too much attention to other new approaches in atomic theory, although he followed the literature in general. Of course, one might wonder whether he regularly looked at the *Annalen der Physik* where Schrödinger's communications appeared, beginning in March 1926, but where not much work on atomic or quantum theory was otherwise published at that time. If, however, he had not seen the first communication (Schrödinger, 1926c), he soon afterwards received a strong hint about it from Werner Heisenberg, who wrote on 9 April from Munich: 'A couple of weeks ago a paper by Schrödinger came out in the *Annalen der Physik* (Volume **79**, issue No. 4, p. 361, 1926), whose content must, in my opinion, be connected mathematically with quantum mechanics.' Heisenberg went on to ask Dirac: 'Have you reflected upon the question of how far this Schrödinger treatment of the hydrogen atom is related to the quantum mechanical one? . . . I am particularly interested in this mathematical problem, since I believe that one can gain quite a lot from it for the physical, fundamental interpretation of the formalism' (Heisenberg to Dirac, 9 April 1926).

Heisenberg had indeed addressed his letter to the right person, because Dirac—in his second paper on quantum mechanics—had treated the problem of the hydrogen atom within the *q*-number theory, a scheme that generalized the previous Göttingen matrix methods and was much closer to Schrödinger's differential equation approach in many respects (Dirac, 1926a). We note with some curiosity Heisenberg's remark that the undulatory theory might help to solve the problem of the physical interpretation of quantum mechanics, a point of view which he later on—when Schrödinger tried to provide such an interpretation—would refute completely. In any case, Heisenberg now hoped to learn from Dirac's mathematical expertise, and he therefore ended his letter with a couple

---

of questions: 'Couldn't you come during the next [few] months to Copenhagen? I would so much like to discuss with you all the new problems. Or will you still be in Cambridge in July? Then perhaps, as I did last year, I would have a great desire to come to England for a short time' (Heisenberg to Dirac, 9 April 1926). Dirac could not go to Denmark until later in the fall of 1926;$^{209}$ still he wrote back to Heisenberg, and their correspondence stimulated his own work which indeed took a turn towards wave mechanics.

The letter, in which Dirac replied to Heisenberg's letter of 9 April 1926, seems to have been lost.$^{210}$ On 26 May 1926, however, Heisenberg answered Dirac from Copenhagen. He reported first about 'the connection between Schrödinger's theory and the quantum mechanics', referring to the results that 'are given in a third paper of Schrödinger [1926e], which may come out in the next weeks.'$^{211}$ Heisenberg may have heard of this paper in April, while he was at Sommerfeld's Institute in Munich, as Schrödinger had already sent it in March to Wilhelm Wien. On the other hand, Heisenberg certainly heard the news of the independent equivalence proof by Wolfgang Pauli, which the latter had formulated in his letter of 12 April to Pascual Jordan, on his passage through Göttingen around 20 April. Indeed, Heisenberg essentially sketched for Dirac the content of Pauli's letter. Thus, for example, he gave the formula for the matrix element of a physical quantity in wave mechanics,

$$f_{mn} = \int f \psi_n \psi_m \, d\Omega, \quad (364)$$

where $\psi_n$ and $\psi_m$ are two eigenfunctions of the system and $\int d\Omega$ denotes the integration over its position variables. He further showed that with the definition (364) the matrix multiplication rule followed for two such quantities, $f$ and $g$, i.e.,

$$(fg)_{nm} = \sum_l f_{nl} g_{lm}. \quad (365)$$

Assuming that the definition

$$(p_k)_{nm} = - \frac{h}{2\pi i} \int \frac{\partial \psi_n}{\partial q_k} \psi_m \, d\Omega \quad (366)$$

yielded the matrix elements for the momentum component $p_k$ of the system, Heisenberg could prove that the quantum mechanical commutation relations did hold automatically. He concluded: 'In a similar way you get from [the Schrödinger

equation] the Hamiltonian function as a function of the matrices $p$ and $q$, and then we know, that [Eqs. (364) and (366)] really give the solution of the quantum mechanical equations. I think, it is not necessary that I write it down' (Heisenberg to Dirac, 26 May 1926).

Heisenberg further presented in his letter a relativistic form of the Schrödinger equation. Then he discussed specific questions, which had essentially been raised before by Dirac. 'I quite agree with your criticism of Schrödinger's paper with regard to the wave theory of matter. This theory must be inconsistent,' he wrote. Nevertheless he also mentioned a more positive aspect by saying: 'I see the real progress made by Schrödinger's theory in this: that the same mathematical equation can be interpreted as point mechanics in a non-classical kinematics *and* as wave theory according to Schrödinger. I always hope, that the solution of the paradoxes in the quantum theory later would be found this way' (Heisenberg to Dirac, 26 May 1926). He then reported on the interest taken by the Copenhagen physicists in Dirac's quantum mechanical treatment of the Compton effect (Dirac, 1926c). Finally, he mentioned his own investigation of the helium problem, especially his success in explaining the large singlet–triplet separation as a consequence of the quantum mechanical resonance effect. 'Really one gets in this way a qualitative explanation of the spectrum with regard as well to the frequency as to the intensities. And I hope, the quantitative agreement is only a question of long numerical work,' he concluded (Heisenberg to Dirac, 26 May 1926).

The last point must have alerted Dirac who had for years been interested in obtaining a satisfactory theory of the helium atom. Actually, Dirac seems to have had (for some time in early 1926) a suitable quantum mechanical action-angle scheme for dealing with that task (Dirac, 1926b).$^{212}$ Probably the preparations for obtaining his Ph.D. degree and the work on the Compton effect, a problem of fundamental importance, had delayed Dirac's final attack on the helium problem. Or did another difficulty exist?

The definite, positive answer to this question can be derived from the introduction to a paper by Dirac that his supervisor Ralph Fowler had communicated to the *Proceedings of the Royal Society of London* in late August 1926 (Dirac, 1926f). There he first described the characteristic feature of the Göttingen–Cambridge approach to quantum mechanics as: 'One can build up a theory [of atomic systems] without knowing anything about the dynamical variables except the algebraic laws that they are subject to, and can show that they may be represented by matrices whenever a set of uniformising variables for the dynamical system exists.' He added: 'It may be shown, however (see §3), that there is no set of uniformising variables for a system containing more than one electron, so that the theory cannot progress very far on these lines' (Dirac, 1926f, p. 661).

The proof of this observation, which Dirac presented in Section 3 of his new paper, ran like this: Consider in quantum mechanics a system consisting of two

760 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

electrons without any interaction. Evidently, its properties must be described by matrices: the particular element (*mn*; *m'n'*) then denotes the transition from a state (*mn*)—the first electron being in the stationary state *m* and the second in the state *n*—to the state (*m'n'*). The question now arises as to whether the two states of the system, (*mn*) and (*nm*), which differ only by the fact that the two electrons have exchanged their individual states, are taken to be identical or not. The assumption that they have to be counted as separate states immediately leads to a contradiction, because only the sum of the intensities due to the transitions (*mn*) → (*m'n'*) and (*nm*) → (*n'm'*) can be determined experimentally. The other alternative, however, results in the identity,

$$x_1(mn; m'n') = x_2(nm; n'm'), \qquad (367)$$

holding for $x_1$ and $x_2$ (denoting corresponding co-ordinates for the electrons 1 and 2) and all values of (*mn*) and (*m'n'*). This would now demand the identity of the two matrices $x_1$ and $x_2$, which is obviously nonsensical. Dirac concluded: ‘We must infer that unsymmetrical functions of the co-ordinates (and momenta) of the two electrons cannot be represented by matrices’ (Dirac, 1926f, p. 667).$^{213}$  
Since Dirac had not addressed the above argument either in his March paper (Dirac, 1926b) or in his April paper on the relativistic extension of the *q*-number theory (1926c), he must have noticed the difficulty later in the spring or early summer of 1926. He remarked many years later: ‘Things which are not pretty obvious are things which take me years before there is a breakthrough. I don’t think it’s any puzzle how someone gets the idea that leads to the break’ (Dirac, Conversations, June 1968, p. 81). Evidently, the many-electron problem was solved only with the help of symmetry arguments, and the latter were indeed available at that time. For example, Heisenberg made use of them in the months from May to July 1926, when he interpreted the results that emerged from his calculation of the helium term-system (Heisenberg, 1926b, c). We are not certain whether the physicists in Cambridge discussed similar ideas; but on 29 July 1926 Max Born arrived from Göttingen to speak at the Kapitza Club on the wave mechanical collision problem.$^{214}$ Dirac, a member of the Kapitza Club, met Born and received some information on Heisenberg’s work on the symmetry properties of wave functions, as he pointed out in a footnote in his later paper: ‘Professor Born has informed me that Heisenberg has independently obtained results equivalent to these’ (Dirac, 1926f, p. 670, footnote †). This statement confirms that at the time of Born’s visit to Cambridge—i.e., before Heisenberg’s first paper on the many-body problem appeared in print (in the *Zeitschrift für Physik*, issue of 10 August 1926)—Dirac had already found the decisive results of his own wave mechanical treatment of many-electron systems.

IV.4 Response to Wave Mechanics II. Applications and Extensions
761

After recognizing the advantage of Schrödinger’s theory, Dirac systematically analysed wave mechanics from a point of view that was more familiar to his own way of thinking.²¹⁵ That is, he recast the scheme first into the general form he had given previously to the *q*-number theory, notably in the paper on ‘relativity quantum mechanics’ (Dirac, 1926c, §2).²¹⁶ So he began by associating with the position variables $q_r$ and the time variable $t$ of a quantum mechanical system the canonically conjugate momentum variables, now in the form of differential operators,

$$
p_r = -i \frac{h}{2\pi} \frac{\partial}{\partial q_r} \tag{368a}
$$

and

$$
- W = -i \frac{h}{2\pi} \frac{\partial}{\partial t}. \tag{368b}
$$

Evidently, all properties of the system could now be expressed in terms of $q_r$ and $t$ and their derivatives, provided they depended only in a rational way on the momenta $p_r$ and the energy $W$. Further, Dirac now noted that to the classical Hamilton–Jacobi equation, i.e.,

$$
H(q_r, p_r, t) - W = F(q_r, p_r, t, W) = 0, \tag{369}
$$

there corresponded the wave equation

$$
F\psi = 0, \tag{369'}
$$

which is nothing other than Schrödinger’s equation. Because of the linearity of Eq. (369') in the wave function $\psi$, a general solution might be written as

$$
\psi = \sum_n c_n \psi_n, \tag{370}
$$

with $c_n$ being arbitrary constants and $\psi_n$ constituting a complete set of independent solutions, called eigenfunctions of the wave equation.²¹⁷

---

Especially, the inclusion of the time variable on the same footing as the position variable is characteristic of both treatments. (For a detailed account of the April paper, we refer to Volume 4, Part 1, Section V.4.)

Then, in general, the right-hand side of Eq. (370) contained an additional integral of the type $\int c_\alpha \psi(\alpha) \, d\alpha$.

762 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

As a second step, Dirac went on to ‘show that any constant of integration of the dynamical system . . . can be represented by a matrix whose elements are constants, there being one row and column of the matrix corresponding to each eigenfunction $\psi_n$’ (Dirac, 1926f, p. 664). Since any such constant $a$ commuted with the ‘Hamiltonian’ $F$ of the system ($aF = Fa$), the function $a\psi_n$ was also a solution of Eq. (369′). As a consequence, its expansion

$$a\psi_n = \sum_m \psi_m a_{mn}, \tag{371}$$

in terms of the complete set of eigenfunctions, $\{\psi_m\}$, provided the elements, $a_{mn}$, of the matrix corresponding to $a$.^{218} Since arbitrary functions, $x$, of the dynamical variables, $p_r$, $q_r$, $W$ and $t$, at a given time $t_0$, provided special examples of such constants of motion, Dirac further concluded that every dynamical variable of the system, $x(t)$, might ‘be represented by a matrix whose elements are functions of $t$ only’ (Dirac, 1926f, p. 665). In the restricted case that $F$ does not depend explicitly on the time variable $t$, $W$ is a constant of motion; and the eigenfunction $\psi_n$ can be chosen to make the matrix representing $W$ a diagonal matrix. Since any such constant $a$ commuted with the ‘Hamiltonian’ $F$ of the system ($aF = Fa$), the function $a\psi_n$ was also a solution of Eq. (369′). As a consequence, its expansion

$$x_{mn} = a_{mn} \exp\left[\frac{2\pi i}{h}(W_m - W_n)t\right]. \tag{372}$$

Consequently, the equivalence of the wave mechanical scheme and the matrix theory of Born, Heisenberg and Jordan was more or less established.^{219} Dirac further concluded that for constants of integration, $a, b, c, \ldots$, which commuted, the same set of eigenfunctions produced diagonal matrices (with elements $a_n$, $b_n$, $c_n$, $\ldots$ representing the corresponding ‘eigenvalues’), i.e., ‘we can have eigenfunctions representing stationary states of an atomic system with definite values for the energy, angular momentum, and other constants of integration’ (Dirac, 1926f, p. 666).

In applying the wave mechanical scheme to systems containing several identical particles, Dirac observed that the difficulties of the previous quantum mechanical formulation (i.e., of matrix mechanics and his $q$-number theory) actually disappeared. This could be recognized immediately in the simplest example, namely a two-electron atom, in which one neglects the interactions between the electrons. The eigenfunctions, $\psi_{mn}$, of this system should be basically given by the product of the eigenfunctions of the individual electrons, $\psi_m(1) \cdot \psi_n(2)$. However, due to the indistinguishability of the two electrons, the states $(mn)$ and $(nm)$ of the
