$^{281}$ Théophile Ernest De Donder was born on 19 August 1872 in Schaerbeek, Belgium. He became professor of mathematical physics at the *Université Libre de Bruxelles* in 1911, a position from which he retired in 1942. His main contributions were in the fields of thermodynamics, statistical mechanics and relativity theory; but he also worked on problems of general relativity and of relativistic quantum field theory. In many articles and books, De Donder made attempts to develop mathematically exact theories of fields and matter. De Donder created a flourishing school of mathematical physics and thermodynamics in Brussels; he died in Brussels on 11 May 1957.

$^{282}$ Frans Henri Antoine van den Dungen, who was born on 4 June 1898 in Saint-Gilles near Brussels, served as professor of analytical mechanancis at the *Université Libre de Bruxelles*. He died in Boitsfort, near Brussels, on 22 May 1965. ‘De Donder and van den Dungen treated dynamical systems of a very general sort, including gravitation and electromagnetism. Their method was essentially a generalized, covariant version of the variational procedure also applied by Schrödinger and Fock. However, the Belgian physicists did not introduce quantum theory explicitly and did not refer to any works of quantum physicists’ (Kragh, 1984, p. 1031). The last remark is not quite correct because they did refer to Schrödinger’s first three papers.

$^{283}$ De Donder had evidently not seen Schrödinger’s fourth communication (Part IV) when he composed his note of 11 October 1926.

It may be mentioned at this point that Norbert Wiener and Dirk J. Struik proposed a similar connection, between general relativity and quantum theory, as did De Donder and van den Dungen in a letter to *Nature*, dated 4 April 1927 (Wiener and Struik, 1927). They also wrote a generally covariant wave equation, which was equivalent to Eq. (426).

Ordnung mit der vielen Vätern,*’ Pauli to Schrödinger, 22 November 1926)<sup>286</sup> without reporting on another work, that of Walter Gordon in Berlin.<sup>287</sup>

Gordon’s paper, ‘*Der Comptoneffekt nach der Schrödingerschen Theorie*’ (‘The Compton Effect According to Schrödinger’s Theory’), was received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* on 29 September 1926 (Gordon, 1926). In Section 1, he presented the ‘*Aufstellung der Differentialgleichung für ψ*’ (‘Establishment of the Differential Equation for ψ’), that is, nothing other than a straightforward procedure for obtaining the relativistic wave equation for a massive, charged, microscopic particle moving in external electric and magnetic fields. Gordon did not refer to Schrödinger’s fourth communication (Part IV), which came out in print at just about the time when he finished his work and which contained parts of his results.

Gordon departed from the classical equation for a relativistic charged particle (electron) with four-momentum $p_\alpha (\alpha = 1, 2, 3, 4)$ in an electromagnetic field.

In the variation process the functions $\psi$ and $\bar{\psi}$ ($\bar{\psi}$ being the complex conjugate of $\psi$) have to be treated as independent variables. Referring to the derivation of the wave equation by Schrödinger in his first communication, Gordon noted: 'From that a generalization of Schrödinger's other rule emerges: one turns the Hamilton-Jacobi equation [(448)] [formally] into a Hermitean equation,
$$
\sum_\alpha \left( \frac{\partial W}{\partial x_\alpha} - \frac{e}{c} \Phi_\alpha \right) \left( \frac{\partial \bar{W}}{\partial x_\alpha} - \frac{e}{c} \Phi_\alpha \right) + m^2 c^2 = 0, \qquad \qquad [(448')]

and introduces the substitution $W = (h/2\pi i) \ln \psi$; then the left-hand side passes over, after multiplication with $(4\pi^2/h^2)\psi\bar{\psi}$, into the expression $H$ [Eq. (451a)]. However, instead of putting $H$ immediately equal to zero [as Schrödinger did in Part I to obtain his nonrelativistic wave equation], one rather puts the variation of the integral, $\int H dx_1 dx_2 dx_3 dx_4$, equal to zero. In the limit $h = 0$, the function $W$ becomes real and Eq. [(450')] passes over into Eq. [(448)]' (Gordon, 1926, pp. 119–120).$^{289}$

The work of Walter Gordon thus provided the most condensed mathematical presentation of the various versions of Schrödinger's equation, especially of the fully relativistic form. Although he was nearly the last to publish the results, this fact justifies the association of his name with Eq. (450') or its special case in the absence of electromagnetic potentials. Finally, Gordon did not stop at the relativistic wave equation, but went on to use it in a crucial problem: to calculate

### Schrödinger’s Visit to Copenhagen

In the *Physikalische Zeitschrift*’s issue of 15 September 1926, there appeared a review article by Ludwig Flamm, entitled ‘*Die Grundlagen der Wellenmechanik*’ (‘The Foundations of Wave Mechanics’), probably the first devoted to the new theory (Flamm, 1926a). The Viennese physicist, a former colleague and friend of Erwin Schrödinger, had followed the publications on undulatory mechanics with great excitement and had come to the conclusion that they signified decisive progress in resolving the earlier difficulties of atomic theory.²⁹⁰ In the introduction to his paper, Flamm remarked:

> In order to remove the difficulties, it was thought already that one had to proceed along a path which means a radical departure from the methods used hitherto in physics . . . , namely to create a “real theory of the discontinuum”. Here we intend to display the foundations of efforts which effect exactly the opposite, namely to incorporate quantum theory into the methods of classical physics. The basis for this has been provided by Louis de Broglie in his *Thèses* [1924e, 1925a]; the further, extraordinarily successful extension we owe to Erwin Schrödinger’s [work on] “*Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem*” [especially, Schrödinger, 1926d]. (Flamm, 1926a, p. 600)

In his review Flamm then gave a simplified introduction to how de Broglie and Schrödinger had proceeded from the variational principles of classical dynamics (see §1), via the wave principles of Christiaan Huygens and William Rowan Hamilton (§2), to the idea of phase waves and its application to quantum theory (§3), and finally to the establishment of wave mechanics (§4).²⁹¹ At the end of the article, Flamm expressed the following view on the theory:

> The engaging aspect of undulatory mechanics consists in the fact that this theory appears to be a further natural development of the great traditions in physics. About half a century has passed since electricity and optics were brought together under one roof by the establishment of Maxwell’s theory. Wave mechanics now seems to

---

²⁹⁰ Evidently, Schrödinger’s friends in Vienna—such as Ludwig Flamm and Hans Thirring—received his undulatory theory with special enthusiasm and wished to contribute their share in propagating the new theory.

²⁹¹ Flamm even mentioned Schrödinger’s recent work on the time-dependent theory in a footnote: ‘The author owes to the kind assistance of E. Schrödinger that he could meanwhile have a look into the fourth communication of [the series on] “*Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem*” already prior to publication in *Annalen der Physik*. The non-stationary quantum problems treated there go beyond the simple foundations reported here’ (Flamm, 1926a, p. 616).

Flamm also discussed the foundations of the non-stationary (time-dependent) theory in a paper presented at the *Naturforscher*versammlung in Düsseldorf in September 1926 (Flamm, 1926b).

put dynamics and optics on a common footing also. Shouldn’t this finally lead to a situation, in which mechanics, optics and electricity flow together harmoniously in a theory that embraces everything? [This would be welcome:] Because the theory of electricity in its present form has not been satisfactory for a long time. One has considered Maxwell’s theory as the beginning of a development, which should replace the old physics of substance (*alte Stoffphysik*) by a new physics of fields. But the further development brought the electron theory of Lorentz, which had to ascribe an equally fundamental role, beside the electromagnetic fields, to the “substance” electricity in the form of the “electrons”. It seems that the phase waves are in a position for the first time to pave the way to a genuine theory of physics. From this point of view one might be inclined to believe that one can already recognize in wave mechanics the aspects of a future, more complete stage of the development of physics. (Flamm, 1926a, p. 616)

Flamm’s review was immediately noticed by Werner Heisenberg who had been invited to present, at the 89th *Naturforscherversammlung* in Düsseldorf, the principal review report on quantum mechanics. He did so on 26 September 1926 and also took the occasion to express his opinion on the continuum interpretation of wave mechanics. In particular, he stated: ‘Recently, the supposition has been expounded sometimes (Flamm, Schrödinger) that, on the basis of Schrödinger’s differential equation, a purely continuum description of the quantum-theoretical experiences, might be possible in about the spirit of the classical theory, and that therefore quantum theory in its present form is illusory. However, if one carries out this point of view consistently, one abandons exactly the foundations of de Broglie’s theory, hence [also] quantum mechanics and quantum theory altogether; and one falls, in my opinion, into a complete contradiction with experience’ (Heisenberg, 1926d, p. 992). In the first place, according to Heisenberg, the blackbody radiation law and also the dispersion phenomena, could not be explained by the ‘classical interpretation’ of undulatory mechanics; moreover, the matter waves of Louis de Broglie—the basis of Schrödinger’s entire theory—‘defy any interpretation on the basis of classical concepts’ (‘*spotten jeder Deutung auf Grund klassischer Begriffe*,’ Heisenberg, 1926d, p. 992). He concluded: ‘The extraordinary physical significance of Schrödinger’s results lies in the observation that a visualizable (*anschauliche*) interpretation of the quantum-theoretical formulae contains typical features of a corpuscular theory, as well as typical features of a wave theory’ (*loc. cit.*).

From the very beginning, Heisenberg had been seriously opposed to the ‘*anschauliche*’ interpretation of wave mechanics. Thus, for instance, he had written to Wolfgang Pauli in June: ‘The more I ponder about the physical part of Schrödinger’s theory, the more horrible I find it. One should imagine the rotating electron, whose charge is distributed over the entire space and which has an axis in a fourth and fifth dimension. What Schrödinger writes on the visualizability of his theory … I find rubbish. The great achievement of Schrödinger’s theory is the calculation of matrix elements’ (‘*Je mehr ich über den physikalischen Teil der Schrödingerschen Theorie nachdenke, desto abscheulicher finde ich ihn. Man*

Die große Leistung der Schrödingerschen Theorie ist die Berechnung der Matrixelemente*’ (Heisenberg to Pauli, 8 June 1926).²⁹² Schrödinger’s colloquium in Munich had merely confirmed Heisenberg’s negative opinion. A few days after the *Kolloquium*, he wrote to Pauli: ‘As nice as Schrödinger is personally, I find his physics so strange: one feels 26 years younger when listening to it. Indeed, Schrödinger throws overboard everything which is “quantum-theoretical”: namely, the photoelectric effect, the Franck[-Hertz] collisions, the Stern–Gerlach effect, etc. It is then not difficult to establish a theory [of the kind that Schrödinger has in mind]. However, it does not agree with experience’ (‘*So nett Schrödinger persönlich ist, so merkwürdig find’ ich seine Physik: man kommt sich ja, wenn man sie hört, um 26 Jahre jünger vor. Schrödinger wirft ja alles “quantentheoretische”: nämlich lichtelektrischen Effekt, Francksche Stöße, Stern–Gerlacheffekt usw. über Bord; dann ist es nicht schwer, eine Theorie zu machen*,’ Heisenberg to Pauli, 28 July 1926). But the unfortunate discussion following Schrödinger’s Munich lecture persuaded Heisenberg of the necessity of having a really detailed and penetrating discussion with Erwin Schrödinger elsewhere, most profitably in Copenhagen where Niels Bohr especially could also participate.²⁹³

In a letter dated 11 September 1926, Bohr actually invited Schrödinger to come to Copenhagen and deliver a lecture to the Danish Physical Society (*Fysisk Forening*) on wave mechanics. At the same time Bohr expressed the hope ‘that you will introduce some discussions for the narrower circle of those who work here at the Institute, in which we can deal more deeply with the open questions of atomic theory’ (‘*daß Sie für den engeren Kreis derer, die hier am Institut arbeiten, einige Diskussionen einleiten werden, bei denen wir tiefer auf die offenen Fragen der Atomtheorie eingehen können*,’ Bohr to Schrödinger, 11 September 1926).²⁹⁴ Among this narrower circle belonged, in particular, Werner Weisenberg—from May 1926 the main *Assistent* and *Lektor* at the Copenhagen Institute for

IV.5 Towards an Undulatory Interpretation of Atomic Phenomena 823

Theoretical Physics—and Oskar Klein; Paul Dirac was also present at Bohr’s Institute at that time. Schrödinger accepted Bohr’s invitation quite readily (in a letter to Bohr, dated 21 September 1926) and announced his arrival in Copenhagen on 1 October (Schrödinger to Bohr, telegram of 28 September 1926). There he was received with great eagerness; thus Heisenberg recalled: ‘Bohr’s discussions with Schrödinger began at the railway station and were continued daily from early morning until late at night. Schrödinger stayed at Bohr’s house so that nothing would interrupt the conversations’ (Heisenberg, 1971, p. 73).

No contemporary notes about the content of the Copenhagen discussions exist; it does not seem to have occurred to anyone—neither Bohr, nor Schrödinger, nor any of the other participants—to keep such notes. However, Heisenberg later gave many lively accounts of the discussions; one may use these, together with information and reports in letters by Bohr and Schrödinger, for a reconstruction of these exciting discussions.<sup>295</sup>

As Heisenberg recalled, in Copenhagen Schrödinger especially attacked the idea of sudden quantum jumps. Schrödinger remarked:

> Surely you realize that the whole idea of quantum jumps is bound to end in nonsense. You claim first of all that if an atom is in a stationary state, the electron revolves periodically but does not emit light, when, according to Maxwell’s theory, it must. Next, the electron is said to jump from one orbit to the next and to emit radiation. Is this jump supposed to be gradual or sudden? If it is gradual, the orbital frequency and energy of the electron must change gradually as well. But in that case, how do you explain the persistence of fine spectral lines? On the other hand, if the jump is sudden, Einstein’s idea of light-quanta will admittedly lead us to the right wave number, but then we must ask ourselves how precisely the electron behaves during the jump. Why does it not emit a continuous spectrum, as electromagnetic theory demands? And what laws govern its motion during the jump? In other words, the whole idea of quantum jumps is sheer fantasy. (Schrödinger, in Heisenberg, 1971, pp. 73–74)<sup>296</sup>

<sup>295</sup> Heisenberg’s main published accounts of the Bohr–Schrödinger discussions are: Heisenberg, 1967, 1971, 1986. Heisenberg talked at length about these discussions to one of the authors (J. Mehra) in April 1954 (Göttingen), July 1962 (Geneva), and June 1968 (Trieste). See also AHQP Interview with Heisenberg, 25 February 1963, p. 10.

Nor should we be surprised to find it so, seeing that the processes involved are not the objects of direct experience.”

Right now I am not concerned with a precise description of this motion, but it ought to be possible to determine in principle how they behave in the stationary state or during the transition from one state to the next. But from the mathematical form of wave or quantum mechanics alone it is clear that we cannot expect reasonable answers to these questions. The moment,

On Bohr’s defence of this concept as being essential in describing the behaviour of atoms and radiation, Schrödinger became quite despondent and finally exclaimed: ‘If all this damned quantum jumping were really here to stay, I should be sorry I ever got involved with quantum theory.’ To which Bohr replied: ‘But the rest of us are extremely grateful that you did; your wave mechanics has contributed so much to the mathematical clarity and simplicity that it represents a gigantic advance over all previous forms of quantum mechanics’ (Heisenberg, 1971, p. 75).$^{297}$

Heisenberg also recalled that the continuous, strenuous discussions and conversations with Bohr exhausted Schrödinger. ‘After a few days Schrödinger fell ill, perhaps as a result of his enormous effort; in any case, he was forced to keep to his bed with a feverish cold. While Mrs. Bohr nursed him and brought in tea and cake, Niels Bohr kept sitting on the edge of the bed talking to Schrödinger: “But you must surely admit that . . .”’ (Heisenberg, 1971, pp. 75–76). In other words Bohr—whom Heisenberg described as having been ‘an almost remorseless fanatic’ (*loc. cit.*, p. 73) in the debate with Schrödinger—still *had to convince* his miserable guest to accept the Copenhagen position. However: ‘No real understanding could be expected since, at the time, neither side was able to offer a complete and coherent interpretation of quantum mechanics. For all that, we in Copenhagen felt convinced toward the end of Schrödinger’s visit that we were

***

however, that we change the picture and say that there are no discrete electrons, only electron waves or waves of matter, then everything looks quite different. We no longer wonder about the fine lines. The emission of light is as easily explained as the transmission of radio waves through the aerial of the transmitter, and what seemed to be insoluble contradictions have suddenly disappeared.”

Bohr: “I beg to disagree. The contradictions do not disappear; they are simply pushed to one side. You speak of the emission of light by the atom or more generally of the interaction between the atom and the surrounding radiation field, and you think that all the problems are solved once we assume that there are material waves but no quantum jumps. But just take the case of thermodynamic equilibrium between the atom and the radiation field—remember, for instance, the Einsteinian derivation of Planck’s radiation law. This derivation demands that the energy of the atom should assume discrete values and change discontinuously from time to time; discrete values for the frequencies cannot help us here. You can’t seriously be trying to cast doubt on the whole basis of quantum theory!”

Schrödinger: “I don’t for a moment claim that all these relationships have been fully explained. But then you, too, have so far failed to discover a satisfactory physical interpretation of quantum mechanics. There is no reason why the application of thermodynamics to the theory of material waves should not yield a satisfactory explanation of Planck’s formula as well—an explanation that will admittedly look somewhat different from all previous ones.”

Bohr: “No, there is no hope of that at all. We have known what Planck’s formula means for the past twenty-five years. And, quite apart from that, we can see the inconsistencies, the sudden jumps in atomic phenomena quite directly, for instance when we watch sudden flashes of light on a scintillation screen or the sudden rush of an electron through a cloud chamber. You cannot simply ignore these observations and behave as if they did not exist at all.” (Heisenberg, 1971, pp. 74–75).

Why should one not forget about Planck’s formula, or, in some way at least, get around it! So, to begin with, Bohr’s argument was not too convincing for Schrödinger. In that way Schrödinger was a bit of a Viennese; he would say, “Well, after all, we don’t know, we don’t worry.” That kind of “*Schlamperei*” [“sloppiness”]. That was contrary to Bohr’s spirit. Bohr would always try to go definitely to the bottom. Bohr would reach the point where one had to say, “Well, this cannot be decided: but at least thus far it is clear.”’ (Heisenberg, AHQP Interview, 25 February 1963, pp. 10–11.)

IV.5 Towards an Undulatory Interpretation of Atomic Phenomena 825

on the right track, though we fully realized how difficult it would be to convince even leading physicists that they must abandon all attempts to construct perceptual models of atomic processes’ (Heisenberg, 1971, p. 76).

Schrödinger, who delivered his lecture entitled ‘*Grundlagen der undulatorischen Mechanik*’ (‘Foundations of the Undulatory Mechanics’) before the Danish Physical Society on 4 October 1926, stayed in Copenhagen for only a few days. A couple of weeks later he reported to Wilhelm Wien: ‘Meanwhile, before going to Vienna, I was in Copenhagen; I did not regret this although I had little time for it and both journeys across Germany provided little pleasure. Still it was very nice that I was able to become thoroughly acquainted with Bohr—whom I had never met before—in his own surroundings, and to talk with him for hours about these matters which now are so very dear to all of us’ (Schrödinger to Wien, 21 October 1926).²⁹⁸ Niels Bohr’s personality had left a deep impression on Schrödinger because: ‘There will hardly come in the near future another man who scores such immense external and inner successes, to whom one pays homage, in his sphere of activity, nearly as to a demigod in the entire world, and who remains at the same time—I don’t say modest and free from presumption—really bashful and shy like a candidate of theology’ (Schrödinger to Wien, 21 October 1926).

In his letter to Wien, Schrödinger also briefly sketched the content of the discussions in Copenhagen, especially the points of disagreement. He wrote: ‘Quite certainly, the point of view of [using] visualizable pictures, which de Broglie and I assume, has not been carried through nearly far enough in order to render an account of the most important facts [of atomic theory]. It is of course probable that here and there a wrong path was taken that must now be abandoned. But that, even if one is Niels Bohr, one believes to be totally sure in stating at this point: the visualizable wave pictures work as little as the visualizable point[-particle] models, there being something in *the results of observation* which cannot be grasped by our erstwhile way of thinking—this I do not believe. I believe it even less since for me the comprehensibility of the external processes in nature is an axiom, say, in the sense: to *grasp* experience means nothing more than establishing the *best possible* organization among the different facts of experience’ (Schrödinger to Wien, 21 October 1926). In Schrödinger’s opinion, the facts of experience could not contradict each other, as Bohr—for many years—had tended to assume in atomic physics; only the ‘theoretical connections’ (‘*gedankliche Verbindungsglieder*’) or the physical interpretations could do so. In particular, it seemed ‘very premature’ (‘*sehr voreilig*’) to give up the ‘completely general conceptions of space and time and the connection of the interaction of neighbouring space-time points’ (‘*ganz allgemeinen Vorstellungen von Raum und Zeit und den Wechselwirkungszusammenhang benachbarter Raumzeitstellen*,’ Schrödinger to Wien, 21 October 1926), concepts that had been preserved even in General Relativity Theory.

Schrödinger also informed Wien of the way in which the discussions with Bohr went in Copenhagen. He reported: ‘The conversation always drives on

826 Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

immediately to philosophical questions; and soon one does not know anymore whether one really adopts the point of view which he fights, or whether one must really fight the point of view which *he* [Bohr] adopts'; it was often difficult to find out what Bohr actually meant, 'partly because he talks often for [several] minutes almost in a dreamlike, visionary and really quite unclear manner, and partly because he is so full of consideration and constantly hesitates—fearing that the other [person] might take an open statement of his (i.e., Bohr’s) point of view as an insufficient appreciation of the achievement of others (i.e., in this case, in particular, of my own work)’ (Schrödinger to Wien, 21 October 1926). Thus Schrödinger found that his work on wave mechanics was highly praised in Copenhagen, although he disliked some of the reasons for the appreciation. He concluded: ‘I can only say that I don’t care at all for this whole play with waves, if it should turn out to be nothing more than a comfortable computational device to evaluate matrix elements. In spite of all these theoretical points of dispute, however, the relationship with Bohr, and especially Heisenberg, both of whom behaved towards me in a touchingly kind, nice, caring and attentive manner, was totally, cloudlessly amiable and cordial’ (Schrödinger to Wien, 21 October 1926).

One need hardly wonder that the reports from Copenhagen on the results of the discussions with Schrödinger sounded a little different. For example, Niels Bohr wrote to Ralph Fowler in Cambridge on 26 October 1926: ‘We had the great pleasure of the visit of Schrödinger. The discussions centred themselves gradually on the problem of the physical reality of the postulates of the atomic theory. We all agreed that a continuity theory in the form indicated in his last paper [Schrödinger, 1926g or h] at a number of points leads to expectations fundamentally different from those of the usual discontinuity theory. Schrödinger himself continued in his hope that the idea of stationary states and transitions was altogether avoidable, but I think that we succeeded at least in convincing him that for the fulfilment of his hope he must be prepared to pay a cost, as regards reformation of fundamental concepts, formidable in comparison with that hitherto contemplated by the supporters of the idea of a continuity theory of atomic phenomena.’ Schrödinger obviously believed that matrix mechanics implied that single stationary states possessed no physical reality, a point of view which Bohr found to be ‘a confounding of the means and aims of Heisenberg’s theory.’ On the other hand, Bohr considered wave mechanics ‘so wonderfully suited to bring out the true correspondence between the quantum theory and the classical ideas’ (Bohr to Fowler, 26 October 1926). This correspondence was explored by Bohr and his collaborators in the months following Schrödinger’s visit to Copenhagen and helped enormously in establishing the physical interpretation of quantum mechanics.²⁹⁹

IV.5 Towards an Undulatory Interpretation of Atomic Phenomena 827

In the discussions of the Copenhagen physicists the essential role of the concept of discontinuity, as well as the alleged non-visualizability (‘*Unanschaulichkeit*’) of the atomic phenomena, resulted in the opinion ‘that all the apparently perceptible pictures should be taken in reality only symbolically’ (‘*daß die ganzen scheinbar anschaulichen Bilder in Wahrheit nur symbolisch zu nehmen seien*,’ Schrödinger to Bohr, 23 October 1926). Schrödinger profoundly disagreed with all these ideas, especially with the conclusion that the amplitudes of the eigen-vibrations might be interpreted only as statistical statements about a large number of atoms, but not as statements on a single atom—a point of view, which had been proposed by Max Born in his papers on the collision processes (Born, 1926a, b) and also adopted by Paul Dirac in applying wave mechanics to the theory of blackbody radiation (see Dirac, 1926f). As Schrödinger wrote to Bohr: ‘I am unable, however, to comfort myself with this preliminary solution. It seems to me that it is as little applicable *generally* as mine’ (‘*Ich vermag mich aber bei dieser vorläufigen Lösung durchaus nicht zu beruhigen. Sie scheint mir ebensowenig allgemein anwendbar, wie die meine*,’ Schrödinger to Bohr, 23 October 1926).

Schrödinger had been confronted with the probability interpretation of the wave function soon after its conception. He had seen the proofs of Max Born’s paper on the collision problem in wave mechanics (Born, 1926b) prior to publication and, in a letter to Wien, he had confided his concern about the probability interpretation of the wave function. He wrote: ‘Today, however, I no longer wish to assume, with Born, that such a single event [i.e., a single collision of an electron or an α-particle with an atom] is “absolutely accidental”, i.e., completely indeterminate. Today I no longer believe that one gains very much with this conception—which I had advocated very actively four years ago.<sup>300</sup> … I believe that Born overlooks—provided this [statistical] picture was available in a completely worked-out formulation—that it would then still remain up to the taste of the observer *what* he wants to consider as *real*, the particle or the pilot field. There is no philosophical criterion of reality unless one wants to say: what is *real* is only the complex of sensations (*sinnfällige Komplex*), everything else is only pictures’ (Schrödinger to Wien, 25 August 1926).

In the discussions in Copenhagen, the question of the probability interpretation did play a role; this follows directly from Schrödinger’s letter to Bohr, dated 23 October 1926, which we have quoted above. Oskar Klein also recalled after several decades: ‘Schrödinger wanted to interpret that which Born interpreted as probability density as really the density of the electrons. Then they [i.e., Bohr and Heisenberg] showed that if that was so and if by means of his currents and densities he coupled the thing to the electromagnetic field, then the probability for the spontaneous emission would be proportional to the number of atoms in the upper state multiplied by the number [of atoms] in the lower state. It would be quite against anything one knew’ (O. Klein, AHQP Interview, 16 July 1963,

<sup>300</sup>By this remark, Schrödinger referred, e.g., to the ideas he had expressed in his inaugural lecture at the University of Zurich. (See Schrödinger, 1929a; we have discussed Schrödinger’s inaugural lecture at the University of Zurich in Chapter II, Section II.3.)

p. 2). Still, Schrödinger remained unshaken, and shortly afterwards he wrote to Max Born: ‘I have, however, the impression that you and others, who essentially share your opinion, are too deeply under the spell of those concepts (like stationary states, quantum jumps, etc.), which have obtained civic rights in our thinking in the last dozen years; hence, you cannot do full justice to an attempt to break away from this scheme of thought’ (Schrödinger to Born, 2 November 1926).

Evidently, Schrödinger counted the probability interpretation among the essential concepts arising from Bohr’s atomic theory of 1913, which he now wanted to abolish. He wrote to Bohr: ‘What is before my eyes, is only one thesis: one should not, even if a hundred trials fail, give up the hope of arriving at the goal—I do not say by means of classical pictures, but by logically consistent conceptions—of the real structure of space–time processes. It is extremely probable that this is possible’ (Schrödinger to Bohr, 23 October 1926).³⁰¹ No, Schrödinger would not easily give up what he considered to be his programme of a visualizable (*anschauliches*) understanding of what happens in atoms and molecules.

### Two Crucial Problems: The Compton Effect and the Photoelectric Effect

Ever since its discovery in late 1922, the Compton effect (Compton, 1923a, b) was considered to represent one of the most typical and crucial quantum phenomena. It seemed to establish firmly Albert Einstein’s concept of the light-quantum, and this in turn created enormous difficulties in the radiation theory during subsequent years, especially after Walther Bothe and Hans Geiger (1925a, b) and Arthur Compton and Alfred Simon (1925c) had practically destroyed the compromising theoretical scheme of Niels Bohr, Hendrik Kramers and John Slater (1924).³⁰² In a letter to *Nature*, dated 29 October 1926, Gilbert N. Lewis from Berkeley, California, summarized the conclusions that could be derived from the experiences of the previous two decades. He wrote:

> Whatever view is held regarding the nature of light, it must now be admitted that the process whereby an atom loses radiant energy, and another near or distant atom receives the same energy, is characterized by a remarkable abruptness and singleness. . . . Had there not seemed to be insuperable objections, one might have been tempted to adopt the hypothesis that we are dealing here with a new type of atom, an identifiable entity, uncreatable and indestructible, which acts as the carrier of radiant energy and, after absorption, persists as an essential constituent of the absorbing atom until it is later sent out again bearing a new amount of energy. If

***

³⁰¹ With this programme, Schrödinger acted against the entire development which atomic theory had pursued from 1913 under the leadership of Niels Bohr and which had eventually led to the quantum mechanical theory proposed by Heisenberg, Born, Jordan and Dirac. (For a detailed description of this development, see Volumes 1–4.)
³⁰² See Volume 1, Sections V.2 and V.5.

IV.5 Towards an Undulatory Interpretation of Atomic Phenomena  
829  

> I now advance this hypothesis of a new kind of atom, I do not claim that it can yet be proved, but only that a consideration of the several objections that might be adduced shows that there is not one of them that can not be overcome. (Lewis, 1926, p. 874)

In order to avoid confusion with the previous conceptions of light—carrier of radiant energy, on the one hand, and structural element within the atom, on the other hand—and also to distinguish the number of the new entity from any of the quantum numbers describing the atom, Lewis took ‘the liberty of proposing for this hypothetical new atom, which is not light but plays an essential part in every process of radiation, the name *photon*’ and postulated the following properties associated with it:  

(1) In any isolated system the total number of photons is constant. (2) All radiant energy is carried by photons, the only difference between the radiation from a wireless station and from an X-ray tube being that the former emits a vastly greater number of photons, each carrying a very much smaller amount of energy. (3) All photons are intrinsically identical. . . . (4) The energy of an isolated photon, divided by the Planck constant, gives the frequency of the photon, which is therefore by definition strictly monochromatic; although two photons coming even from similar atoms would never have precisely the same frequency. (5) All photons are alike in one property which has the dimensions of action or of angular momentum, and is invariant to a relativity transformation. (6) The condition that the frequency of a photon emitted by a certain system be equal to some physical frequency existing within that system, is not in general fulfilled, but comes nearer to fulfilment the lower the frequency is. (Lewis, 1926, p. 874)

Lewis succeeded in essentially resolving the conceivable objections against his photon concept, but also admitted that he had not yet been able ‘to derive certain familiar selection principles from the conservation of photons’ (Lewis, 1926, p. 875).<sup>303</sup> On the other hand, he found that the rule ‘that one, and only one, photon is lost in each elementary radiation process . . . predicts that many atomic processes will be inhibited at very low temperatures, and for this there seems to be some experimental evidence’ (Lewis, 1926, p. 875).  
The ingenious introduction of the concept of the photon, which may be considered as the most radical formulation of Einstein’s light-quantum hypothesis of 1905, would soon (in 1927) be taken up by several physicists—especially, Paul Dirac and Pascual Jordan—who developed quantum field theory. In quantum field theory, the radiation occurred in the form of photons, that is, Lewis’ photons exactly constituted the systematically quantized description of radiation. However, for the wave mechanical theory of 1926 the light-quantum and even more the photon concept certainly meant a challenge, because the fundamental problem arose as to how to describe a directed, moving, indestructible object  

<sup>303</sup> Among the possible objections which Lewis discussed were: the situation with cavity radiation and thermodynamical equilibrium, and the detailed spectroscopic processes occurring in an atom.

with polarization and concentrated (at a given moment) in space.$^{304}$ But even if this question had been answered positively, what would happen to the originally concentrated wave packets after they were scattered by atoms or electrons? Special physical examples of that situation were provided by the discussions of the photoelectric and the Compton effects in wave mechanics. Concerning the latter, Pauli wrote to Wentzel on 5 July 1926: ‘I want to translate the Compton effect *à la* Dirac into the language of Schrödinger!’ (‘*Comptoneffekt nach Dirac möchte ich in die Schrödingersche Sprache umsetzen!*’). Apparently he did not make much progress with the problem, because we find no results either in Pauli’s subsequent correspondence or in a publication.

As for the photoelectric effect, Wilhelm Wien, Schrödinger’s close discussion partner, was particularly worried. So he wrote in the summer of 1926: ‘One of the most serious difficulties for wave mechanics seems to me to be the photoelectric effect. I talked about this question in detail with Bohr and Born in Oxford; both of them are convinced that the photoelectric effect is incompatible with wave mechanics’ (Wien to Schrödinger, 20 August 1926).$^{305}$ Although the specific arguments of Bohr and Born had not convinced Wien, he did not see how to fit the known empirical facts observed with the photoelectric effect into Schrödinger’s theory. After a discussion of the main problems in the latter, he concluded: ‘It seems to me that one cannot get at the photoelectric effect without involving statistics. However, perhaps this is quite possible in the case of the Compton effect, but the theory of this effect will probably demand still larger preparations’ (Wien to Schrödinger, 20 August 1926).

In his immediate reply, Schrödinger admitted ‘that the photoelectric effect presents—besides the experimentally confirmed space quantization—the biggest conceptual difficulty for the execution of a classicistic theory’ (‘*daß der lichtelektrische Effekt (neben der experimentell sichergestellten Richtungsquantelung) die größte begriffliche Schwierigkeit für die Durchführung einer klassizistischen Theorie darbietet*’), and that he did not have the slightest idea of how to attack its calculation (Schrödinger to Wien, 25 August 1926). He just suggested that the key to the problem might lie in the ‘*identity* which exists between energy and frequency for the microscopic processes’ which ‘we do not yet understand sufficiently’ (‘*Identität, die im mikroskopischen Geschehen zwischen Energie und Frequenz besteht*’, ... ‘*wir noch nicht genügend verstehen,*’ Schrödinger to Wien, 25 August 1926). Three months later Schrödinger returned to the problem of the Compton effect in another letter to Wien. He reported: 'The Compton effect has now been treated by wave [mechanical] methods, and not by me but by a—as it seems—very clever and gifted Mr. W. Gordon in Berlin' ('*Der Comptoneffekt ist nun auch wellenmäßig behandelt und zwar nicht von mir, sondern von einem, wie es scheint, sehr klugen und geschickten Herrn W. Gordon in Berlin*,' Schrödinger to Wien, 28 November 1926). Some time before Gordon had sent to Schrödinger a copy of his paper on the Compton effect (Gordon, 1926), which was submitted in late September to *Zeitschrift für Physik* and which appeared in issue No. 1–2 of Volume **40** (dated 29 November 1926). Schrödinger had some difficulty in understanding the contents of the paper and he remarked to Wien: 'It is not palatable at all. Only after some considerable time did I succeed in recognizing the true factual situation. Without formulae it is now indeed so simple and so easily comprehensible to anyone, that I consider it to be appropriate to publish it in this [non-technical] form myself—many people will be happy about it' ('*Genießbar ist sie allerdings gar nicht. Erst nach längerer Zeit ist es mir gelungen, den wahren Sachverhalt zu erkennen. Dieser ist nun allerdings so einfach und sozusagen ohne Formeln für jedermann verständlich, daß ich es für richtig halte, ihn in dieser Form zu publizieren—viele werden sich freuen darüber*,' Schrödinger to Wien, 28 November 1926). The manuscript of the short communication, entitled '*Über den Comptoneffekt*' ('On the Compton Effect'), which Schrödinger announced (in his letter of 28 November to Wien, and which was submitted simultaneously), was indeed received by the *Annalen der Physik* on 30 November 1926 (Schrödinger, 1927a). Before dealing with it, we shall first analyse the particular contents of Gordon's paper.

Gordon began his paper on the Compton effect—as we have already mentioned—by establishing a suitable relativistic wave equation, i.e., Eq. (450'), in Section 1. In the next Section 2, he showed how to use this equation in order to obtain the emission of radiation from an atomic system. In particular, by multiplying Eq. (450') with $\bar{\psi}$, and the corresponding equation for $\bar{\psi}$ with $\psi$, and subtracting the two results, he obtained the equation

$$ \sum_{\alpha} \frac{\partial s_{\alpha}}{\partial x_{\alpha}} = 0, \qquad (452) $$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0473 -->

where the four-vector \(s_\alpha\) had the form  

\[
s_\alpha = \frac{1}{i} \left( \bar{\psi} \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial x_\alpha} - \psi \frac{\partial \bar{\psi}}{\partial x_\alpha} - \frac{4\pi i e}{h c} \Phi_\alpha \psi \bar{\psi} \right).
\]  
(453)  

Equation (452) evidently constituted a continuity relation for \(s_\alpha\), which in turn could be interpreted easily by considering the space-components \(s_k\), \(k = 1, 2, 3\) and the time-component \(s_4 = i c \rho\) separately. Gordon concluded: 'Therefore, we are justified in calling \(s_k\) the components of a current density and \(\rho\) a charge density, because these quantities satisfy the continuity equation  

\[
\left[ \sum_{k=1} \frac{\partial s_k}{\partial x_k} + \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} = 0,
\right]
\]  
(452')  

and *a priori* they do not have to satisfy any other condition for being able to act as the source of an electromagnetic field in the Maxwell equations' (Gordon, 1926, p. 121).  

The four-current (of the matter wave) thus defined could also be obtained from the variational principle, Eq. (451), namely through the equation  

\[
s_\alpha = -\frac{h e}{2 \pi c} \frac{\partial H}{\partial \Phi_\alpha},
\]  
(453')  

where \(H\) denotes the invariant (see Eq. 451). The electromagnetic field created by the source \(s_\alpha\)—i.e., by the atomic system—will then be described by the retarded potentials  

\[
\Phi_\alpha^{\text{ret}} = \frac{1}{c} \int \frac{[s_\alpha]}{R} \, dx_1 \, dx_2 \, dx_3,
\]  
(454)  

with \(R\) denoting the distance of the volume element \((dx_1 \, dx_2 \, dx_3)\) from the point of observation, and \([s_\alpha]\) denoting the value of the current-components at the retarded time \(t - R/c\). Equation (454) now gives the radiation emitted by the motion of the electrical centre of the atomic system.  

Going on to consider the Compton effect (in Section 3), Gordon represented the primary X-radiation by a linear polarized wave which has the direction cosines \(n_1\), \(n_2\) and \(n_3\) and the frequency \(\nu\). The X-rays then create an external potential  

\[
\Phi_\alpha = a_\alpha \cos \phi,
\]  
(455)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0474 -->

IV.5  Towards an Undulatory Interpretation of Atomic Phenomena  
833

with the phase $\phi$ given by$^{306}$

$$\phi = \sum_\alpha l_\alpha x_\alpha, \text{ where } \begin{cases} l_k = \frac{2\pi\nu}{c} n_k \text{ for } k = 1, 2, 3, \\ l_4 = i \frac{2\pi\nu}{c}. \end{cases} \tag{455a}$$

These potentials have now to be inserted into Eq. (450') and yield the wave equation describing the Compton effect, i.e.,

$$\sum_\alpha \frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial x_\alpha^2} - \frac{4\pi i}{h} \left( \frac{e}{c} \sum_\alpha a_\alpha \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial x_\alpha} \right) \cos \phi - \frac{4\pi^2}{h^2} m^2 c^2 \psi = 0. \tag{456}$$

In order to solve it Gordon made the *Ansatz* for the wave function $\psi, ^{307}$

$$\psi = \exp \left( \frac{2\pi i}{h} W \right), \tag{457}$$

with

$$W = \sum_\alpha p_\alpha x_\alpha + \left( \frac{e}{c} \sum_\alpha p_\alpha a_\alpha / \sum_\alpha p_\alpha l_\alpha \right) \sin \phi. \tag{457a}$$

For the calculation of the effect one actually needs the four-vector of the current $s_\alpha$, for which a detailed expression was obtained after straightforward calculation. This expression then had to be inserted into Eq. (454), and yielded the emission radiation from the atom; the radiation contained, of course, the frequency of the X-rays shifted by the Compton effect. In particular, Gordon found that the result implied an equation,

$$p_\alpha + \pi_\alpha = p'_\alpha + \pi'_\alpha, \tag{458}$$

which stated the energy-momentum conservation for the system consisting of the atom (four-momenta $p_\alpha$ and $p'_\alpha$ before and after the impact of the X-radiation) and the radiation (four-momenta of the quanta being $\pi_\alpha$ and $\pi'_\alpha$, respectively), i.e., just as the old relation of Compton and Debye. Further, the well-known

---

$^{307}$Gordon emphasized that the *Ansatz* (457) was valid not only for small $h$, but could also be taken to be strictly valid if a term proportional to $a^2_\alpha$ was taken into account in the definition of $W$, Eq. (457), namely the term:
$$- \left( \frac{e^2}{c^2} \frac{\sum_\alpha a^2_\alpha}{8 \sum_\alpha p_\alpha l_\alpha} \right) \cdot (2\phi + \sin 2\phi).$$

834 | Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

frequency relation followed. Finally, Gordon calculated the intensity $I$ of the Compton radiation, obtaining the result

$$I = \sqrt{I_{\text{cl}} \cdot I'_{\text{cl}}}, \tag{459}$$

that is, the quantum-theoretical intensity was equal to the geometrical average of the corresponding classical quantities in the initial ($I_{\text{cl}}$) and the final ($I'_{\text{cl}}$) states. The same result had already been obtained earlier by Gregory Breit on the basis of correspondence considerations (Breit, 1926) and by Paul Dirac in his relativistic $q$-number theory (Dirac, 1926c).

Schrödinger approached the wave mechanical treatment of the Compton effect in his own paper (Schrödinger, 1927a)—as he had mentioned to Wien—on a far less technical level. He practically went back to the optical analogies that had stimulated the whole development in November 1925, and in which the properties of microscopic particles were described by matter waves and their propagation in homogeneous media. From such considerations he now—a year later—drew the following conclusion: ‘It is to be expected, nay, even demanded, that we should be able, by means of quite simple phase considerations . . . , to explain the connection between the changes in direction and frequency of the ether wave which occur in the Compton effect and the change of velocity of the electron. For according to de Broglie’s idea the latter also can be described as the change of direction and frequency of a wave, namely, of a de Broglie wave’ (Schrödinger, 1927a, pp. 257–258; English translation, pp. 124–125). Such a procedure then made ‘a more detailed investigation of the wave mechanics of the process, such as W. Gordon has recently carried out with complete success, unnecessary, except for the determination of the intensities’ (Schrödinger, 1927a, p. 258; English translation, p. 125).

In pursuing the attempted goal of a ‘simple intuitive treatment’ (*loc. cit.*), Schrödinger remembered one of his earlier papers, in which he had investigated the reflection of light waves (of wavelength $\lambda$) from a compression, i.e., a sound wave (of wavelength $\Lambda$); he had shown then that the famous Bragg relation of the classical radiation theory, i.e., the law accounting for the reflection of first order of the X-rays from a lattice with lattice constant $\Lambda$,

$$2\Lambda \sin \theta = \lambda, \tag{460}$$

could be taken over into quantum theory, provided he applied the light-quantum hypothesis to both radiation and sound phenomena (Schrödinger, 1924b). The situation in Compton scattering resembled the old light–sound scattering; hence the question arose as to whether an equation of the type of Eq. (460) would also follow from a wave mechanical calculation, and further, if so, whether then the known frequency shift of X-rays when scattered by electrons bound in atoms would result.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0476 -->

IV.5 Towards an Undulatory Interpretation of Atomic Phenomena | 835

Schrödinger proceeded in the most simple manner. He first wrote the wave equation determining the propagation of a free electron in space, i.e.,

$$\Delta \psi - \frac{1}{c^2} \frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial t^2} - \frac{4\pi^2 \nu_0^2}{c^2} \psi = 0. \tag{461}$$

This wave equation possessed, as the simplest solution, a plane wave,

$$\psi \sim \exp \left\{ \frac{2\pi i}{h} \left[ h\nu t - \frac{h\sqrt{\nu^2 - \nu_0^2}}{c} (\alpha x + \beta y + \gamma z) \right] \right\}, \tag{462}$$

where $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ denoted the direction cosines ($\alpha^2 + \beta^2 + \gamma^2 = 1$), $h\nu$ the energy of the moving electron and $h\nu_0$ ($=mc^2$) the energy of the electron at rest. According to the discussion in Part IV, a $\psi$-wave of the type (462) creates a density distribution which is constant in time. If, however, one superposes two such plane waves—the second one having frequency $\nu'$ and direction cosines $\alpha', \beta', \gamma'$—a ‘wave of electrical density’ (‘*Welle elektrischer Dichte*,’ Schrödinger, 1927a, p. 260) is created which has a structure similar to the sound wave considered in the old paper of 1924. The reflection of a light wave then indeed followed Bragg’s law, Eq. (460). One of the immediate consequences was that the energy-momentum four-vectors of the incident and scattered radiation and the corresponding four-vectors of the electron (which is initially bound in the atom and finally leaves it as a free electron) satisfy the Compton–Debye relation, Eq. (458). Schrödinger concluded this simple, quite visualizable (*anschauliche*), undulatory treatment with the words: ‘The direction and frequency laws of the Compton effect are completely equivalent to the statement that the pair of light waves and the pair of $\psi$-waves concerned stand in the Bragg relationship for reflection of the first order (generalized for a moving crystal) to one and the same “space lattice”. The space lattice considered can at the outset have an arbitrary position and an arbitrary distance between the plane layers, and a velocity of translation less than that of light but otherwise arbitrary’ (Schrödinger, 1927a, p. 263; English translation p. 129).$^{308}$

A little earlier, before Schrödinger’s investigation of the Compton effect was completed, Gregor Wentzel from Leipzig submitted a paper, ‘Zur Theorie des photoelektrischen Effekts’ (‘On the Theory of the Photoelectric Effect’) to *Zeitschrift für Physik*: it was received on 19 November 1926 (Wentzel, 1926e). Since Wentzel wrote in the abstract: ‘Schrödinger’s wave mechanical formulae on

$^{308}$ Of course, it may be felt to be quite unusual to consider an electron to be represented by a space lattice; especially, one may ask why one should represent the electron by two waves. In his paper, Schrödinger answered these questions by referring to the optical analogues, in which one discusses simple phase considerations in exactly the same way. Hence: ‘By means of these simple considerations we investigate the Compton effect *in a steady state*, so-to-speak, in which the primary wave of one kind is continually transformed into a secondary wave by reflection at the system of interference fringes of the other kind, and *vice versa*’ (Schrödinger, 1927a, p. 264; English translation, p. 129).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0477 -->

836 | Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

dispersion theory involve unique statements about the probability of the photoelectric effect’ (*loc. cit.*, p. 574), and also cited Born’s papers on collision processes (Born, 1926a, b), one may argue that his treatment was not entirely in accordance with the spirit of Schrödinger’s intentions; that is, the difficulties addressed by Wilhelm Wien in his letter to Schrödinger, dated 20 August 1926, could not be considered as having been completely solved. However, the whole question, whether any of the applications of wave mechanics satisfied Schrödinger’s goal concerning an *anschauliche* interpretation, had not nearly been settled at that time, i.e., in the autumn of 1926. In any case, Wentzel opened the path dealing with the photoelectric effect in wave mechanics.

Wentzel did not start his approach from scratch by writing a wave equation for the physical problem; he rather took over a result from Schrödinger’s dispersion theory in Part IV, namely the expression for the wave function of the atomic system in the case of a continuous spectrum, i.e.,

$$\psi = u(x, E_0) \exp \left[ \frac{2\pi i}{h} (mc^2 + E_0)t \right] + \frac{1}{2} \int \frac{a(E_0, E')u(x, E')}{E_0 + h\nu - E'} \exp \left[ \frac{2\pi i}{h} (mc^2 + E_0 + h\nu)t \right] dE'. \tag{463}$$

In Eq. (463), $u(x, E_0)$ and $u(x, E')$ are the normalized wave functions of the ground state (discrete energy $E_0$) and the excited state (energy $E'$ of the continuum) of the atomic system; the function $a(E_0, E')$ describes the corresponding vibration excited by the incident radiation (i.e., the partial vibration of the electric moment multiplied by the electric field strength of the incident light wave), hence the quotient $a(E_0, E')/(E_0 + h\nu - E')$ ‘obviously determines the probability that a photoelectron comes out with the energy $E'$’ (Wentzel, 1926e, p. 575).$^{309}$

Wentzel noticed that the integral on the right-hand side of Eq. (463) was divergent for the zero denominator of the integrand, i.e., for $E' = E_0 + h\nu$. This difficulty could, however, be avoided by the method of complex integration; in particular, one distorts the path of the integration a little into the positive or negative imaginary half-plane, a procedure which was physically meaningful because of the following fact: ‘The integrand in [Eq. (463)] actually represents a *standing* vibration, which may be decomposed into a *convergent* (in-coming) and a *divergent* (out-going) wave. According to the choice of the path of integration one of the two waves will be *suppressed* by the integration. Since physically only

$^{309}$ In taking over expression (463) from Schrödinger’s paper (Schrödinger, 1926h, Eq. (12) and (14’)), Wentzel neglected the term with the discrete eigenvibrations of the atom as being inessential for the discussion of the photoelectric effect—the originally bound electron actually is liberated—as well as the term multiplied by the frequency factor $\exp[(2\pi i/h)(mc^2 + E_0 - h\nu)t]$—which corresponds to negative incident radiation and cannot be made responsible for the photoelectric effect.

# IV.5  Towards an Undulatory Interpretation of Atomic Phenomena  837

the *out-going* wave makes sense, we always choose the path of integration in the *positive* half-plane' (Wentzel, 1926e, pp. 575–576).$^{310}$

In order to obtain his main result, namely the intensity of photoelectrons, Wentzel just had to insert the appropriate eigenfunctions of the atom. As a particular example, he selected those of the hydrogen atom and carried out the evaluation of the integral by introducing a system of polar co-ordinates, $r$, $\theta$ and $\phi$, whose axis is parallel to that of the electric field vector of the incident X-ray. The calculation finally yielded: 'The intensity of the current of photoelectrons, and respectively the probability of the emission of a photoelectron per unit of the angle of aperture is therefore proportional to $\cos^2 \theta$. Hence the emission is strongest parallel to the electric field vector' (Wentzel, 1926e, p. 577).$^{311}$ This result more or less agreed with the experimental observations made by Frank W. Bubb (1924a) and especially the more recent observations by Fritz Kirchner (1926a), except for one fact: 'The direction of the maximum of photoelectric emission is not exactly parallel to the electric vector, but is slightly bent in the direction of the ray [of the incident light]. This asymmetry has already been connected with the momentum of the absorbed primary radiation by various people. The latter, however, does not enter into our calculation, since we have neglected the magnetic part of the light wave; in this point the theory must therefore be supplemented' (Wentzel, 1926e, p. 579).

In a second short note, '*Über die Richtungsverteilung der Photoelektronen*' ('On the Directional Distribution of the Photoelectrons')—submitted two months later (in January 1927)—Wentzel completed his treatment of the photoelectric effect in wave mechanics by adding the above-mentioned supplement, i.e., including in his calculation the influence of the magnetic field of the incident radiation (Wentzel, 1927a). The evaluation was based on the relativistic formalism of Gordon (1926) and the time-dependent perturbation theory of Schrödinger (1926h). It led to the following corrections of the previous results: 'The photoelectrons obtain an additive velocity component in the direction of the ray of the amount ($h\nu/mc$) [with $\nu$ the frequency of the incident light, $m$ the mass of the electron]. The maximum of the photoelectric current, which according to the earlier calculation fell in the direction of the electric field vector, now bends forward towards the direction of the [incident] ray, in full agreement with experience' (Wentzel, 1927a, p. 828). Indeed, the older observations, notably those of Walther Bothe (1924b), seemed to confirm Wentzel's new formula for

---
$^{310}$Wentzel found yet another difficulty with the expression for $\psi$: if one calculated $\psi\bar{\psi}$ and integrated over the three-dimensional space, the result diverged (because $u(x, E)$ behaved at infinity like $\cos(kr)/r$, with $k$ the wave vector). On the other hand, the space-integral of $\psi\bar{\psi}$ had to be finite, i.e., should be normalized to unity. However, considering the back-coupling of the emitted $\psi$-radiation on the atom—here the fact that the inside of the atom loses electric charge (by the emission of the photoelectron)—creates an experimental damping factor under the integral which makes the integral converge and even assume the value unity. (See Wentzel, 1926e, Section 5, pp. 585–588.)

For other initial states of the atom, the calculation is a little more involved but leads practically to the same result. (See Wentzel, 1926e, Sections 3 and 4.)

$$\cos \theta' = \frac{h\nu}{c} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2m(h\nu - |E_0|)}}, \tag{464}$$

where $|E_0|$ denotes the energy required to liberate an electron from an atom.$^{312}$

## Further Successes of Wave Mechanics in the Second Half of 1926

From the middle of the year 1926 onwards, wave mechanics occupied an increasing importance in the physical literature on atomic theory. The number of theoreticians using Schrödinger's methods in order to treat a variety of old and new problems grew considerably. The works submitted for publication at that time included, for example, Hendrik Kramers' paper on '*Wellenmechanik und halbzahlige Quantisierung*' ('Wave Mechanics and Half-Integral Quantization,' Kramers, 1926) and Fritz London's '*Winkelvariable und kanonische Transformationen in der Undulationsmechanik*' ('Angle Variables and Canonical Transformations in Undulatory Mechanics,' London, 1926d), both of which helped to establish a deeper relation between the different schemes of quantum mechanics.$^{313}$ Among the contributors to the applications of wave mechanics were physicists, who had for years made a name for themselves in atomic and quantum theory—like Peter Debye, Hendrik Kramers, Ralph Kronig and Fritz

---
$^{312}$In 1929 Arnold Sommerfeld and G. Schur carried out a systematic wave mechanical calculation of the effect of the radiation pressure (i.e., of the action of the electric and magnetic fields of the incident radiation) on the intensity distribution of the photoelectrons (Sommerfeld and Schur, 1930). In particular, they found that Wentzel's formula, Eq. (464)—which he had obtained by simply considering the momentum of the incident light-quantum—must be improved. Actually, the maximum of the photoelectric current is bent even more strongly into the direction of the incident radiation than is given by Eq. (464).

$^{313}$We shall, therefore, not deal here with the above-mentioned publications of Kramers and London, but we will analyze them in Volume 6.

Reiche—as well as newcomers like the Dane Øyvind Burrau, the Belgian Charles Manneback, and the Americans J. Robert Oppenheimer and Isidor I. Rabi. Especially, the fact that the youngsters also demonstrated their ability to master Schrödinger's methods, so soon after their publication, provided a signal for what later became the triumphant march of wave mechanics.

On 5 December 1926, Wolfgang Pauli wrote in a letter to Gregor Wentzel: 'In Göttingen, one has dealt with the problem of applying quantum mechanics to the absorption of X-rays: a Mr. Oppenheimer has performed calculations on it, but I don't know any more details' ('*Mit der Frage der Anwendung der Quantenmechanik auf die Röntgenabsorption hat man sich in Göttingen beschäftigt; ein Herr Oppenheimer hat darüber gerechnet, ich weiß aber nichts Näheres,*' Pauli to Wentzel, 5 December 1926). About three weeks later a letter, dated 1 November and signed by Oppenheimer, appeared in the issue of 24 December of *Naturwissenschaften* (Oppenheimer, 1926c). In this short communication entitled '*Quantentheorie des kontinuierlichen Absorptionsspektrums*' ('Quantum Theory of the Continuous Absorption Spectrum'), Oppenheimer drew attention to his recent work of applying undulatory mechanics 'to the hyperbolic orbits of the hydrogen atom (*auf die Hyperbelbahnen des Wasserstoffatoms*)' that had been published recently in the *Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society* (Oppenheimer, 1926a; see also Oppenheimer, 1926b). He wrote further: 'The formulae [obtained] are too intricate for this communication; they provide an estimate of the intensity of the continuous X-ray absorption spectrum. This [estimate] is—I believe—the first experimental check of these parts of the [undulatory] theory' (Oppenheimer, 1926c, p. 1282). According to the results obtained by Oppenheimer, the absorption of the X-rays suddenly begins—the atomic electron being in an orbit described by the quantum numbers $n$ (principal) and $k$ (azimuthal)—at the limit of the corresponding series, assuming there a value proportional to the wavelength of the series limit. Further, for very hard (short-wavelength) X-rays, the absorption coefficient is proportional to the product of a certain power of the wavelength and another power of the effective charge of the atomic nucleus; the calculated numerical values for these power coefficients agreed with the corresponding values derived from the empirical formulae.

As Oppenheimer indicated, by referring to the detailed publication in the Cambridge journal, he had already obtained the results earlier in England. J. Robert Oppenheimer had gone there a year previously from America to continue his studies under Joseph John Thomson at Cambridge University.$^{314}$ In the

---
$^{314}$J. Robert Oppenheimer was born on 22 April 1904 in New York. He studied physics at Harvard University from 1922 to 1925, after which he spent the academic year 1925–1926 at Cambridge University and the year 1926–1927 with Max Born in Göttingen. After an intermediate year back home (with a National Research Fellowship at Harvard and the California Institute of Technology), he again travelled in Europe on a fellowship of the International Education Board (1928–1929: Leyden and Zurich). He then served for a long period at the University of California at Berkeley: assistant professor (1929), associate professor (1930); full professor (1935). From 1943 to 1945 he directed the Los Alamos Laboratory (the atomic bomb project) near Santa Fe, New Mexico, and from 1947 to 1967 he served as Director of the Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton, New Jersey. He died on 20 February 1967 in Princeton.

summer of 1926 news of Schrödinger's theory had reached England. Max Born had even discussed his very recent application of wave mechanical methods describing atomic collisions in the talk he gave on 10 August at the Oxford meeting of the British Association.$^{315}$ Born's pioneering work had provided Oppenheimer with a suitable guide to his own work in wave mechanics; after dealing with the problem of X-ray absorption, he even came to Göttingen in the autumn of 1926 with the intention of obtaining his doctoral degree under the supervision of Max Born.

The newcomer turned out to be an extremely talented and quick learner, and completed the work on his thesis a few months after his arrival in Göttingen. On 24 December 1926, the *Zeitschrift für Physik* received an article, '*Zur Quantentheorie kontinuierlicher Spektren*' ('On the Quantum Theory of Continuous Spectra'), which Oppenheimer noted as 'abridged Göttingen dissertation' and which was published in a February issue of the journal (Oppenheimer, 1927). Oppenheimer had organized the material of the dissertation into three parts for the publication: I. General Theory (*Allgemeine Theorie*, pp. 268–275); II. Application to the Two-Body Problem (*Anwendung auf das Zweikörperproblem*, pp. 275–283); III. Physical Results (*Physikalische Ergebnisse*, pp. 283–293). In Part I, he displayed the solution of the (time-independent) Schrödinger equation of a general atomic system which possesses a discrete and continuous energy spectrum. He treated the latter on the basis of the mathematical work of Ernst Hellinger (1909) and Hermann Weyl (1910a), the main problem being the proper normalization of the continuous spectrum.$^{316}$ By combining in a clever way the ideas of Paul Dirac (on the calculation of atomic transition amplitudes excited by the incident radiation: from Dirac, 1926f) and Max Born (on the weight of continuous states: from Born, 1926b), Oppenheimer arrived at a general expression for the so-called 'normalized eigendifferential', i.e.,

$$\Delta\Theta(\lambda) = \int_{\lambda}^{\lambda+\Delta\lambda} \frac{h}{8\pi^2 \mu g^2} \psi \, d\lambda, \tag{465}$$

where $\psi$ denotes the wave function, $\mu$ a mass (e.g., the mass of the particle in a one-body problem), $g$ a measure factor (determining the length element in the space of position co-ordinates) and $h$ Planck's constant.$^{317}$

---
$^{315}$Oppenheimer later translated an extended version of Born's Oxford lecture into English; it was published under the title 'Physical Aspects of Quantum Mechanics' in the issue of 5 March 1927 of *Nature* (Born, 1927a).

$^{316}$Erwin Fues had already pioneered the treatment of continuous spectra in the case of diatomic molecules, also starting from the same basic mathematical investigations—see Section IV.4. Oppenheimer knew of Fues' paper and quoted it at various points (Oppenheimer, 1927, p. 273, footnote 3; p. 275, footnote 2; p. 281, footnote 2).

$^{317}$Equation (465) has the same structure as Fues' equation (275a) for the eigendifferential; one just has to replace $u(\mathcal{E}, x)$ with the expression $h/8\pi^2 \mu g^2$.

IV.5 Towards an Undulatory Interpretation of Atomic Phenomena \hfill 841

Oppenheimer applied the general theory thus developed to the class of atoms consisting of a heavy nucleus of mass $M$ and electric charge $Ze$, which attracts an electron with a distorted (Coulomb potential)

$$V = -\frac{Ze^2}{r} - \frac{b}{r^2}, \tag{466}$$

where $b$ denotes a small constant. He solved the wave equation of this system in the standard way, making use of Ludwig Schlesinger's book on differential equations in the same way as Schrödinger had done in his first calculation of the hydrogen atom (see Schrödinger, 1926c). The spatial part of the eigenfunctions could then be expressed—as in the case of the (nonrelativistic) hydrogen atom—in terms of bounded integral transcendental functions for positive (continuous) energy eigenvalues, and in a power series (of $r$) for negative (discrete) eigenvalues—as in the case of hydrogen. Oppenheimer calculated the normalization factors of the eigenfunctions for both types of solutions, and finally the matrix elements of those position co-ordinates which determine the transition probabilities of the atom; he arrived at extended sum expressions (see Oppenheimer 1927, Section II.3, pp. 279–283).

In Part III of Oppenheimer's paper, the above results were applied to the simplest case, the hydrogen atom (where the second term in the potential drops out: $b = 0$ in Eq. (466)). That is, Oppenheimer calculated the properties of the continuous absorption spectra which join the discrete series spectra of atomic hydrogen on the short wavelength side. Especially, he found an explicit formula for the coefficient of absorption $\alpha$, expressed as a function of the wavelength $\lambda$ of the absorbed radiation. This coefficient $\alpha$ can be written as const. $\lambda^n$: at the series limit of the Lyman spectrum the exponent $n$ assumes the value 3.3, for shorter wavelengths it first decreases towards 2.5, and finally rises again to 3.5 for ultra-short wavelengths. Similar behaviour followed from Oppenheimer's theory for the continuous absorption spectrum extending beyond the Balmer series limit. Oppenheimer noted that his results agreed with the available experimental information. He then turned to the continuous X-ray absorption spectra, i.e., those which occur in the case of heavier atoms by the absorption of a free electron to an unoccupied $K$-, $L$- or $M$-orbit. Again the calculated absorption coefficient had the general form const. $\lambda^n$, with the exponent $n$ assuming values around 3 for the $K$-spectrum and a little larger for the $L$-spectrum; all these results seemed to agree with recent data (e.g., of S. J. M. Allen, 1926).

Oppenheimer also used his theory to deal with two other physical problems, namely the photoelectric effect and *Bremsstrahlung*. In the first case, the production rate of photoelectrons should be proportional to the absorption coefficient $\alpha (=\alpha(\nu))$ divided by the energy quantum $h\nu$ of the incident radiation; the experimental data were also described rather well here by Oppenheimer's theory. For the intensity distribution of the photoelectrons, Oppenheimer derived the

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v05_p02 p0483 -->

proportionality with $\cos^2 \phi$, where $\phi$ denoted the angle between the directions of the scattered electron and the electric field vector of the incident radiation;$^{318}$ he could not explain, however, the fact that for harder incident radiation the maximum of distribution turned away from the direction of the electric field vector towards the direction of propagation of the incident radiation. Finally, in the case of *Bremsstrahlung*, Oppenheimer derived an approximate formula for the radiation energy emitted per unit time and unit frequency interval with the frequency $\nu$ ($R$ being Rydberg’s constant),

$$ \nu = RZ^2(n^{-2} - n'^{-2}), \quad (467a) $$

namely,

$$ i_\nu = \frac{64\pi}{3c^3} \frac{Z^2 e^6}{m^2 v^2} n, \quad (467b) $$

which was valid when an electron of mass $m$ and velocity $v$ hit a heavy nucleus of charge $Ze$ and $n \ll n'$. Equation (467b) deviated from a previous result, derived by Hendrik Kramers within the old quantum theory using correspondence arguments, only by the factor $(2\sqrt{3}/\pi) n$. $^{319}$

Thus the young scholar’s thesis work yielded quite a few definite results, most of which were in fair agreement with the empirical data. In spite of the fact that Oppenheimer obviously wrote the thesis, and the paper based on it, in a great hurry—some of the considerations lacked the thoroughness of his senior colleagues—his name had become known for the first time among quantum physicists. During the same period, when Oppenheimer performed the above work, other physicists had also started to concern themselves with the applications of wave mechanics. Two problems attracted special attention and were taken up and treated independently by several people in different places: the symmetrical top and the hydrogen molecule-ion.

Before embarking upon the discussion of the work on the symmetrical top, we wish to report on the wave mechanical solution of a related problem by Charles Manneback. Manneback, who was then working with Peter Debye at the E.T.H. in Zurich, signed on 17 July 1926 a paper on ‘*Die Dielektrizitätskonstante der zweiatomigen Dipolgase nach der Wellenmechanik*’ (‘The Dielectric

This is the radiation of frequency intervals ($\nu$ and $\nu + d\nu$), emitted per second from a surface element $d\sigma$ of an infinitely thin target containing $A$ atoms of atomic number $Z$ per $\text{cm}^2$, which is bombarded by an electron beam of velocity $v$ such that $s$ electrons per second pass across a cross-section of $1 \text{ cm}^2$.

IV.5  Towards an Undulatory Interpretation of Atomic Phenomena 843

Constant of Diatomic Dipole Gases According to Wave Mechanics') and submitted it to *Physikalische Zeitschrift* (Manneback, 1926).$^{320}$ This problem was a rather fashionable one in those days, besides being of considerable interest for Manneback's host Debye. Especially, Lucie (Lucy) Mensing and Wolfgang Pauli had very recently—in June 1926—obtained a result with the help of matrix mechanical methods which appeared to be more satisfactory than the result based on the old quantum theory, insofar as it passed over into the classical solution of Debye (1912a) in the limit of high temperatures (Mensing and Pauli, 1926).$^{321}$ The question now arose whether a similar result would follow from a wave mechanical calculation.

The dielectric polarization $M$ of $N$ molecules bearing a permanent dipole moment in an electric field of strength $F$ can be defined by the equation

$$M = NkT \frac{\partial \ln \zeta}{\partial F}, \tag{468}$$

with $k$ denoting Boltzmann's constant, $T$ the (absolute) temperature and $\zeta$ the (quantum) statistical sum (*Zustandssumme*) over the discrete energy states $E_i$,

$$\zeta = \sum_i \rho_i \exp\left(-\frac{E_i}{kT}\right). \tag{468a}$$

(The $\rho_i$ are the statistical weights associated with the energy state $E_i$.) Manneback's task was, of course, to calculate the energy states of the diatomic molecule in the electric field by using Schrödinger's (nonrelativistic) wave equation

$$\text{div grad } \psi + \frac{8\pi^2}{h^2}(E - V)\psi = 0, \tag{469}$$

where the potential energy $V$ is given by the expression

$$V = -\mu F \cos \theta, \tag{469a}$$

with $\mu$ being the electric moment of the permanent dipole (associated with each molecule) and $\theta$ the angle between the axis of the dipole moment and the vector of the electric field. If one introduces polar co-ordinates $\theta$ and $\phi$ for the motion of the axis of the dipole—$\phi$ being the azimuthal angle with respect to the direction

***

$^{320}$Charles Lambert Manneback was born on 9 March 1894 in Etterbeck near Brussels. In 1922 he became *Chargé de Cours* at the Catholic University of Louvain; in 1924 he was promoted to *professeur ordinaire* at the same university, a position from which he retired in 1964. Manneback worked especially on the theory of molecules. He died on 15 December 1975 in Brussels.

$^{321}$We have reported on the matrix mechanical treatment of the diatomic molecule in Volume 3, Section IV.6.

844
Chapter IV Early Response and Applications

of the electric field—Eq. (469) is replaced by the equation

$$
\frac{1}{\sin \theta} \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \left( \sin \theta \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial \theta} \right) + \frac{1}{\sin^2 \theta} \frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial \phi^2} + \frac{8\pi^2 A}{h^2} (E + \mu F \cos \theta) \psi = 0, \quad (469')
$$

where the solution $\psi$ had to be finite and unique on the whole sphere, especially for the critical points $\theta = 0$ and $\theta = \pi$.
Manneback considered this problem to be one of wave mechanical perturbation theory, provided the product $\mu F$ was small compared to the energy eigenvalues of the free diatomic molecule (in a zero electric field). The latter energy values were exactly those of the rotator, and could be taken over from Schrödinger's second communication (see Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 521, Eq. (34')), i.e.,

$$
E_n^{(0)} = \frac{n(n + 1) h^2}{8\pi^2 A}, \quad n = 0, 1, 2, \dots \quad (470)
$$

(The constant $A$ in the denominator represents the moment of inertia of the molecule with respect to an axis which is perpendicular to the axis of the dipole.)
But for the lowest state, $n = 0$, the standard perturbation theory (Schrödinger's Part III) provided the first-order correction to the energy terms

$$
E_{n,p}^{(1)} = \frac{1}{2} \frac{(\mu F)^2}{E_n^{(0)}} \left[ \frac{(n + 1)(n + p)(n - p)}{(2n + 1)(2n - 1)} - \frac{n(n + 1 + p)(n + 1 - p)}{(2n + 3)(2n + 1)} \right], \quad (471)
$$

with $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$, and $p = -n, -n + 1, \dots, +n$. In the case of $n = 0$, where the free molecule does not exhibit any rotation, the second term on the left-hand side of Eq. (469') drops out, hence it becomes an ordinary differential equation of second order which can be written (with $\cos \theta = x$) as

$$
\frac{d}{dx} (1 - x^2) \frac{d\psi}{dx} + (\mathcal{E}^* + kx)\psi = 0, \quad (472)
$$

with

$$
\mathcal{E}^* = \frac{8\pi^2 A}{h^2} E_{00} \quad (472a)
$$

and

$$
k = \frac{8\pi^2 A}{h^2} \mu F. \quad (472b)
$$

This equation has to be solved in successive approximations, that is, the eigenvalue parameter $\mathcal{E}^*$ may be written as a power series in $k$,

$$
\mathcal{E}^* = \mathcal{E} + k\mathcal{E}' + k^2\mathcal{E}''. \quad (472a')
$$
